Sports.title: Inside Rangers' summer transfer window - but will it deliver success?
Sports.content:
We have passed the 100-day landmark in the Derek McInnes era at Rangers, and it has certainly been a rollercoaster ride.

His first four games were winless, followed by that humiliating European exit to Jablonec.

However, when Rangers return from the international break, they will have their sights set on going top of the Scottish Premiership for the first time this season.

That's down to a new-look squad and six consecutive wins, including back-to-back Old Firm victories. There is a feel-good factor in the stands at Ibrox once again.

Here, we look at how a key summer transfer window helped pave the way for a remarkable turnaround - one McInnes knows he must keep on track against Kilmarnock on October 10.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights as Rangers made it back-to-back wins over Celtic within a week as they won at Parkhead

How do transfers at Rangers work?

Before we get into the fine detail, it's important to take a look at the bigger picture.

This was the second consecutive summer that Rangers signed 14 players. However, the two windows couldn't be more different.

For full context, you need to go back 12 months. It was a new era (yes, another one) at Ibrox. Russell Martin had been appointed head coach, and the club were being led by CEO Patrick Stewart and sporting director Kevin Thelwell. However, that fresh start proved to be a false dawn.

As Rangers went off track, Martin was sacked after 123 days, before Stewart and Thelwell followed soon after. Meanwhile, of the 14 signings sanctioned by the likes of the aforementioned, only four remain. Chairman Andrew Cavenagh admitted mistakes had been made, and after issuing the P45's, he took a more hands-on role at the club.

Image: Kevin Thelwell, Russell Martin and Patrick Stewart were all sacked by Rangers last year

Some might think it was Robbie Thelwell, who has the title "head of recruitment", who was in charge of the signings. In truth, his title does not reflect his responsibility, and he works in the scouting team.

Instead, fast-forward 12 months and working alongside Cavenagh were the likes of CEO Jim Gillespie, who joined in March, now outgoing technical director Dan Purdy, Paraag Marathe and Gretar Steinsson of the 49ers, plus Stig Inge Bjornebye, who was appointed performance director in June following a spell as consultant.

Image: Former Everton head of recruitment Dan Purdy has stepped down from his role as technical director but will continue assisting Rangers this season after helping rebuild the squad

Rangers were not only looking at players' attributes, but also how they'd fit in the dressing room, their injury history, trading value and so on. Things which in the past were not always prioritised but are now all part of the equation.

The likes of Purdy would identify the options, Cavenagh and Gillespie were among those signing off on the deals, all done with the backing of the 49ers and ultimately the manager.

While there will always be successes and failures, this time Rangers had a united approach.

Image: CEO Jim Gillespie joined in March and led the search for manager Derek McInnes who both played a key role in summer transfers

So what was the plan this summer?

Rangers' initial target was to sign fewer players than they did the previous summer, but opportunities and injuries saw that number rise from around 10 to 14.

The club's leadership group set the parameters, the model of how Rangers should play both domestically and in Europe was in place, and it was over to the new powers that be to sign the players - just like they did in January when Tuur Rommens, Tochi Chukwuani and Ryan Naderi were permanent additions.

Image: Ryan Naderi and Tochi Chukwuani have impressed after joining Rangers in January

Rangers' goal this season - under McInnes, who knows the Scottish game inside out - was to taste domestic success once again.

So what was the plan to end Celtic's Premiership stranglehold? Well, rather than trying to copy their Old Firm rivals' possession-based style of play, Rangers were focussing on physicality and speed. The view was that to beat Celtic, they couldn't be like Celtic - they had to work differently.

Furthermore, following the departures of captain James Tavernier, vice-captain Jack Butland and co, they needed leaders in the squad, plus wanted to reduce the overall age of the group - something they had achieved over the previous windows.

Image: Dan Neil was captain at Sunderland and Lawrence Shankland was Hearts skipper before both joined Rangers in the summer

Finally, while chairman Cavenagh was willing to splash the cash for the right players, many signings would still need to have the potential to grow in value and help the club flourish.

Did they deliver?

It was a complex checklist and not everything has been fixed at Ibrox over a few months. This was always going to take multiple windows. However, there are positive signs.

The average age of the team that beat Celtic in their two games before the international break was less than 24 - compared to their rivals, who were closer to 27.

The starting XI in those games comprised of a new-look spine and six summer signings: goalkeeper Ivor Pandur, defender Olwethu Makhanya, captain Dan Neil in midfield along with James Penrice, Minsu Kim out wide and Kevin Kelsy leading the line.

Image: Kevin Kelsy and Olwethu Makhanya, both 22, have impressed since joining Rangers in the summer

At Ibrox in their League Cup quarter-final triumph, Rangers played like a team with an identity and style. They were strong, physical, fast and dominated the battle for second balls. That was reaffirmed at Parkhead in the Premiership a week later, while their rivals changed shape in a search for answers that didn't arrive.

Both in January and this summer, Rangers have been adding to their squad with a clear plan in place. They now have a group boasting speed, physicality, desire and the types of players who could attract interest from bigger leagues across Europe.

That recognition is coming on the international front too, with 13 of the squad selected by their country for this three-week window. Of those away with their countries, 12 of the 13 are 26 or under too - a clear sign of the change in direction at Ibrox.

Rangers starting XI vs Celtic age Ivor Pandur (26); Dujon Sterling (26), Emmanuel Fernandez (24), Olwethu Makhanya (22); Kim Minsu (20), Nicolas Raskin (25), Dan Neil (24), James Penrice (27), Djeidi Gassama (23); Ryan Naderi (23), Kevin Kelsy (22)

There has been significant work to alter Rangers' recruitment process since last summer, and while the early signs are positive, nothing is won in September.

Rangers still need to catch Celtic in the Premiership and face a tough test in Aberdeen, if they're to book a spot in the League Cup final, where Hearts or Hibs would await.

However, for the first time in years, after a busy transfer window and consecutive Old Firm victories - they head into Autumn with a platform that will allow them to deliver.

Sports.title: Ocon to leave Haas at end of 2026 season
Sports.content:
Esteban Ocon will leave Haas at the end of the 2026 Formula 1 season, both driver and team have confirmed.

Confirmation of the Ocon's exit came on Wednesday morning after months of speculation over the 30-year-old Frenchman's future with the team.

Along with confirming Ocon's departure, Haas said that there would be no imminent news on his replacement, despite reports that Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara has been lined up to partner Britain's Oliver Bearman next season.

Ocon wrote on social media: "My time with Haas F1 Team will come to an end at the end of the 2026 season.

"I leave this project with my head held high and proud of my performances in what were not always the easiest of circumstances for various reasons and factors outside of my control."

Ocon joined Haas from Alpine for the 2025 season but has been outperformed by 21-year-old Bearman across their two campaigns together.

'This is not the end of my F1 career'

The timing of the announcement, with just eight rounds of the 2026 season remaining, means Ocon is highly likely to be without an F1 seat next year.

Sports.title: Williams aiming to change course of Warrington's history with Grand Final victory
Sports.content:
Warrington Wolves captain George Williams is looking to leave on a high by bringing home the club's first Grand Final win; watch Warrington Wolves take on Wakefield Trinity in the Super League Grand Final on Saturday October 3, live on Sky Sports from 5pm

Super League Grand Final: George Williams hoping to change course of Warrington Wolves' history with victory in his final game

It's Grand Final time with Warrington Wolves set to face Wakefield Trinity in the chase to become the sixth team to be Super League champions

George Williams has set himself one task for when he steps out in the Super League Grand Final as Warrington Wolves skipper: Make sure he leaves the club with a trophy.

When Williams returned from the NRL in 2021, he made the bold decision to not go back to his hometown club of Wigan and instead headed to Warrington.

After five years there, he is poised to return to Australia and has one last opportunity to try and depart with a trophy.

It is set to be a pretty-evenly-matched Grand Final as third- and fourth-placed Warrington and Wakefield Trinity do battle. Two underdog teams who beat the first- and second-placed sides to make it to Old Trafford.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Super League semi-final clash between Leeds Rhinos and Warrington Wolves

It is not lost on Williams how big this match is as he could lead Warrington to their maiden Grand Final triumph to become just the sixth team in the history of the competition to lift the Super League trophy.

He has tasted that glory with Wigan as a youngster and now wants to leave the Wolves with another career highlight and change the direction of the club.

"It is crucial, there are so many different narratives that you want to get the win, but personally, I was pretty vocal, I came here to change history and win with Warrington," Williams told Sky Sports.

"It is pretty fitting it is my last game and I've got the opportunity to do that. Personally, that would be brilliant, a great way to go out, but there's a lot more different narratives we have got for the club and the town to do it."

Warrington take on a Wakefield team who pulled off an almighty shock with their 33-6 victory over favourites Wigan in their own backyard.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Wakefield Trinity booked their place in their first-ever Super League Grand Final as they produced a huge upset to defeat Wigan Warriors

Williams knows if Trinity turn up in that form again, Warrington will need to be on their A-game.

"We know Wakefield play a good brand of rugby, they have been posting points all year, we played them three or four weeks ago and they beat us, so we know what they're capable of," he added.

"I think everyone saw Wigan as favourites and we were surprised by that one.

"Both teams have been pretty consistent all year, third and fourth, I think that's probably the word I want to use for us this year, consistent.

"Now we've just got to bring it one more time and are 80 minutes away from history which is the biggest key for us."

How to watch the Super League Grand Final

The Super League Grand Final takes place at Old Trafford on Saturday October 3, live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports+.

The match will kick-off at 6pm, with coverage on Sky Sports from 5pm.

Sports.title: Carra: Man City should be stripped of titles and have owners removed
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher believes Manchester City should be stripped of the titles they won during the years they have been found guilty of financial breaches - and says the club's owners should be removed from their positions.

City have been found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission.

The club continue to deny the breaches, with chief executive Ferran Soriano calling the process a "Premier League conspiracy theory" in a video message to players and staff. The club have confirmed they will appeal against the ruling and have until Friday October 2 to do so.

During the period between the 2009/10 season and 2017/18 season, City won three Premier League titles, one FA Cup, three League Cups and one Community Shield.

"I do think Manchester City's titles they've won in this time, or trophies, should be taken off their list," Sky Sports pundit Carragher said.

However, Carragher is less convinced whether those honours should then be passed onto teams and players who finished second to City in those competitions. Ultimately, he says, the most important part of winning in football - the feeling at the time - has been taken from those players, clubs and their fans by City's actions.

"Whether other clubs should get them is slightly different," said Carragher. "But what Manchester City have done is, they've not just hurt their own players in terms of no one looks at their trophies and medals now in the same way...

"I've been very lucky to win a few medals. I never look at the medal years later. But my mind goes back to a moment, I get a feeling in my stomach. I remember the referee blowing a final whistle of a big game.

"Those players will never get that feeling and it was robbed by Manchester City. That's what they haven't got. I don't think any player will care if you go and give them a medal, and he puts it in the house, in his trophy room, he'll never look at it.

"It's not about medals, it's about feelings, and that's what Manchester City have robbed."

Carragher says while he expects Man City as a club to be punished, the owners must pay for their involvement by losing their leadership roles.

"The club are going to get punished," he said. "You've got supporters, players, the club and owners. For me this is all about the owners, the people who are at the top of the club.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Carragher says he's 'not surprised' that Man City have been found guilty on all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.

"Man City are a wonderful club and have been for a hundred years and will be for hundreds of years going forward. But in terms of what we're finding out now, I don't know how the owners can continue in English football.

"We talk about a fit and proper test for owners. What they've done for 10 years - and left this stain that will be there for the next 10 years - it starts because they don't like the word no. When you see the statements - the one from [CEO Ferran] Soriano last night - it's beggars belief what you're hearing.

"They have so much power and finance behind them, nobody ever tells them no. Until they move away from the club, I don't know how this stain is removed from the club.

"City will move on - they will have great teams in the future. But I don't see how the ownership can continue after what's happened here and their reaction to it. How can they be surprised? They've got irrefutable evidence - well where is it? Put it out there."

Carra: Revenue claims were 'impossible' "I'm shocked but also not surprised. I always felt they were guilty for two simple reasons.



"It would be impossible for Man City ever to have the commercial revenue of Liverpool, Man Utd or Real Madrid. They said for years they had that type of income coming in. It's impossible for that to ever happen, no matter how successful Man City are.



"And number two, as they said yesterday and have continually said over this period, 'they've done nothing wrong, they have irrefutable evidence'. Every man and his dog knows if you're charged by the police and had irrefutable evidence it would be over in a day or a week - this has dragged on for years. This idea that nothing has gone on and it has dragged on this long tells you something was there.



"The reason I'm shocked is because I never believed the Premier League would be able to beat them in a court of law because of the power and finances Man City have behind them.



"A huge well done to the Premier League for the result it seems they have right now. For the Premier League to not just win this case but people talk about 114 charges out of 115 - they had to win it like that for it to be convincing."

Carra: If I was a City player 'I'd be furious'

Carragher also discussed what the news means for the legacy of City's greatest players of the period and the current squad, saying he is sympathetic to their situation, even if some former players are continuing to defend City's actions right now.

"I'd be furious and I actually feel for the Man City players," said Carragher. "As a team, what they've done is wrong. The Premier League have called it a sham five times in their statement.

Who were Man City's major signings during period of breaches? 2009/10: Carlos Tevez, Emmanuel Adebayor, Joleon Lescott, Roque Santa Cruz, Kolo Toure, Gareth Barry

2010/11: Edin Dzeko, Yaya Toure, Mario Balotelli, David Silva, Aleksandar Kolarov, James Milner, Jerome Boateng

2011/12: Sergio Aguero, Samir Nasri, Stefan Savic

2012/13: Javi Garcia, Matija Nastasic, Jack Rodwell

2013/14: Fernandinho, Stevan Jovetic, Alvaro Negredo, Jesus Navas

2014/15: Eliaquim Mangala, Wilfried Bony, Fernando

2015/16: Kevin De Bruyne, Raheem Sterling, Nicolas Otamendi, Fabian Delph

2016/17: John Stones, Leroy Sane, Gabriel Jesus, Ilkay Gundogan, Nolito, Claudio Bravo

2017/18: Aymeric Laporte, Benjamin Mendy, Kyle Walker, Bernardo Silva, Ederson, Danilo, Douglas Luiz

"But in terms of individual players, some of them are coming out to bat for the club, that's normal right now. It must be very difficult for them to see anything that's going on and to almost feel like a lot of their career is going to have an asterisk with it, or people are just going to call it a sham.

"I think of Kevin De Bruyne, who's one of the greatest players I've ever seen. He could have played for any team in the world and he still would have been one of the best players. He was fantastic.

"But he chose his club to be Manchester City. Now, one of those reasons he may have chosen, maybe was his wages, that maybe were inflated because of the situation around Man City and what they've been charged with.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dave Reed takes a look the independent commission's key findings on the 'Disguised Funding Scheme' used by Manchester City.

"But if he sits there at the end of his career now and the whole world looks at his Manchester City career of 10 years of service and look at it as a sham, and I keep using that word, that's the word the Premier League used, I'd be furious. Absolutely furious that around the world people are looking at my career like that because of what's going on upstairs.

"Those people have continually told those players - because I have spoken to certain players about it - that everything was fine. They were not going to get done for anything.

"We keep talking about Liverpool or Manchester United, all these players who maybe could get Premier League titles now. And that's absolutely spot on,

"But I've actually been thinking about the Manchester City players and how they feel. What Manchester City's hierarchy are coming out with in the last couple of days as well, they're just gaslighting the players, their ex-players, their supporters, because those people want to believe them so much. They've got such strong relationships with them, they want to believe it right now.

"I think the longer this goes on, the more you'll see less support from maybe ex-City players and more frustration about maybe how their careers are going to be viewed by the outside world."

Sports.title: Mind games to start today? 'Fury will try every trick in the book to get to AJ'
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's first press conference is expected to go ahead in London on Wednesday ahead of their blockbuster heavyweight fight on December 11, and Sky Sports' Matthew Macklin has spoken of what he expects when the two British rivals face off....

I think the press conference will be important.

The psychological, mental aspect of boxing is huge. It's an individual sport - one on one - so if you can get into the other guy's head and help put him in a negative headspace, you're halfway there.

Confidence is key. And if someone's struggling with confidence, if you can put some seeds of doubt in their mind, that's a real benefit to you.

Sports.title: Could Willis switch allegiance from England to Ireland?
Sports.content:
Jack Willis hinted he could be open to switching allegiances to play for Ireland, as the flanker remains ineligible for England selection.

The 29-year-old Toulouse back row has enjoyed another standout season in the Top 14, being crowned the league's Player of the Season for the second year running this week.

The Rugby Football Union (RFU) currently restricts overseas-based players from representing England, meaning Willis has been unable to add to his 14 international caps since the 2023 Rugby World Cup. He won his last cap during England's group-stage victory over Chile and remains under contract with Toulouse until 2029.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Steve Borthwick's side currently have a restriction on selecting overseas-based players

He was given a special dispensation to play for England at the tournament, having joined Toulouse in November 2022, after his former club, Wasps, entered administration.

The RFU has come under pressure to loosen the restrictions, and Willis had previously hoped the governing body would reconsider the policy.

The flanker is eligible to play for Ireland through his grandfather, who was born in Belfast, and could, hypothetically, switch allegiances to play for Andy Farrell's side.

Image: Willis remains determined to play international rugby

It would be a huge coup for Ireland. But, like England, Farrell's side also has restrictions on overseas-based players, meaning prospective internationals must represent one of the country's four provinces: Munster, Ulster, Leinster or Connacht.

Willis has not given up on the prospect of playing Test rugby, and jokingly challenged reporters at this week's Nuit du Rugby in Paris to find a way around the rules.

"I'm a quarter Irish. But they have the same rules as England," Willis told The Telegraph and The Times.

Image: The Toulouse flanker claimed his second successive Top 14 Player of the Season award earlier this week

He joked to reporters: "You need to do some digging, that's your job, you find the way [around the rules]."

World Rugby relaxed its international eligibility rules in 2021, allowing players to switch national sides under certain conditions, including having a parent or grandparent born in the respective country and serving a three-year stand-down period from international rugby.

Willis has continued to impress for Toulouse since moving to the south of France and once again proved pivotal as the French club secured a fourth consecutive Top 14 title last season, scoring six tries and making 173 tackles.

Although he admitted he "missed" playing for England, Willis said it was his choice to continue his career in France.

"You know what you sacrifice," the flanker said.

"It's something I still want to do, but rules are rules."

Sports.title: Humphries, Wade progress at World Grand Prix as Rock dumped out
Sports.content:
Luke Humphries was not punished for a raft of missed finishing doubles as he beat a below-par Dave Chisnall to reach the second round of the World Grand Prix in Leicester.

Humphries - who has made the last three finals in this event, winning in 2023 ahead of two runners-up finishes since - is the new favourite to triumph this year following defending champion Luke Littler's shock defeat to Luke Woodhouse on the opening night.

Cool Hand, sporting a scab on his forehead he put down to an allergic reaction, defeated Chisnall 2-0 while averaging only 80.41 and going at 26 per cent on his doubles as he secured a second-round meeting with Chris Dobey's conqueror Jermaine Wattimena.

Image: Humphries will take on Jermaine Wattimena in the second round on Thursday evening

Chisnall had a chance to break Humphries and push for a deciding set only to bust his score, before the world No 2 wrapped up victory on double four and then appeared to shush someone in the crowd.

Dobey was one of two seeds to tumble on Tuesday evening, alongside Josh Rock, who fell to Niels Zonneveld as the Dutch debutant peeled off three ton-plus finishes in the third set to book a last-16 date with Gary Anderson.

Rock - who at one point attempted an audacious 101 finish with bullseye, one, bullseye - had lit up proceedings by following a 180 with a roof-raising 151 to break Zonneveld and ensure a deciding set.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Josh Rock produced six brilliant darts to win the second set against Niels Zonneveld before losing in a decider

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rock took a unique route as he attempted a checkout of 101, leaving Sky Sports' Wayne Mardle with a lot to say!

Dobey, meanwhile, suffered a first-round exit for the third year running.

'Hollywood' - who burned four darts to break Wattimena in the opening leg - averaged below 80 and really struggled to hit the mandatory starting double in legs, with a sizzling 128 finish at the start of the second set his only moment of magic as he lost 2-0.

Wade progresses but more Grand Prix woe for Heta

James Wade fought back from a set down and shrugged off six missed match darts in the space of two visits to beat Joe Cullen 2-1 as he resumed his bid for a third Grand Prix title and first in 16 years.

A key moment came in the fourth leg of the second set when Wade hit the bull for a finish of 81, just as Cullen was eyeing a break that would have left him throwing for victory.

Wade faffed about before getting over the line, squandering arrows at double top and double 10 in the third leg of the deciding set before pinning double 10 in the next to advance.

Image: James Wade won the World Grand Prix in 2007 and 2010

Wade's reward is a clash with Stephen Bunting, who defeated Andrew Gilding 2-1 in the final match of the round.

There was further Grand Prix despair for Damon Heta as he suffered a sixth-straight first-round loss - the Australian has never won a match here - after surrendering a one-set lead and wasting a match dart at double five in the second set against Anderson.

Anderson, runner-up in 2016 to Michael van Gerwen, swept the third set 3-0 while averaging 110.

Gian van Veen saw off fellow Dutchman Dirk van Duijvenbode in straight sets for his first victory on this stage after round-one exits in 2024 and 2025, to Ross Smith and Littler respectively.

However, Van Duijvenbode missed two tries at double 16 to set up a decider having belatedly found his scoring form after an abject display while losing the first five legs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player William O'Connor took out 95 with two double 19s against Ryan Searle in their World Grand Prix clash

Van Veen will play Ryan Searle next after 'Heavy Metal' punished four missed match darts from William O'Connor to progress as he won the final three legs of their encounter having lost the previous five.

O'Connor's electric run after losing the first set included taking out 95 with back-to-back double 19s but the Irishman - appearing at this event for the first time in over a decade - then lost his way.

Sports.title: Gordon-inspired England seal much-needed win over Czech Republic
Sports.content:
Pavel Sulc's first-half red card helped England recover from a nervy start to register an Anthony Gordon-inspired 2-0 Nations League win over the Czech Republic in Prague.

While the Three Lions toiled in the early stages and nearly fell behind twice to presentable chances wasted by Sulc, Barcelona winger Gordon, supported by former Newcastle team-mate Lewis Hall, was a threat throughout. He came close to teeing up an opener while the two sides were still 11 vs 11, but saw Morgan Rogers curl his low cross against the far post on the turn.

Even once Sulc had been dismissed following a VAR review for a studs-up challenge on the shin of Elliot Anderson, it took a reshuffle from Thomas Tuchel and the half-time arrival of Eberechi Eze for many of his team-mates to catch up following a particularly nervous and passive opening period from the Three Lions.

But once they did, it was Gordon who took full advantage less than two minutes after the restart to stoop and turn Trent Alexander-Arnold's typically inviting cross home, netting for the third competitive game in a row.

England ratings Trafford (7), Alexander-Arnold (7), Chalobah (5), Guehi (6), Hall (7), Anderson (6), Lewis-Skelly (6), Saka (5), Rogers (7), Rogers (8), Kane (7).



Subs: Eze (7), Scott (7), Ngumoha (7), Bellingham (6), Gibbs-White (6).

Alexander-Arnold later revealed to ITV: "I spoke to Anthony at half-time and I said if I'm getting in the half spaces and putting them [crosses] in, make sure you get to the back post.

"You don't expect it to happen that quickly, but it did and it worked."

Hall, too, nearly got his just desserts when his dangerous low delivery was turned onto his own post by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci with Rogers sniffing.

Coincidentally it would be a mix of Rogers and a deflection off Krejci that would tee-up Harry Kane, who else, to sweep home a second with England's next attack to put the result beyond doubt and add his 87th international goal.

Image: Harry Kane added another to his record tally with an 87th international goal to seal victory, his ninth England goal in 11 games in 2026

That gave Tuchel the confidence to give out two competitive debuts to Alex Scott and Rio Ngumoha, both introduced shortly afterwards.

Scott would come within inches of a debut goal while Rogers and Eze both also went lose to adding to England's lead, but the Three Lions would at least see out a comfortable and much-needed win to get their Nations League campaign off the ground at the second attempt.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Rob Dorsett gives his player ratings for England players during win over Czech Republic in the Nations League.

The key moments from Prague

5: CHANCE! A simple ball over the top is misjudged by Anderson and reaches Sulc, who holds off Trevor Chalobah but is denied by James Trafford when the goalkeeper is quick off his line.

13: SULC AGAIN! Sulc is given space to run in outside the area and is hesitant to take a shot, before eventually seeing an effort blocked by Chalobah's head.

16: OFF THE POST! Out of nothing England nearly strike as Rogers turns on the ball and fires against the far post from Gordon's low cross.

21: CLOSE! Gordon himself goes close next, bending just wide after cutting in off the flank.

25: RED CARD! Having twice gone close for the hosts, Czech player of the year Sulc sees a yellow card upgraded to a red by VAR for a high lunge on Anderson.

38: GORDON DANGER! The flying winger gets beyond his man and whips a low ball in which Michal Sadilek bundles behind, only just beyond his own goalframe.

45: KANE CHANCE! Captain Kane goes close in his first chance of the game, turning and shooting from 20 yards and forcing Matej Kovar into a one-handed stop.

46: SUB! Eze is brought on for Myles Lewis-Skelly at the interval to give England's midfield more attacking threat.

47: GOAL! The Three Lions get their second half off to the perfect start as Alexander-Arnold's wicked cross is headed home by a stooping Gordon.

63: OFF THE POST! Another low cross nearly results in an own goal as Hall's delivery is turned onto his own post by Krejci.

69: GOAL! Rogers and Krejci compete for a loose ball which falls to Kane, who makes no mistake sweeping home into the far corner.

72: SUBS! Kane and Gordon make way to give Ngumoha and Scott their competitive debuts.

87: CHANCE! Scott goes close on debut with a rising effort which flies just over from 20 yards.

Tuchel: We needed more dynamism

England head coach Thomas Tuchel on ITV:

"We played very professionally in the second half. We stepped up, we needed to be a bit more dynamic and put a bit more urgency into our play.

"We kept the intensity going and it was very professional. The effort was still there, it was a deserved victory. It's a bit strange to get an early red card, it's not the best for the spectators or the teams.

"But we got an important win, and that's what counts."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England captain Harry Kane admitted he only found out about Manchester City's charges after the game and that he is only focused on his country at the moment.

Gordon: I've been dying to play with Trent

England goalscorer and man-of-the-match Anthony Gordon on ITV:

"I make that run time and time again and only a certain type of player has got the technique, ability and bravery to make the mistake playing that pass.

"Credit to Trent, that's why he's so good. I've been dying to play with him for that reason.

"Trent's had his own journey with England. He would have liked to have played more than he has but he's a great character. He's a great addition."

Image: Gordon celebrates his goal with Trent Alexander-Arnold

England returnee Trent Alexander-Arnold on ITV:

"It was amazing, always an honour and pleasure to represent my country.

"It's been a long time but I've always believed that I can play for England and I always want to.

"The belief is always there, it's about proving it at club level. The manager gave me the chance tonight to play and to try to follow what he asked of me to the best of my ability. Hopefully he's happy with how I played."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Tuchel praised Trent Alexander-Arnold's performance during England's 2-0 win over the Czech Republic.

Analysis: Alexander-Arnold showed what England have been missing

Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett in Prague:

"Trent Alexander-Arnold was always going to make the headlines in his first start for two years.

"There was one moment of real class and plenty of other impressive cameos which showed Tuchel - and the England supporters - what they've been missing for so long.

"His curling cross at the start of the second half which pin-pointed Anthony Gordon's head was joyous, as was the gleeful way the Barcelona man scored his third England goal in as many matches. Gordon has really blossomed into one of England's most exciting and important attacking players.

"Overall, England did enough. There will be plenty of fans who will think they should have put Czech Republic to the sword, especially seeing as the home side played for over an hour with 10-men.

"But against the deepest of deep blocks, England worked hard to eventually get the breakthrough and Kane's sharp finish sealed a solid if unspectacular victory.

"There were no obvious injuries, which is a plus. The second of four matches in 11 days won't live long in the memory, but job done for Tuchel."

Sports.title: Sham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severe | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
How bad could it be, really? How serious can a breach of arcane financial regulations be, really? Just how damning can accountancy be? Even after Friday’s revelation that Manchester City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League, it was perhaps difficult to grasp the scale of what that meant. After the publication of the independent commission’s findings, there can be no doubt: the commission found that Manchester City cheated, that they did so deliberately, and that they have sought to cover that up with a campaign of calculated misinformation.

City continue to maintain their innocence and issued a statement insisting that “the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. It referred, once again, to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of all of its positions”, and, again, insisted that “the club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”.

The chief executive, Ferran Soriano, released a video reiterating many of the same points and vowing that the club would appeal – it has until Friday to do so – and pursue “all other legal avenues” to prove its innocence. He dismissed the Premier League’s charges as “a conspiracy theory” – and pointedly referred to the independent commission as a “Premier League Commission” – claiming that they were based on “a single false accusation” of diverting funds from the owner to the club under the guise of sponsorship payments. This, he said, “could not happen and … did not happen”. The commission’s view, it’s fair to say, is very different.

Any sanction will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission, but it is impossible to read the verdict without thinking that it will have to be extremely severe. Everton were docked a total of eight points over two accounting windows for an inadvertent breach of profitability and sustainability rules amounting to around £20m, having cooperated with the investigation. Exactly what City’s breach would turn out to be remains to be calculated, but the verdict found that they overstated income by around £855m and understated outgoings by around £66m. And this was not a cock-up but a calculated attempt to circumvent the rules.

View image in fullscreen The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. Photograph: Carl Recine/Reuters

The verdict makes for astonishing reading. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters, shredded in careful, measured legal prose. The appendices, as and when they are made public, might make it even worse. Even if some technicality is found that mitigates the punishment, their standing cannot surely recover. The findings show this is the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football. This is not breaching the maximum wage and being caught when most clubs were doing similar, which lay at the heart of the three previous huge top-division financial scandals: Manchester City in 1906, Leeds City in 1919 and Sunderland in 1957. This was deception on a massive scale.

Sponsorship deals are described as “shams” to obscure investment and overstated by £830m over the nine years in question as part of “a plan to disguise shareholder funding … as ‘commercial partner revenue’”. The Fordham Agreement, an arrangement by which an entity bought player image rights, was “little more than a front”. Attempts to claim that the Premier League had misunderstood how the sponsorship deals worked were “an ‘explanation’ that the club concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal and obscure the realities of the disguised funding scheme”.

The level of mendacity identified is extraordinary. In regards to the “sham” sponsorship arrangements there was “intentional conduct” to “disguise the true nature of certain revenues and liabilities/expenses, to give the appearance of minimising the club’s financial dependence on ADUG” and give “a misleading impression in the club’s financial statements that the club’s financial position was better than it in fact was”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Having been charged, City “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation”. The panel found “evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects” and “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”. On occasions, the panel concluded it “should not accept the opinion of an expert”; the precise reasons why are set out in an appendix but, in context, an inference can be drawn.

The one charge on which City were not found guilty was of breaching “duties of cooperation” with the Premier League in relation to one tranche of accusations. That, clearly, is not the get-out many City fans have hoped for since Friday. The verdict is damning.

The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. They have lied consistently and deliberately. The continued denials only enhance the sense that this is a club that has no respect for the regulations.

There must now be a very good argument for expulsion. How can City, at least under the current ownership, ever be trusted again? How can they go on playing even this season, pretending all is well, awaiting appeal and sanction, when they have been found guilty of charges of such magnitude?

When the club has behaved like this, how can its continued existence in the Premier League be tolerated? And when they have cheated as they have been shown to do between 2009-10 and 2017-18, how can their name appear on the Premier League’s roll of honour?

Sports.title: ‘Throw your medals in the bin,’ Roy Keane tells Manchester City players
Sports.content:
Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane said he would throw the “medals in the bin” if he were a Manchester City player following Premier League confirmation on Tuesday that the club were guilty of all charges related to their financial rules and boosted their income by more than £900m after arranging “sham ­contracts” with commercial partners.

City, who continue to deny any wrongdoing, won eight trophies, including three Premier League titles between 2009 and 2018, the period under investigation. Keane said the achievements of City’s players had become redundant because of the “cheating” that took place during that time.

“If I was a player, I’d be 100% sticking those medals in the bin. Of course you would, it’s cheating,” the ITV football pundit stated during the coverage of England’s match against the Czech Republic in the Nations League. “They won it on the pitch because cheating was going on.” And on the club he added: “They knew it would hurt a lot of people, but they’ve still done it.”

Meanwhile, the former City defender Micah Richards says the damning verdict on the club has left him devastated and heartbroken. City were found to have engaged in an almost £1bn scheme to either inflate revenues or reduce costs through a series of “sham” arrangements in order to avoid breaching league and Uefa financial regulations.

Speaking on The Rest is Football podcast, Richards said: “The reports were troubling. I saw the words which were used by the Premier League in sham contracts and I felt absolutely devastated.

“I’ve been at that club since I was 14 years old, I would die for that club. I achieved my dream at Manchester City, but then to hear these reports, and not only me as an ex-player, but the fans, what they have to go through, absolutely devastating.”

Richards described speaking to the fan he used to live with as a young player at the club, adding: “My digs man, he rang me and he was literally in tears and asking me about information, which I don’t know, I haven’t got the answers to tell him.

“And that’s someone who’s supported the club for 60-odd years, and the uncertainty around it is just heartbreaking. To have a headline of this nature for a club that I love so much, it’s been difficult. If you listen to the reports, they are damning. I feel saddened, I feel angry, I feel a lit bit confused because, on the other side, you have City’s side of the story.”

Sports.title: Disguised funding and dishonest witnesses: key findings in Manchester City case
Sports.content:
Agreements were ‘shams’

The independent commission’s “core decision” is a 40-page document which appears to confirm the worst interpretation of Manchester City’s behaviour. Central to the finding that the club were guilty of all charges of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules is the conclusion that City’s lucrative sponsorship arrangements were “shams”.

When a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, bought the club in 2008 he set out “ambitious plans” for City. But those ambitions could not be met by the finances then being generated. “The club appreciated from the early days of [Mansour’s] ownership that very significant funds would be required if the steps needed to realise … ambitions were to be fulfilled,” the commission said.

In the first instance the club relied on extra injections from Mansour, or “owner equity”. But according to the commission: “The club recognised that [this] was not a sustainable model”, and that with owner equity to be excluded from financial fair play rules it “needed to grow its commercial operations”. One way of doing this, the club decided, was to “seek high-value sponsorship arrangements in the UAE generally and in Abu Dhabi in particular”.

What resulted was what the commission call the “Disguised Funding Scheme” (DFS). Traditional sponsorship valuations would not be enough for City to meet their ambitions and forestall financial losses. So City applied a different approach. In the words of the commission: “The club would enter into sponsorship agreements with Abu Dhabi sponsors which contained substantial [fees] at well above fair market value. However, the sponsor would not be liable to pay the recorded sponsorship fee, and would not do so.” Instead the sponsor would pay only a small percentage of the fee, described by the commission as the “base sum”. The rest, or the “tagged sum”, would be paid for by Mansour, or at least the company that he had formed to control City, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

The DFS, the commission said, allowed the club to state that “its commercial revenues from Abu Dhabi sponsorship agreements (and so its income generally) were far, far greater than was in fact the case”, and also “conceal from third parties the true extent of the equity contributions in fact being made into the club by ADUG”. As a result, it said: “Each of the Abu Dhabi sponsorship agreements was a sham.”

City had argued in their defence that sponsors had paid all the money but that the sponsors had required, “from time to time”, financial assistance from the Abu Dhabi government and its crown prince court to meet their sponsors’ obligations. City’s argument therefore was that although money was given by the Abu Dhabi government to sponsors, the club was not involved.

The scale of the funding

The commission calculated that, over the course of the nine seasons under investigation, from 2009-10 to 2017-18, City had booked £949.94m in sponsorship revenues from Abu Dhabi-based companies. Of that total, only £119.25m had been paid in “base fee”. The rest, £830.69m, were “tagged sums” paid by ADUG to the club.

By some estimates, the £830m accounted for as much as 30% of City’s revenue over the period of the investigation. It was a sum far greater than the total revenue of most of their Premier League rivals. The scale of the funding also grew heavily over time. In 2009-10, the commission identified £22.5m in “tagged sums” paid by ADUG. By the 2017-18 that figure had risen to £134.73m, the highest total across the seasons under investigation.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans show their appreciation for their wealthy owner in 2014. Photograph: Matt West/BPI/Shutterstock

The knock-on effect

The commission broke the charges into four blocks and once the first had been proven – relating to the provision of accurate financial information – a domino effect ensued. Blocks two and three related to City’s requirement to meet the financial rules of first Uefa then the Premier League. Removing the “tagged sums” from any balance sheet meant that City had failed to comply with either set of regulations “in any of the seasons” under which they were charged.

The submission of inaccurate financial information meant that City were also in breach of group four of the charges, relating to the “duties of cooperation” it owed to the Premier League. But City’s behaviour went further in this regard. The commission found that the club had “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation” and had “concocted” explanations for the DFS “well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the reality”.

Dishonest witnesses

The commission also made damning comments on the behaviour of witnesses called by City during the hearings. “Evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects,” the commission wrote, arguing that some of falsehoods had been deliberate. “Certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest,” it said. Also contained in the verdict is the detail that, in the event of City being found guilty, the Premier League had reserved the right to challenge “additional and perhaps more egregious acts of non-cooperation” relating to City’s behaviour during the League’s own investigation.

Further wrongdoing

Further, smaller charges were proven against City. Payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”, totalling more than £15m, were found to have been made to three former employees, understood to include Roberto Mancini and Yaya Touré. Equally, a scheme known as the “Fordham arrangement”, was shown to be another sham whereby City sold their players’ image rights to a third party which was “in reality little more than a front for ADUG”.

The only charge City were cleared on related to one subset of the club’s obligations to act “in the utmost good faith” towards the Premier League.

View image in fullscreen Roberto Mancini (right) and Yaya Touré (centre) were found to have had payments not recorded in their employment contracts. Photograph: Marc Atkins/Shutterstock

No love lost

The commission describes the case as having been “fiercely contested” and there is no sense of either side pulling their punches. City were revealed to have sought to dismiss the Premier League’s investigation, its decision to charge the club and its decision to prosecute the charges. The verdict was published after one party failed in an attempt to keep it private. “The proceedings were at all times extremely hard fought on both sides,” the commission said. “We in no way mean that as a criticism of either party; it is simply fact. No stone was left unturned.”

The competitive nature of the proceedings will have been a key factor in turning the case into such a substantial endeavour that the verdict could be published only more than two years after proceedings began. The commission said evidence submissions ran to “many, many thousands of pages”, the core bundle of documents to “tens of thousands” of pages, and even the index to the documents used in the hearing was 1,000 pages long.

“It has taken us much longer than we would have wished, and much longer than we had anticipated would be the case when the hearing concluded, to produce our decision,” the commission wrote. “That is regrettable.”

The submissions are likely to continue given City intend to appeal against the decision before Friday. The commission must also meet to decide upon its sanction.

What do City say?

The club continue to deny wrongdoing. City have said they will appeal “on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. Their chief executive, Ferran Soriano, said in a video to employees that the decision was based on a “Premier League conspiracy theory”.

Sports.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
Sports.content:
In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years go we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation mark The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation mark The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

Sports.title: Dropping Kelly and Toone could prove a World Cup masterstroke by Wiegman | Tom Garry
Sports.content:
Sarina Wiegman sent a clear message to two of England’s biggest names on Tuesday and – in doing so, irrespective of reputations – fired the same warning to every player: perform for your club or you will not go to the World Cup.

Wiegman was unequivocal with her reasoning for leaving Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly out of her squad for October’s playoff against Greece. Her straight-to-the-point and typically honest style made it inescapably clear, when she said: “The main reason is that I think the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Amid reports of Kelly struggling with an injury, Wiegman was asked to clarify if any concerns about fitness had played a part in her decision and she said: “Well, I had a conversation with Chloe and, for me, it was just what I saw on the pitch, so I kept it [to the] football.”

With those blunt words, the Dutchwoman emphasised that she was picking her squad on form, and it is a message that has an extra urgency given there are just under nine months to go until the start of the World Cup, which England will attempt to qualify for over the next 10 weeks across two rounds of playoffs, starting with October’s tie against Greece, and ultimately seek to go one better than 2023’s second-placed finish.

For England fans who have enjoyed the past three major tournaments and seen Toone and Kelly “come up clutch” in numerous big moments, having these two household names omitted from a squad may feel strange. Both were on the scoresheet in the 2022 European Championship final and they have been relied upon in the crucial games at tournaments that have defined this successful era, whether it was Toone dragging England level in their 2022 Euros quarter-final against Spain, lobbing Germany’s goalkeeper at Wembley in the final or firing into the top corner in the World Cup semi-final in 2023. Or whether it was Kelly repeatedly holding her nerve from the penalty spot in the dramatic summers of 2023 and 2025 or her cross that created England’s all-important goal in Basel. Their contributions will make them almost immortal in English women’s football history.

Wiegman has, however, frequently demonstrated that she will not be sentimental when it comes to squad selections, no matter the pedigree of any player and no matter the contributions they may have made to either the team or the wider English game. Examples include omitting the former England captain Steph Houghton, choosing Hannah Hampton as England’s No 1 over Mary Earps for Euro 2025 and how the international careers of successful servants such as Rachel Daly and Fran Kirby came to an end earlier than expected. The 56-year-old does not afford major-tournament winners the luxury of saying “you helped us win a tournament so you can keep your place ahead of an in-form, younger player”, and it has evidently served her well as she has evolved the team repeatedly and reached three finals in a row with England, winning two.

To be fair to Toone and Kelly, there are extenuating circumstances to their form. Toone has been part of a Manchester United side where very few players excelled in their opening two matches as they all appeared to take time to adjust to the ideas of their new manager, Eva Olid. Kelly, meanwhile, appears to be struggling with a hamstring problem, with her Arsenal head coach Renée Slegers confirming later on Tuesday that Kelly is unavailable for Arsenal’s Women’s Champions League game away against Paris FC on Wednesday. Slegers said: “She’s had some issues with her hamstring. There’s nothing we could see from an injury perspective [from scans] but [Kelly is] managing something.”

View image in fullscreen Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly were key cogs in England’s winning machine at Euro 2025. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/Sportsphoto

Nevertheless, neither player has been at their best in recent months and neither could say they finished last season in red-hot form. Therefore it is understandable that Wiegman has opted to give opportunities to players such as the London City Lionesses winger Freya Godfrey and the Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter, who was mightily impressive during Chelsea’s win over Arsenal on Sunday.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It would also be wrong to imply Wiegman is closing the door on Toone, 27, and Kelly, 28. She added at her press conference at St George’s Park: “I still believe in them, they’re not in the squad but I believe in them.

“We expect a bit more and we know they can bring more. That was the message. There is also competition going on. It’s about talent, it’s about playing minutes – I hope they can step up and show what they can do. I’m convinced they can do better, I think they are convinced about that too. I think they took the feedback in a good and in a positive way but it’s hard to take at the same time of course, it’s not a nice message.”

Crucially, she concluded: “I hope they come back even better than they were before.” And therein lies the opportunity for this top-class duo. Rediscover their form and Brazil awaits. If they do start to click again for their clubs – which every England fan should hope they do – and they deliver next summer, this will all look like a masterstroke in management from Wiegman. Equally, Godfrey and Potter being rewarded for their domestic form has to be applauded too. And in the meantime, every England player, however strong their CV, however integral the role they may have played in 2025’s glorious summer, will now be on notice. The battle is on for World Cup selections, and time is of the essence.

Sports.title: Nations League roundup: Lamine Yamal sinks Croatia in Spain’s World Cup homecoming
Sports.content:
Lamine Yamal scored two goals and set up another as Spain hammered Croatia 4-1 on Tuesday in the Nations League in their first home game since lifting the World Cup.

Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring within two minutes against England in Saturday’s Wembley win and took just 75 seconds to do so against Slaven Bilic’s side in Andalusia. The teenager’s left-footed finish took his tally of international goals to nine in 36 appearances.

Just before the half-hour mark, the visitors equalised through Dion Beljo’s header as the 6ft 4in attacker headed home from an Ivan Perisic cross.

Two minutes later the hosts restored their lead as Marc Pubill fired home a header from a pinpoint Lamine Yamal cross before provider turned scorer again on 63 minutes, beating Barcelona teammate and Croatia goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic at his near post. With fewer than two minutes to play Athletic Bilbao’s Nico Williams notched up a fourth for Spain with a crisp dribble and finish.

La Roja next play Czechia on Saturday in Group A3.

Lamine Yamal’s contribution strengthened his case for the Ballon d’Or, with voting having closed on Monday and the winner announced on 26 October.

Spain’s captain, Rodri, showed off the World Cup trophy before kick-off at the packed Estadio Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán, being handed it by Sevilla legend Jesús Navas, a winner with Spain in 2010.

“We were very excited to bring the cup here,” Lamine Yamal said. “To be able to win the game and bring it home is great.”

In Group B1, Slovenia beat North Macedonia 2-0 with goals from Sandi Lovric and Aljosa Matko.

Moldova were held to a 1-1 draw at home to the Faroe Islands and Slovakia beat Kazakhstan 2-1, while Iceland were 3-0 winners in Luxembourg and Estonia drew 1-1 in Bulgaria. Finland and Belarus played to a scoreless draw in Helsinki.

Sports.title: Tuchel praises Alexander-Arnold for ‘decisive’ display on England return
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel praised Trent ­Alexander-Arnold after the right-back impressed on his first England appearance since June 2025.

Alexander-Arnold, who has a point to prove after missing out on a World Cup spot, was one of the big positives as Tuchel’s side recovered from their defeat to Spain by recording a comfortable 2-0 win away to Czechia in the Nations League on Tuesday.

The Real Madrid defender shone in possession, particularly after the Czechs lost Pavel Sulc to a red card at 0-0, and helped England take the lead when he crossed for Anthony Gordon to score early in the second half.

“We never doubted that he can produce these kind of assists,” Tuchel said. “I think the second half the position, a bit of a deeper position, suited him more than the higher position in the first half. Overall, I think we had a good and professional performance. Of course the red card is such a heavy influence in the game.

“We need to keep focused, and Trent was a big help in this, because he’s very secure on the ball and can be decisive with his crosses. He did this solid defending and one decisive action that helped us score, so a good performance overall.”

Jude Bellingham started on the bench but the midfielder wore the captain’s armband after replacing Harry Kane during the closing stages. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup,” Tuchel said. “It is always a reward and always an honour. If you’re the captain at the end of these matches you can for sure be the permanent captain.

“He loves to be with us at the moment. We had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts to say: ‘Let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that. But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench.”
