In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White

It's on. At last. Finally. Confirmed by the almighty Turki.

Reconfirmed by the late, late word sent out that the face to face stare down between our two heavyweight titans will definitely take place at a press conference launch this Wednesday.

The fight that almost got away. AJ versus the Gypsy King. So close to being another of boxing's lost jewels that we almost gave up hope.

May the lords of the rings be praised.

Whether or not Dana White, the American interloper from UFC cage fighting who is demanding a share of the action, is present despite the protestations of Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, who won the battle for this fight to take place if not at Wembley but not as far, far west of London as New York.

Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury has been rescued for the British fight fans, by Cardiff. Although like the 70-odd thousand in the Principality Stadium the TV majority will have to stay awake into the wee small hours on the Friday night of December 11.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will face each other down at a press conference on Wednesday

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 2am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

First bell about 2am so that the tens of millions of Netflix subscribers can stream at peak time in America.

Assuming they buy into this as being a mega fight for all time. Or are satisfied that it is a spectacle unto itself.

Maybe a world heavyweight title adding spice to the occasion. Maybe not. Maybe just two good old Brits sorting differences that should have been settled a decade ago.

And why not? Fury and Joshua may be past their prime but they are not yet the walking dead.

They have enough fight left in their late 30s to put on a show.

And a future to fight for. For the winner there can be challenges to meet from the new generation of champions and a few million dollars more to add to the 75 million each will receive as an early Christmas present.

Always assuming no more spanners are thrown into these on-off-on works.

Good luck to both. Even more so to the Welsh constabulary who will have to deal with all those fans spilling out into darkened streets on what will already be a typically wild Friday night in Cardiff.

Sports.title: For Scottish boxing, the cupboard is bare. All that remains are memories of better times
Sports.content:
For Scottish boxing, the cupboard is bare. All that remains are memories of better times

Given the endless nonsense that continues to surround the Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight, it’s no surprise that it has dominated all the recent headlines in boxing.

Will they? Won’t they? Does anyone even really care any more? Is it happening in the UK? America? Saudi Arabia? Maybe on the moon? For a gazillion dollars?

It felt like a degree of certainty had been reached last week with the announcement that the fight will go ahead at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff in December.

That was until Dana White, the UFC supremo and one of the fight’s chief promoters, said only a few days ago that he ‘doesn’t know’ if it will go ahead.

Perhaps we will get a clearer picture tomorrow afternoon, with Fury and Joshua set to face-off at a media conference in London.

Either way, this tiresome circus act involving two fighters long past their prime continues to be pretty much the only thing anyone is speaking about in boxing right now.

Josh Taylor is dominated by Jack Catterall in Leeds as his ring supremacy is left in ruins

Nathaniel Collins had been Scotland's biggest hope until he suffered two successive defeats

Taylor's rise to the top of the fight game was an incredible achievement that will long be lauded

It perhaps escaped your attention, then, that Scotland’s Nathaniel Collins was back in the ring last weekend. Quite an important fight it was, too.

Taking on European featherweight champion Liam Davies in Birmingham, this was supposed to be Collins’ comeback fight after he lost to Spain’s Cristobal Llorente in Glasgow in April in their world title eliminator.

It did not go well. Collins was floored in the first round and never really recovered, before his trainer put a stop to it all and said enough was enough at the end of the seventh round.

There was a sadness to it all. Not only that Collins had suffered a second successive defeat, but also in terms of the wider implications for himself and for Scottish boxing as a whole.

The defeat to Llorente at The Hydro had been the first loss of Collins’ career. It had been a tough night, albeit not disastrous. There was a chance to bounce back and come again.

But, in terms of challenging at world level, he now looks further away than ever. The same would surely apply to Scottish boxing as a whole after this latest blow.

Not so long ago, Scottish boxing felt like it had a pulse. Josh Taylor climbed the mountain and was, in his pomp, one of the best pound-for-pound fighters on the planet.

The Tartan Tornado put together one of the greatest runs by any British fighter in history to become our first undisputed world champion in the four-belt era. Achieving that in just 18 fights was truly phenomenal.

When Taylor’s career then fizzled out due to a combination of burn-out, inactivity and promotional mismanagement, it had been hoped that Collins would be the next cab off the rank.

The late Ken Buchanan won multiple titles at lightweight and fought between 1965 and 1982

The Nightmare, as he’s known, was supposed to be the fighter who kept the lights on and continued to fly the flag in the post-Taylor era.

That’s not to say he was ever going to be quite as good as Taylor. That always looked unrealistic. But there was genuine hope that Collins could at least be a contender for a world title.

The brutal yet stylish manner in which he dismantled fellow Scot Lee McGregor at The Hydro in May 2025 gave the look of a fighter with all the credentials to go on and box at world level.

But the defeat to Davies in Birmingham last weekend has surely ended that conversation. In the post-Taylor era, the cupboard is depressingly bare for Scottish boxing. Completely and utterly empty.

No one is selling out arenas in Scotland. No one is forcing their way on to Sky Sports and the likes. No one is even close to holding box-office appeal or appearing on pay-per-views.

The amateur and club scene are still doing their bit. The numbers are OK, even if a lot of people use boxing clubs as fitness classes these days rather than having any desire to actually enter a ring.

But when you speak to people involved with boxing clubs across Scotland, the majority of them all share a similar concern.

Plainly, that we have no one even remotely close to following in Taylor’s footsteps and fighting at the top level of the sport. The outlook is bleak.

Listen, Scotland is a relatively small country. We do not have an endless pool of talent. Boxing is not a mainstream sport like football or rugby.

The two successive defeats for Collins have signaled a barren period for Scottish boxing

Kids learn to play football in various different ways; at school, at coaching sessions, or with a club. Maybe even down the local park or on the streets in some very rare and old-fashioned instances.

Rugby is a non-negotiable for those in private education. Even golf now has far more reach and appeal with the younger generation than boxing.

With the awareness around long-term brain damage now greater than ever, you can hardly blame any parent if they aren’t overly enthused by the idea of their kids being involved in a sport where they get punched in the head.

When a generational talent like Taylor comes along and then leaves, the gap is enormous. There is no conveyor belt of world-class operators waiting in the wings.

Sadly, it also now appears that Scotland can’t even offer up any fighters in the bracket just below world level either.

Collins has already come through a serious health scare – a life-threatening twisted bowel caused by infant scar tissue – that put much more than just his boxing career at risk. He has shown heart. No one questions that. He gave it a good go.

But his latest defeat is emblematic of the wider malaise that continues to be so prevalent across Scottish boxing as a whole.

There have been lean times in the past. After Ken Buchanan and Jim Watt, there were quiet periods. After Scott Harrison’s turbulent reign at featherweight the scene thinned out again until Ricky Burns and then Taylor arrived.

Cycles exist. The problem now is that the cycle feels stuck in the downward phase with no obvious sign of it moving back up again.

Where is the next boxing superstar in Scotland? It is beginning to feel like the sport is dying a death. That is the uncomfortable truth.

When Collins fought Llorente at The Hydro in April, it wasn’t even close to being a sell-out. The whole top tier of the arena was closed. Make of that what you will.

And that was a world title eliminator involving the guy who was supposed to be our next big hope. Taylor himself has acknowledged the lack of young fighters breaking through.

The Tornado’s retirement left a void. Collins’ latest defeat has made it wider and deeper. The Hydro still stands ready for big nights, but it’s hard to see a major promoter going back there any time soon.

The Scottish public still loves a fighter who will dig in and go to war. But the fighters of genuine world-class pedigree are simply not here at present.

These are the lean years. The barren stretch. And that should worry anyone who cares about the sport north of the border.

The cupboard is bare. The stars have gone. Until someone steps forward and proves otherwise, Scottish boxing is living on memories of Taylor and on nostalgia about some of the other great names of the past.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury enrolls in drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott London press conference ahead of £150m Cardiff bout
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury enrolls in drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott London press conference ahead of £150m Cardiff bout

Tyson Fury has now enrolled in the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association (VADA)'s testing programme ahead of his blockbuster showdown with Anthony Joshua, his camp has confirmed.

The development comes just 24 hours after Joshua threatened to boycott Wednesday's first press conference in London unless Fury could prove he had entered the VADA testing pool.

Joshua had already enrolled, while Fury's camp maintained that the terms of their agreement gave him longer to do so.

But with the first face-to-face meeting between the two heavyweights this Wednesday, Fury has now completed his enrolment and provided his whereabouts to VADA.

Fury's manager, Spencer Brown, told Playbook Boxing: 'We are enrolled in VADA. We are enrolled in VADA. Just to confirm that.'

Asked about the timing of Fury's enrolment, they added: 'He did it a bit earlier than when the fight was announced. In our contract, we had more time, but you know, it doesn't matter. We've done it. We've done everything we've been asked to do. Everything.'

Tyson Fury has agreed to join a drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott their press conference

The Gypsy King's manager also explained that enrolment and testing are separate stages of the VADA process.

Asked whether Fury had already been tested, they said: 'No, you have to enrol first, don't you? That part of it's all been done, then the testing comes second.'

Brown stressed that the nature of VADA's programme means fighters are not given advance warning of when testers will arrive.

'You could be tested in a week, you could be sitting there on your toilet and they knock on the door,' he said. 'That's the way they work. They don't tell you a time. They don't say we're coming round tomorrow. That's the way. That's why it works.'

The dispute had threatened to become an unwanted subplot to a fight more than a decade in the making.

Joshua's camp had raised concerns after it emerged that the two fighters had different timelines under their respective contractual arrangements, with promoter Eddie Hearn subsequently making clear that he expected Fury to enter the programme.

There is now another significant issue to resolve before December 11: exactly when the fight will take place.

The heavyweight blockbuster will be staged at Cardiff's Principality Stadium and streamed globally by Netflix, with organisers targeting the US primetime market. The main event is expected to take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in Britain, with a ring walk potentially as late as 2am.

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on Friday December 11. The pair are set to meet for a press conference on September 30

Brown has now revealed that the precise timing is still being negotiated and made clear that he does not want the fight to start at 2am.

'I think 2am is far too late,' he said.

'I think that the general public in England will want to watch it in the pubs, the clubs, you know, round each other's houses. There'll be a party atmosphere, and I just think it needs to be earlier. Simple as that.'

Brown added: 'It's all in negotiation at the moment, but it shouldn't be at 2 o'clock in the morning. I certainly wouldn't like to sit there at 2 o'clock in the morning, would you?'

And Brown also questioned the experience for the thousands of fans expected to attend in Cardiff.

'I think 99 per cent of the people will probably tell you that if you're in the stadium, you don't want to be sitting in the stadium till 2 o'clock in the morning, freezing your nuts off.'

The late start has been driven by the fact Netflix is looking to maximise its US audience, while Cardiff's Principality Stadium was selected after the proposed venues in London could not accommodate the required late finish.

The venue can accommodate the late finish, but the event's licensing arrangements have also required negotiation because of the proposed early-hours schedule.

Fury and Joshua are due to meet for the first time in public since their long-awaited fight was officially confirmed at Wednesday's press conference in London.

The bout, which will be contested at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on December 11, is the culmination of years of failed negotiations between the former world champions.

Both men have won their respective comeback fights this year, clearing the way for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight showdown.

Now, with Fury's VADA enrolment confirmed, attention can turn back to the build-up and whether organisers can find a start time that works for both the global Netflix audience and the British fans inside and outside the stadium.

Sports.title: Dana White admits he 'doesn't know' if Tyson Fury's fight with Anthony Joshua will go ahead after Gypsy King claimed rival wants to pull OUT of the £150m bout amid Eddie Hearn's feud with promoter
Sports.content:
Dana White has cast doubt over Tyson Fury's heavyweight blockbuster against Anthony Joshua, admitting that he has 'no idea' whether the £150million showdown will go ahead on December 11.

The battle between British boxing's biggest names was plunged into jeopardy over the weekend, with Fury claiming his arch rival 'wants to pull out' of the fight amid a dispute between White and Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn.

Fury's claim made for a dramatic escalation, with the pair announcing their Cardiff bout just over 24 hours earlier.

White, who runs Zuffa Boxing alongside Saudi Arabia's boxing supremo Turki Al-Sheikh, has been billed as the main promoter for the heavyweight showdown and had fought for the contest to take place in New York City.

Hearn, who successfully wrestled the fight back to Cardiff, has claimed that the contract Joshua signed stipulates that White cannot be involved in the contest and threatened crunch talks with broadcaster Netflix over White's attendance at Fury and Joshua's press conference on Wednesday in London.

That warning appears to have thrown the event into chaos, with Fury claiming Hearn's 'ego' is presenting a major stumbling block in the long-awaited bout taking place.

Dana White has admitted he has 'no idea' if Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua will go ahead

Tyson Fury announced on Saturday that Joshua 'wants to pull out' of the December 11 contest

White, whose involvement has been criticised by sections of the British boxing public, was grilled by the media in a cagey press conference on Saturday night, where he labelled the bout a 's***show' while conceding he has 'no idea' if the contest will take place.

'I don't know. The guy who is supposed to be helping the fight has been hurting the fight the entire time. He hasn't done the fight any favours. I don't know anybody who is more full of s*** than Eddie Hearn.'

When asked whether he would step aside to allow the fight to go ahead, White said: 'That's not up to me. I'm involved in the f***ing fight.

'If Eddie Hearn really cared about this f***ing fight — first of all the fight would've happened a f***ing long time ago, one. Number two, he could finance the thing himself.

'Listen, this whole thing's a s***show right now. We'll all know a lot more in the next three, four days, see how this thing plays out.'

White's comments follow Fury's expletive-laden Instagram video, in which he labelled Joshua and Hearn 'cowards'.

He said: 'Breaking News: Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight they are saying he is not going to fight now.

'They're little s*** house cowards, mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego, he's making up a million different things and threatening that "we're not going to fight" you little coward.

Fury and Joshua have been on a collision course for 15 years but a fight has never transpired

Fury and Joshua's fight was due to take place on Friday December 11. The pair are set to meet for a press conference on September 30

'AJ pull your finger out you white flag, yellow-bellied coward. You know now we're coming home, now I'm coming home the Gypsy King is coming back to the United Kingdom to thrash you in front of all my fans in Wales.'

Fury went on to call Joshua a 'body-building sausage'.

He also claimed that boxing supremo Turki Al-Sheikh is now looking to find a new person to fight Fury at 'the drop of a hat'.

Fury continued: 'So I hope [Hearn and Joshua] are happy you little cowardly b*******, I've never seen anything like [Hearn and Joshua] you pure s*** houses and this is mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego. What a little p****.'

The 38-year-old then posted a mocked up poster of himself and light heavyweight champion David Benavidez, hinting that the 29-year-old American could replace AJ in the Cardiff contest.

It is understood that both men are set to pocket around £75million for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil, if it goes ahead.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua in chaos as Gypsy King claims rival wants to pull OUT of  £150m Cardiff mega fight just over 24 hours after bout was confirmed
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury’s heavyweight blockbuster with Anthony Joshua has been thrown into chaos after the Gypsy King claimed his rival is pulling out of the Cardiff contest.

In a dramatic escalation a little over 24 hours after their £150million bout was confirmed, Fury took to Instagram to say the fight is now in jeopardy owing to a feud between Joshua’s promoter Eddie Hearn and the UFC’s Dana White.

White, who runs Zuffa Boxing alongside Saudi Arabia’s boxing supremo Turki Al-Sheikh, has been billed as the main promoter for the heavyweight showdown and had fought for the contest to take place in New York City.

Hearn, who successfully wrestled the fight back to Cardiff, has claimed that the contract Joshua signed stipulates that White cannot be involved in the contest.

In an expletive-laden Instagram video, Fury claimed the fight has been cancelled because of Hearn's ego – and that he is 'making up a million different things'.

He said: 'Breaking News: Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight they are saying he is not going to fight now.

'They're little s*** house cowards, mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego, he's making up a million different things and threatening that "we're not going to fight" you little coward.

'AJ pull your finger out you white flag, yellow-bellied coward. You know now we're coming home, now I'm coming home the Gypsy King is coming back to the United Kingdom to thrash you in front of all my fans in Wales.'

Tyson Fury announced the news in a video on social media

Fury and Joshua's fight was due to take place on Friday December 11. The pair were set to meet for a press conference next week on September 30

Fury exchanges words with Anthony Joshua after his fight in April 2026

Fury went on to call Joshua a 'body-building sausage'.

He also claimed that Al-Sheikh is now looking to find a new person to fight Fury at 'the drop of a hat'.

Fury continued: 'So I hope [Hearn and Joshua] are happy you little cowardly b*******, I've never seen anything like [Hearn and Joshua] you pure s*** houses and this is mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego. What a little p****.'

The 38-year-old then posted a mocked up poster of himself and light heavyweight champion David Benavidez, hinting that the 29-year-old American could replace AJ in the Cardiff contest.

Fury and Joshua, 36, are due to meet on September 30 in a pre-fight press conference, but Hearn warned that White – who he labelled a ‘loser’ and a ‘soppy t**’ after the fight was confirmed – must not be present at the London face off.

But Fury now claims that this latest demand could see the fight unravel. In a stinging response, Al-Sheikh also threw his weight behind White by posting a photo of the American smoking a cigar on Instagram.

It is understood that both men would have pocketed around £75million for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil.

Hearn had also succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York.

Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff.

The event, broadcast on Netflix, was expected to take place around 2am to accommodate a US audience.

This is a breaking news story. More to follow.

Sports.title: Former world heavyweight champion boxer, 53, loses sad comeback against club fighter after 12 years retired
Sports.content:
Hasim Rahman shocked the boxing world when he knocked out Lennox Lewis to become heavyweight champion in 2001.

But 25 years later, he was fighting in front of just a handful of people in Lowell, Indiana and losing a split decision to a club fighter on Thursday night.

Rahman made a sad return to the ring 12 years after his last fight at VFW Post 6841, fighting against 4-4 opponent Phillip Triantafillo for the Indiana State heavyweight belt.

And he lost a six-round unanimous decision, with two judges' scorecards scoring the bout 59-55 and the other 58-56. The loss drops his record to 50-10-2 in a fight that was a far cry from his glory days as the king of boxing's biggest division.

Rahman has been threatening a comeback for years, finally announcing in May he would return to the ring and claiming he had ambitions of becoming boxing's oldest heavyweight champion.

That record is held by George Foreman, who regained the heavyweight championship at 45, eight years younger than Rahman.

Hasim Rahman lost a unanimous decision as he made a sad comeback to boxing at the age of 53

Rahman was once the IBC and WBC heavyweight boxing champion back in 2001

His low-key loss against Triantafillo drew criticism from those within the boxing community.

Legendary promoter Lou DiBella wrote on X: 'In the early hours of this morning, in Lowell, Indiana, 53 yr. old former heavyweight champion Hasim Rahman lost a six round sanctioned #boxing match to a 3-4 guy... a SANCTIONED fight.

'Every day, in many ways, across borders, from billionaire and corporate supported events to unsafe silliness in tiny venues, boxing is showing you what it is in 2026. You can have it!'.

Boxing writer Dan Rafael wrote: 'Just watched some sad s***: Utterly washed former heavyweight champion Hasim Rahman, age 53, ending a 13-year retirement & losing a slow motion 6-rounder to 40-year-old novice Phillip Triantafillo (now 5-4) in what looked like a community center gym in front of maybe a dozen people. #Boxing is unforgiving.'

Baltimore, Maryland native Rahman last fought professionally in June 2014, losing a three-round decision in Auckland, New Zealand against Anthony Nansen.

Two years earlier, he had been knocked out in the second round by Alexander Povetkin in a fight that marked the end of his career at the top level.

Rahman produced one of the sport's great upsets when he beat Lewis in April 2001 in South Africa, knocking him out in the fifth round before losing a rematch later that year.

He went on to fight the likes of Evander Holyfield, James Toney and Wladimir Klitchsko in his long career which has now featured another chapter long past his 50th birthday.

Rahman was beaten by his 4-4 opponent in a six-round contest in front of barely any people

Rahman shocked the boxing world when he knocked out Lennox Lewis in South Africa in 2001

Another former world heavyweight champion, Mike Tyson, made headlines for his return to the ring in 2024 aged 58 against Jake Paul.

He recently insisted he would 'never' return again, saying: 'That’s why I did the last fight. So I never have to do it again.'

Tyson earned a reported $20 million payday for that return to the ring, which ended with a sad unanimous decision loss, but he later wrote: 'This is one of those situations when you lost but still won.

'I’m grateful for last night. No regrets to get in ring one last time. I almost died in June. Had 8 blood transfusions. Lost half my blood and 25lbs in hospital and had to fight to get healthy to fight so I won.

'To have my children see me stand toe to toe and finish 8 rounds with a talented fighter half my age in front of a packed Dallas Cowboy stadium is an experience that no man has the right to ask for. Thank you.'

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - and Netflix reveal price it will cost to watch
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua's long-awaited fight with Tyson Fury has finally been confirmed for December 11 at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium – and it will save Joshua around £7.5million in tax. It is understood each man will pocket around £75m for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil after Joshua’s team, led by Eddie Hearn, succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York. Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff. The ring walk is expected to take place around 2am to suit a US-based audience, in line with the demands of Netflix, which will broadcast the heavyweight showdown. Although the delivery of the fight in Wales will be positioned as a victory for British fight fans, pragmatism around tax was also a key consideration in Hearn’s argument against Madison Square Garden in New York. As Daily Mail Sport revealed earlier this month, the two fighters would have been taxed around 30 per cent of their purses in America, compared to 20 per cent in the UK, with Joshua particularly unhappy about the prospect of an extra £7.5m being added to his bill. The two-time world champion instead demanded that his contract be honoured, which stipulated a British-based fight. Boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh said: 'Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. 'The time for talking is over. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua. Years in the making. One night to settle it. December 11th. LIVE on Netflix.' Netflix today confirmed the fight would be available 'at no additional cost' to subscribers. Their general membership pricing starts at £7.99 a month in the UK. Bookmaker Betfair make Fury the early favourite to win, pricing him at 8/15. Joshua is priced at 13/8. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been announced for Friday, December 11 The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects Joshua tweeted: 'I am inspiring a generation', alongside an emoji of the British flag. His promoter Eddie Hearn, who fought relentlessly to keep the fight in the UK, wrote: 'WE DID IT. Forever indebted to the U.K. public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn’t have got this over the line without you.' Fury's name appearing first on the card for the Battle of Britain will be an early win for the Gypsy King in his constant PR war with Joshua. The pair had originally been pencilled in to fight on November 20 at Madison Square Garden in New York, but a determined push from Joshua and Hearn saw the contracts re-negotiated to bring the fight back to British soil. Hearn had been adamant that British fans deserved the opportunity to watch two of the country's biggest sporting stars go head-to-head at home, and fought hard to make that happen. Fury, too, wanted the fight in the UK, but had been prepared to accept a move to America because of his concerns that the bout could once again slip away. Now those fears, after ten years of frustration, have been put to bed. The fight will take place in Cardiff, with the later-than-usual start time expected to mean ring walks at around 2am UK time as organisers attempt to satisfy the American audience watching on Netflix. Wembley had been the preferred venue for the showdown, but the major stumbling block was securing the necessary late-night permit. With Netflix and Turki Alalshikh keen for the event to cater to viewers in the United States, organisers required a start time significantly later than would normally be permitted at Wembley. Cardiff, however, was able to secure the required permit - clearing the final obstacle to bringing the fight back to Britain. Cardiff's Principality Stadium has come out on top to host the fight after weeks of negotiations

Your browser does not support iframes.

The scale of the occasion is already being felt in the Welsh capital, with hotels in Cardiff now understood to be sold out as supporters scramble to secure accommodation for one of the biggest fights in British boxing. For Joshua, the move represents the culmination of a push to ensure the fight was staged in the UK. The former two-times world champion and Hearn had been clear that, after years of watching British heavyweight stars travel overseas for major fights, Joshua-Fury belonged in front of their home crowd. Fury was willing to compromise on the location if necessary, however, with his priority being to finally get the fight over the line. The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects. Joshua won Olympic gold at London 2012 before turning professional, while Fury had already made his professional debut in 2008 and was building an unbeaten record of his own. For years, the prospect of the two eventually sharing a ring became one of British boxing's great hypothetical match-ups. Fury's stunning victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015 elevated him to the summit of the heavyweight division, while Joshua was rapidly closing in on world-title status himself. FURY VS JOSHUA - BIG FIGHT ODDS Fury to win - 8/15 Draw - 16/1 Joshua to win- 13/8 Victory method: Tyson Fury by Points or Decision - 16/5 Fury by TKO/KO/DQ - 13/10 Anthony Joshua by Dec/Tech Dec - 15/2 Joshua TKO/KO/DQ - 13/5 Fight to go the distance: Yes - 13/8 No - 4/9 Odds courtesy of Betfair Joshua claimed the IBF heavyweight title by stopping Charles Martin in 2016 before adding the WBA and IBO belts to his collection. By 2017, Joshua-Fury had evolved from a fantasy fight into a genuine target. But the negotiations repeatedly broke down. The closest it came to fruition was in 2021, when the two camps appeared to be on the brink of agreeing a two-fight deal. The proposed showdown was publicly discussed and appeared to be edging towards reality, only for Fury to become contractually obligated to face Deontay Wilder after an arbitration ruling. That fight ultimately took place, with Fury beating Wilder for a third time, while Joshua embarked on his own defining chapter against Oleksandr Usyk. Joshua lost his WBA, IBF and WBO titles to Usyk in 2021 before suffering a second defeat to the Ukrainian in their 2022 rematch. Once again, Joshua-Fury seemed to drift further away. Then came another tantalising opportunity. Negotiations accelerated in late 2022, with both camps discussing a potential December showdown, but the fight again failed to materialise. Fury moved on to other opponents while Joshua began rebuilding his career following the two defeats by Usyk. The emergence of Alalshikh and the rapid expansion of Saudi Arabia's influence over boxing created a fresh route to making the fight. And this time, the years of disappointment are finally over. The contracts have been signed. Joshua-Fury is no longer a fight being negotiated, teased or promised. It will take place in Cardiff on December 11.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's torture training! Boxer uses ancient Cossack warriors' stretching machine to prepare himself to fight Tyson Fury in a painful-looking workout routine
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has been summoning the strength of an ancient warrior as he prepares for his long-awaited bout with Tyson Fury on a stretching machine.

Boxing's biggest battle of the year is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in early December, after a venue war that saw it move from Madison Square Garden in New York.

Despite the superfight being shrouded in uncertainty for much of the year, both Joshua and Fury have been knuckling down in the gym in preparation for their showdown.

Away from the usual training drills associated with boxing, it appears that Joshua is trying something new in order to get the best out of himself when he faces the Gypsy King.

The two-time heavyweight world champion has posted a video to Instagram of him using a Pravilo machine, a stretching machine used by warriors in medieval times.

The machine is a training and conditioning device that originates from Slavic and Russian traditions. It is best-known for being used by historical Cossack warriors for over 1,000 years.

Anthony Josshua has posted a video of him using the ancient warrior Pravilo machine

And if the video posted by Joshua is anything to go by, it can be somewhat of a torturous bit of equipment, based on how it stretches out each limb of the human body.

The 36-year-old can be seen being pulled into a starfish position by the modern version of the machine, which he keeps in his new training gym in Dubai.

Earlier this year, Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic due to the conflict in the Middle East.

The post on Instagram – which is captioned 'When the instructor says, relax and breathe' – also shows the 251.0lb (113.9kg) frame of Joshua being easily rotated 180 degrees, displaying the strength of his core.

Joshua will be returning to the Welsh capital where he has won twice previously, beating Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker in 2017 and 2018 respectively.

Wembley had looked an ideal venue for the fight, but the strict 11pm curfew has been a sticking point, despite London mayor Sadiq Khan saying he wanted to ensure allowances were made to host the fight.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury could now be set to fight in Cardiff, Wales in December

Boxing dealmaker Turki Al-Sheikh has been insistent on a start time of 2am.

The streaming giant Netflix has yet to sign off on Cardiff, but American sportswriter Dan Rafael last week reported he had asked Netflix if they would approve, with a source telling him: 'I think they're OK.'

A spokesperson for the Welsh Rugby Union said: 'We'd be delighted to host this fight.

'We are very keen to attract more boxing to the stadium, which has a rich history in the sport, enhanced by its closable roof, unrivalled sight lines and unique city-centre location.'

Sports.title: Ocon to leave Haas at the end of F1 2026
Sports.content:
Esteban Ocon will officially leave Haas at the end of the 2026 Formula 1 campaign with his replacement yet to be announced.

The 30-year-old joined the American squad from Alpine for 2025, but a very disappointing 18 months means the one-time grand prix winner will depart Haas after just two seasons.

Ocon spent both 2025 and 2026 alongside youngster Oliver Bearman, who was a rookie last year, but has scored 45 points to the Briton’s 61 meaning this announcement was expected.

“I’d like to thank Esteban for everything he’s contributed to the team since joining us in 2025,” said Haas team boss Ayao Komatsu. “His professionalism and commitment have proved valuable as we continue to grow as an organisation.

“Together this year we tackled the challenge of a major regulation change, where Esteban’s driving experience and inputs were significant as we’ve worked hard to develop the VF-26 across the season.

“There’s still plenty of racing ahead and our focus remains on working together to maximise every opportunity through to the final race of the year.”

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

Ocon had always made it clear that his struggles stemmed from the inconsistencies of the Haas car, an issue that plagued him more than Bearman, arguing it wasn’t his driving at fault.

The issue has improved of late for the Frenchman, scoring points in Baku last weekend, but he still lags behind Bearman in qualifying with a losing 13-6 record against him in 2026.

So Ocon may leave at the end of the year with what should be 203 grand prix starts to his name, one victory at Hungary in 2021 and four podiums, all scored with Alpine.

He said on social media: "My time with Haas F1 Team will come to an end at the end of the 2026 season.

"I leave this project with my head held high and proud of my performances in what were not always the easiest of circumstances for various reasons and factors outside of my control.

"My immediate focus is the next race weekend. I will continue to work hard with the team, maximise every opportunity, and keep extracting every bit of performance from the car.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

"There are still many races to go this season and, as always, I will give it my everything behind the wheel for myself and for my team.

"I am still motivated. I am still hungry. This is absolutely not the end of my Formula 1 career."

His next step is not yet known, nor is his replacement, though reigning Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and current F2 leader Rafael Camara are understood to be the candidates.

Ocon is currently 16th in the 2026 drivers' standings, three spots behind Bearman, with Haas seventh in the constructors' championship after 15 of 23 rounds.

Sports.title: Was Baku really Red Bull's last opportunity of winning in F1 2026?
Sports.content:
When Max Verstappen walked into the Red Bull hospitality on Friday for his Dutch Formula 1 media session – which in Azerbaijan, incidentally, consisted of just two Dutch journalists – the message was clear. The Baku City Circuit offered Red Bull its best opportunity to win a race this year, but Verstappen added: "We’ve done a great job messing it up."

A day later, he still came remarkably close to victory. Admittedly, he felt the gap of just 0.196 seconds at the finish line was somewhat misleading due to Valtteri Bottas' crash and George Russell's boost issue, but Red Bull's race pace was undeniably good – particularly on the softs.

That was not only down to the impressive top speed on the longest straight of the F1 calendar, but also to the upgrades Red Bull introduced in Baku. It was the final significant package for the RB22 and, according to both drivers, the upgrade – which included a new floor and revised sidepods – delivered what had been hoped for.

Besides outright performance, the upgrade also made both drivers more comfortable in the car, at least on the Baku layout.

"Baku is a very specific track, with specific tarmac, but the way the car was behaving in terms of through-corner balance this weekend, from lap one in FP1, I was like, 'Okay, this is looking pretty good'," Isack Hadjar said.

"Then the second half of the car [the power unit], we’re definitely lacking compared to Mercedes. But in terms of handling on the brakes, the car was definitely a step better than in Budapest," Hadjar said, referring to the last race before his wrist injury. "So, yeah, I’m really pleased with that [feeling in the car]."

Verstappen shared that view and felt the confidence to attack the corners that is so important at a track like Baku. "Yeah, I mean, it’s a unique track. It has mainly 90-degree corners, but it probably felt a little bit more together balance-wise," the Dutchman said.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"But like I said, we have other issues in the car that we really need to fix because there is just free lap time in that. That’s what we are working on. But the performance items, they worked well and we’ve been fairly happy all weekend with what I had from the car."

By the problems costing 'free' lap time, Verstappen is referring to the 'car degradation' issues and the deployment on the electrical side of the power unit, which is not optimal compared with Mercedes.

Despite the upgrades from the technical team led by Pierre Wache working well, Verstappen maintains that the Baku race weekend was Red Bull’s best chance of victory in 2026.

That is not only because of the layout, but also because Mercedes will have its long-awaited upgrade package for the W17 in Malaysia – with an ADUO upgrade for the power unit in the pipeline as well.

"If they’re bringing an upgrade to Malaysia, then it’s going to look a little bit more difficult for us," the four-time world champion said.

"If Mercedes is bringing an upgrade and it works, then they’ll take another step ahead, and that’s not what you want. It will make it even more difficult to win, but we’ll try every single weekend and, of course, if the opportunity is there, we go for it."

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

When Autosport asked Mekies whether he sees it the same way, or whether the race pace in Baku instead gives him confidence that there will be more opportunities, the team principal responds:

"I think both statements are correct. I think it's fair what Max is saying in terms of assessing this track as, on paper, the one that was favouring us the most. So I think that is correct, it has probably been the most favourable track for us in terms of car characteristics.

"Equally I think that the performance we've shown in the race is giving us decent hope that we will get another couple of occasions before the end of the year."

Moreover, Mekies stresses that the remaining race weekends this year are not only about securing that much-coveted victory. At least as important is for Red Bull to learn for 2027, ideally allowing it to produce a car that can consistently fight at the front next season.

Verstappen has already said several times that certain bigger changes are no longer possible in 2026, but that they are necessary to mount a championship challenge next year. Mekies acknowledges that and says the remaining race weekends are important in that respect as well.

"On top of getting a couple of other occasions to get that first win, it's also good to go to tracks where it's going to be more difficult for us, because that is exactly what we need to be confronted with to continue to progress," he said.

Nevertheless, a year without a victory would be remarkable, as it would be the first time since 2015 for both Verstappen and Red Bull.

Sports.title: Aston Martin retains Alonso and Stroll for F1 2027
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso has finally confirmed that he will continue with Aston Martin into the 2027 Formula 1 campaign, ending all speculation surrounding his future.

For months the 45-year-old had been answering questions about whether or not he will stick with F1, given his then Aston Martin contract expired at the end of the current 2026 campaign.

The double champion claimed it depended on which direction the regulations would take, as he strongly dislikes the new-for-2026 ruleset that has more emphasis on electric power.

But Alonso not publicly committing was partly an effort to increase pressure on F1, particularly as he’d held meetings with Stefano Domenicali and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

So now has come the news that the F1 paddock expected: Alonso has signed a new deal with Aston Martin, which he joined in a shock move from Alpine for the 2023 season.

"I'm very happy to sign a new contract with Aston Martin," said the 32-time race winner. "I took my time to make this decision, but racing is my life, my passion, and I know I still have the speed and determination to compete at the highest level.

"I'm committed for the long term with this team and to helping us succeed. I truly believe in what we are building: we have strong leadership, incredible people, partners and facilities.

"I look forward to making more memories on the racetrack in front of the passionate fans. Their energy creates an atmosphere that inspires me and is what makes our sport special."

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

The Spaniard has endured a real up-and-down journey with the Silverstone outfit, having made a blistering start with six podiums in his opening eight grands prix before two more that year.

But since then it has been mainly lows, as Aston Martin was outdeveloped by its rivals before making a horrendous start to the 2026 regulations, partly due to its uncompetitive Honda engine.

Aston Martin sits 10th in the standings with just three points - all scored by Alonso - after 15 rounds and is only ahead of newcomer Cadillac.

The Silverstone squad has also announced the extension of Lance Stroll's contract, so he is set for his ninth season at Team Silverstone after joining from Williams.

"I'm very happy to continue with Aston Martin for the long term," said Stroll. "I've been on this journey since the beginning and I believe we have the resources and the people to become a winning team.

"There is so much hard work going on at Silverstone with real progress being made, and the determination I see in every department is a huge motivation for me.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin, Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I know we are heading in the right direction, and my commitment is stronger than ever to help us achieve our goals."

Team owner Lawrence Stroll added: "Lance and Fernando have been a crucial part of our journey and we are very pleased to confirm that they will continue with us into the next chapter for the team.

"Having two drivers with their level of experience, commitment and knowledge provides tremendous value to the whole organisation.

"We are here to win, and whilst our short-term focus remains on improving performance, I believe we have the world-class talent we need to achieve our long-term objectives."

Sports.title: Azerbaijan GP was a step forward for upgraded Williams - but real test is still to come
Sports.content:
If there is a definition of a mixed bag, that's what the Baku weekend was to Williams. It progressed to Q3 for the first time in 2026, but didn't start there due to a grid penalty for Carlos Sainz. It scored points for the first time since Monaco, with some fortune, but also saw Alex Albon crash out.

Azerbaijan was a key weekend circled in red on Williams' calendar as it finally upgraded an FW48 starved of significant improvements for months. The Grove team wheeled out an all-new chassis, which was finally on the required weight, as well as a new floor and other aerodynamic parts.

The car's long run pace in FP2 looked encouraging, unlocking a long-shut door to the midfield ballpark that includes the likes of Haas, Racing Bulls and Audi.

In qualifying, Sainz claimed ninth but a grid penalty dumped him back to 14th behind Albon. From the belly of the pack it was looking like a long-awaited chance to score points went begging until Franco Colapinto took out Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris at a restart.

"It's been a mammoth effort to bring the update that we have here this weekend and it's nice to walk away with a point," said team principal James Vowles. "You can see we didn't have the pace on that first stint, and we need to dig and understand that because that was a critical part of the race where we weren't able to make progress."

The point for 10th was a reward for all the hard work in the factory, but did the Williams B-spec really deliver as much as hoped? "I think it's exactly the step we expected," Albon insisted. "Maybe we didn't expect Q3, to be fair to you. But yes, it put us in a midfield fight."



Sainz added: "Our initial feel is that the car feels just a bit quicker. But we were so far away that even though we've been bringing such a big upgrade, it still feels like we are playing a lot of catch-up. So as promised, no big massive surprises in terms of pace, a healthy step forward."

James Vowles, Williams Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

An additional factor is that Baku was a real Williams track, which can't be said from Malaysia's Sepang and the Singapore street circuit which will put a much bigger emphasis on downforce. So, coming away with a point and a DNF feels like at least half of a missed opportunity if it means Williams will regress again over the remainder of the triple header.



"This track, even without the upgrade, it would have favoured us," Albon said. "Malaysia will be telling to see where we are on a much more downforce-focused circuit. We've also got now a few days to actually understand the package.

"If you look at the big picture, we'll make the car go faster in terms of optimising it. But we'll be slower relative to the rest of the field, because that track will not suit us. Expect us to fall back in Malaysia, and then maybe in Singapore we can come somewhere in between."



As far as Albon's crash is concerned, which brought out the safety car on lap 31, he took responsibility for outbraking himself but felt it also further exposed of a key Williams weakness which has carried over across regulations.

"It was odd," he explained. "I braked a little bit later, but not much later. Then we had a big wind gust. I thought I would run a little bit wide, but I never thought I would hit the wall.

"I'm sure I have to hold my hand up in that situation, but at the same time we've had these issues before. We know our car likes to lift the front wheel and we three-wheel. We know when we brake a little bit late, we can expose ourselves to that three-wheeling. And sometimes when it does that, the penalty for front locking is huge on our car. It happens.

"For sure, with the wind gust and braking late at the same time, it just tips it over the edge. It wasn't a huge amount; it was a few metres, but that's too much."

Alexander Albon, Williams Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Williams fans may have expected more from such a long-awaited upgrade on a circuit that historically suited the team. But 2026 is already a lost season for Williams, at least on the track as it languished in ninth in the standings.

Perhaps it is more constructive to view the process of redesigning its chassis while adding aero performance as a stress test for the team. And a round of evidence gathering for Vowles that the Grove-based squad is now more capable of bringing through new parts than it was 12 months ago, and a way to course correct as the 2027 car project gathers steam.

With the latest chassis expected carry over into the 2027 campaign, that's already one big-ticket item out of the way.



"I'm confident you're going to see us stepping forward now that that big rule change is behind us," Vowles told Sky. "There's an aero change for next year, there's a power unit change for next year. But it's smaller in size so we can absorb it.

"But it's going to take a little bit of time to catch up on the mess that's happened this winter. My real learning from it is we need a lot more investment to bring us just the ability to keep up with those in front. And the cost cap restrains us from doing that.



"[The upgrade] is directionally right. I think more importantly, it's the foundation we wanted to set ourselves for next year. We recognise this year's a little bit behind us, unfortunately, but there's a lot to do in going into 2027."

Sports.title: Herta still aiming for F1 by 2028
Sports.content:
“It would be foolish to sit here and think that I will be on the pace right away, that I will be on the pace and ready to win in my first race. I may be older, but speed-wise, these guys are just as fast as anybody out there.”

This was how Colton Herta viewed his gamble of a Formula 2 switch from IndyCar as he pursued his Formula 1 dream, and he has so far been proven right – actually more than he initially imagined.

Cadillac’s protege was well aware that F2 was a tricky championship for rookies, especially when bypassing F3 and having to master the Pirelli tyres from the get-go, but he certainly didn’t expect to struggle to the extent that he has.

The Hitech driver lies 19th in the drivers’ standings, with 26 points to his name and fifth place in the Barcelona sprint race as his best result – from third on the reversed grid. He is at a loss to explain such a lack of performance.

Asked by Autosport in an exclusive interview what exactly has been tough for him to get his head around, Herta responded: “Nothing in particular, it's just been the whole thing. Unfortunately, there hasn't been a whole bunch of positives at any point. For whatever reason, there's been zero pace, and nothing has really changed.

“It's unclear why we can't put a weekend together from start to finish and it be completely strong. I think it's just a head-scratcher to be qualified three seconds off here [in Baku]. It just makes zero sense to me.”

Colton Herta, Hitech Photo by: Getty Images

Pressed on whether he struggled to get used to the car or to the tyres, Herta clarified: “Initially, no. Through the winter testing, we were fairly strong. All the private testing that I’d done, I was strong, but for some reason on race weekends, it just hasn't ever translated.”

The American’s analysis is accurate. He was joint 11th-fastest in pre-season testing at Barcelona, 0.574s down on pacesetter Rafael Camara – also a rookie as the reigning F3 champion. That performance clearly was encouraging.

But it didn’t last. Herta qualified 14th on average in the first five rounds, with a 0.848s deficit to the top, and his form gradually worsened, as he averaged 18th across the next eight qualifying sessions. Over the latter period, the mean gap was 1.088s – discounting the latest Baku event, where his deficit inexplicably ballooned to 2.484s in Q1 and 3.091s in Q2.

Crashes also have been more and more frequent, with no fewer than three across the recent Monza and Madrid rounds.

“It's frustrating, but all we can do is just keep trying,” Herta added. “I guess, unsure if that's the last one [of the season, with Qatar and Abu Dhabi at threat due to the Iran war] or if we have more, but we'll keep working like we have two more races to do. I'll try to get the most out of it.”

It’s fair to say this season hasn’t exactly been amazing for Herta’s F1 prospects, especially given Cadillac F1 CEO Dan Towriss expected a top-10 finish in the championship, which is all but mathematically out of reach.

Cadillac had been clear that its test and development driver had a real chance of an F1 seat in a not-too-distant future if he did well enough in F2, but Herta said he hadn’t had feedback from the team about his performance in the feeder series.

Colton Herta, Hitech Photo by: Getty Images

The former IndyCar frontrunner added that he was currently in talks with the F1 outfit regarding his 2027 plans and clarified, amid conflicting media reports, that he wasn’t ruling out a second season in F2 – though this clearly isn’t his priority.

“I said ‘I don't have an interest’,” Herta pointed out. “This year, I think if there was clear progression and whatnot, it would be more interesting to return, but there's zero progression.

“I've been doing a lot more with the F1 team now as far as sim stuff. I just did a TPC [Testing of Previous Cars] day on Monday, which was very strong. On the F1 sim and the TPC stuff, the pace has been really strong, but for whatever reason, it's just not translating to F2.”

Yet, asked if he was still firmly on Cadillac’s books for 2027, Herta replied: “I don't have anything for next year at the moment, but we're discussing, getting through that as far as what the opportunities are for me within the team.”

And when we inquired whether the 2024 IndyCar runner-up would consider a return to the series, Herta made it clear where his priority lay: “It all depends on what next year looks like. My focus is still on getting to F1, and I still think I have a chance of that in these next two years. But I don't know exactly, I have to sit back and see what the plan is for Cadillac for me.

“And once I know that, then I can make more decisions on maybe if I'm in Formula 1, if I'm not. What does that look like in terms of, is it a reserve role? Is it still a test role? If that's the case, what other series can I race in during that to stay busy?

“So, there's a lot of just, like, nothing to say at the moment, unfortunately, until I have more solidified plans for next year – then I can build everything out around that.”
