World.title: Liberia: MODA Distances Itself from Agriculture Minister Nuetah, Says He Is Not and Has Never Been a Member
World.content:
According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah “is not a member of the Movement for Democratic Alliance, has never been a member of MODA, and has not communicated any intention to become a member of the Movement.”

GBARNGA, Bong County – The Movement for Democratic Alliance (MODA) has clarified that the Minister of Agriculture, Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah, is not a member of the organization. It also rejected claims that his support for a youth training initiative in Bong County signals a political alliance or an effort to form a political party.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

In a press statement issued Tuesday in Gbarnga, MODA said it had taken note of recent public discussions and media reports that sought to link the Minister to the Movement and to present his backing of a youth skills-development program as evidence of political collaboration.



“MODA considers it important to place the facts on record and to correct any misunderstanding surrounding the matter,” said Acting Chairman Lawrence N. Yallah, who signed the statement.

“Not a Political Party”

MODA first clarified its own status, stating that it is “not a political party” but a “political movement.” It then addressed Minister Nuetah’s relationship with the group directly.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah “is not a member of the Movement for Democratic Alliance, has never been a member of MODA, and has not communicated any intention to become a member of the Movement.”

The Movement said it therefore “rejects any representation suggesting that the Minister is a member, official, political leader, financier, or representative” of MODA.

Describing itself as a people-centered movement founded on democratic participation, integrity, unity, equity, inclusion, public service and sustainable development, MODA said it remains open to working with individuals, institutions, organizations and public officials when such engagement serves the legitimate interests of the Liberian people. However, it cautioned that cooperation on a specific development project should not be read as political membership, affiliation or endorsement.

Origin of the Excavator Training Slots

The statement traced the controversy to July 14, 2026, when Minister Nuetah made five excavator-training slots available for young people from Bong County. MODA said this followed an appeal from its Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Jomah B. Dolo, for more opportunities for the county’s youth.

The Movement described the slots as an initial contribution toward skills development.

The five slots reportedly drew 252 applicants, who then went through an independent vetting and selection process.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah made the opportunity available, while the individual who received it, who is associated with MODA’s leadership, chose to place the selection process in the hands of the Movement. MODA said it then facilitated the exercise with the stated aim of ensuring the five beneficiaries were chosen through a transparent and competitive process

MODA stressed that the Minister did not personally select the five beneficiaries and did not set up any political recruitment process through the Movement.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah made the opportunity available, while the individual who received it, who is associated with MODA’s leadership, chose to place the selection process in the hands of the Movement. MODA said it then facilitated the exercise with the stated aim of ensuring the five beneficiaries were chosen through a transparent and competitive process.

The Movement added that it was “even more excited” that all five selected individuals turned out to be supporters of the Unity Party, even though party affiliation was not a requirement for applying.

The five young people are expected to begin their excavator training at For Life Zoe in the coming days. MODA said it regards the initiative “strictly” as an opportunity for young Liberians to acquire practical skills that can improve their employment prospects and economic participation.

It noted that the Ministry of Agriculture has itself publicly emphasized youth empowerment, agricultural mechanization and practical skills development as part of its broader agenda.

MODA Dismisses New Party Speculation

The Movement also responded to commentary suggesting that the Minister’s support for the training slots through MODA means he has established a political party to challenge President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s potential bid for a second term.

MODA dismissed the suggestion in strong terms, describing it as “blatant mendacity coming from the mouth of back-door politicians who are afraid of youth progression.”

The Movement called on individuals, commentators, political actors and media practitioners to distinguish between a development initiative and political affiliation.

“A public official providing opportunities for young people does not, by itself, establish membership in MODA or demonstrate an intention to form or lead a political party,” the statement said.

MODA further stated that Minister Nuetah’s political affiliation and future decisions are matters that should be addressed through his own public statements and actions, not attributed to the Movement.

“For the avoidance of doubt, MODA does not claim Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah as a member of the Movement, and the Movement has no authority to speak on his behalf regarding his political affiliation or future political plans,” the statement said. It added that the group has known the Minister only as a people-centered leader, not through “the opinions of agent provocateurs.”

Outlining its position, MODA said the country’s political and development environment should allow people and institutions to cooperate on matters of national and community interest without every act of cooperation being treated as partisan politics. It encouraged public discussion to remain grounded in facts, particularly where individuals, political organizations, public officials and opportunities for young people are concerned.

The Movement also urged everyone discussing the excavator-training initiative to respect the integrity of the 252 applicants and the five young people chosen. “Their opportunity should not be reduced to political speculation,” the statement said.

MODA reaffirmed its commitment to its stated principles and to engaging anyone prepared to support initiatives that advance the interests of the Liberian people, noting again that such engagement does not automatically create political membership or affiliation.

It pledged to continue supporting efforts that expand opportunities for young Liberians, promote skills development, encourage transparency and contribute to national development.

World.title: Liberia: Beyond Survival: WONGOSOL Gives FGM Survivors Dignity Today and Livelihoods for Tomorrow
World.content:
MONROVIA — For women and girls who have survived female genital mutilation (FGM) and other forms of gender-based violence, the road to recovery often extends far beyond the immediate trauma.

By Patience M. Jones

It can mean having access to basic hygiene supplies, clothing and personal-care items while receiving support—and, for some survivors, having the means to earn an income and rebuild their lives.



That is the focus of the Liberia Fight FGM Project, implemented by the Women NGOs Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL) with support from the United Nations Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women.

As part of the project’s third consignment of support, WONGOSOL is distributing more than 600 dignity kits to FGM and gender-based violence (GBV) survivors through one-stop centers across six counties, while also preparing livelihood assistance for 365 women trained in vocational skills, business management and Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) approaches.

Speaking to journalists on Friday, WONGOSOL Executive Director Esther S. David Yango said the initiative is designed to address both the immediate needs of survivors and the economic challenges that can leave women vulnerable.

“The FGM project connects immediate survivor support with long-term economic empowerment, providing dignity today while helping women and communities build safer, more resilient and sustainable futures,” Yango said.

A Kit Designed to Restore Dignity

The dignity packages are intended to provide practical assistance to survivors during periods of vulnerability.

According to the project team, the packages include toothpaste and toothbrushes, sanitary pads, towels, grease, slippers, bath soap and lappa.

Separate packages are being prepared for younger survivors, with additional items such as snacks and toys intended to make their experience at one-stop centers less distressing.

Clothing, including blouses and dresses, will also be provided to survivors.

Jeneba M. Vessellie, Project Officer of the Liberia Fight FGM Project, explained that the materials are meant to respond to survivors’ immediate needs while they access health, psychosocial, legal and protection services.

The intervention, officials said, recognizes that recovery is not only about medical or legal assistance, but also about helping survivors maintain dignity during a difficult period.

From Training to Economic Independence

While the dignity kits address immediate needs, the livelihood component is intended to provide a longer-term pathway toward economic independence.

The project has trained 365 women in livelihood and vocational skills, business management and VSLA approaches. The beneficiaries include FGM practitioners, FGM survivors, single mothers, youth and women leaders.

Livelihood support will include materials for activities such as soap making, tailoring, pastry and baking, among other income-generating activities.

The project team said the assistance is intended to help trained women put their skills into practice, establish or strengthen businesses and build economic resilience after the project ends.

For women involved in agriculture, support will also include farm materials and tools.

The program team cited women survivors involved in agriculture in Bong County as among those expected to receive agricultural support.

The project also links livelihood support to savings.

Officials said beneficiaries trained in savings and loan approaches will be able to save from the income generated through their activities, helping them sustain their businesses beyond the life of the project.

Reaching Communities Across Six Counties

The Liberia Fight FGM Project is being implemented in 38 communities across Bomi, Bong, Gbarpolu, Grand Cape Mount, Margibi and Montserrado Counties, in partnership with local organizations.

The project has also established 40 community coalitions comprising 600 members who have been trained to advocate for the protection of women and girls against harmful practices, including FGM and sexual and gender-based violence.

The coalitions are also supporting advocacy for the passage of the Women and Girls Protection Act.

The implementing partners include Women Care Initiative (WOCI) in Bomi; Community Women Peace Initiative (CWPI) in Bong; Paramount Young Women Initiative (PAYWO) in Gbarpolu; Sister Hands Liberia (SHL) in Grand Cape Mount; Women Education and Development Organization of Liberia (WEDOL) in Margibi; and WEPS and INSURED in Montserrado.

Two Needs, One Intervention

For WONGOSOL, the distribution represents two connected sides of survivor support.

The dignity kits respond to immediate needs, helping survivors meet basic personal-care and hygiene needs and restore a measure of dignity during vulnerable periods.

The livelihood assistance, meanwhile, addresses longer-term economic vulnerability by helping women transform training into sustainable economic opportunities.

Together, the interventions form what WONGOSOL describes as an integrated approach to prevention, protection and women’s economic empowerment.

The project, which began in October 2023, was initially scheduled to end in September 2026. A five-month no-cost extension has now extended implementation through February 28, 2027.

For the women at the center of the intervention, the assistance is therefore about more than receiving a package or business materials.

It is about having something to meet a need today and, through skills and economic opportunities, something to build on tomorrow.

World.title: Liberia: WONGOSOL Urges Pres. Boakai to Put Women, Justice at Heart of Liberia’s Trust-Building Agenda
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Women NGOs Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL) has called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to place women’s leadership, transitional justice and reconciliation at the center of Liberia’s efforts to restore public trust and consolidate peace.

By Patience M. Jones

The call comes in response to President Boakai’s address to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on September 24, where he spoke on restoring trust, managing transformation, strengthening multilateralism, advancing peace and security, inclusive development and reform of global governance.



While welcoming the President’s recognition of women’s leadership as important to sustainable peace, economic growth and accountable governance, WONGOSOL said Liberia’s message to the international community could have gone further by explicitly addressing the country’s transitional justice process and the role of women in peacebuilding, justice and reconciliation.

“Liberia’s journey from conflict to constitutional democracy cannot be fully understood without acknowledging the contributions of women to peacebuilding, the experiences of victims and survivors, and the unfinished work of transitional justice,” said Esther S. Davis Yango, Executive Director of WONGOSOL.

Women Must Move From Recognition to Decision-Making

WONGOSOL said the President’s emphasis on preventive diplomacy, mediation and early warning must be matched by meaningful participation of women in those processes.

According to the organization, Liberia’s history demonstrates that women have played critical roles not only as victims of conflict, but also as peacebuilders, mediators, community leaders, early-warning actors and advocates for reconciliation.

The organization is therefore calling for Liberia’s Women, Peace and Security commitments to move beyond recognition toward implementation, financing, participation and accountability.

WONGOSOL said women should be fully integrated into the structures through which conflict prevention and sustainable peace are designed and implemented.

The call comes as Liberia has also launched its third National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security, with the government hosting a high-level side event on the margins of the 81st UNGA under the theme, “From Pioneers to Global Leaders: Liberia’s Journey in Women, Peace and Security.”

WONGOSOL Demands Resources Behind Gender Commitments

WONGOSOL also challenged government to translate commitments on women’s leadership into tangible access to political decision-making, economic resources, security institutions, peace processes and national development planning.

The organization referenced President Boakai’s statement that, “When women lead, peace agreements last longer, economies grow faster, and governance becomes more accountable.”

But WONGOSOL stressed that such commitments must be supported by adequate and predictable financing, implementation plans and affirmative legislative and governance reforms.

“Commitments without resources, implementation mechanisms and accountability cannot become sustainable policy,” the organization said.

Transitional Justice at the Center of National Reconciliation

One of WONGOSOL’s strongest concerns is what it described as the limited explicit attention given to transitional justice in the President’s formal UNGA address.

The organization noted that the address focused heavily on restoring trust, strengthening institutions, accountability, the rule of law and Liberia’s transition from conflict to constitutional democracy—issues it says are closely linked to the country’s transitional justice agenda.

WONGOSOL said the address could have highlighted Liberia’s outstanding transitional justice priorities, including the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, accountability for conflict-era crimes, victims and survivors, reparations, reconciliation and memorialization.

The organization is particularly urging government to clearly articulate what is required to establish and operationalize the War and Economic Crimes Court (WECC) and strengthen the Office of War and Economic Crimes Courts (OWECC).

It also called for sustained political commitment, adequate funding, institutional capacity and meaningful engagement with victims, survivors and civil society.

“The UN General Assembly was a significant opportunity for Liberia to tell the world not only that we are committed to transitional justice, but also what it will take to deliver it,” Yango said.

She added that establishing and operationalizing the War and Economic Crimes Court and successfully transitioning the OWECC into a viable judicial entity would require sustained political commitment, adequate resources, institutional capacity and meaningful engagement with victims, survivors and civil society.

WONGOSOL further called for strengthening the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission as part of a broader accountability and rule-of-law framework.

Calls for Gender-Responsive Transitional Justice

WONGOSOL said Liberia’s transitional justice process must also respond directly to the experiences of women and girls affected by the civil conflict.

The organization is calling for the meaningful participation of women victims and survivors, recognition and documentation of conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence, gender-responsive reparations and survivor-centered approaches to justice.

It also wants stronger protection for victims, witnesses and survivors; preservation of women’s testimonies and historical records; meaningful participation of women in truth-seeking and reconciliation; and memorialization initiatives that recognize women’s experiences.

According to WONGOSOL, women must not be remembered solely as victims of Liberia’s conflicts but also recognized as agents of peace, justice and national transformation.

The organization is further calling for initial start-up funding for the War and Economic Crimes Court and the National Anti-Corruption Commission to be intentionally provided for within the national budget, alongside the establishment of a National Reparations Trust Fund.

Development Must Also Deliver for Women

WONGOSOL also wants Liberia’s ARREST Agenda and other national development initiatives implemented through a gender-responsive approach.

It said sectors including agriculture, infrastructure, education, rule of law, sanitation and tourism directly affect women and girls and should therefore address structural barriers to land, finance, markets, education, technology, justice and decision-making.

The organization is calling for practical affirmative measures to ensure that national development policies produce measurable improvements in the lives of women and girls.

It also urged government to ensure that climate action recognizes the particular vulnerabilities of women while supporting their leadership in building community resilience.

‘Restoring Trust Requires Justice’

WONGOSOL said Liberia has an opportunity to draw on its history and experience to strengthen its voice in global discussions on peacebuilding, women’s leadership, reconciliation and democratic recovery.

As Liberia calls for a United Nations that “delivers for all,” the organization said the definition of “all” must include women, victims and survivors, young people, rural communities and others historically excluded from decision-making.

WONGOSOL acknowledged President Boakai’s UNGA message as an important foundation but said international commitments must now be translated into measurable action at home.

The organization is calling for clear implementation measures and technically competent bodies insulated from political interference to mobilize the expertise and resources needed to advance Liberia’s national priorities.

“Restoring trust requires justice. Managing transformation requires inclusion. Sustaining peace requires women’s leadership. And reconciliation requires that we confront the past while building a more inclusive future,” Yango said.

WONGOSOL maintains that gender equality, Women, Peace and Security, transitional justice, accountability and reconciliation should be treated as interconnected pillars of Liberia’s democratic transformation.

World.title: Who Shut the Courts? State Points to Security Services
World.content:
Security Agencies, Not the Judiciary, Ordered August Court Shutdown, Attorney-General Tells ConCourt

The three-day closure of Zambia’s courts in August was ordered by the country’s security agencies, not by the Judiciary. Attorney-General Mulilo Kabesha has told the Constitutional Court that the Judiciary’s Chief Administrator merely communicated directives issued by the defence and national security services. He made the disclosure while asking the court to dismiss, with costs, a petition by Chapter One Foundation challenging the shutdown of court operations from August 24 to 26, 2026. The Attorney-General argued that the Constitution does not impose an absolute duty to keep every courthouse physically open during an assessed security threat. His submissions for the first time place responsibility for one of the most contested episodes of the post-election period on the security establishment.

The closure began on August 24, the last day under Article 105 of the Constitution for lodging a challenge to the presidential election result. The High Courts in Lusaka, Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court in Lusaka were shut, along with some Local Courts. A judiciary memo cited security concerns and instructed staff not to report for work. Police presence restricted access to court premises. Civil society groups and opposition figures questioned the timing of the shutdown.

Chapter One Foundation petitioned the Constitutional Court, arguing that the closure and restrictions on access to judicial services violated Articles 118, 119 and 122 of the Constitution. It says the shutdown undermined judicial authority and denied citizens access to justice. The organisation is seeking declarations that the closure was unconstitutional, unlawful and null and void. It also wants the State compelled to disclose the nature of the security concerns and the authority under which the action was taken. It further wants the identities of those who authorised or carried out the closure made public.

Mr Kabesha has raised preliminary objections under Article 128(3) of the Constitution and the Constitutional Court Rules 2026, arguing that the petition does not meet the requirements for the court to hear it. He submitted that there was a mismatch between the constitutional provisions relied on by the petitioner and the administrative steps being challenged. He said the decision to close the court precincts was prompted by security concerns. National security matters, he argued, fall under the Defence Force and National Security Services established under Part XV of the Constitution.

The Attorney-General said the Judiciary’s Chief Administrator had only relayed the security directives to staff and the public. He also argued that Chapter One Foundation had not cited any constitutional provision requiring security agencies to disclose full details of the threats they were addressing against a person, State organ or institution. In his submissions, he defended the measures as a precaution to protect lives.

“The precautionary measures pursued legitimate public safety objectives, protecting human life, court users and public officers, and were lifted once the threat de-escalated, also affecting institutions like the Ministry of Justice and the National Prosecution Authority,” Mr Kabesha said.

He said the State had acted under the precautionary principle in responding to the threat. He contended that the foundation had failed to present evidence proving violations of Articles 1(3), 118, 119 and 122. The petitioner had therefore failed to discharge the burden of proof required in constitutional proceedings, he argued. Mr Kabesha assured the court that judicial authority remained fully intact and asked it to dismiss the petition with costs.

The State’s answer leaves the central questions in Chapter One’s petition unresolved. It does not identify which security agency issued the directive, what the threat was or who assessed it. Those are the disclosures the foundation is asking the court to order, and the tate maintains it has no constitutional duty to make them. The Constitutional Court must now decide whether the petition can proceed to a hearing on its merits

World.title: Zambia to Spend K212 Billion Servicing Debt Over Three Years,
World.content:
Zambia to Spend K212 Billion Servicing Debt Over Three Years, Outstripping Combined Budget for FISP, CDF and Free Education

Zambia will spend K212.2 billion servicing its debt between 2027 and 2029. That is K63.6 billion more than the Government plans to spend over the same period on transfers covering the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), the Constituency Development Fund (CDF), free education and school feeding combined. The figures are set out in the 2027-2029 Medium-Term Budget Plan Green Paper, the Treasury’s first spending blueprint for the new presidential term. Debt service in 2027 alone is projected at K68.4 billion, equivalent to 6.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). The bill covers interest payments on domestic and external debt as well as principal repayments.

The debt bill rises every year in kwacha terms but shrinks as a share of the economy. It is projected to reach K70.9 billion in 2028, equal to 6.2 percent of GDP, and K72.9 billion in 2029, or 5.7 percent of GDP. Over the same three years, the Government plans to spend K148.6 billion on transfers. These cover FISP, CDF, free education, the school feeding programme and support to the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) to strengthen revenue collection. The transfers allocation starts at K45.7 billion in 2027, rises to K47 billion in 2028 and reaches K55.9 billion in 2029.

The Green Paper comes as the country’s external debt stock falls. The Ministry of Finance and National Planning said external debt stood at US$15.36 billion at the end of June 2026, down five percent from US$16.15 billion at the end of December 2025. The ministry attributed the decline to a liability management operation in the second quarter of 2026. That operation included the partial repurchase of Eurobond obligations through a debt-for-energy conversion supported by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

Beyond its creditors, the Government also owes money at home. It plans to set aside K37.8 billion to clear domestic arrears over the three years: K15 billion in 2027, K10 billion in 2028 and K12.9 billion in 2029. These arrears are unpaid bills owed to suppliers, contractors and other local creditors. That brings the combined sum earmarked for external and domestic obligations to about K250 billion over the medium term.

Social protection receives K63.2 billion over the period to fund the Social Cash Transfer, the Food Security Pack and pension payments. That allocation grows from K17.3 billion in 2027 to K22.1 billion in 2028 and K23.8 billion in 2029. The Government also plans to spend K140.4 billion on assets, made up of K125.1 billion in non-financial assets and K15.3 billion in financial assets. Taken together, social benefits and capital spending over the three years still fall short of the debt service bill by only about K8.6 billion.

The capital programme is led by roads, which take K42.1 billion over the three years. Construction of hospitals and public universities receives K26 billion, and provincial aerodromes K9.9 billion. Water and sanitation infrastructure is allocated K6.9 billion and the rural electrification programme K2.4 billion. Roads alone therefore attract more money than water, electrification and aerodromes combined.

To pay for these commitments, the Treasury is turning to the taxpayer. The Green Paper says the Government will continue to prioritise domestic resource mobilisation to create sustainable fiscal space for development. It is developing a Medium-Term Revenue Strategy for 2027-2031, designed to widen the tax base and improve collection. Proposed measures include reviewing and streamlining tax incentives, strengthening property taxation, and using mobile digital payment platforms to improve compliance. The strategy also aims to bring informal businesses and small and medium-sized enterprises into the tax net, including artisanal miners.

The Government has also signalled a tougher line on tax evasion, including smuggling, which it says undermines revenue sustainability and hurts local production. The push to widen the tax base comes as the administration courts foreign investors under the Grow Zambia Agenda, whose stated goal is to double the size of the economy. Special Assistant to the President for Finance and Investment Jito Kayumba said a larger economy would generate more transactions, more government revenue and more liquidity. He argued that this would ultimately lower the cost of living.

“The higher the transactions, the more government revenue, liquidity in circulation, and economic stimulation,” Mr Kayumba said.

The Green Paper’s figures lay out the arithmetic the new term must solve. Debt service falls as a share of GDP only if the economy grows as projected. Every kwacha collected in new taxes must also stretch across creditors, farmers, pupils, pensioners and road contractors. The Green Paper will now go through consultations before the 2027 national budget is presented to Parliament.

World.title: Possession is not proof: the State must show its evidence against Archbishop Banda
World.content:
Possession is not proof: the State must show its evidence against Archbishop Banda

I understand that receiving or possessing property and unlawfully disposing of government property are two different legal questions. The question I think the State now needs to answer is this: what specific evidence does it have against Archbishop Alick Banda beyond the fact that he ended up with a vehicle which the State says was improperly disposed of by the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA)?

The Archbishop faces a separate charge relating to possession of the Toyota Hilux. As publicly reported, the State’s case is not that he took part in the ZRA officials’ disposal process. It is that he possessed property reasonably suspected of having been unlawfully obtained. That distinction matters.

The facts on the record so far are thin. The Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) alleges that between April 2021 and December 2023, the Archbishop was in possession of a blue Toyota Hilux, registration number ALF 7734, reasonably suspected to have been unlawfully obtained from ZRA. He has denied the charge under Section 319 of the Penal Code. His side says the vehicle was a gift from a well-wisher who bought it from ZRA through an internal process.

If ZRA officials unlawfully disposed of government vehicles, those responsible should be held accountable. But the unlawful conduct of whoever disposed of government property does not automatically make every person who later came into possession of that property criminally liable.

In this case, those responsible are not hypothetical. Former ZRA Commissioner General Kingsley Chanda and former Director of Administration Callistus Kaoma were convicted in October 2025 over the disposals and are awaiting the outcome of their appeals. The State has already found the people who disposed of these vehicles. What it has not yet shown is what the Archbishop did wrong by receiving one.

The prosecution itself says the Hilux is part of a wider investigation into about 22 ZRA vehicles that allegedly left the authority’s fleet without proper procedure. That raises an obvious question. Who bought the rest of those vehicles, who drives them today, and has every one of those people been arrested, charged and held in a cell overnight? If not, the public is entitled to know why one recipient became the face of the case.

The Anti-Corruption Commission this week called for stronger systems to safeguard, manage and dispose of recovered assets, motor vehicles among them, in a transparent and accountable manner. That is a reminder that the weakness often lies in how public institutions dispose of property, not with the citizen at the end of the chain.

So what evidence does the State have that Archbishop Banda knew, or had reason to know, that this particular vehicle had been unlawfully acquired when it came into his possession? And what evidence directly connects him to the alleged irregular disposal itself? These are legitimate questions, and they should be answered through evidence and due process, not political assumptions.

The manner of his detention has not helped. The Archbishop met every bail condition set by Resident Magistrate Mwandu Nakazwe: K80,000 in his own recognisance, three working sureties bound at K50,000 each, and the surrender of his travel documents. Even so, he spent Monday night at Chimbokaila while his sureties were interviewed, and walked out only on Tuesday afternoon. For a 62-year-old cleric who has denied the charge and been convicted of nothing, that night in a cell sends a message that goes well beyond a Toyota Hilux.

I am also concerned about the wider political context. For years, the Catholic Church in Zambia has spoken on governance, accountability and national affairs, sometimes supporting government positions and at other times challenging those in power. That role did not begin with the current government, and it should not become unacceptable simply because a particular Church leader is critical of those in power.

The Church has also stood with the State when the cause was just. The Roman Catholic Church is among the churches the DEC has partnered with in its outreach against drug abuse. A Church that is a partner when the State needs it should not be treated as a suspect when it speaks.

I have seen calls from some UPND supporters for Archbishop Banda to be arrested or removed. The ruling party’s deputy spokesperson, Elvis Nkandu, now says the case should be separated from the Catholic Church and left to the courts. On that, I agree with him. But separating the case from the Church must work both ways: it also means separating it from party supporters who have already decided the verdict.

The president of the Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops, Archbishop Ignatius Chama of Kasama, has called for fairness and due process free of prejudice or intimidation, and has accused the ruling party of seeking to silence the Church. Voices outside the Church, among them Organised Peoples Party president Dr Brian Mushimba, have spoken of what appears to be the continued targeting of the Archbishop. The quickest way for the State to answer those concerns is not with statements, but with evidence.

The Archbishop’s name has also surfaced in the Lumezi South election petition. There, a losing candidate alleged that handouts were distributed at his farm, then conceded under cross-examination that he had no photographs or video to prove it. Allegations must be proven, not merely pronounced.

Political reactions should not decide whether a criminal case has merit. The proper test should be the evidence, the law and due process.

The trial opens on November 3. If the State has evidence against the Archbishop, it should present that evidence before the courts and have it tested according to law. If there is no evidence beyond his possession of a vehicle whose disposal is alleged to have been irregular, then the public deserves a clear explanation of why possession alone is enough to sustain the charge.

The rule of law must apply equally, whether the person involved is a politician, a businessman, a Church leader or an ordinary citizen. We should also be careful not to turn legitimate law enforcement into a means of silencing institutions that have historically spoken truth to successive governments.

The Catholic Church should be free to speak, just as the government should be free to investigate genuine criminal conduct. The answer to disagreement should be evidence, transparency and due process, not intimidation or political retaliation.

By Illness Kalimukwa

World.title: Nabwalya GMA records five more anthrax deaths
World.content:
The country has recorded additional five cases of anthrax mortalities in Nabwalya Game Management area.

This takes the cumulative total to 49 hippos, nine elephants and six buffalos, while the cumulative number of reported human cases now stands at 26.

Following the multi-sectoral rapid response deployment conducted from 21st to 25th September 2026, the Animal Health-Wildlife and Laboratory Team undertook carcass assessments, specimen collection and environmental sampling in the affected areas.

According to Disaster Risk Management Division (DRMD) National Coordinator Norman Chipakupaku, disclosed that three Hippo and two elephant mortalities were related to anthrax.

Mr Chipakupaku explained that during the field investigation, three elephant and seven hippo carcasses were sighted around Kalimba-Chipangu Village, Talwe Village, the Munyamazi River, and the Munyamazi–Musipazi confluence.

He observed that continued occurrence of wildlife mortalities, particularly among hippos and elephants, underscores the need to maintain heightened surveillance, prompt reporting and rapid investigation of any newly detected carcasses within the affected and surrounding areas.

“Some carcasses could not be sampled because they were inaccessible or already significantly decomposed.

Evidence of community access to some carcass sites was also observed during the investigation,” Mr chipakupaku stated.

The Permanent Secretary indicated that routine surveillance should continue and include environmental sampling of soil and water, as well as biological sampling of suitable carcass tissues, to monitor the outbreak, assess ongoing transmission risk and guide subsequent interventions.

“The response team recommends urgent and safe disposal of carcasses, together with appropriate decontamination of affected sites,” he added.

Mr Chipakupaku added that community sensitisation should also be sustained to discourage handling, opening or consumption of carcasses and to promote immediate reporting of suspected animal deaths.

He said that DNPW, working in collaboration with the relevant sectors, will continue to monitor the situation closely and provide further updates as additional surveillance information and laboratory results become available.

World.title: Maamba Solar starts 100mw power injection
World.content:
Maamba Solar Energy Limited (MSEL) has commenced evacuating 100 megawatts (MW) of electricity into the ZESCO national grid.

The 100 MW solar project complements Maamba Energy Limited’s 600 MW thermal power generation portfolio, comprising 300 MW currently operational and a further 300 MW under construction at Maamba.

According to a statement issued by the MSEL Corporate Affairs Department, the solar power project entered the commissioning phase on September 24, 2026, with electricity injection into the national grid forming part of the commissioning process.

MSEL Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Lieutenant Colonel Cyrus Minwalla (Retired), said the commencement of the commissioning phase of the 100 MW solar power project was an important milestone for both MSEL and Zambia.

Mr Minwalla said the project will significantly increase renewable energy generation capacity in Zambia’s power system and contribute to the diversification of the country’s energy mix.

“The project is aligned with Government ‘s target to achieve 1000 MW Solar power in this year and cumulative 10,000 MW by 2031,” he stated.

He disclosed that the project incorporates modern tracking technology that enables solar modules to follow the movement of the sun during the day, thereby improving solar energy capture.

World.title: Public workers urged to support Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Nalolo District Commissioner Namatama Mupo has urged civil servants in the district to remain committed to their duties and contribute effectively to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mrs Mupo said the Grow Zambia Agenda can only be achieved if everyone performs their duties effectively and contributes to the economic development of the country.

She said public workers should be at the forefront of explaining government policies to citizens and ensuring that services reach everyone, regardless of their location.

“Our people will understand and contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda if they are well informed of the policies being implemented,” Mrs Mupo stated.

Mrs Mupo expressed concern that some officers were not reporting for work daily, saying the situation undermines service delivery in the district.

She said civil servants should respect their jobs and demonstrate commitment, as the government relies on them to drive development at district level.

Mrs Mupo was speaking during the Third Quarter District Development Coordinating Committee (DDCC) meeting held at her office.

Mrs Mupo has since called on heads of departments to monitor officers under their supervision and ensure that disciplinary measures are applied to those who abscond from work.

World.title: Govt approves first-ever male breast cancer awareness materials
World.content:
In a landmark move for inclusive healthcare, the Ministry of Health has officially approved Zambia’s first Social Behaviour Change (SBC) communication materials dedicated to male breast cancer.

The approval was granted to the Male Breast Cancer Foundation.

And Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary for Donor Coordination George Sinyangwe explained that the approval enables the Foundation to print and disseminate the resources in support of awareness-raising of male breast cancer among men.

“The Ministry greatly appreciates and values the Male Breast Cancer Foundation’s continued collaboration and partnership in advancing public health priorities towards achieving national development objective” Dr Sinyangwe stated.

founder of Male Breast Cancer Foundation Boaz Musamvu, the move breaks a decades-long silence that has left men out of national breast cancer campaigns and fueled the dangerous myth that breast cancer is only a women’s disease.

Mr Musamvu added that while male breast cancer is less common, Zambian men do develop the disease and are often diagnosed late due to low awareness, stigma, and lack of male-specific information.

He indicated that the new posters will be rolled out nationally to educate men and communities on warning signs, self-examination, and the critical need to seek early medical attention.

“This is more than an approval; it is a life-saving shift in narrative. For too long, men have suffered in silence. These materials ensure men are finally seen, informed, and included in the fight against breast cancer,” Mr Musamvu stated.

He thanked the Ministry of Health for its leadership in championing inclusive awareness, its global strategic partner the Male Breast Cancer Global Alliance (MBCGA) for sustained advocacy and technical support, and its Patron, Chief Mumena XI, for his instrumental leadership in advancing the cause.

“The milestone is expected to improve early detection, reduce stigma, and save lives,” Mr Musamvu noted.

World.title: Chisamba launches HIV, Syphilis screening
World.content:
Chisamba Rural Health Centre, in collaboration with the AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF), has launched a screening exercise for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in Chisamba District.

The exercise, which focuses on HIV and syphilis testing, is targeting people within the health facility’s catchment area, with the aim of detecting infections early and ensuring timely treatment.

Monday Mobile Market, where the exercise was underway, Chisamba Rural Health Centre In-Charge Merry Muyembe said the exercise follows community sensitisation on HIV and syphilis, as well as the identification of STI hotspot areas, including Chawama Compound.

“We identified our hotspots for STIs under HIV and Syphilis, that is Chawama and we have a number of positive cases from there. So we wanted to take advantage of mass sensitisation and identification of the cases and early treatment,” Ms Muyembe said.

She said those who tested positive have since been started on treatment and will continue receiving care at the health facility.

Ms Muyembe expressed optimism that more positive cases would be detected if the screening exercise is extended to Chawama Compound.

She further said that the health centre aims to screen at least 1,000 people, but that limited resources and logistical challenges have hampered the exercise.
