The parents hurried to the hospital where they found Christian in the pediatric ICU, unresponsive and on a ventilator. The doctor explained that Christian suffered a massive brain injury. There was little hope for a recovery.

Bobbie and DeForrest spent hours at Christian's bedside. He was declared "brain dead." The parents made the decision to withdraw life support.

On July 10, 2024, Christian Williams — 15-years-old, son, brother, foster child — was pronounced dead. Cause of death: "diabetic ketoacidosis," caused by a lack of insulin.

Not one staffer trained in diabetes care

An investigator for the Arizona Department of Child Safety found that — even after the weeks of Christian being in their facility and struggling — staff at Logos House said they'd never received training in diabetes care.

"All of the direct care workers interviewed denied any training or knowledge of Type 1 diabetes," the investigator wrote. "Not one staff member could explain what the signs or symptoms of hypoglycemia are or the range for blood sugar levels."

The facility didn't keep complete medication logs, the investigator found. Nor were there records that tracked when, or if, Christian took his insulin and the readings from his glucose monitors.

After Christian Williams died, the director of the Arizona Department of Child Safety (DCS) told Phoenix news station, ABC15, that the agency was consulting experts to revise its diabetes care guidelines.

NPR asked DCS to respond to our findings. Public Information Officer Darren DaRonco said: "We are going to decline to comment due to the pending litigation."

The month after Christian died, the Catalyst Corporation won accreditation from the state and an accreditation agency to operate for another three years.

How many other children have been harmed?

It shouldn't have been a surprise to Arizona officials that the state's training for diabetes care in foster care was lacking.

Another Arizona foster child — 9-year-old Jakob Blodgett — died under similar circumstances a few days before Christmas in 2022.

toggle caption Blodgett family

He had been living in foster care less than two weeks when he was rushed from a foster care group home to the hospital. The boy's parents said he was unable to manage his insulin on his own. In depositions, group home staff members said that the home never trained them on the care and management of Type 1 diabetes.

"How many other children are there who have been harmed and that we don't know about?" asks Phoenix attorney Robert Pastor who represents the Williams family and the Blodgett family in separate lawsuits against the state and health care providers. "For the children who find themselves just bouncing from group home to group home or foster placement to foster placement, they must truly be alone in whatever it is that they are going through."

The high rate of death for disabled kids in foster care

All children in foster care face a significantly elevated risk of death — and those with disabilities are at substantially higher risk. One study found foster youth are 42% more likely to die, compared to other children.

Other research found children in foster care with physical disabilities, which include diabetes, are nine times more likely to die than non-disabled children in foster care. Children with intellectual disabilities are more than three times at higher risk of death.

The researcher, Jill McLeigh at Rees-Jones Center for Foster Care Excellence at Children's Health in Dallas, looked at data for more than 3 million children in foster care from 2005 to 2019, one of the only studies to use federal data to measure outcomes for disabled foster youth over a long period of time.

McLeigh told NPR she was stunned by the extreme differences in death rates. "Although we had hypothesized that mortality rates would be higher," she said, "we were surprised by the degree to which risk levels for dying while in care were higher for children with physical disabilities, emotional disabilities, and other medical conditions relative to children in care without disabilities."

NPR found many cases of children and youth with disabilities dying in foster care, including other children with diabetes — the result of poorly trained staff or the lack of proper support for a child's disability.

Other common problems that contribute to deaths include shortages of staff and a lack of adequate housing, especially for children with behavioral health disabilities.

Last September, 16-year-old Kanaiyah Ward died by suicide in Baltimore when she was able to grab a bottle of pills, unseen by a staffer who was working a 53-hour shift.

Ward, on a suicide watch, was living in a Baltimore hotel with a staffer who was forced to work for more than two days straight when other staff didn't show up.

A recent federal audit, by the inspector general for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, found that thousands of foster children sleep in hotels, child welfare office buildings and other unlicensed settings because state agencies don't have enough suitable places for them.

Most of those children, according to the federal audit, go to those temporary placements because they have disabilities that need attention — like behavioral health conditions. But then sometimes the children end up being watched by staff with little or no training to help them.

State child welfare directors say providing care for children with behavioral health needs has always been difficult — and has gotten harder in recent years, especially as states deal with cuts to social service budgets.

"We never have enough money. We never have enough quality services," said Christine Norbut Beyer who ran New Jersey's system until earlier this year and now works for Think of Us, a child welfare reform group.

And Mike Leach, who ran South Carolina's department until last year and also works for Think of Us, said problems start for families long before children even go into the child welfare system. In many states, there are long waiting lists for services that can help families stay together. "Over time, you've seen a decrease in budgets, a decrease in high-intensive psychiatric treatment," said Leach.

We were promised

toggle caption David Fouts for NPR

Avery Habelitz, at four, finally was sleeping through the night. The autistic girl had stopped hurting herself by banging her head on the floor when she was frustrated.

She didn't speak but she had ways to communicate, like taking her mother's hand and walking her to the refrigerator when she was hungry.

"She can't say, 'Hey, my stomach hurts.' Or, 'I'm hungry,' " her father, Jeremy Habelitz, explained. "So it took time to learn what certain things were with her. But we actually got to a point where we were really good at that. When she was having her moments of disarray, if you will, we were able to quickly soothe her."

Avery was making friends at her preschool and the three hours of speech therapy and Applied Behavior Analysis therapy in the afternoons seemed to be helping, her parents said.

Avery, at four, said her first word: "Da da."

toggle caption David Fouts for NPR

"Avery was just a bundle of joy," said her father. "She loved her family. She was just a happy kid."

But someone unknown to the parents reported Habelitz and Kaitlyn Morrow to child protective services in San Bernardino County, California, for using drugs.

Avery and her younger sister were removed from the family — even though they lived with Habelitz's mother and grandparents, who, he noted, weren't using drugs — and placed with a foster family.

That was on September 25, 2025. On the morning of December 23, 2025, the girl was found unresponsive and struggling to breathe in her room at the foster home, tied up in the sweatshirt her foster mother had used to restrain her to keep her in bed.

toggle caption David Fouts for NPR

Habelitz and Morrow are suing San Bernardino county for the wrongful death of their child.

"We were promised that her needs were going to be met," said Habelitz.

But, according to court documents, when Avery moved to foster care, her schooling and the many hours of therapy stopped.

The girl became anxious and her behavior regressed. She started banging her head on the floor again. She slept only an hour or two a night. She ran out of her bedroom and through the house of her foster parents.

On one difficult night, the foster mother put both of the girl's legs into the single leg of her pajamas to stop her from kicking and tied her in an adult sweatshirt with both of her arms restrained inside. She put on the girl's protective helmet with the hood of the sweatshirt over it, to prevent Avery from taking off the helmet.

In the morning, the foster mother found the girl unresponsive. When Avery was whisked to the hospital, Habelitz and Morrow were notified and rushed there, too. But by then, the girl was being transported, by another ambulance, to a hospital in Loma Linda.

Habelitz and Morrow drove frantically to that hospital to be by their daughter's bedside — but the hospital would not let them see her.

Hours later, the girl was pronounced dead.

The county coroner would declare the cause of death: "combined hyperthermia with positional restraint, hours."

"Just caring for Avery as long as we did, I've always said that we live in a world that is not meant for or willing to work with kids and teens and adults with disabilities," said Morrow. "It's just not a world made out for them."

toggle caption David Fouts for NPR

For foster youth, an ignored awareness about treating trauma

At her clinic in Arkansas, Elizabeth Cleveland treats a young boy in foster care who gets in trouble for frequent meltdowns.

The boy, she said, has a sensory processing disorder. He gets overwhelmed by loud sounds. Noise-canceling headphones can keep him calm.

But when he acts out, he gets disciplined. The residential facility where he lives takes away the headphones and requires him to build up points with good behavior to get them back.

Deprived of his headphones, the boy gets more anxious and acts out more, creating a cycle of more stress and more discipline — and moving him further and further from the reward he needs to stay calm.

"I probably hear a story like that once a month," said Cleveland, an assistant professor in the department of pediatrics at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences. She runs a clinic that specializes in treating children with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders, a vastly underestimated disability in foster care, she believes.

There's been a revolution in recent decades in understanding how children's brains develop and are changed by trauma. But foster care lags far behind in adopting the new thinking, said psychologist Karyn Harvey.

Behavioral therapies, which are standard in foster care settings, use punishments and rewards to get children to control outbursts, anger and other problematic behaviors.

This kind of behavior modification technique dates to the early 20th century.

But a disciplinary approach is often the opposite of what works with "neurodiverse" children — kids whose brains work differently because of disability or trauma, argued Harvey, who, for 35 years, has specialized in treating children and adults with disabilities.

Meltdowns are often an involuntary reaction to severe stress and anxiety. These children are "in states of hyper-arousal because their amygdala is firing danger signals and they're freaking out and their brains are filled with cortisol and adrenaline," according to Harvey. "And so they're breaking things and running away because they're in this heightened state due to the trauma and their trauma responses. And that's looked at as manipulative. It's looked at as attention seeking. They're punished repeatedly."

At school, kids who have a meltdown are sometimes put in physical restraints or secluded in closets and classrooms, creating more stress. In foster care, they're then moved from one placement to another and often end up in therapeutic group homes or residential treatment centers that use more punishment techniques.

They're "almost couch surfing facilities in foster homes," said Nancy Thaler who leads a federally-funded project through The Link Center to understand these "complex" children and how to best help them.

A gift of life

toggle caption Courtney Pedroza for NPR

The gravestone for Christian Williams, flush to the ground, is a rectangular, gray piece of marble, decorated with a cross, a basketball and a football. It reads: "In Loving Memory of Christian Avery Williams. January 3, 2009 - July 10, 2024."

Bobbie and DeForrest Williams visited their son's grave on a summer evening after the 100-plus degree temperature began to drop. The sky was blue and pink as the sun set.

DeForrest likes to visit here, usually once a week, after he's finished his job driving a school bus. He brings a rag to wipe down the headstone, and scissors to cut back the grass.

Bobbie, a school aide, and DeForrest heard that their son's donated organs — his lungs, liver and kidneys — went to four women on transplant lists. One woman sent them a hand-written card, expressing her sorrow at their loss and her thanks for the kidney she had waited for.

"He helped people," said his mother. "That's what he would have wanted."

"It means that he went away leaving a legacy and that he was a hero," said DeForrest. "He helped to give the gift of life to others."

These kids can recover

toggle caption Donaven Doughty for NPR

JoJo Kimble, a former foster youth in South Carolina, found a path to success — but largely on her own.

Kimble was diagnosed as autistic when she was 12. At school, she got an individualized education plan and accommodations around her autism. But when she went into foster care at 15, she said the system erased her autism diagnosis and gave her new labels: Depression, bipolar disorder, ADHD, borderline personality disorder.

She was prescribed antipsychotic medications — the overuse of such powerful drugs is a long-time problem in foster care — and sent to therapeutic treatment facilities and psychiatric hospitals.

Kimble, 23, has no doubt — nor do her current medical providers — that she is autistic. "It's easier to treat," she says of a behavioral health issue. "You can't treat autism with medication," she says. But you can "treat depression … with medication and all types of therapy."

Now she's living on her own and going to Coker University where she is studying nursing. She helps a professor research the impact of childhood cancer on families.

The "goal" of foster care, she says, "should be to raise healthy citizens for your society and to have people who are contributing." Instead, Kimble said, "you're just shoving these people back into a corner so that you don't have to deal with them."

NPR's Robert Benincasa contributed to this story.

World.title: Montana starts enforcing Medicaid work requirements on Oct 1. Patients are confused
World.content:
Montana starts enforcing Medicaid work requirements on Oct 1. Patients are confused

toggle caption Aaron Bolton/MTPR



Bethany Zulick went back to school in January to become a high school English teacher.

Years ago, she taught English as a second language overseas and loved it.

"It's so exciting to me to watch someone learn a new word or have that spark of understanding," said Zulick, who lives in Missoula.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Zulick knew she could earn enough money as a substitute teacher to make going back to school financially viable — except for the cost of health insurance. She didn't want to risk being unable to see her doctor for her allergies or for preventive care.

The health insurance offered through Montana State University was too expensive, Zulick said, almost as much as her tuition. But then she found a solution that allowed her to make the leap: Medicaid. She wouldn't have to pay any monthly premiums.

Sponsor Message

It worked well for a few months, as Zulick taught by day and took online classes at night.

But in June, the state sent a letter that she said left her "completely confused." She knew Montana was rolling out a system for Medicaid work requirements over the summer, but she thought she wouldn't have to prove she met the requirements until next year, when her Medicaid enrollment came up for renewal.

Yet the letter from the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services outlining the new requirements gave conflicting information on when Zulick would have to prove she was meeting them. First, it said at her next renewal, which would be sometime next spring.

Lower down, it told her she would have to submit paperwork to prove compliance much earlier — "within 30 days" of the date on the letter, June 26. She wondered: Was it a boilerplate mass-mailing letter she could ignore, or was her insurance on the line?

All states must implement the new work requirements by Jan. 1, but three states — Montana, Nebraska and Arkansas — have already gotten started.

Medicaid advocates worry that the expedited timeline in those states will lead to thousands of people losing coverage because they're confused about the new rules, even if they are eligible for the program — and that Montana may offer a troubling preview of what will happen nationwide next year.

Sponsor Message

State health department officials maintain they are well prepared and told state lawmakers they plan to process roughly 5,000 enrollees monthly.

Growing confusion and dwindling help

State Rep. SJ Howell of the Montana House has gotten dozens of calls from confused constituents, specifically about letters like the one Zulick received.

"The notices coming from the department are very, very confusing, and it's very hard to find help figuring out what's going on," said the Democratic legislator, who asked health department leaders about those letters at a hearing in early September.

toggle caption Aaron Bolton/MTPR



Letters being sent to enrollees have been updated to be clearer, state health officials told lawmakers at the hearing.

In Montana, nearly 71,000 people are subject to the new rules. Medicaid costs are split between the federal and state governments, and states are responsible for administering the program, which provides health insurance for people with low incomes or disabilities.

Under the new work requirements, enrollees must document that they're working, volunteering, or studying 80 hours per month — or they must show that they qualify for one of a range of exemptions, such as being "medically frail" or being the primary caretaker for a family member.

Montana began with a soft launch of the work requirements in July and gave enrollees until Oct. 1 to comply.

Critics contend that isn't enough time, because the state hasn't finished setting up new computer systems or hiring the staff it said it would need. Of the 59 positions, only about 20 were filled, state health department officials told state lawmakers during the Sept. 9 hearing.

The state had already hired over half of those workers earlier this summer, but officials said they lost staff to turnover.

State health officials have said they'll eventually be able to automatically verify that students are enrolled in public universities. However, that computer system isn't expected to be up and running until next year, leaving students like Zulick to track down and submit the correct paperwork to prove their college enrollment.

Sponsor Message

However, there are fewer outside resources to help residents with these bureaucratic tasks.

For example, Cover Montana, a nonprofit that helps Montanans fill out such paperwork, lost federal funding last year, going from a staff of 18 to two part-time employees working a phone line.

The state does operate a helpline, but federal data shows that Montanans stay on hold much longer than the national average and that many callers hang up before they connect with a state employee.

"We were worried about chaos that could be generated by the state rushing," said Aaron Wernham, CEO of the Montana Healthcare Foundation, a nonprofit aimed at improving health in the state.

"Given how little information the state has provided about what they are doing, I'm much more worried about chaos," Wernham added.

Wernham pointed to a similar upheaval in 2023, when states undertook a massive process to redetermine the eligibility of all Medicaid enrollees, after regular eligibility checks were paused during the pandemic.

Many Montanans who were financially eligible lost Medicaid coverage for technical reasons, such as incorrectly filling out paperwork — roughly 87,000, according to state data from two years ago.

Even vulnerable Montanans who didn't need to file paperwork, because their coverage should have been automatically renewed, were dropped from the Medicaid rolls, including people who were homeless.

Long-sought requirements in the state

The Montana Legislature passed a measure in 2019 expressing its desire to add work requirements to Medicaid, but the state didn't have permission from the federal government to move forward until now.

Having work requirements creates accountability for people who rely on the social safety net, said Montana Senate President Matt Regier, a Republican.

"In an economy like this, if you're an able-bodied adult that's able to work, you really do need to step up," he said.

Asked about confusion among enrollees about the rules, Regier responded that the Oct. 1 deadline offered more than enough time to work out the kinks in the new system.

Sponsor Message

In the end, Zulick learned she didn't need to worry about that deadline, because she got married in July and no longer qualified for Medicaid, although she didn't know that would be the case when she got the June letter.

But others remain scared about losing coverage, including Heather Reel, who attended a rally at the state capitol in July to push back against Montana's early rollout.

Reel relies on Medicaid for its mental health coverage. Without it, she said, she would struggle to care for her teenage son, who has autism and is nonverbal. Between her shifts at a fast food restaurant and caring for her son, she's scared she'll be too busy to figure out how to report her work hours.

Montana's rollout is a potential preview

The handful of states that are implementing the Medicaid work requirements early are building the plane as they're taking off, said Akeiisa Coleman, who provides Medicaid analysis for The Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit focused on making healthcare more equitable.

"Montana is going to be an example for what we might see nationally as things roll out," she said.

Although most other states are sticking to the Jan. 1 deadline to build and test their Medicaid systems, they still might not have all the components in place, she said.

If states can't automatically renew or deny coverage based on the new rules, state workers will have to do so manually, on a case-by-case basis. That could create backlogs and more disruption, leading more people to lose coverage, Coleman said.

Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson for the state's health department, said in a statement that Montana's Medicaid office is ready for the change on Oct. 1.

"We are committed to ensuring eligible Montanans maintain coverage while meeting requirements, and we will continue to monitor implementation closely," Ebelt said.

Sponsor Message

Democratic state lawmakers have repeatedly asked state health officials to extend the Oct. 1 deadline for enrollees to comply with the new rules, but state health department leadership said they have no plans to do so.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with Montana Public Radio and KFF Health News.

World.title: One year after the end of the EV tax credit, is the future still electric?
World.content:
One year after the end of the EV tax credit, is the future still electric?

toggle caption Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

One year ago today, the auto industry bid farewell to a hefty federal tax credit that helped bring down the cost of electric vehicles. Congress had voted to kill it as part of 2025's One Big Beautiful Bill Act — and car buyers rushed to take advantage of the credit before it ended on September 30, 2025.

So, how have EV sales fared since?

Ask around, and you get two answers. One is that EV sales are down, according to data from car analytics companies like Cox Automotive and Edmunds. No one is the least bit surprised.

Sponsor Message

When the Inflation Reduction Act took effect in August 2022, expanding the credit to more buyers, EVs made up about 5% of new car sales. Over the following three years, EV sales grew, ticking past 6, then 7, then 8%. They swelled to 11.4% in September 2025, as people rushed to take advantage of the tax credit's final days, according to data from Edmunds.

Data from Cox Automotive shows a similar bounce. EV sales peaked around September — then dropped in the following two quarters once the credit expired. Compared to the year before, in late 2025, they fell 36%. They were down 27% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2026.

This year, new EV sales have been more sluggish — but they're stable. EVs have steadily accounted for somewhere between 5 and 6% of all new car sales throughout 2026, according to Edmunds. Cox Automotive reports similar figures. This trajectory is " clearly nothing like what it was previously, but it has not fallen off of a cliff, which is what some people's predictions would've been," said Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds.

But ask Sal Iqbal how EV sales have fared over the last year, and you'll get another answer — and this one is more surprising. He's the general sales manager of the Toyota franchise in Massapequa, New York, where he's worked for nearly 10 years. And this year he noticed: Hybrid sales are way up.

toggle caption Willa Rubin/NPR

"We used to have Siennas sit on the lot before," Iqbal said, referring to the Toyota model which, like other hybrids, uses a gas engine and battery-powered electric motor. " We used to have to literally beg people to take a Sienna, and now we can't keep them on the shelf. People are lining up for Siennas."

Sponsor Message

Drury concurs: Siennas are a whole thing. Years ago, he said, minivans like these were considered undesirable, "and now it's like, 'Oh, if I could get my hands on a sweet Sienna, I'd do anything.'" The same thing, he said, is happening with Toyota's RAV4, a small hybrid SUV.

And nationally, American car buyers are really gravitating towards hybrids. Sales are up almost 27% in the past year, according to data from Edmunds.

Is it because the federal EV tax credit went away? Maybe. Is it because gasoline prices are still hovering around $4.50 per gallon nationally? Also maybe. Data from Edmunds shows hybrid sales jumped up in March, shortly after the U.S. began its war in Iran — a geopolitical shift that was not on analysts' radars when they made their forecasts for 2026.

The rise of the hybrid has been a kind of bright spot in a year that's been flat for the EV industry.

" Hybrids are having their moment, are continuing to have their moment," said Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive and who studies the transition to EVs.

Drury put it this way: " The downfall of the EV has highlighted how good the hybrid is."

How the federal tax credit worked

The EV tax credit was created by Congress in 2008, but it received a big boost from 2022's Inflation Reduction Act, which restructured how the credit could be used and adjusted some of the rules for which cars could qualify. It also added a credit for purchasing used cars, an expansion designed to extend benefits to low-and-middle-income buyers.

In the credits' most recent form, people who bought or leased a new electric vehicle could earn a federal tax credit worth up to $7,500, which could be stacked on top of state incentives. The credit for used vehicles was up to $4,000 on qualifying vehicles.

Sponsor Message

For people buying new cars to qualify , they needed to purchase EVs that were made in, and contained a certain percentage of parts from, North America. There was also an income cap for buyers.

That was a good deal, but it was an even better deal for people leasing EVs. They could use that credit toward any EV car — without limits on price, where the vehicle was made, or their income.

"The program was so good, it almost made no sense to buy the car," Iqbal said.

Either way, the credit helped juice interest in EVs, and overcome some of the reservations drivers have about them. EVs generally have a higher sticker price than gas-powered cars; the average EV transaction price was over $54,000 in August, compared to an average of just under $50,000 for gas-powered vehicles, according to Cox Automotive. Drivers have long worried about limited range , or a lack of charging points, or the expense of replacing an enormous lithium-ion battery that can cost thousands of dollars.

Congressional Republicans got rid of the EV tax credit last year after long arguing that markets, not the government, should influence what Americans drive, and dubbed the tax credit wasteful spending.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration chipped away at other policies that promoted electric vehicles. It scrapped California's ability to set strict emissions standards. It nixed penalties on carmakers who don't meet federal standards for making enough fuel-efficient vehicles. This week, it scaled back those standards altogether .

When Iqbal heard the EV federal tax credit was going away, he was nervous.

"We didn't know what was going to happen," Iqbal said. Even though about 10% of the vehicles sold at the dealership where he works are electric, he said, "We can't just sit on inventory. It's only going to depreciate more and more."

Sure enough, after Sept. 30, 2025, Iqbal says they didn't sell another EV until mid-November.

Sponsor Message

That trend bore out nationally. People rushed to buy electric vehicles months leading up to the tax credit going away, but EV sales slumped in the next few months; over 11% of car buyers bought electric vehicles in September 2025, but only 5.8% did a month later, Edmunds data shows.

Over the last year, Iqbal says, EVs overall have been a tougher sell without the help of that credit. After all, Iqbal said, some people are still nervous about EV batteries, or about charging.

"A lot of people are still scared of the electrical side of EVs because it gives them anxiety of losing charge on the middle of the road," he said.

Hybrids, though, inspire no such worries. The hybrid is, he said, "the best of both worlds."

Hybrids are having a moment

Part-electric, but still powered by gas, hybrids have greater fuel economy than traditional gas vehicles, and a lower price point than EVs.

"Hybrids were always there. They're always kind of lurking in the background of attention," said Drury.

But after the war with Iran began, they got a lot more attention. Drury said traffic on the Edmunds site for both hybrids and EVs climbed. But ultimately, he said, "many consumers either did not move forward with their EV plans or they just bought a hybrid instead," most likely because of the lower price point.

To him, the clearest victor in 2026 has been Toyota, a company with a hybrid-heavy lineup and a long history of making them. In the past couple of years, Toyota's transitioned some of its most popular cars, like the RAV4 and the Camry, to be hybrid-only.

"Toyota had their 'I told you so' moment many times over now," Drury said.

Valdez Streaty of Cox agrees. " Toyota is definitely, I think, capitalizing on this period where we have high gas prices," she said. "So you can save money on gas. If you care about the environment, you get some of those environmental benefits. And also, you don't have to worry about charging, so it takes away that friction point."

Sponsor Message

Toyota didn't return requests for an interview or for sales statistics. But Drury says you can learn a lot about demand for vehicles by seeing how long they spend on the lot.

And in Massapequa, Iqbal said, hybrids are flying off the lot. On average, over the past year, Iqbal said they've had a 12-day supply. "That means if I don't get another vehicle from the factory, it will take me 12 days to sell out of my whole inventory," he said.

Those kinds of numbers are basically unheard of, said Drury, and indicate the high demand for Toyota vehicles: "We consider anything under 14 days basically sold out."

The momentum for hybrids goes beyond Toyota. Hyundai sold 33% more hybrid vehicles in August compared to the year before — making up almost 30% of its total August sales. Kia's August hybrid sales rose 99% compared to the previous year.

toggle caption Willa Rubin/NPR

Iqbal said when potential hybrid buyers come in to the Toyota dealership in Massapequa, they have done their homework.

"They know more about the cars than we do sometimes," he said. " They are literally in-depth with every little feature. They know the cubic feet of the trunk."

But most of all, he said, they know that they won't be spending as much on gas. "They know that same $50 in gas is taking them two weeks instead of one week, and that can make or break somebody, depending on who you are," Iqbal said.

After all, he said, " Nobody wants gas prices to be high. We all want them to be lower. But what can we do? Am I not going to drive?"

The market for used EVs is growing

There is a second possible bright spot that's beginning to glow for EV buyers and sellers — and that's a burgeoning used car market.

It's a legacy from the era of the tax credit: because so many people used it to lease EVs, as more and more of these vehicles come off lease, they are showing up on used car lots as inventory.

Sponsor Message

Even though used EVs make up less than 3% of the used car market, that number is growing, said Valdez Streaty of Cox Automotive. In the next year, more than 300,000 vehicles will come off lease, she said — and she expects those numbers to keep rising.

This means EVs could be more accessible to buyers at lower price points, since used cars are generally cheaper than new ones. And, Nick Nigro , founder of the climate-focused think tank Atlas Public Policy said, seeing more EVs around will help normalize them.

" That's probably the single best  for electric vehicles in the last several years," Nigro said. " The vast majority of people buy used vehicles, and that's what makes up most of the vehicles on the road."

Valdez Streaty says that even without the tax credit, American automakers are under some pressure to keep making EVs. After all, they must compete globally. Outside the U.S., the market for electric vehicles is picking up speed. In China, more than half of new cars sold in 2025 were electric, and over 30% of cars sold last year in Europe were electric, according to the International Energy Agency.

Meanwhile, demand for Chinese-made electric vehicles continues to grow; the Chinese EV company BYD Auto sells more electric cars than Tesla .

The loss of the tax credit won't stop automakers from producing EVs, she said: "It's kind of just shifted their timeline and the way they roll things out."

Valdez Streaty sees the EV market in 2026 as finding a new equilibrium.

"There's still underlying demand for new EVs, but at a lower and more stable level, while growth is stronger in used EVs and hybrids," she said.

EV adoption may be slower, Valdez Streaty said. But, she continued, "I think the future's still electric."

World.title: Why pro-Trump ads — paid for with public money — are airing on U.S. TV
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With crucial midterm elections just weeks away, the White House is using taxpayer funds to air campaign-style TV ads featuring U.S. President Donald Trump.

The ads have aired in top timeslots on national and local television, including during last weekend's NFL games, costing at least $1.4 million US so far, according to analysis by advertising tracking firm AdImpact.

The White House's decision to spend public money on the campaign is drawing widespread criticism, including from Republicans.

"I like the message, but it shouldn't be paid for by taxpayer dollars," Senate majority leader John Thune told reporters on Capitol Hill on Monday.

The ads are running as Trump's approval rating hits an all-time low and his Republican Party faces what could be a disastrous midterm result on Nov. 3, potentially ceding control of the U.S. Congress to the Democrats for the remainder of his presidency.

Although U.S. law forbids use of government funds for "publicity and propaganda," Trump's officials insist there's nothing illegal about the advertising campaign.

U.S. tax dollars paid for this TV ad, featuring Donald Trump:

"These public service announcements are unapologetically American ," the White House said in a statement. "The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads. President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action."

While it's true that Trump is not up for re-election in the midterms, he did urge the audience watching this month's Republican convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot," an attempt to boost turnout for GOP candidates in tight House and Senate races.

'Love Me'

Richard Painter, who served as White House ethics lawyer during then-president George W. Bush's second term, says the ads could be an impeachable offence because Trump cannot use taxpayer money to campaign.

"All three ads, they're sheer propaganda," Painter told the Associated Press. "This is increasingly looking like what authoritarian governments do to promote their leaders."

The first ad features rapid-fire montages of photos of Trump, as a choir repeatedly sings the title lyrics of Love Me, a song by musician JMSN.

"If President Trump wants people to love him, he can pay for it himself," a group of Democratic lawmakers wrote to Trump's chief of staff in a letter calling for the ad to be pulled.

'Together we will defeat communism,' says Trump in ad, as choir sings 'Love Me':

"This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and utterly illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars," the Democrats wrote.

The 'Love Me' ad begins with grainy black-and-white video of Trump as his voice is heard saying "Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America."

The 30-second ad then shows slides declaring in all-caps "Largest Tax Cuts in History" and "Reigniting American Manufacturing."

UFC boss praises Trump in ad

It concludes with video of Trump with Dana White, CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship mixed-martial arts empire, as the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" appear at the bottom of the screen.

"He's the toughest, most resilient person that I've ever met, and nothing was going to stop him for fighting so hard for the country he loves," White said in the voice-over, audio from his introduction of Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention.

Another of the government-funded ads is nearly identical to a Trump campaign ad from 2024.

'We will expel the warmongers from our government,' says Trump in government-funded ad:

" This is the final battle," Trump said in the ad. "With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state, we will expel the warmongers from our government."

Another ad uses clips and video from Trump's speech at Mount Rushmore on July 3, the night before the 250th anniversary of the U.S. Declaration of Independence.

"We are the freest people on earth," Trump said in the minute-long TV commercial. "This is only the beginning of the golden age of America."

The taxpayer money for the ads comes from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, an agency of the Department of Homeland Security, the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday.

Scott Talan, a professor of communication at American University in Washington, D.C., describes the message of the ads as "love Trump, love his policies" but he's doubtful they will have much impact on the president's sagging polls.

"I can't imagine much movement," Talan told CBC News. "People pretty much have their opinions formed."

He noted that the ads ran heavily during pro and college football games. "I don't know how many people watching those games haven't made up their mind already," he said.

Past administrations have used taxpayer funds on public service advertising, such as a $10 million US campaign under Joe Biden urging people to get vaccinated against COVID-19 and national TV ads promoting government subsidies for health insurance during Barack Obama's time in the White House.

The top Democrat in the U.S. Senate, Chuck Schumer, said the Trump administration's ads are "anything but" public service announcements.

"They were pure propaganda," Schumer said Tuesday on the Senate floor. "Trump is getting you, American taxpayer, to use your dollars to pay for his political ads."

World.title: Now that you know the truth, what do you do about reconciliation?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Reconciliation through friendship and forests: Unreserved 54:00 Reconciliation through friendships and forests!

When Jenny Davis was about to meet an Indigenous elder for the first time through her work at Toronto's High Park Nature Centre, she was nervous.

Davis, the centre's special events co-ordinator at the time, said she's embarrassed looking back at her internal monologue when meeting Donna Powless, director of the Taiaiako'n Historical Preservation Society.

"I was saying, 'just act natural. This is such an important person. I just have to act natural,'" she said. "Obviously, I'm not acting natural if I'm saying to myself, 'Act natural.'"

The two were meeting because Powless would soon be leading the Nature Centre's first Indigenous family nature walks — a collaboration that's still happening eight years later.

By now, nearly 11 years after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission released its final report and 94 calls to action , most of us have learned at least some of the truth about the impacts of colonization.

But as a non-Indigenous person, Davis said she understands how fear of making a misstep can leave people unsure how to participate even in small acts of reconciliation.

An old shed in Toronto's High Park now houses supplies used to help protect snapping turtles. Its mural was created by Macie Dixon and Claudia Luz Doare. (James Beaton)

Elin Sandberg Miller, co-author of Everyday Reconciliation: A Guide to Action and Change for All of Us, said she understands that uncertainty.

"It's not always easy as a non-Indigenous person to do the right thing, to say the right thing, and so then we don't do anything because we're worried of overstepping boundaries," she told Unreserved host Rosanna Deerchild.

"A lot of people feel guilt, and they don't know what to do with that guilt."

Sandberg Miller, originally from Sweden, points out that the Sami people in her home country have suffered similarly under colonization.

But both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people say there are countless ways to contribute to reconciliation, from supporting Indigenous artists by streaming their music to volunteering to help protect sensitive ecosystems and species.

"Once you begin, you can see all the ways reconciliation can be part of your life," Davis said.

Here are some ideas to consider on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and beyond.

Derek Aronhie:nens Montour is the co-author of Everyday Reconciliation: A Guide to Action and Change for All of Us. (Submitted by Derek Aronhie:nens Montour)

Explore Indigenous music, films and books

Derek Aronhie:nens Montour, who is Mohawk from Kahnawà:ke, located across the St. Lawrence River from Montreal, said part of the work of reconciliation is about "trying to shift and change the way we see things."

He said that's part of what he and Sandberg Miller are trying to do with their book. He encourages people to get to know some of the many Indigenous authors and filmmakers out there.

"That's what I think Canadians need to do is try to put on a different set of glasses," said Aronhie:nens Montour. "It could be something as simple as starting to listen to more Indigenous YouTube artists because those push up and start to make Indigenous music more popular."

The St. John's Mi'kmaw Women's Circle sang and drummed at the sunrise ceremony on National Indigenous People's Day, June 21, 2025. (Abby Cole/CBC)

Attend a ceremony

Jenny Davis encourages other non-Indigenous people to attend one of the many Indigenous ceremonies that are open to the public. These include powwows or the sunrise ceremonies held to mark summer solstice, usually coinciding with National Indigenous Peoples Day every year on June 21.

"What I've experienced is that the elders who are leading these public ceremonies are so incredible at making sure we know what we should do," said Davis. "If you can get there, just really trust that these elders or grandmothers will lead you."

Learn who lives near you

Aronhie:nens Montour said some Indigenous people find themselves doing a lot of labour to help educate others.

Indigenous people didn't create the colonial system, he said, "so, really, reconciliation is a non-Indigenous task."

But there's a ton of good-quality, easily accessible information that people can use to direct their own learning, he said. A good place to start, according to Aronhie:nens Montour, is by considering who lives near you.

"Which Indigenous nation had the land first in that surrounding area? But once you learn that, pick another nation."

Echoing the need for personal initiative, Sandberg Miller noted that while many didn't learn about these issues in school, "it's not too late and that's the good thing."

Elin Sandberg Miller says a lot of people feel guilt about colonization but don't know what to do about it. (Submitted by Elin Sandberg Miller)

Listen to first-hand accounts

Sandberg Miller said she's learned a lot just from listening to the personal stories of individual Indigenous people, including that of her co-author, Aronhie:nens Montour.

"I think for many non-Indigenous people, when you read about a residential school, you read land rights being violated, you read the treaties and how the obligations were not fulfilled, and it's still so abstract," she said.

"But to hear it first-hand from someone who has grown up on a reserve and who has been impacted so deeply at the personal level by all those decisions, it changes how you see it."

Restore native plants

Done in a way that's informed by Indigenous land practices, an act of service to the environment and the other beings living there can also be a form of reconciliation.

Lena Ouse-Hicks is part of a group of Indigenous and non-Indigenous people called Friends of Tryon Creek who are restoring native plants to a forest in Portland, Ore.

Tryon State Natural Area was once rich with Western red cedar, salmonberry and hazel. But with the arrival of settlers came new species, like ivy, a popular evergreen climbing vine that Ouse-Hicks said almost took over the forest completely.

"The wonderful thing about the native plants here is they are so resilient," said Ouse-Hicks, who is a member of the Coast Miwok tribe. "You see that through just the areas where you pull a little ivy and that next year … those native plants come up when they're just given that space."

Ouse-Hicks said caring for the land is more than ecological repair. "I think inherently it should be environmental restoration as a means of cultural restoration. To me it's one and the same."

Protect a turtle

In Toronto, an effort to reconcile human impacts on a revered animal relative unfolded from a fateful day in 2021 when Carolynne Crawley came upon a snapping turtle laying her eggs in a high-traffic area of High Park.

"She called me and she said, 'You've got to come and help me keep people away,'" said Jenny Davis.

The encounter inspired the two women to co-found Turtle Protectors, an Indigenous-led program whose staff and volunteers raise awareness of urban turtles among visitors to 11 Toronto parks, protect turtle nests and run a hotline to field reports of vulnerable or injured turtles.

Jenny Davis helps a juvenile turtle to water in Toronto's High Park, in August. (James Beaton)

It's an especially meaningful effort given the turtle is part of the Anishinaabe creation story, which says the first woman to arrive on Earth was given a home on a great turtle's back .

Davis said prospective volunteers must complete a workshop with Crawley called "Indigenous ways of knowing," and a second one called "Turtles 101."

Speak up

Elin Sandberg Miller said everyone has a role to play.

"It could be that you talk to your elected representative and ask them what they are doing about the 94 calls to action. You can talk to your children's school teacher about what they're teaching. You can intervene when you hear someone say something racist or hear prejudice," she said.

"There's so much you can do on a daily basis, that we can all do. And if we don't, that's a choice too."

World.title: Victory for separatist Parti Québécois would present a new political test for Carney
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There is an immediate political test looming for Prime Minister Mark Carney and his government as early as Monday — one that has not been on the political radar federally for more than a decade.

And it's one that does not seem to be front and centre of the federal agenda yet.

This week has so far seen the expansion of an LNG plant on the West Coast and the referral of a high-speed rail strategy in Alberta to the Major Projects Office. It is widely expected the West Coast pipeline will be designated a project of national interest to speed the approval process along.

The prime minister is banking on these projects to grow the Canadian economy, but also help deal with the very real political challenges in the West. That includes, of course, the Oct. 19 Alberta referendum on whether the province should start a process to leave Canada.

WATCH | PQ entering majority territory, polls show: PQ enters majority territory in latest election polls | Duration closed caption 4:27 Qc125 polling analyst Philippe J. Fournier breaks down provincial polling one week out from the election with CBC News Montreal at 6 guest host Sudha Krishnan.

But before that, Quebec will choose a new government. Public opinion polling shows it is likely that the Parti Québécois will win, with the party now closing in on majority territory.

The last time Quebec had a sovereignist government was 2014 when Premier Pauline Marois's PQ was voted out after less than two years in office. But there was little to no talk of a referendum from that government . In fact, you have to go all the way back to the last Quebec election I covered, in 2003, when Bernard Landry tried to pick up the mantle of Lucien Bouchard and promised a referendum if he had the "mortal certainty" he would win it.

Landry lost that election to Quebec Liberal Leader Jean Charest.

The current PQ leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, has promised not to hold a referendum until after Donald Trump is no longer president, citing the volatility of that administration and how it could impact results.

But federal leaders should not mistake that decision for lack of commitment to the sovereignist cause. In fact, St-Pierre Plamondon says he remains optimistic despite what most polls show, namely that only 30 per cent of Quebecers are interested in a referendum at all.

St-Pierre Plamondon's lead in the polls has expanded in recent days. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

In the last debate of the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon pointed to something former premier and PQ leader Jacques Parizeau would say: "We shouldn't be afraid of democracy."

It is not just the real threat of a referendum — that will become a contentious issue should the Parti Québécois pull off a victory. Ottawa will also have to be prepared for a more aggressive stance from the PQ leader.

"I think it is difficult to find more evident declines and reversals than over the past 10 years," St-Pierre Plamondon said in an editorial board interview this week with La Presse.

"It is not referendums that are to blame for the decline of French, the decline in our demands for health transfers and that of immigration, that has been sabotaged by the federal government."

All premiers and provinces fight for their jurisdictions and to get more from Ottawa. But only one of them will make those demands elected with the mandate to hold a referendum on independence.

Case in point for what awaits Carney's government: as premier, St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to get rid of an intergovernmental affairs minister. Instead he would have a minister of independence, tasked with making gains for Quebec.

In an era where working as Team Canada has been key to the response to the trade war with the United States, that team may now become fractured and more difficult to manage.

Polls suggest Carney's popularity remains high across Canada, including in Quebec, which also happens to be his political power base — holding 44 of the 78 ridings.

But his ability to manage the country through a crisis and prove to Quebec it is a valued part of the federation without giving further fodder to a no longer dormant separatist movement is about to be tested in real time.

World.title: After 'doom and gloom' decade, Fort McMurray readies for a boom
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Alberta community synonymous with meteoric oil booms and crippling busts is now staring down another potential wave of economic fortune.

Already signs are pointing to a boost in growth in Fort McMurray with rising home prices, increased investment in the oilpatch, widespread hiring and longer lines at the Tim Hortons drive-thru.

Much of the growth is in anticipation of a new oil pipeline to the West Coast, as proposed by the Alberta government. On Thursday, the federal government is expected to declare the project is in the national interest.

As more families and businesses move in, roofer William Gilbert sees his business growing alongside Fort McMurray.

With nail guns and roofing hammers, one of Gilbert's crews finishes up attaching shingles on a black two-storey house on the western edge of the community. His 20 employees are working as much as they can to keep up with demand. Though business hasn't spiked overnight, Gilbert expects steady hiring over the next few years.

"I see us doubling, if not tripling," he said. "We're slowly getting a boom."

A series of federal and provincial announcements aimed at growing oil production over the last 12 months are fuelling the sense of optimism, including a new West Coast oil pipeline being developed by Alberta and Ottawa.

In addition, the federal government has wiped away certain environmental policies such as the oilpatch emissions cap , while speeding up the regulatory process to approve major projects and introducing new financial incentives for investors.

The Alberta government aims to double oilsands production to eight million barrels per day by 2035.

The Syncrude oilsands mining facility operates north of Fort McMurray. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

The last decade in the region has been lacklustre for many businesses, with little economic growth and a declining population. However, the period was useful in allowing the local government to catch up on building roads and other important infrastructure.

Now, people are moving back, pushing the population to an all-time high.

"It's been very doom and gloom here since 2015," said Kyle Vandecasteyen, a councillor with the Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo. "We're ready for growth."

Excitement building

Some construction crews have seen a threefold increase in work, said Dianna De Sousa, the president of the local chamber of commerce.

"It's organized chaos. They have to turn away work," she said.

After several years of a stagnant economy, she said there is excitement and anticipation, mixed with some trepidation.

"The challenge is going to be labour and workforce without a doubt," said De Sousa, since some tradespeople are already in short supply.

Fort McMurray is prepared for a possible oil boom after several years of infrastructure improvements, says Kyle Vandecasteyen, a councillor for the Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

An oil boom will require a plethora of workers from drivers and engineers to mechanics and pipefitters.

The local college is trying to gear up, but it faces a similar predicament in finding enough instructors.

"I'm hoping when this boom happens, we have the manpower," said Shane Ganong, a heavy-duty mechanic and instructor at Keyano College.

He worked in the oilsands during the last boom, including long shifts at all hours of the day.

"We don't need to put people through such extreme workloads that they put in the past," he said.

Housing demand is up about 30 per cent this summer compared to last year, said realtor Paige Cyr, "So we are eating up our housing supply quite quickly."

The real estate market hasn't been this strong in many years, and while prices are rising, Cyr said some houses are still selling $200,000 below when they were purchased 10 or 15 years ago.

"People are coming back to the region. People are ready to invest," she said.

The common sentiment in the community is a need for a slow and controlled pace of growth, since Fort McMurray was unprepared during past booms.

A gold rush-type atmosphere brought workers from across Canada, lured by the highest wages in the country. There were too few houses, daycares and schools. Businesses were poaching workers from each other. Grocery stores had never-ending lineups.

"All of a sudden the bust happens and so many people that are local here are underwater in their mortgages. And that's happened a few times," said Kris Yarish, the chief operating officer of Alcor Facilities Management, which has operated in Fort McMurray for over 50 years, providing construction, work camps and other services.

He remembers the 2006 boom in particular, when it took four times as long to drive to oilsands sites because of so much traffic on the highway.

As he stood in front of his company's booth during a recent oil trade show, the largest such event in nearly a decade with more than 200 businesses, he couldn't help but notice the positive atmosphere.

"Having a new pipeline makes a difference, 100 per cent," he said, providing confidence throughout the industry.

No guarantees

Still, he's cautious knowing how a potential oil boom could always be derailed.

Large oilsands companies have been reluctant to invest tens of billions of dollars and take on sizeable debts to build megaprojects, of which the last one was completed in 2018. Investors no longer prioritize a company's growth as they once did, instead focusing on regular returns of cash and share buybacks.

Past oil booms in Fort McMurray were driven by multiple oilsands companies all building at once, which meant competing for labour, equipment and supplies. These days, there are only a handful of major oilsands producers after several years of consolidation.

There are other factors too, said Yarish, such as the ongoing trade war with the United States and continued turmoil with global oil prices.

An aerial view of Fort McMurray's downtown. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Major infrastructure work continues in Fort McMurray as heavy machinery moves dirt along the riverbank to better protect the downtown from flooding. The municipality has invested in sewer, water, road and other projects to better position the community for the next wave of growth.

Still, there's more to do, including a continued push by some locals for a new highway to better connect the community.

The $1.5-billion East Clearwater Highway has been discussed since the devastating 2016 wildfire, which highlighted how Fort McMurray only has one highway out of the community.

The proposed project would add a second route to the east, which would also improve access to some oilsands facilities in the region.

"If the oilsands is going to be growing and have a new pipeline, you want to build that highway, not only because it makes business sense for the industry, but for safety as well," said Marty Giles with NorthStar Ford, who has lived in the community for more than 30 years.

His dealership in Fort McMurray sells about 1,200 F-Series trucks each year and he sees all the signs of economic growth.

That's why he is hiring another 30 people to push his staffing level to about 300 workers.

"I haven't seen this much optimism actually in Fort McMurray for the last decade as I do today," he said.

World.title: Commercial plane travelling from Dubai to Israel diverted to Saudi Arabia after distress call
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes.

Israeli media, citing security officials, said the incident stemmed from a feud between the plane's two pilots, and everyone on board was safe. The plane landed in Tabuk, a civilian and military base in the kingdom.

The FlyDubai plane transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff, according to publicly available flight-tracking information.

A regional official briefed on the incident said a fight broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved pilots. It wasn't immediately clear what had caused the fight, the official said.

Israel scrambles warplanes

A second official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking of a plane carrying dozens of its citizens. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalated security threats.

Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was still under investigation.

Netanyahu's office later said the situation was under control and Israel was working to bring the passengers home.

Emergency landings for personnel reasons are rare, yet not unheard of. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after fighting in the cockpit on a Geneva-Paris flight, though it did not have to be diverted and landed as planned.

Plane dipped steeply, passengers say

Passengers on the plane told Israel's Channel 12 by phone that they heard shouts from passengers toward the front of the plane who heard the altercation between the pilots, and the plane dipped steeply before landing in Saudi Arabia.

They also said that all the passengers were staying on the plane and that there was a heavy presence of Saudi security forces surrounding them.

FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines. The U.A.E. has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalized ties in 2020.

A screengrab taken from Flightradar24 shows the flight path of the FlyDubai flight to Israel, which was diverted to Saudi Arabia. (Flightradar24.com/Reuters)

According to Flight Radar, the incident occurred about 2½ hours after takeoff.

FlyDubai later confirmed that Flight FZ 1073, en route to Ben Gurion, experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday.

"Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities," the carrier said. "Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available."

Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including often invasive check-in procedures for Israel-bound flights.

World.title: Are the raspberries in my fridge OK to eat? What to know about chemical levels on Driscoll's berries
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You may be having second thoughts about eating the berries in your fridge after CBC News spoke with a whistleblower who made a startling claim about the amount of chemicals on fruit that a U.S. company allegedly shipped to Canada.

David Harada, a former employee for California-based Driscoll's, alleged in a lawsuit that about half of the company's exports to Canada contained pesticide levels that exceeded Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) standards.

Driscoll's supplies raspberries, strawberries, blueberries and blackberries that are largely grown in California and Mexico, but with some products coming from other places seasonally — including parts of Canada.

Harada says the excess chemical levels were due to over-spraying and the removal of food safety compliance parameters for berries sent to Canada.

The CFIA confirmed higher-than-permissible levels of pesticides on the company's berries. Driscoll's has said that it's amended its controls to comply with Canadian standards.

But that may not be enough to put some Canadian consumers' minds at ease, especially parents. Meanwhile, food safety experts say this has prompted an important conversation about the chemicals used on the produce we eat.

Here's a quick look at what you need to know.

Are the berries in my fridge safe to eat?

Harada's lawsuit alleges that millions of pounds of berries with chemical levels exceeding CFIA guidelines were imported between 2022 and 2024, so it's highly unlikely those would have survived in your fridge since then — and you certainly shouldn't eat them if they are still in there.

Maria Corradini, an associate professor in the University of Guelph's food sciences department, says the chemical compounds sprayed on produce do degrade over time.

But the issue, she says, is ensuring that the right amount is applied and that enough time has passed so that there isn't leftover residue come harvest time.

WATCH | Driscoll's berries shipped to Canada with excess chemicals, lawsuit alleges: Driscoll's sent berries with excess chemicals to Canada: whistleblower | Duration 3:06 A whistleblower lawsuit in California alleges millions of trays of fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border between 2022 and 2024. The suit also accuses Driscoll’s fruit company of trying to cover it up.

Environmental toxicologist Daniel Green says that even if you actually consumed berries with higher than permissible levels of chemical residue, it probably wouldn't be enough to harm you.

You would likely need to eat something like 19 kilograms of berries in a short period of time to really feel any adverse effects.

"This issue isn't one serving of berries," he told CBC Montreal's Gloria Henríquez, explaining that it's like "one speck" of the chemicals to which people are exposed in their daily lives.

What chemicals were found on the berries?

The three chemicals found were bifenthrin, iprodione and captan.

Iprodione is used to prevent and control mould, mildew and stem and root rot on a variety of crops. Captan is also a fungicide that is used on field, greenhouse and orchard crops.

Bifenthrin is an insecticide that accounts for more than a quarter of commercially used pesticides globally. In addition to various produce, it is used on certain flowers, shrubs and trees. It attacks insects by targeting their nervous systems, eventually paralyzing them and causing death.

A worker at an unidentified farm in Mexico's Guanajuato state sprays a field of strawberries that will be distributed to different states in Mexico and exported to the U.S. (Mario Armas/AFP/Getty Images)

Bifenthrin is considered to be of low toxicity to humans, though large quantities can induce adverse effects, including headaches, dizziness or skin or nasal irritations when inhaled, or a sore throat, nausea and vomiting if ingested.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also classifies it as a possible human carcinogen, but only based on incidences of tumours in mice.

However, Corradini says that workers on berry farms would be more likely to face any sort of health risks from acute exposure.

Can I wash these chemicals off berries?

It may not do much, Corradini says, especially when it comes to berries, because of how soft they are and all of the tiny crevices in their skin.

She says there have been some studies showing that soaking them for a few minutes in a mixture of water and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) may help, but that there's not enough evidence to conclusively say it's effective.

Are organic berries better?

Buying organic is your best bet in avoiding these chemicals, but it's not foolproof, Corradini says.

"If you are in a facility that is having half of the production organic and half not, well, there is always a risk that there is a mistake," she said.

Driscoll's also markets a line of organically grown berries, including strawberries, that it says adhere to U.S. Department of Agriculture standards. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

She also pointed out that chemical pesticides are why fruits and vegetables can be grown so plentifully and at a relatively affordable cost.

Organic crops, she says, may also be more prone to infestations. And like non-organic produce, organic foods are not immune to pathogens and parasites that can cause food-borne illnesses such as E. coli and norovirus.

WATCH | The parasite that caused a nationwide outbreak in the U.S.: What is cyclospora? A diarrhea-causing parasite | Duration 2:37 A diarrhea-causing parasite has led to a growing outbreak in the United States that has sickened more than 1,000 people and sent dozens to hospital. As of Wednesday, multiple states had reported cyclospora infections, which can cause watery diarrhea, bloating, fever and nausea. While cases are common in the spring and summer, the current outbreak has led to an unusually high number, making it one of the largest the country has seen. No deaths have been reported.

Is Driscoll's facing any sort of investigation?

Driscoll's says that it "never knowingly shipped product that we believed to be unsafe."

Harada's lawsuit is still in progress and the company wouldn't comment on it other than to deny his allegations.

Driscoll's is also facing a separate class-action lawsuit filed earlier this year by six plaintiffs living in New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts and Illinois.

SFGate reported that the suit accuses the company of consumer fraud and deceptive practices by allegedly "greenwashing" the amount of so-called forever chemicals, known as PFAS, on its strawberries.

World.title: G20 trade ministers are meeting in Wisconsin. Many will be discussing deals without their U.S. host
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When trade ministers from some of the world's largest economies gather in Wisconsin today, it will be hard to ignore the red white and blue elephant in the room.

Most of the officials attending the G20 trade ministers' meeting in Milwaukee find themselves in challenging positions, largely because of U.S. President Donald Trump's global tariff agenda.

Some, including Canada, have been forced to rethink and reshape trading relationships due to the new tariffs, barriers, and uncertainty imposed by the Trump administration as it pursues what it describes as an America-first agenda.

All of this makes for a potentially unusual summit, with high-level meetings on the sidelines where different countries discuss plans to work around the host.

That is part of Canada's goal here, as it seeks to advance talks with global trading partners as the government works to reduce dependency on the U.S. economy where it can.

"In a more unpredictable world, trade diversification is Canada's Plan A," said International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu.

"In the past year, our non-U.S. trade has increased by 17 per cent, or $33 billion, and nearly one-third of Canadian exports now go to destinations outside the United States, the highest share in 40 years," he said in an email sent in response to multiple questions from CBC News.

The Pfister Hotel in Milwaukee, Wisc., pictured on Tuesday, is set to host the meeting of G20 trade ministers. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)

Sidhu is leading the Canadian delegation, not Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, since this is a gathering of international counterparts.

While Sidhu is expected to cross paths with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, the top Trump administration negotiator, this is not expected to be a forum to potentially resuscitate Canada-U.S. trade talks.

Negotiations between the two countries broke down in August, after Canada rejected the latest U.S. deal. Greer and LeBlanc both say they have spoken by phone multiple times per week ever since, including as recently as last Friday.

The latest American shot against Canada in its trade war landed Tuesday, when an import ban on certain Canadians products, including most alcoholic drinks, came into effect.

WATCH | U.S. bans certain Canadian imports: New U.S. import ban takes aim at Canadian alcohol | Duration closed caption 2:49 A U.S. ban on select Canadian goods takes effect Tuesday, hitting alcohol producers particularly hard. The move shuts many Canadian spirits, beer and cider products out of their biggest export market as the trade war escalates.

Sidhu said he has meetings planned with the delegations from the European Union and India, in the hopes of advancing negotiations with both trading partners.

"We are moving at pace to secure greater access to some of the world's largest and fastest-growing economies," he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before a meeting at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Sept. 16. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

U.S. pushes for WTO changes

The priorities of the Trump administration, including its tariff agenda, will be showcased over two days of meetings at the summit, according to a news release from the U.S. trade representative's office.

Among the discussions will be "eliminating forced labour in global supply chains" and "addressing structural and excess capacity and production," including a meeting dedicated to steel.

But the issue that stands out the most is the American push to change the World Trade Organization's Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) rules, says Martha Harrison, a Toronto-based trade lawyer who co-leads the international trade and investment team at McCarthy Tétrault.

To simplify a deeply technical and complicated system, the MFN principle is meant to prevent discriminating against another WTO member country.

"You have to give equal treatment to members of the WTO community," and "it has to be the same tariff rate across the board," Harrison told CBC News.

"It is not dramatic to say that if the MFN rule is softened … it will create distinctions and a trade environment globally that is even more unpredictable than it is now."

WATCH | Sidhu hopeful of free-trade deal with India: Canada, India will 'hopefully' reach a trade deal by end of year: Sidhu | Duration closed caption 10:03 International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu tells Power & Politics that Canada's trade diversification trip to India, Australia and Japan will open dialogue for new partnership and investment opportunities — including first steps toward a free trade deal with India.

The Trump administration has long complained about WTO rules, with Greer laying out his case for reform in an opinion essay published in August 2025 by the New York Times.

"The bulk of global manufacturing shifted to jurisdictions such as China, Vietnam, and Mexico where companies could exploit vulnerable workers or benefit from expansive state support while the United States ran up what in absolute terms is the highest trade deficit in the history of the world," Greer wrote.

"The rules of international trade cannot be a suicide pact," he continued, adding that the U.S. has "laid the foundation for a new global trading order," citing an agreement that the U.S. had just signed with the European Union.

Harrison said the U.S. position is that “MFN was designed for a world where countries broadly played by similar rules."

"Washington now argues that some countries benefit from WTO access while pursuing state-led industrial policies or maintaining non-market practices."

WATCH | Carney seeks stronger ties with European Union: Carney pledges deeper ties in EU speech but offers few details | Duration closed caption 3:07 A day after the door was opened for Canada to become an 'associate member' of the EU, Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered a speech at the European Parliament pledging deeper ties with Europe, though questions remain on what that includes.

However, changing the MFN rules would lead to more uncertainty and confusion for businesses that rely on international supply chains, Harrison said.

"It impacts, ultimately, not just the trading relationship between Canada and the U.S., but trading relationships around the world that are governed by the rules based system," she said.

The WTO has long struggled to find ⁠agreement on reforms in the consensus-based organization, as its 166 members are at different stages of economic development and often have ​conflicting interests.

On Sept. 15, the organization urged its members to reform global trade rules or risk a slide into fragmentation that could significantly reduce ‌economic output and hit poorer countries hardest.

In its annual report, the WTO said existing rules have struggled to keep pace with shifts in economic power, the rise of industrial policy, digital trade and escalating political tensions between major powers.

World.title: Russian airstrikes kill 4 in Kyiv region, including child, Ukraine officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and nearby areas killed four people, damaged energy infrastructure and shrouded the ‌capital in smoke, Ukrainian officials said Wednesday.
