Prime Minister Godwin Friday of St. Vincent and the Grenadines took the witness stand on 29 September 2026 in an election petition over his Canadian citizenship. His foreign minister, Dwight Fitzgerald Bramble, faced the same questions in the High Court in Kingstown, the capital.

Who Is Being Challenged, and Why

St. Vincent and the Grenadines is an island nation of the eastern Caribbean and a member of the Commonwealth. Friday’s New Democratic Party (NDP) won 14 of its 15 elected seats on 27 November 2025.

It was the second-largest win in the country’s history, after the NDP took all 15 seats in 1989. It ended the long rule of the Unity Labour Party (ULP) of Ralph Gonsalves, now opposition leader.

Two defeated ULP candidates then filed election petitions, court cases that challenge the result in a constituency.

Carlos Williams contests Friday’s win in the Northern Grenadines, where Friday took 2,185 votes to his 339. Luke Browne contests Bramble’s win in East Kingstown, which Bramble won by 1,001 votes.

What the Constitution Says

Section 25 of the 1979 Constitution says a candidate must be a Commonwealth citizen aged 21 or older.

Section 26(1)(a) then sets a bar. It disqualifies anyone who, “by virtue of his own act”, is under “acknowledgment of allegiance” to “a foreign power or state”.

The dispute began before the vote. Electors lodged objections to both nominations on Nomination Day, 10 November 2025, and notices urged voters not to back either man.

The petitioners argue that Canada is a foreign state. Both men applied for Canadian citizenship themselves, took its oath and hold Canadian passports, they say.

The defence argues that Canada, as a Commonwealth country, is not foreign in the sense the Constitution means. Friday has sat in Parliament since 2001 and Bramble since 2020, and both held Canadian citizenship before they were first elected.

Godwin Friday, Prime Minister of St. Vincent and the Grenadines, who was cross-examined on 29 September over his Canadian citizenship.

A Day on the Witness Stand

Justice Gertel Thom, a retired appeal judge sitting in the High Court, heard the case. The petitioners’ lawyers asked both men what their oath of allegiance to Canada means and where their loyalties lie, iWitness News reported.

They asked when the men obtained Canadian passports and why they never gave up Canadian citizenship. Friday was also questioned on a report he prepared on his status and on earlier comments to the media.

Professor Hamid Ghany, a Caribbean expert on constitutions and parliaments, testified by video on the same day. On 28 September a Canadian lawyer, Joel Goberman, explained the meaning of Canada’s citizenship oath.

Two Legal Teams From Trinidad

Both sides hired senior lawyers from Trinidad and Tobago. Stuart Young, a former prime minister of that country, leads the petitioners’ team.

Young said the question put again and again was why the two men kept Canadian citizenship while seeking to serve Vincentians. “He chooses to hold a Canadian passport,” Young told reporters.

Anand Ramlogan, a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago, leads the defence. He called Canada’s oath “symbolic” and said Friday had never hidden his dual citizenship.

A street in central Kingstown, the capital where the election petitions over dual citizenship are being heard.

The Bills Waiting in Parliament

In April 2026 the government tabled two bills to “clarify what is a foreign power or state”, in Friday’s words. One would amend the Constitution and the other the election law.

Friday said the bills would go to a parliamentary committee for public input. iWitness News reported that the government would not pass them before the petitions are decided.

The opposition called the bills an insurance policy against the petitions. Young raised them in court, saying that if a change is not necessary, “that becomes a question”.

What Happens Next

Hearings were set to continue on 30 September, with more expert witnesses. Young said the evidence should close this week, after which both sides return for closing arguments.

The court has not set a date for its judgment. Friday said on 28 September that his side respects the court and is “confident about the case”.

What It Means for Residents and Investors

The case matters beyond two seats, because many Vincentians live abroad. The ruling will show whether a second citizenship is compatible with a seat in Parliament.

For investors, the NDP’s majority is wide, and it would keep 12 of 15 seats even if both men lost theirs. The larger question is continuity at the top, which the judge’s ruling will settle in its own time.

Two defeated opposition candidates say Prime Minister Godwin Friday and minister Dwight Fitzgerald Bramble were not qualified to stand in November 2025. They argue that Canadian citizenship is allegiance to a foreign state under Section 26 of the Constitution.

Who won the 2025 election in St. Vincent and the Grenadines?

Godwin Friday’s New Democratic Party won 14 of 15 seats on 27 November 2025. Ralph Gonsalves of the Unity Labour Party became opposition leader.

No date has been set. Evidence was expected to close in the week of 28 September 2026, followed by closing arguments from both sides.

World.title: Missing Surinamese Men: Guyana Police Detain ‘Demon’ Cromwell’s Relatives
World.content:
GUYANA · CRIME

Key Facts — Who is missing Siegello Lorenzo Van Dalen, 28, and Derryl Danillo Bont, 29, were last seen on 29 August 2026 in Nickerie, Suriname, heading for Guyana by boat (Guyanese and Surinamese police).

— Detentions The wife and a brother of Mark ‘Demon’ Cromwell were in Guyana police custody on 29 September 2026 as part of the probe (Demerara Waves, Kaieteur News).

— Blocked search Villagers in Vigilance, east of Georgetown, stopped police from searching Cromwell’s house on 29 September; roads were blocked with burning debris and a truck was torched (Kaieteur News).

— The link Police sources say the two men were last seen alive getting into a white car registered to Cromwell’s wife (Demerara Waves, 29 September 2026).

— Background Cromwell, a former policeman, was sanctioned by the US Treasury on 5 June 2025 over alleged cocaine trafficking; he has not been charged in Guyana over those allegations (Demerara Waves).

The search for two missing Surinamese men has led Guyana police to the family of a US-sanctioned former officer. It also brought a tense night in his village.

Guyana police detained the wife and a brother of Mark “Demon” Cromwell on 29 September 2026 over two missing Surinamese men. Their attempt to search his house in the village of Vigilance was blocked by residents, and a night of unrest followed.

Two Men Who Never Arrived

Siegello Lorenzo Van Dalen, 28, and Derryl Danillo Bont, 29, come from the Surinamese districts of Saramacca and Wanica. On 28 August they left home in a Toyota Vitz for Nickerie, the town on Suriname’s border with Guyana.

Police say they were last seen on 29 August, getting out of the car at Clarasluis in Nickerie. From there they planned to cross to Guyana by boat, across the Corentyne River that divides the two countries.

Suriname’s police and the Guyana Police Force issued separate missing-person bulletins on 19 September. The next day Wendell Blanhum, head of Guyana’s Criminal Investigations Department, said the men had not been seen in Guyana.

A Car Leads Police to Vigilance

The investigation then turned to Vigilance, a village on the East Coast of Demerara, east of the capital Georgetown. Police sources told the news site Demerara Waves that the men were last seen alive entering a white car.

That car, the sources said, is registered in the name of Cromwell’s wife. Police called his house “a building of prime interest” and obtained a search warrant.

On 29 September officers tried to carry out the search but were stopped by people in the village. Cromwell was not at home, the Surinamese newspaper Suriname Herald reported.

Guyana Police Force vehicles lined up in a row; officers detained two relatives of Mark Cromwell over the missing Surinamese men.

Fire on the Public Road

Later that day, residents blocked roads with burning debris, Kaieteur News reported. A lorry belonging to a road construction crew was set on fire on the Vigilance Public Road.

Suriname Herald, citing Guyanese reports, said two masked men on a motorcycle attacked the road crew in the afternoon. Several shots were then heard in the village, and it is not known who fired them.

Officers who tried to put out the fires met a hostile reaction, Kaieteur News said. The flames also threatened power poles belonging to Guyana Power and Light, the state electricity company.

Who Is ‘Demon’

Cromwell, also known as “Diamond”, is a former Guyanese policeman. On 5 June 2025 the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which runs American sanctions, listed him.

OFAC described him as a violent drug trafficker and an associate of Paul Daby Jr, who was sanctioned the same day. Senior police superintendent Himnauth Sawh was also named in that action over alleged cocaine trafficking.

None of the Guyanese named has been charged locally over those allegations, and the United States has not requested their extradition. Separately, Guyana police have sought Cromwell since 2024 over the abduction of former policeman Delon Alexander in Buxton.

A church and parsonage in Nieuw Nickerie, the Surinamese border town from which the two missing men planned to cross the Corentyne by boat.

What Police Have and Have Not Said

Police said the wife and brother remained in custody as part of the probe, Demerara Waves reported late on 29 September. The Guyana Police Force has not officially named them or said whether they are suspects or witnesses.

The police have made no public statement on the blocked search, the fires or Cromwell’s own role. No official link has been drawn between the missing men and the earlier cases against him.

The families in Suriname have now waited a month for news. Both police forces are asking anyone with information to come forward.

A Shared River, a Shared Problem

Guyana and Suriname are neighbours on the northern coast of South America. The Corentyne River separates Nickerie from the Guyanese region of Berbice, and small passenger boats cross it.

The case shows how quickly a crime on one bank becomes a matter for both states. The two police forces worked together on the bulletins, and cooperation between them is the main hope for an answer.

What It Means for Travellers and Residents

For travellers between the two countries, crossings through official border posts leave a record of who crossed and when. Such records help police trace a person’s route if something goes wrong.

For residents of the East Coast of Demerara, the unrest showed how tense the area can become around police operations. The next step to watch is whether police complete the search and give the families an account.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the missing Surinamese men in Guyana?

They are Siegello Lorenzo Van Dalen, 28, and Derryl Danillo Bont, 29, from the districts of Saramacca and Wanica. They were last seen on 29 August 2026 in Nickerie, preparing to cross to Guyana by boat.

Who is Mark ‘Demon’ Cromwell?

He is a former Guyanese policeman, placed on a US Treasury sanctions list on 5 June 2025 over alleged drug trafficking. Guyana police have also sought him since 2024 over the abduction of a former officer.

Has anyone been charged in the case?

No charges had been announced by 30 September 2026. Police said Cromwell’s wife and brother were in custody, but they have not said whether the two are suspects.





What is the background to Missing Surinamese Men?





Cromwell, a former policeman, was sanctioned by the US Treasury on 5 June 2025 over alleged cocaine trafficking; he has not been charged in Guyana over those allegations (Demerara Waves).

World.title: French Guiana Homicides Reach 45 in 2026 as Prefect Orders Weapons Checks
World.content:
FRENCH GUIANA · SECURITY

Key Facts — Killings this year French Guiana has recorded 45 homicides since 1 January 2026, already above the 43 of all 2025 (prefecture count, 28 September 2026).

— Guns seized Police and gendarmes have seized 370 firearms so far in 2026, against about 300 at the same point in 2025 (state services, via France-Guyane).

— New sanctions The prefect has started procedures to bar two party organisers and venues from holding events for three months after a shooting on 6 September 2026.

— Main pattern More than half of the killings in the territory are settlings of scores between criminals, according to the authorities (28 September 2026).

— Longer trend Homicides fell from 53 in 2024 to 43 in 2025, and armed robberies dropped 29% (prefecture 2025 security review, February 2026).

French Guiana has recorded 45 homicides so far in 2026, more than in all of 2025. The prefect, the French state’s top official there, wants more firearms seized and has moved to ban two event venues.

What the Prefect Announced

French Guiana is an overseas department of France on the northeast coast of South America, between Brazil and Suriname. Prefect Antoine Poussier spoke to reporters on 28 September 2026, the newspaper France-Guyane reported.

He said he has asked for more police and gendarmerie checks, above all to find firearms. Security forces have seized 370 guns since January, against about 300 at the same point last year.

“We want to make the circulation of weapons as difficult as possible,” Poussier said. “It is firearms that turn crime in French Guiana into very violent crime”.

Two Venues Face Three-Month Bans

The prefect also wants to use administrative sanctions more often, meaning penalties imposed by the state without a court trial. He has opened a procedure to bar the venue Le Diamant from hosting events for three months.

A second procedure would bar La Soyana, the organiser of a party on 6 September, from organising events for three months. The prefecture’s formal order had not yet been published on 29 September.

The sanctions follow a shooting at that party in the Zone Collery district of Cayenne, the capital. Four men aged 20 to 30 were shot at about 4:40 a.m., mostly in the legs, and survived.

Two men have since been placed in pre-trial detention. La Soyana said it “deplores the facts” and sent its thoughts to the wounded.

Creole houses at a street corner in Cayenne, capital of French Guiana, where homicides this year have already passed the 2025 total.

A Month of Deadly Shootings

On 4 September Anderson Marcellus, a 14-year-old handball fan, was shot dead in the Eau-Lisette housing estate in Cayenne. His family and a citizens’ group called a silent march in his memory on 16 September.

Early on 23 September a woman of about 50 was shot dead in Kourou, home of Europe’s space centre. Gendarmes arrested a Brazilian suspect, reportedly her former partner, later that morning.

The same afternoon, gunmen killed the popular singer Badbay Mono, whose real name was Christopher Robinson, outside a family home in Cayenne. The prefect gave no details on that case, and police have not named a suspect.

The latest killing came on 25 September on the Oyapock, the river that forms the border with Brazil.

Guns and Organised Crime

More than half of the killings are settlings of scores between criminals, according to the authorities. In 2025, nearly two thirds were such settlings of scores, tied to illegal gold mining or control of territory.

“Police and gendarmes share the feeling that some of these crimes and settlings of scores are linked to Brazilian factions,” Poussier said. In Brazil, factions are organised criminal gangs, several of which began inside prisons.

In late 2024 the gendarmerie counted nearly 400 people loyal to such factions in French Guiana. Most belonged to Comando Vermelho, from Rio de Janeiro, or Família Terror do Amapá, from the neighbouring Brazilian state.

The gendarmerie station in Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, one of the police posts behind the prefect’s push to seize more firearms in French Guiana.

What Has Been Improving

The rise follows a calmer year. In 2025 homicides fell to 43 from 53, and armed robberies dropped 29% to 593, the prefecture said in February.

Total recorded crime fell 4.6% in 2025, to 19,918 offences. Gun seizures, however, slipped from 528 in 2024 to 482 in 2025.

The faster pace of seizures this year reverses that trend.

Even in the better year, homicide rates in French Guiana stayed close to ten times the French national average. The territory’s worst recent year was 2023, with about 60 killings.

Local Leaders Call for Calm

The Territorial Collectivity of French Guiana (CTG), the elected local government, said on 24 September that “no violence must ever become ordinary”. It called for calm and described security as a shared responsibility.

The citizens’ group Tròp Violans, which organised the march for Anderson Marcellus, spoke of a general weariness with violence. “We cannot accept that a young person can die under bullets in his neighbourhood,” it wrote.

What It Means for Residents and Visitors

For residents, the practical change is more frequent police checks and a harder line on events where guns appear. Organisers of parties and concerts now face the risk of a temporary ban.

Most of the violence is concentrated in disputes between criminal groups, not in attacks on visitors. The real test will be whether seizures and sanctions bring the count back toward last year’s lower level.

How many homicides has French Guiana recorded in 2026?

The prefecture counted 45 homicides between 1 January and late September 2026. That is already more than the 43 recorded in all of 2025.

What is the prefect of French Guiana doing about gun violence?

Prefect Antoine Poussier has ordered more checks to find firearms, and 370 have been seized so far in 2026. He has also opened procedures to ban two event organisers and venues for three months after a shooting.

Who is behind the violence in French Guiana?

The authorities say more than half of killings are settlings of scores between criminals. The prefect said police and gendarmes suspect links to Brazilian criminal factions in some cases.

World.title: ICE Arrests of Cubans Up 463% as US Agents Shift to Quieter, Wider Tactics

CUBA · MIGRATION

Key Facts — What happened US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has replaced large raids with quick, low-profile arrests, Periódico Cubano reported on 29 September 2026.

— The Cuban figure Arrests of Cubans rose 463% between late 2024 and early 2026, from fewer than 200 a month to more than 1,000.

— Who is exposed More than 42,000 Cubans in the United States hold final deportation orders, Periódico Cubano reported, citing The Guardian.

— The brake Removals have stayed near 1,200 people a day, held back by a lack of flights and limits set by receiving countries.

— The court backdrop On 29 September 2026 the US Supreme Court let deportations to third countries resume until it hears the case in December.

ICE arrests of Cubans have multiplied as US agents trade armoured raids for 90-second street arrests and deals with local police.

ICE arrests of Cubans in the US rose 463% between late 2024 and early 2026, as agents turned to quieter, faster methods. More than 42,000 Cubans now hold final deportation orders, the Cuban news site Periódico Cubano reported on 29 September 2026.

From armoured raids to 90-second arrests

ICE, the US agency that detains and deports migrants, changed course after its 2025 raids drew political criticism. Those operations used armoured vehicles in residential areas and patrols in public spaces.

In February, President Donald Trump said, “I learned that maybe we could use a little bit of a softer touch”. In March, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told senators he wanted the department out of the daily headlines within six months.

The volume of arrests did not fall with the noise. Arrests now happen as people leave home, wait for a school bus, buy fuel or drive to work, Periódico Cubano reported.

“The detentions are happening in a flash,” said Gracie Willis, a rapid-response lawyer with the National Immigration Project. She put the time from ICE’s arrival to the car leaving at about 90 seconds.

Local police join the effort

A key tool is the 287(g) programme, named after a section of US immigration law. It lets state and local police carry out some immigration duties for ICE.

By 15 September, ICE had signed more than 2,500 such agreements. In July, local and state forces took part in 13% of ICE-linked arrests, against under 5% a year earlier.

Willis describes an enforcement made invisible, with agents in unmarked cars, behind masks and inside local police departments. She says the programme multiplies ICE’s reach far beyond its own officers.

The Department of Homeland Security now has more than 22,000 officers and staff. Congress approved US$75 billion in extra funding for its operations.

Calle Ocho in Miami’s Little Havana, heart of the Cuban community in the United States, where many families now follow ICE arrests closely.

Why Cubans are among the most exposed

The 463% rise in arrests of Cubans first appeared in an April study by the Cato Institute, a Washington think tank. It found monthly arrests went from under 200 in late 2024 to over 1,000 by early 2026.

Periódico Cubano reported that more than 42,000 Cuban citizens have final deportation orders pending in the United States. A final order means the immigration courts have finished with the case.

One Cuban resident of Miami was detained outside his own home during everyday errands. The profile of detainees has also changed: in July, fewer than a quarter had criminal records.

In December 2024, that share had been almost 60%, Periódico Cubano reported. The widening net therefore reaches many people with no criminal past.

The brake on deportations

More arrests have not produced the same rise in deportations. Removals have stayed at about 1,200 people a day, even though August saw more arrests than earlier months.

Periódico Cubano named three limits: logistics, a shortage of available flights and restrictions set by some receiving countries. For Cubans, the receiving country is often not Cuba itself.

The Versailles restaurant in Little Havana, a long-standing meeting place for Miami’s Cuban exile community.

The Supreme Court backdrop

On 29 September 2026 the US Supreme Court paused a Boston ruling that required notice before deportation to a third country. A third country is one that is not the migrant’s own.

The case, D.V.D. v. Department of Homeland Security, carries the initials of its lead plaintiff, a Cuban man ordered removed in 2017. He fears being sent to a country where he would lose access to psychiatric treatment, his lawyers told the court.

Three of the nine justices said they would have refused the government’s request. The full case will be heard in December 2026.

Until then, the government can apply its own, shorter notice rules for third-country removals. It has not said how many Cubans it plans to send to third countries.

Complaints of profiling and force

Immigration lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said, “We are seeing a lot of racial profiling”. She cited Brian José Morales García, born in Denver, who was deported to Mexico although he says he is a US citizen.

On 20 September an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan delivery worker, in Austin, Texas. Four days later a Guatemalan man died in a road crash in Grand Rapids, Michigan, while fleeing federal agents.

What it means for Cuban families

For Cubans in the United States, the risk now sits less in large raids than in ordinary daily routines. Families with a relative under a final order face the greatest uncertainty.

ICE has not published a breakdown of how many arrested Cubans have since been deported. The December hearing will shape where those removals can lead.

More: Cuba news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much have ICE arrests of Cubans increased?

Arrests of Cubans rose 463% between late 2024 and early 2026, from under 200 a month to over 1,000, according to a Cato Institute study cited by Cuban media. Periódico Cubano repeated the figure on 29 September 2026, citing The Guardian.

What is a 287(g) agreement?

It is a section 287(g) deal under US immigration law, letting state and local police perform some immigration duties for ICE. By 15 September 2026, ICE had signed more than 2,500 of them.

Are deportations rising as fast as arrests?

No. Removals have stayed near 1,200 people a day, Periódico Cubano reported. Logistics, a lack of flights and limits set by receiving countries hold them back.





What is the background to ICE Arrests Of Cubans?





On 29 September 2026 the US Supreme Court let deportations to third countries resume until it hears the case in December.

World.title: Haiti Moïse Assassination Trial: Pastor Christian Sanon Faces Miami Jury
World.content:
HAITI · JUSTICE

Key Facts — What happened The trial of Christian Emmanuel Sanon, 67, opened with jury selection in Miami federal court on Monday 28 September 2026.

— The charges Sanon, a Haitian-American pastor and physician, has pleaded not guilty to eight charges, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Haiti’s president.

— The court US District Judge Jacqueline Becerra of the Southern District of Florida is presiding, as in the case’s first trial.

— The case so far A jury convicted four men in May 2026, and eight co-conspirators had already pleaded guilty, the US Attorney’s Office said.

— Still open No trial date has been made public for the 18 suspects Haiti handed to US agents on 20 September 2026.

The Moïse assassination trial is back in a Miami courtroom, where a Haitian-American pastor denies plotting the 2021 killing of Haiti’s president.

Haiti’s Moïse assassination trial resumed in Miami on 28 September 2026, with Haitian-American pastor Christian Emmanuel Sanon in the dock. He is accused of plotting to kill or kidnap President Jovenel Moïse, and opening statements followed on Tuesday 29 September.

A pastor on trial five years later

Sanon, 67, is a physician and pastor who lives in Palm Beach County, Florida, and holds both Haitian and US citizenship. He has pleaded not guilty to eight charges, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person outside the United States.

That charge carries a possible life sentence. US District Judge Jacqueline Becerra, who presided over the first trial in the case, is hearing this one too.

Jury selection took place on Monday 28 September. Gunmen had killed Moïse, 53, at his home in Port-au-Prince, Haiti’s capital, on 7 July 2021.

Two portraits in the opening statements

Assistant US Attorney Sean T. McLaughlin told jurors that Sanon was driven by “greed, arrogance and power,” the Miami Herald reported. He said Sanon flew to Haiti on a private jet with ballistic vests for a Colombian team.

Early plans to kidnap Moïse and put Sanon in his place failed, the prosecutor said, but Sanon pressed on. “Sanon doesn’t give up,” McLaughlin told the jury.

Defence lawyer Humberto Dominguez did not dispute that Moïse was killed, but said his client was not responsible. He placed Sanon’s ambitions in the turmoil of 2021, when Moïse’s term of office was in dispute.

Dominguez also attacked the credibility of cooperating witnesses who have pleaded guilty. “A person who kills another person, what would they not do for freedom to reduce their time?” he asked.

Jovenel Moïse, Haiti’s president, during a state visit to Taiwan in 2018; he was killed at his home in July 2021.

The widow’s testimony

Former first lady Martine Moïse was the first witness, as she was in the earlier trial. She described being woken by gunfire in the middle of the night and her husband saying, “Honey, we are dead”.

She was shot in the arm in their bedroom and watched as her husband was killed. The couple’s two children hid in a bathroom downstairs.

Defence lawyers began their cross-examination on Tuesday and aim to show that the president had many enemies. Martine Moïse was due back on the stand on Wednesday 30 September.

How the case reached Miami

US prosecutors say the plot was planned and financed largely in South Florida. That gives US federal courts jurisdiction over the conspiracy.

In May 2026, a federal jury convicted four men: Arcángel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages. The charges included conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person outside the United States, and they await sentencing.

Eight co-conspirators had pleaded guilty before that trial, and six of them testified, the US Attorney’s Office said on 8 May. Those guilty pleas are why cooperating witnesses now sit at the centre of the defence strategy.

Houses on the hills of Pétion-Ville above Port-au-Prince, the area where President Jovenel Moïse lived and was killed in July 2021.

A prosecution that keeps growing

On 20 September Haiti handed 18 suspects to US agents, as we reported. They include former Justice Ministry official Joseph Félix Badio and former Colombian soldiers, and belong to a 30-defendant indictment unsealed in Miami.

The same indictment alleges that pandemic relief loans were fraudulently obtained and laundered to help pay for the plot. Sanon’s lawyers called it a “surprising new indictment” days before his trial, the Associated Press reported.

One of the transferred Colombians, Victor Albeiro Pineda Cardona, pleaded not guilty on 28 September and was denied bail. Prosecutors say he belonged to the team that entered the president’s house first.

What it means for Haiti

Haiti’s own investigation has not reached trial in five years, slowed by gang violence and judges stepping down. For many Haitians, the Miami courtroom is where the facts of the plot are being tested in public.

The trial also shows how far Haiti still depends on outside institutions. Its government cited major difficulties in its own proceedings when it sent the 18 suspects to Miami.

No court has yet ruled on who in Haiti knew of the plot. On Tuesday, Martine Moïse declined to name the people she had once suspected.

What comes next

The trial continues this week with the cross-examination of Martine Moïse. The court has not published an expected end date.

No trial date has been made public for Badio and the other newly transferred defendants. Their cases will move through the same Miami court in the months ahead.

More: Haiti news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is on trial for the assassination of Jovenel Moïse in Miami?

Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a 67-year-old Haitian-American pastor and physician from Florida, is on trial. He has pleaded not guilty to eight charges, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person outside the United States.

Why is the Moïse case being tried in the United States?

US prosecutors say the plot was planned and financed largely in South Florida, which gives US federal courts jurisdiction. Haiti’s own investigation has stalled for five years amid gang violence.

Has anyone been convicted over the killing?

Yes. A Miami jury convicted four men in May 2026, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida. Eight co-conspirators had pleaded guilty before that trial.





What is the background to Moïse Assassination Trial?





No trial date has been made public for the 18 suspects Haiti handed to US agents on 20 September 2026.

World.title: Dominican Republic Debt Interest Passes Education Spending by 18 September
World.content:
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · PUBLIC FINANCES

Key Facts — Spent so far From 1 January to 18 September 2026 the state paid RD$234.6 billion (about US$3.94 billion) in debt interest and fees, against RD$230.4 billion (about US$3.87 billion) spent by the Education Ministry (Hoy, citing the budget office).

— The gap Interest was ahead by RD$4.2 billion (about US$71 million), a timing effect: at the end of June education was still ahead (DIGEPRES).

— Full-year budget The revised 2026 budget still gives education more: RD$330.0 billion (about US$5.55 billion) versus RD$311.0 billion for interest (Hoy, Ministry of Finance and Economy).

— 2027 draft The 2027 budget bill sent to Congress in September 2026 plans RD$365.6 billion (about US$6.15 billion) for the Education Ministry and RD$351.3 billion for interest (Ministry of Finance and Economy, DIGEPRES).

— Exchange rate Conversions use the central bank buying rate of RD$59.49 per US$1 on 29 September 2026.

Dominican Republic debt interest paid this year has edged past what the Education Ministry has spent. Schools still hold the larger annual budget.

The Dominican Republic paid RD$234.6 billion (about US$3.94 billion) in public debt interest between 1 January and 18 September 2026. That is RD$4.2 billion (about US$71 million) more than the Education Ministry spent in the same period. The newspaper Hoy reported the figures from budget office data.

What the Budget Data Show

Hoy based its front-page report on the execution data of the General Budget Directorate (DIGEPRES), the office that tracks state spending. The Education Ministry, known as Minerd, spent RD$230.4 billion (about US$3.87 billion) in the period.

Of the interest bill, RD$151.3 billion (about US$2.54 billion) went to foreign creditors and RD$82.3 billion to domestic ones. Fees and other bank charges on the debt added RD$1.0 billion (about US$17 million).

Hoy put the interest paid so far at 2.7% of gross domestic product (GDP), the total value of the economy’s output. It noted that interest had overtaken education spending at least once before this year.

A Question of Timing, Not of Budgets

The headline gap is small and partly a matter of calendar. Interest falls due on fixed dates, while ministries spend their budgets gradually through the year.

At the end of June the picture was reversed. DIGEPRES data show Minerd had spent RD$148.4 billion (about US$2.49 billion), while interest and debt fees reached RD$142.6 billion.

For the full year, education keeps the larger share. The revised 2026 budget gives Minerd RD$330.0 billion (about US$5.55 billion) and interest RD$311.0 billion (about US$5.23 billion).

Children in a computer class at a school in Guaricano, Santo Domingo; the Education Ministry still holds the larger annual budget.

Why the 2026 Budget Was Revised

In July 2026 the government sent Congress a bill to modify the 2026 budget law, Law 99-25. It cited volatile international markets, trade swings and a new tax law, Law 30-26.

The bill cut the net allocation for public debt and moved money towards health, security and public works. It reclassified RD$2.0 billion (about US$34 million) of Minerd’s budget within the ministry, without a net cut, the finance ministry said.

Congress approved the changes, and the president signed them into law as Law 43-26 on 27 July 2026. Hoy’s comparison uses these revised figures.

What the 2027 Draft Budget Plans

On 23 September 2026 the Ministry of Finance and Economy sent the 2027 budget bill to Congress. It gives Minerd RD$365.6 billion (about US$6.14 billion), 10.1% more than the approved 2026 budget.

DIGEPRES projects RD$351.3 billion (about US$5.91 billion) for debt interest in 2027. Interest would take 22.9% of the central government’s current spending.

The government says the education function keeps its long-standing target of 4% of GDP. The draft also sets aside RD$30.8 billion (about US$518 million) for school meals for about 1.96 million pupils.

Health would get RD$198.7 billion (about US$3.34 billion), 10.0% more than in 2026. Capital spending on investment projects would rise 19.7% to RD$257.8 billion (about US$4.33 billion), the largest on record, the ministry says.

Calle las Damas in the colonial quarter of Santo Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic, where debt interest now outpaces school spending. Photo: "Calle las Damas, Santo Domingo, Zona Colonial" by Desox7x, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The Debt Behind the Interest Bill

Non-financial public sector debt stood at US$68.0 billion on 31 May 2026, equal to 48.3% of GDP, according to DIGEPRES. About 71% of it is owed to foreign lenders.

The average interest rate on foreign debt was 6.5% in March 2026. The government projects debt to fall to 46.3% of GDP by the end of 2026 and to about 44.5% by 2030.

The 2027 plan keeps a small primary surplus, meaning revenue covers spending before interest. The overall deficit, interest included, is set at 3.4% of GDP.

Pressures and Buffers

Interest payments did not rise this year. In the first half of 2026 they were 5.5% lower than a year earlier, DIGEPRES data show.

The budget office still sees risk abroad. It warns that slightly higher long-term US Treasury yields could make long-term foreign borrowing more expensive for the country.

The Dominican economy is still growing, and the government expects real growth of 4.75% in 2027. Growth makes a given debt easier to carry, which is why the ratio is projected to fall.

What It Means for Residents and Investors

For families, the comparison shows how much of each tax peso goes to past borrowing rather than classrooms. Schools still receive more over a full year, but the margin is narrow.

For bondholders, the data point to a government paying on time and planning a slowly falling debt ratio. Congress must approve the 2027 budget before it takes effect on 1 January 2027.

More: Dominican Republic news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the Dominican Republic now spend more on debt interest than on education?

Only in year-to-date payments. Between 1 January and 18 September 2026, interest reached RD$234.6 billion (about US$3.94 billion) against RD$230.4 billion spent by the Education Ministry. The full 2026 budget still gives education more.

How much will the Dominican Republic pay in interest in 2027?

The budget office projects RD$351.3 billion, about US$5.91 billion, in the 2027 draft budget. The Education Ministry would receive RD$365.6 billion (about US$6.15 billion).

How large is Dominican public debt?

Non-financial public sector debt was US$68.0 billion on 31 May 2026, or 48.3% of GDP. The government expects the ratio to fall to 46.3% by the end of 2026.





What is the background to Dominican Republic Debt Interest?





Conversions use the central bank buying rate of RD$59.49 per US$1 on 29 September 2026.

World.title: El Salvador CAF Talks: Pledge on Health and Schools but No New Loan Figure
World.content:
EL SALVADOR · DEVELOPMENT FINANCE

Key Facts — Meeting CAF chief Sergio Díaz-Granados met President Nayib Bukele in San Salvador on 28 September 2026 (CAF).

— The commitment Both sides agreed to deepen CAF’s support in education, health, aeronautics and the recovery of public spaces; CAF named no new loan amount (CAF, 28 September 2026).

— Airports CAF approved US$320 million in July 2024 for the ‘El Salvador Vuela’ programme, including the new Pacific International Airport (CAF).

— Schools CAF has approved US$400 million in credits since 2022 for El Salvador’s education modernisation reform (CAF, 28 September 2026).

— Membership El Salvador joined CAF in 2022; the bank also lent US$145 million in 2024 for the country’s first submarine internet cable (CAF).

The El Salvador CAF meeting produced a promise of more support for health, schools, airports and public spaces. It builds on loans approved since 2022.

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele and CAF, a regional development bank, agreed on 28 September 2026 to deepen the bank’s support. The four areas are education, health, aeronautics and the recovery of public spaces, but CAF announced no new loan amount.

A Meeting at the Presidential Palace

Sergio Díaz-Granados, executive president of CAF, met Bukele at Casa Presidencial, the presidential palace in San Salvador. CAF published its account the same day, and the Salvadoran news site La Página reported it on 29 September.

CAF, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, is owned by its member countries. Its board is made up of finance ministers, central bank governors and senior economic officials of those states.

According to CAF, the two men reviewed the relationship since El Salvador joined the bank in 2022. They then discussed the country’s next priorities.

What CAF Actually Committed

The concrete outcome is a pledge, not a signed loan. CAF said both sides agreed to deepen its support ‘with financial capacity, agility and mobilisation of resources from strategic partners’.

The four named areas are education, health, aeronautical development and the recovery of public spaces. CAF did not publish a figure, a timetable or a specific health project.

Díaz-Granados described the link as a mature, long-term relationship. He said CAF is willing to keep mobilising its own funds and those of partners for new investments, especially new enabling infrastructure.

El Salvador’s international airport near San Salvador; aeronautics is one of the four areas in the new CAF commitment. Photo: Mauricio G. Campos, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

The Airport Loan Already on the Table

The most visible CAF project is ‘El Salvador Vuela’ (El Salvador Flies), an aviation programme. CAF’s board approved a US$320 million loan for it on 18 July 2024.

The programme has three parts. It covers the new Pacific International Airport in the east, a remodelled Ilopango airport near San Salvador and a new Tonalá aerodrome.

CAF said in 2024 that the plan follows the Infrastructure Master Plan 2030 and the National Tourism Plan. Both plans belong to the Bukele government’s own development programme.

During his visit, Díaz-Granados toured the Pacific airport site. CAF says the programme aims to cut the cost and time of air travel, lift tourism and improve disaster response.

Schools and the Internet Cable

Education is the second pillar. Since 2022 CAF has approved US$400 million in credits for El Salvador’s Education System Modernisation Reform.

The money goes to school buildings, digital equipment, teacher training and closing the digital gap. Díaz-Granados visited the Escuela OEI school in Santa Tecla with Education Minister Karla Trigueros.

CAF says the reform is already showing positive results, without publishing figures. It will keep funding the reform and offering technical help so that it reaches the whole school system.

In the same July 2024 decision, CAF approved US$145 million for El Salvador’s first submarine internet cable. The bank said then that faster internet would support online education, telemedicine and electronic public services.

That cable project is now moving through tenders and contracts. It links the school agenda to the country’s wider push for digital connectivity.

The historic centre of San Salvador, where the recovery of public spaces is one of the areas CAF has pledged to support.

Why a Small Country Borrows From CAF

El Salvador uses the US dollar, so all these amounts are in dollars. Development banks such as CAF usually lend for longer periods than private markets, which suits airports and schools.

Since joining, El Salvador has widened its work with CAF from single projects to a broader investment agenda, the bank says. That agenda so far covers connectivity, aviation, infrastructure, education and digital transformation.

The Other Side of the Ledger

Every CAF credit is a loan the state must repay with interest. In El Salvador, foreign loans to the state also need approval from the Legislative Assembly before money flows.

The new pledge therefore sets a direction rather than a sum. Its real weight will show only when specific health or public-space loans reach CAF’s board and the Assembly.

What It Means for Residents and Investors

For residents, the visible results so far are building sites: an eastern airport, school upgrades and a planned cable. Health is now named as a priority, but no project has been described.

For contractors, CAF-financed work has included international tenders, such as the recent consultancy for the submarine cable. The next signal will be the first new operation CAF approves under this agenda.

More: El Salvador’s first submarine cable. El Salvador news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did CAF promise El Salvador on 28 September 2026?

CAF and President Bukele agreed to deepen the bank’s support in education, health, aeronautics and the recovery of public spaces. CAF did not announce a new loan amount or a specific new project.

How much has CAF already lent El Salvador for airports and schools?

CAF approved US$320 million in July 2024 for the ‘El Salvador Vuela’ aviation programme. It has also approved US$400 million in credits since 2022 for the education modernisation reform.

What is CAF?

CAF is the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, owned by its member countries. El Salvador became a member in 2022.





What is the background to El Salvador CAF?





El Salvador joined CAF in 2022; the bank also lent US$145 million in 2024 for the country's first submarine internet cable (CAF).
