World.title: Costa Rica Tripled Tourism Advertising Spending Without Proven Visitor Impact
World.content:
Costa Rica more than tripled the amount of money it spent promoting itself to international tourists between 2022 and 2025, but government auditors say there is not enough evidence to show the additional spending produced a significant increase in visitors. The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT), spent $8.59 million on international advertising and marketing in 2022. By 2025, that figure had climbed to $27.75 million, an increase of 223%.

During the same period, the number of international tourists arriving in Costa Rica by air increased by 27%, from approximately 2.12 million in 2022 to 2.69 million in 2025. The figures come from a new audit by Costa Rica’s Comptroller General examining how effectively the ICT used its resources to attract international visitors between January 2022 and December 2025.

As advertising spending increased, the estimated amount spent to attract each tourist also climbed. In 2022, the figure was approximately $4 per visitor. By 2025, it had reached about $10. The Comptroller analyzed whether countries targeted by Costa Rica’s international advertising campaigns produced stronger growth in tourist arrivals than markets where the ICT did not spend money on campaigns.

The audit found differences between the two groups, but after conducting statistical tests, auditors said there was not enough evidence to conclude that the countries receiving advertising experienced significantly stronger growth because of those campaigns. That does not mean Costa Rica’s tourism advertising failed or that advertising didn’t bring any visitors here.

Instead, the audit found that the ICT has not been able to clearly demonstrate that the large increase in spending produced a corresponding increase in international arrivals. The issue is important because Costa Rica spent nearly $67 million on international tourism marketing during the four years examined by auditors.

The audit also found changes in how long tourists stay here. Visitors spent an average of 12.23 nights in Costa Rica between 2022 and 2025, but the annual average declined during that period. By 2025, the average stay had fallen to 10.3 nights, about 3.2 nights shorter than in 2022.

Tourists nevertheless continued to give Costa Rica high marks as a destination, with an average satisfaction score of 86.87% during the period examined. Employment numbers also raised concerns. Tourism represented 7.85% of national employment in 2022. By 2025, that figure had slipped to 7.61%.

Costa Rica recorded 16,475 fewer tourism jobs in 2025 than it had the previous year, according to figures included in the audit. The report comes at a complicated time for Costa Rica’s tourism industry. International arrivals have continued recovering in 2026. Between January and August, Costa Rica received about 2.19 million visitors, 5.3% more than during the same period in 2025 and close to the number recorded before the pandemic in 2019.

The United States and Canada remain by far Costa Rica’s most important tourism markets, accounting for about 67% of visitors during the first eight months of this year. At the same time, tourism businesses have raised concerns about Costa Rica becoming more expensive for international visitors, particularly because of the strong colón and rising operating costs.

The Comptroller also examined whether tourism growth was producing broader social and environmental benefits. Eight of Costa Rica’s 33 designated tourism development centers remained below 70 points on the Tourism Social Progress Index in 2024. Auditors also found limited participation among tourism businesses in several ICT programs designed to encourage sustainable and socially responsible tourism.

Businesses participating in programs such as the Certification for Sustainable Tourism, the Sofía Network and the tourism industry’s Code of Conduct represented only about 1% to 2% of the estimated number of lodging businesses here. The Comptroller concluded that the ICT needs better ways to measure whether its international marketing campaigns are actually delivering results and whether tourism promotion is producing economic, social and environmental benefits.

The ICT said it is reviewing the Comptroller’s findings and recommendations and will determine which measures can be implemented within the agency’s authority. The audit does not call for Costa Rica to stop advertising internationally. Instead, it raises a more basic question about the sharp increase in spending: whether Costa Rica has enough information to know which campaigns are working and whether the additional millions of dollars being spent are producing enough results to justify the cost.

World.title: Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska’s Comeback Gains Momentum in São Paulo
World.content:
Nadia Podoroska’s return to professional tennis has moved well beyond simply testing whether her body could handle competition again. Six months after returning from a 14-month injury layoff, the 29-year-old Argentine reached the first WTA Tour final of her career at the São Paulo Open, a result that lifted her 117 places in the rankings and provided the clearest sign yet that the former Roland Garros semifinalist is again becoming a factor on the women’s tour.

Podoroska entered the WTA 250 event ranked No. 317 and unseeded, but worked her way through the draw before producing the biggest result of her week in the semifinals. She defeated former world No. 2 Paula Badosa 6-3, 6-4, ending an 0-4 career record in WTA Tour semifinals and becoming the first Argentine woman to reach a tour-level singles final since Paula Ormaechea in Bogotá in 2013.

The title ultimately went to Spain’s Kaitlin Quevedo. After Podoroska took the opening set, the 20-year-old Spaniard rallied for a 4-6, 6-4, 6-2 victory in two hours and eight minutes to claim her first WTA title. The final was played Monday, after rain prevented its completion on Sunday. For Podoroska, however, reaching the final may have carried greater significance than the result itself.

She climbed from No. 317 to No. 200 following São Paulo, continuing a remarkable ranking recovery for a player who began the season outside the Top 1,000 and returned to competition without a ranking after more than a year away. Podoroska had not played for 440 days when she returned earlier this year. Her absence began with a hip problem and was complicated by a shoulder injury, leaving her uncertain whether she would play professionally again. During her recovery, she acknowledged that she had seriously considered retirement.

Her comeback began quietly in Argentina before gathering momentum in Europe. In April, Podoroska returned to the rankings after winning an ITF W15 tournament in Madrid, where she came through qualifying and played eight matches during the week. She followed that with a W35 title in San Gregorio in June.

The results became increasingly significant as the summer progressed. At the U.S. Open, Podoroska used a protected ranking to enter the main draw and defeated Switzerland’s Simona Waltert in the first round. It was her first Grand Slam main-draw victory since the 2024 Australian Open and another important step in a comeback that initially centered more on staying healthy than chasing rankings.

São Paulo changed the scale of the conversation. Podoroska was no longer collecting matches at lower-level tournaments. She was beating established WTA players and playing for a tour-level championship.

That carries particular weight because of where she has been before. Podoroska produced one of the biggest breakthroughs in Argentine tennis in recent years when she came through qualifying to reach the 2020 Roland Garros semifinals, defeating then-world No. 5 Elina Svitolina along the way. She eventually reached a career-high ranking of No. 36 in July 2021.

Injuries repeatedly interrupted the seasons that followed, including another lengthy absence after that French Open run. Now the ranking is moving quickly in the other direction. Podoroska started 2026 around No. 1,200, climbed to No. 574 by the end of June and reached No. 317 shortly before São Paulo. Her run to the final pushed her back to No. 200.

A return to the Top 100 remains a considerable climb, but it is no longer a distant target. More importantly, Podoroska has demonstrated that she can again compete with players much higher in the rankings. After spending much of the past two years fighting simply to stay on the court, São Paulo offered something different: evidence that the Argentine’s comeback may be turning into a genuine second chapter of her career.

World.title: Murder accused Anthony Carballo Jr. seeks sentencing indication, signaling possible guilty plea
World.content:
Murder accused Anthony Carballo Jr. seeks sentencing indication, signaling possible guilty plea

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Anthony Carballo Jr., one of two men accused of the 2023 murder of Sylvian Nigel Swift, has asked the High Court for a sentencing indication — a move signaling that he is considering a guilty plea.

Carballo Jr. and his co-accused, Christopher Pitts Jr., appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday in connection with Swift’s April 27, 2023 murder in Belize City.

During the hearing, Carballo’s attorney, Nazira Myles-Espat, informed the court that she had recently been able to review the complete disclosure and requested a sentencing indication on behalf of her client.

A sentencing indication would give Carballo an idea of the sentence the court could impose should he decide to plead guilty to murder. No guilty plea was entered on Tuesday.

Justice Pilgrim adjourned the matter to October 8, 2026, when he is expected to give the indication. The Crown has been ordered to file agreed facts by October 5.

Pitts, who is represented by attorney Andrew Bennett, remains jointly charged with Carballo.

Swift, 30, was fatally shot on Antelope Street shortly before 8 p.m. on April 27, 2023. Contemporary reports said he was standing near his home when two men on a motorcycle opened fire. Swift was struck in the arm and neck and died from his injuries.

Police pursued the fleeing motorcycle, and a 9mm pistol and the motorcycle were recovered after the suspects reportedly fell from the bike and escaped on foot.

Carballo was arraigned for Swift’s murder on May 2, 2023, while Pitts was charged several days later on May 8. The pair were subsequently indicted jointly for murder before the High Court in 2025 and initially pleaded not guilty.

The case returns to court next week for Carballo’s sentencing indication.

World.title: Dead doctor’s statement sparks legal battle in weed gummies case against former Police Exhibit Keeper
World.content:
Dead doctor’s statement sparks legal battle in weed gummies case against former Police Exhibit Keeper

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The High Court will have to determine whether a statement given by the late Dr. Cecilio Eck can be admitted into evidence in the upcoming trial of former Belize Police Department exhibit keeper Mario Bustillos over the infamous 2023 cannabis-infused gummies incident.

The issue arose during a Case Management Conference before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday, September 29.

Bustillos’ attorney, Nazira Myles-Espat, is challenging the contents and reliability of Dr. Eck’s statement. The Crown has indicated that a voir dire, or hearing within the trial to determine the admissibility of disputed evidence, will therefore be required.

Prosecutors will have to establish that Dr. Eck, who died earlier this year, is deceased and provide the circumstances under which his statement was obtained before seeking to rely on it at trial.

Dr. Eck reportedly treated two of the minors affected after cannabis-infused candies made their way into public circulation in April 2023. His medical evidence forms part of the Crown’s case against Bustillos.

Bustillos is accused of acting in excess of his authority as the Police Department’s exhibit keeper on April 21, 2023, by allegedly disposing of bags containing cannabis-infused gummies that had been placed in the police exhibit room for safekeeping.

Police previously said the gummies had been seized after entering Belize and were later discarded in a garbage trailer at the Queen Street Police Station compound before being taken to the Belize City transfer station. Some subsequently made their way back into circulation and were sold to members of the public. More than 30 children and several adults were hospitalized after consuming the marijuana-laced sweets.

Bustillos was initially charged with 10 counts of negligent harm involving minors affected by the incident. Those charges were later discontinued and he was subsequently charged with willful oppression.

The Crown is expected to call more than 20 witnesses when the matter goes to trial. Bustillos remains on bail and on interdiction from the Police Department.

His trial, which had been scheduled to begin in September, has since been pushed back to March 9, 2027, because of the High Court’s trial calendar.

World.title: Evan Gillett fined $6,000 for almost 3lbs of weed; Pleads guilty so father-in-law isn’t charged
World.content:
Evan Gillett fined $6,000 for almost 3lbs of weed; Pleads guilty so father-in-law isn’t charged

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 46-year-old Belize City businessman has avoided immediate jail time after pleading guilty to possession of 1,295 grams of marijuana with intent to supply.

Evan Michael Gillett appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday alongside his 69-year-old father-in-law, Bert Foreman, following a police search conducted on Sunday, September 27.

Gillett pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply, while Foreman pleaded not guilty.

According to the facts presented in court, police received information from the Fusion Center about a vehicle suspected of transporting drugs. Officers were later directed to a residence on Nurse Seay Street, where they allegedly saw Gillett running from the house.

Police say that after he was detained, Gillett told officers that marijuana was inside a drum and expressed concern that his father-in-law could be taken to jail. A search reportedly led to the discovery of a yellow bag containing suspected cannabis weighing 1,295 grams.

In court, Gillett accepted responsibility but disputed the allegation that he had run from police. He also told the court that he had not intended to supply the marijuana to anyone.

The Magistrate initially considered a starting sentence of two years’ imprisonment and an $8,000 fine. Gillett’s previous drug conviction was treated as an aggravating factor, increasing the prospective sentence to two years and six months and the fine to $9,000.

However, a one-third reduction was applied for his early guilty plea.

Gillett was ultimately sentenced to one year and nine months in prison, suspended for two years, and fined $6,000. He was ordered to pay $2,000 immediately, with the remaining $4,000 due by June 30, 2027.

The court explained that the suspended sentence means Gillett will not immediately serve the one-year-nine-month prison term, but it remains hanging over him during the two-year suspension period and could be activated if he is convicted of another offence.

Following Gillett’s guilty plea, the prosecution withdrew the charge against Foreman, who was free to leave the court.

World.title: Nicaraguan woman charged for presenting fake driver’s license at Cemetery Road checkpoint
World.content:
Nicaraguan woman charged for presenting fake driver’s license at Cemetery Road checkpoint

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 35-year-old Nicaraguan woman has been charged after police say she presented a Belize driver’s licence that appeared to have been tampered with and could not be verified in official records.

Yadira De Los Angeles Aldana, a permanent resident of Belize, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, September 28, where she was arraigned on a single charge of uttering upon a false document.

Police allege that on September 24, Aldana was driving a gold Chrysler Aspen SUV when she was stopped at a vehicular checkpoint on Cemetery Road near Constitution Park.

An enforcement officer reportedly inspected the licence Aldana presented and noticed several inconsistencies. Checks were then made with internal records and the Transport Department, but police were reportedly unable to locate any record of a driver’s licence issued in Aldana’s name.

Aldana was subsequently detained and charged.

No plea was taken during Monday’s arraignment after the police prosecutor informed the court that instructions are being sought from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions on whether the matter will proceed summarily in the Magistrate’s Court or on indictment before the High Court.

Aldana’s attorney, Leeroy Banner, told the court that his client has lived in Belize for approximately 23 years and holds permanent resident status. He also said she had travelled to Belize City to make funeral arrangements for her father when she was detained.

Banner raised concern about the length of time Aldana remained in police custody before she was formally charged.

The prosecution did not object to bail, and Aldana was granted bail in the sum of $2,000 with one surety in the same amount, which she met.

She is scheduled to return to court on November 26, 2026, when disclosure is expected to be provided.

World.title: Magistrate dismisses aggravated assault charge against interdicted cop
World.content:
Magistrate dismisses aggravated assault charge against interdicted cop

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An aggravated assault charge against Police Constable Luwis Pascascio has been dismissed after the prosecution was unable to produce a case file in the matter.

Pascascio, who had been placed on interdiction following his arraignment in May, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, September 28, where the sitting Magistrate dismissed the charge. Public reporting confirms that the court was informed that no case file had been produced.

The 31-year-old officer had been charged with aggravated assault upon fellow police officer PC Jose Mejia following an incident at the Puma Gas Station on Freetown Road in May.

Police alleged that Mejia and PC Mario Coye were on motorcycle patrol when they observed a vehicle run a red light at the intersection of St. Thomas and St. Joseph streets. The vehicle was followed to the gas station, where Mejia approached it with his service firearm drawn because its windows were heavily tinted.

Police alleged that Pascascio exited the vehicle and continued advancing toward Mejia after being ordered to stop. Mejia alleged that Pascascio later slapped him across the face, causing a small cut to his lower lip. Pascascio was subsequently detained and charged. He was granted bail with a condition that he remain at least 100 feet away from Mejia.

Speaking following Monday’s dismissal, Pascascio said he had appeared in court about five times since May but had never been provided with disclosure.

He complained that police “can’t get their act together” and said he and his attorney, Oscar Selgado, will now discuss pursuing legal action following the dismissal.

Pascascio has previously faced another aggravated assault allegation. In September 2024, he was charged with aggravated assault with a firearm involving Belizean athlete Shaun Christopher Gill after Gill alleged that an officer assaulted him with a firearm. That case was subsequently withdrawn after Gill requested no further court action.

Monday’s dismissal means Pascascio no longer faces the aggravated assault charge arising from the May incident with his fellow officer.

World.title: Nearly four years after guilty pleas, two men still awaiting sentence for 2018 manslaughter killing of PC Osbourne Martinez
World.content:
Nearly four years after guilty pleas, two men still awaiting sentence for 2018 manslaughter killing of PC Osbourne Martinez

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly four years after pleading guilty to manslaughter in the killing of Police Constable Osbourne Martinez, two Belize City men are still waiting to be sentenced.

Tyrique Myles and Glen Lopez appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim in the High Court this week as the court moved to finally conclude sentencing proceedings stemming from the November 2, 2018 killing of the 27-year-old police officer.

The two men pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter in November 2022 after initially being charged jointly with murder alongside Rayford Mejia. At the time, Justice Ricardo O’Neil Sandcroft had been presiding over the matter.

Justice Pilgrim reportedly acknowledged the lengthy delay and indicated that the court does not want the matter prolonged any further. The Crown, represented by Senior Crown Counsel Riis Cattouse, and defence attorneys Norman Rodriguez and Orson “OJ” Elrington have been instructed to put together the material necessary for sentencing, including an agreed statement of facts and mitigation submissions.

The matter has now been adjourned to October 8, 2026, for sentencing.

The case dates back almost eight years. Martinez was shot while responding to an armed robbery at the Belcove Hotel on Regent Street West in downtown Belize City. Police reports at the time said three armed men entered the hotel and robbed persons inside before officers arrived. Martinez was shot in the abdomen and later died while undergoing treatment at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Myles, Lopez and Mejia were subsequently arrested and jointly charged with murder and robbery-related offences. Police also recovered firearms following the confrontation near the Haulover Creek.

While Myles and Lopez opted to plead guilty to manslaughter, Mejia maintained his innocence and went to trial. In May 2023, Justice Sandcroft found Mejia guilty of murder after accepting prosecution evidence that he had fired the shot that killed Martinez.

On June 29, 2023, Mejia was sentenced to life imprisonment and ordered to serve 25 years before becoming eligible for parole, with time already spent on remand deducted from that period.

During sentencing, Sandcroft stressed the seriousness of killing a police officer in the execution of his duties and noted that Martinez had lost his life while responding to an emergency and attempting to protect members of the public.

Nearly three years after Mejia was sentenced — and almost four years after their own guilty pleas — Myles and Lopez are now expected to learn their sentences when the matter returns to court on October 8.

World.title: High Court finds Rupert Codd guilty of raping sick woman on picnic table outside KHMH
World.content:
High Court finds Rupert Codd guilty of raping sick woman on picnic table outside KHMH

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Rupert Codd, a 25-year-old resident of Mile 5 on the Philip Goldson Highway, was found guilty of rape on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, by High Court Justice Derick F. Sylvester.

The verdict was handed down at 9:30 a.m. following a bench trial in the High Court of Belize. Codd was accused of raping a 35-year-old woman on picnic table in the early morning hours of April 2, 2023, outside the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH).

According to the evidence presented in court, the victim was unwell and walking to KHMH to seek medical attention around 3:00 a.m. when she was accosted before entering the facility. Codd physically assaulted her, dragged her onto a nearby picnic table, and raped her.

During the trial, Crown Prosecutor Maria Santana Nembhard called 11 witnesses and submitted key evidence, including a 37-second video showing a man in yellow shorts and red sneakers walking near Brad’s Store toward Freetown Road. A police officer who attended primary school with Codd positively identified him from the footage.

Codd, who was represented by attorney Michael Peyrefitte, admitted to being at the scene and physically assaulting the woman, but denied having sex with her. He claimed he had left a nightclub, stopped to urinate behind a building near the Belcan area, and placed his wallet and phone on a picnic table. Codd alleged that when he returned, his items were missing and he confronted the woman, claiming he found his missing belongings inside her bosom. In his 30-page judgment, Justice Sylvester rejected Codd’s narrative as a fabricated story concocted to explain his presence at the crime scene.

Although there was no DNA testing linking hair found on Codd’s clothing to the victim, Justice Sylvester concluded that the Crown successfully proved all essential elements of the crime: that penetration occurred, that it was committed by Codd, and that it was without consent. Justice Sylvester noted minor inconsistencies in the victim’s testimony but deemed them irrelevant to the charge, finding her account credible and reliable while rejecting Codd’s defense.

Following the verdict, Codd was remanded back into custody until his sentencing hearing on November 9, 2026, when Justice Sylvester will consider a mitigation plea on his behalf. Prior to sentencing, the court ordered a Social Inquiry Report, a Victim Impact Statement, an Antecedent Report detailing Codd’s criminal history, and a Prison Report. Under Belizean law, Codd faces a minimum penalty of eight years up to life imprisonment.

World.title: Minister of Health calls for renewed CARICOM action on Non-Communicable Diseases
World.content:
Minister of Health calls for renewed CARICOM action on Non-Communicable Diseases

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Health and Wellness Kevin Bernard is calling for renewed regional action to address non-communicable diseases (NCDs) as CARICOM prepares to mark the 20th anniversary of the Port-of-Spain Declaration in 2027.

The declaration was adopted by CARICOM Heads of Government in 2007, committing the region to bold action against NCDs.

Bernard highlighted the upcoming anniversary during the 53rd Meeting of the CARICOM Council for Human and Social Development (COHSOD) – Health.

The Minister said the milestone should serve not only as an opportunity to reflect on progress but also as a call for stronger engagement beyond the health sector and greater accountability for results.

He also emphasized the need for continued regional cooperation to strengthen health systems against infectious disease outbreaks and climate-related shocks, while protecting the health and resilience of Caribbean communities.

World.title: Sugar tax shortfall
World.content:
The new sugar sweetened drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year.

The Government collected $3 billion less than it had budgeted from the local special consumption tax (SCT) during the April-June quarter, with the Ministry of Finance pointing, in part, to non-compliance following the introduction of the sugar-sweetened drinks tax.

But the country’s fiscal watchdog, the Independent Fiscal Commission (IFC), says the explanation does not go far enough.

The IFC said information provided by the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service (MoFPS) was inadequate to determine whether the explanation for the 35.5 per cent shortfall was reasonable.

According to the IFC’s latest statement on fiscal performance that was tabled in Parliament last week, the Government collected $5.52 billion in local SCT during the first quarter of the 2026/27 financial year, well below the $8.57 billion that had been budgeted.

The resulting $3.04-billion gap was the largest shortfall recorded under the local SCT heading among the production and consumption taxes for the quarter.

The ministry attributed the underperformance to several factors, with the introduction of the new tax on non-alcoholic, sugar-sweetened beverages forming only part of its explanation.

“The shortfall reflects lower-than-expected collections from new revenue measures in Q1 (quarter one), due in part to non-compliance by some firms in remitting SCT for May 2026 following the introduction of the sweetened drinks tax. Changes in production and consumption behaviour in anticipation of the scheduled tax increases announced under the FY [financial year] 2026/27 revenue measures also contributed to the shortfall.

“Lower remittances from Petrojam Limited, together with weaker-than-expected performance in the automotive, petroleum distribution, and beverage/tobacco industries, further reduced SCT collections,” the ministry told the IFC.

However, the IFC was not satisfied that the explanation provided enough information to properly assess the reasons for the shortfall.

The new sweetened-drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year. The Government had initially proposed a charge of two cents per millilitre on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages, but subsequently changed the structure following consultations with industry. The revised measure applies SCT at 22 cents per gram of added sugar or sweetener.

The Government had said the measure was intended not only to raise revenue but also to support public-health objectives. It was originally projected to generate $10.1 billion during the fiscal year.

The implementation itself also encountered administrative challenges. Tax Administration Jamaica extended the deadline for beverage manufacturers to complete licensing under the new SCT regime to May 15, after the tax took effect.

The local SCT shortfall formed part of a wider revenue gap during the quarter. Central Government revenue and grants came in $28.7 billion, or 9.8 per cent, below budget, while tax revenue was $18.8 billion, or 6.9 per cent below target.

The IFC noted that nearly $9 billion of the overall $28.7-billion gap was related to timing differences, including tax revenue that had been projected for April but was collected in March as some companies paid early, and a $2.9-billion transfer from the National Housing Trust that was budgeted for June but was received in September.

The delayed implementation of the Environmental Protection Levy also contributed to the revenue shortfall. The IFC estimated that the delay resulted in approximately $700 million in revenue not being collected during the June quarter and projected a $1.8-billion revenue fallout for the 2026/27 FY if implementation remained delayed.

The legislation for the Environmental Protection Levy was passed by the Senate last Friday with the higher 0.85 per cent levy set to take effect on October 1.

World.title: Road repair ‘blame game’
World.content:
MORGAN... when local authorities demand additional public funds, taxpayers have a right to inspect how existing funds are managed

WHILE Jamaicans continue to express concern over deteriorating parochial roads, central government and local representatives elected on an Opposition ticket are trading barbs, with each side contending that the other is culpable.

At the core of the dispute, minister without portfolio with responsibility for works Robert Morgan insists that municipal corporations are not doing enough to fulfil their responsibility for sustaining roads, while the National Caucus of People’s National Party (PNP) Councillors argue that they are being hobbled by inadequate resources.

In a media release Tuesday morning, Mayor of Spanish Town Norman Scott strongly rejected comments Morgan previously made to the media, regarding poor management of parochial roads by local authorities. Scott argued that the Government should provide municipal corporations with adequate funding instead of engaging in a “blame game”.

He said that of Jamaica’s 25,000 to 27,000 kilometres of roads, municipal corporations are responsible for more than 15,000 kilometres of parochial roads, while the National Works Agency (NWA) maintains approximately 5,000 kilometres. The mayor contended that an annual budget of just over $6 billion across all parishes is simply not enough.

Arguing his point, Scott highlighted disparities in the budget available to works being carried out by the State, including the $45-billion Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to our Road Network (SPARK) programme. Scott also pointed to the $4-billion Relief Emergency Assistance and Community Help (REACH) Programme which addresses road and infrastructure needs in rural communities.

“The Parochial Revenue Fund, from which municipal roads are maintained, is not a personal road fund at the disposal of individual councillors. Resources are allocated through municipal corporations, which must contend with competing demands for road maintenance, drainage, disaster mitigation and other municipal responsibilities as well as being saddled with offsetting the shortfalls in salaries,” he argued said.

“The National Caucus of PNP Councillors is also calling for increased allocations to the Parochial Revenue Fund and a sustainable financing framework that gives municipal corporations the capacity and resources to properly maintain roads for which they have statutory responsibility,” added Scott.

But Morgan was unrelenting in his position, arguing that the issue is not simply a lack of funding but how existing resources are administered.

“When local authorities demand additional public funds, taxpayers have a right to inspect how existing funds are managed. This call for accountability is not coming from the minister of works alone. In her July 2020 audit of Mayor Scott’s own St Catherine Municipal Corporation [covering financial years 2014/15 through 2018/19], the Auditor General [Pamela Monroe Ellis], uncovered severe administrative deficiencies,” said Morgan, adding that the audit magnified flaws in strategic planning, incomplete road inventories, an absence of documented criteria for selecting roadworks, and defective contract records.

He further noted that the caucus failed to disclose in its statement that municipalities collect independent revenue from approximately 30 distinct internal sources, including trade, shop, and market fees, as well as from subdivision, billboard, and parking charges, directly boosting their annual budget.

Against that backdrop, Morgan debated whether an increase in budget would see any changes in the management of parochial roads, arguing that previous increases have only resulted in “close to $2 billion of misappropriation and fraud by municipal corporations under the leadership of the People’s National Party, including the Manchester Municipal Corporation and Mayor Scott’s own St Catherine Municipal Corporation”.

The works minister also sought to put to bed what he deemed an unfair comparison between his ministry’s spending for long-term projects, and funds available to municipalities.

“In the release, they have attempted to compare the municipal corporations’ annual Parochial Revenue Fund allocation of just over $6 billion alongside the $45-billion SPARK allocation to claim financial neglect. This comparison is fundamentally flawed. The Parochial Revenue Fund figure used represents a single year’s allocation, whereas SPARK is a multi-year capital investment programme,” Morgan stressed.

He added that the SPARK programme does not only fund road infrastructure, but also has a portion of its budget dedicated to sewerage, fibre infrastructure, water infrastructure and sidewalks as well as drainage construction.

“The contrast in public disclosure is equally stark. While the central government publishes extensive digital tracking for SPARK and has launched the interactive Jamaica Road Register to map every road, a search of the St Catherine Municipal Corporation website and other municipal portals reveals zero listed ongoing projects. This is not demonstrating accountability and transparency. I welcome Mayor Scott’s call for transparency, and I challenge him and the National Caucus of PNP Councillors to join me in achieving it,” charged the minister.

World.title: St Elizabeth student injured by falling boulder still unconscious at UHWI
World.content:
A loosened boulder on the train track in St Elizabeth where three students were injured, one of whom remains unconscious.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The young schoolgirl, Kendra Rose, who was one of three students injured by a falling boulder as they made their way to Merrywood Primary School in St Elizabeth earlier this month, remains hospitalised in an unconscious state at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI).

Member of Parliament for St Elizabeth North West, Andrew Morris, provided the update on Tuesday during his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in the House of Representatives. He also shared that all medical fees for Rose’s treatment have been waived.

Morris noted that the “heartbreaking incident” occurred on the Merrywood to Breadnut Walk stretch. “Three children were severely injured by falling boulders while forced to use an abandoned train track as an alternative route to get to Merrywood Primary School. No child should risk life and limb just to seek an education,” he said.

READ: Three children injured after being hit by boulder in St Elizabeth

The first-term MP told the House that following dialogue with Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon and Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton and his team, “I am relieved to announce that all medical fees related to care for Kendra Rose have been waived…,” Morris said.

He also shared that the other two children were treated and released from hospital but are still undergoing treatment.

“I have made visits to the hospital and their homes and offered support to the families. Furthermore, I have engaged in constructive dialogue with the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries, Minister Floyd Green, concerning the rehabilitation of the road from Merrywood to Breadnut Walk under the Farm Road Programme to ensure this tragedy is never repeated,” Morris said.

He also pointed out that his constituents face dangerous roadway breakaways that threaten to cut off entire communities, specifically in Ginger Hill, Pisgah, Cornwall, Retirement and Jointwood.

— Lynford Simpson

World.title: US Supreme Court lifts limits on third-country deportations
World.content:
This image released by the Department of Defense shows US Northern Command supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flights via military airlift, at Fort Bliss, Texas, February 7, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — The United States (US) Supreme Court on Tuesday lifted restrictions until further notice on the deportation of undocumented immigrants to third countries.

The high court granted a request from the Trump administration to suspend a lower court ruling that restricted a policy of deporting undocumented immigrants to countries that are not their own.

In a brief statement, the court ruled that it will hear the case on its merits in December.

World.title: Profound sorrow
World.content:
A police vehicle seen on the campus of Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after the death of a fourth-form student. Photo: Joseph wellington

DEEP sorrow and grief shrouded Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after a fourth-form student collapsed in class and died.

“I don’t think we’ve ever had such a situation; meaning, it’s typical for us to have students fall ill, we take them for medical attention, and we see them back in school. It’s the first that we’re having an experience where a student has been taken for medical attention and will not be back with us,” Principal Dwight Pennycooke told journalists at the school in the Corporate Area.

The principal said he was unable to give a detailed account of the school’s initial reaction to the incident, as, after receiving the call from the school nurse informing him of the situation, he had been at Medical Associates Hospital where the student was rushed.

However, he shared that his students were compassionate and empathetic and he expected that the school would be in a period of mourning for quite some time.

“I know over the next few days it’s going to be a difficult one for his peers, his teachers, and for us the administration. We’ve never had to walk through something like this, but we will, through the grace of God, and the help of the support, walk through this and ensure that we provide the necessary support to his peers as well,” said Pennycooke.

He added that, in his absence, vice-principals had been ensuring that the school remained settled, while an early dismissal gave students and staff time to “decompress and to process” what had happened.

He further noted that he could not speak to the specifics surrounding the medical emergency, but recalled seeing the school nurse’s urgent response after receiving her call.

“I saw her running. She’s heavily pregnant, and you see her running, and so I think you would appreciate that she had the sense that this is an emergency, and so she dealt with whatever the call was… in that moment. So that is all I’m aware of,” he said.

Pennycooke reiterated that the school would continue to provide necessary support to those in mourning, noting that the Ministry of Education responded to the incident, and that counsellors were immediately deployed.

“Our young men are quite sensitive, and when it comes down to empathy and compassion, I know I’m going to have to support them quite a bit over the next couple of days… We had a counselling team here earlier. We had our women’s girls’ school counsellors come over. Now we have persons from the Ministry of Education, and no doubt we will have them again for the next couple of days,” he said.

The principal’s update followed a statement released by Wolmer’s Joint Board of Management, which detailed that the student was rushed to hospital where he was later pronounced dead after he collapsed at school.

The board expressed profound sorrow for the loss of the student and further extended its condolence to his parents, relatives, friends, classmates, teachers, and all whose lives he touched.

The board also said that affected peers and staff were being provided with emotional support and asked that the privacy of the student’s family and the school community be respected at this time.

“We also urge the public to refrain from speculation or the circulation of unverified information concerning the circumstances of his passing. The Wolmer’s family stands together in grief and will continue to support the student’s loved ones in the days ahead,” the board said.

World.title: ‘We are not breaking ranks’
World.content:
TWO defence lawyers representing murder accused Andre Ruddock appeared in court on Monday as his trial continued, despite colleagues maintaining a pledge to withdraw legal services from all criminal matters islandwide in pursuit of amendments to the Firearms Prohibition Restriction and Regulation Act 2022.

But according to attorney Anthony Williams, he and fellow counsel Venice Brown did not break ranks with their colleagues. Instead they had a duty to their client which had to be fulfilled.

“We want to make it very clear that we are not breaking ranks with our colleagues. Myself and Miss Brown are 150 per cent in support of our colleagues. However, there is a difference — the Jamaica Bar Association knows about it and they also sanctioned it. The difference is that when you are in a part-heard matter you can’t just go and strike like that. You have to seek the permission of your client in writing,” Williams told the Jamaica Observer.

“If you don’t seek the permission of your client in writing, then you can be deemed to have neglected your client and you can be sanctioned as well. Also, the court can proceed with the matter and the judge can possibly cite you for contempt of court,” Williams explained.

He added that in the absence of defence attorneys a judge may decide to proceed in a part-heard matter because lawyers are expected to be present. He said that if they don’t turn up, they do so at their own peril.

“The situation is different when you are in a part-heard matter, and the lawyer, whoever he or she is, cannot just abandon their client just like that; they have to seek the client’s permission. And in this particular case our client said, ‘Run with it.’ There are many other lawyers who are in the same position, but we have not abandoned our colleagues,” Williams stressed.

In addition to Williams and Brown, a number of attorneys showed up for their clients on Monday at the Home Circuit Court for various reasons, including that some were not in agreement with the protest action.

Essentially, the defence lawyers are arguing that the Act removes discretionary powers from judges, as it mandates a 15-year minimum sentence for an illegal gun possession conviction.

Williams’ client, Ruddock, is being tried in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner in what has been described as a human sacrifice ritual at Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion St James. Ruddock allegedly cut Gardner’s throat on the instruction of his now deceased pastor, Kevin Smith.

Smith died in a car crash in St Catherine a few days later while being transported to Kingston to be charged with the incident.

On Monday the fourth witness in the case, a police sergeant based in St James, returned to complete his testimony which he started last week.

He described the scene at the church as “evil, fluid and chaotic”.

“People were moving from one direction to the next. One body was seen close to the pool area,” the witness recalled.

He explained that members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) made their way through barbed wires to gain access to the compound of the church where three people, including Gardner and two male members of the church, lay dead.

One of the men was allegedly killed by Smith, while the police were said to have shot dead the other man who had rushed toward them with a knife. Based on the sustained gunfire and the sacrificial-type activities that were taking place at the church, the security forces had to call for adequate back-up, which included support from the military.

“The soldiers got to the barbed wire. I saw them climbing over and onto the church premises. On reaching the premises I shouted out to them. Police, accompanied by army personnel, proceeded towards a person who was kneeling behind the column at the entrance gate. I observed them accosting this person. They arrested him and carried out a search of him. The police and soldiers then forced open the big entrance gate,” the witness said.

“When they got there, the man was still in the kneeling position with white cloth over his head. He stood up and the officers searched him. When he stood up, from where I was standing [on the roof] I couldn’t see his face. I could only see the height of the person who was about 5 feet two or three inches tall. At that time there were a lot of police personnel and soldiers around this man. They took him on[to] the roadway and I couldn’t see what took place from there,” the witness said, without being able to say who the man was.

World.title: Stitchie: A legacy that connected dancehall, gospel
World.content:
Lieutenant Stitchie at the 2019 Sterling Gospel Music Awards

Lieutenant Stitchie’s voice may have fallen silent, but the influence of the veteran deejay — who commanded respect in both secular dancehall and gospel music spheres — is expected to continue reverberating across generations.

The veteran artiste, whose given name was Cleveland “Cleve” Laing, died at Kingston Public Hospital on Monday morning, one day shy of his 61st birthday.

The news comes less than 24 hours after his wife, Sophia Laing, confirmed that the entertainer had been hospitalised with a low blood count and was receiving treatment.

His passing closes a remarkable chapter in Jamaican music — one that began in dancehall and found a path to gospel.

For distinguished cultural analyst, Professor Donna Hope, Lieutenant Stitchie’s ability to remain loved across musical boundaries was rooted not only in his talent, but also in his personality that endeared him to audiences.

“Stitchie was loved because a lot of his songs were humorous. They were fun and they made people happy,” Hope said. She pointed to his enduring early hit Wear Yu Size, noting that the song was “digestible”, catchy and non-combative — qualities that helped establish his connection with listeners.

“Stitchie had an excellent career in dancehall and that followed him into gospel,” Hope continued. “I saw Mr Vegas made a post and I’m sure several others will as the news spreads because a lot of the artistes he would have came up with in that era were still close to him even though they were doing different genres.”

Entertainers and government officials took to social media to pay tribute to the deejay. Among them Prime Minister Andrew Holness, Tarrus Riley and Chevelle Franklyn (who also transitioned from dancehall to gospel).

Professor Hope shared that Stitchie’s significance extended beyond his music.

“Having a relationship with secular artistes was something Stitchie did well because he understood that it was important to minister to the sheep that ought to be brought into the fold,” she said. “This loss will be felt across genres and eras. He is a part of the industry in a way few artistes were, and so he will never be forgotten.”

Basillia Barnaby-Cuff, founder and director of Sterling Gospel Music Awards, agreed.

“I think Stitchie set a beautiful example of how you can remain an influence with people even when you’re in a different season of your life,” she said. “He was able to bridge the gap between the secular and gospel. He was still able to be on stage with secular artistes, singing gospel without compromising his walk with Christ.”

For Barnaby-Cuff, that was the essence of Stitchie’s ministry — not simply preaching to people already inside the church, but allowing his life and testimony to reach those outside it.

“It is about allowing your life to minister to those you wish will come over to Christianity,” she said.

The Sterling Gospel Music Awards family shared a particularly close connection with the artiste in his later years. A few years ago, Stitchie was honoured at the awards with the KFC Big Deal Award, an occasion Barnaby-Cuff now views with gratitude.

“I am just so happy we were able to give him his flowers while he was alive,” she said. “The gospel fraternity and we here at the Sterling Gospel Music Awards are really saddened by this news.”

Even as his health deteriorated, the organisation continued to support him, raising funds towards his care in the hope that his condition would improve.

“As the body of Christ, we are so grateful that he used the latter part of his years in ministry, and that he brought so many other persons to Christ,” she said. “He truly lived a full life and, as children of God, we don’t mourn as if we don’t have hope, and so that hope is something we hold on to and that one day we will see him again in the great resurrection.

Stitchie emerged from the competitive sound-system culture of Spanish Town in the early 1980s, working alongside artistes including Papa San and Wickerman. His breakthrough came in 1986 with the humorous Wear Yu Size, followed by songs such as Natty Dread, as his distinctive delivery and ability to connect with audiences propelled him beyond Jamaica. In 1988, he secured a recording deal with Atlantic Records, marking another significant milestone in a career that was increasingly taking him onto the international stage.

But it was his decision to walk away from secular music and embrace Christianity in 1997 that would ultimately redefine his legacy.

In 2014 he published his autobiography and among his accolades was honoured with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer in 2021 for his contribution to music.

World.title: Debutants Tru-Juice remaining calm despite table-topping JPL start
World.content:
Tru-Juice FC striker Daniel Roberts celebrates after scoring the winning goal in the club’s 1-0 victory over Molynes United in the Jamaica Premier League at Stadium East on Sunday. (Photo: JPL)

DESPITE Tru-Juice FC’s strong start to their debut Jamaica Premier League (JPL) season, Assistant Coach Craig Richards says it’s too early to be thinking about the play-offs.

The newly promoted club lead the JPL stadings on seven points after a 1-0 win over Molynes United at Stadium East on Sunday. Striker Daniel Roberts’s 62nd-minute strike was enough as Tru-Juice stay unbeaten after their first three games. They also join Montego Bay United and Waterhouse as the only two clubs who have yet to concede.

Richards says he was pleased with the team’s execution, after nearly a week of preparation.

“We knew that it was going to be a tough-fought game. We know how the Molynes team plays and we’ve been training all week to nullify them — and we also worked on ways to hurt them and it paid dividends,” he said.

“When we play against certain teams, we really assess them and train accordingly, so I’m very pleased. There are parts of the game that I’m disappointed with but there are aspects that I’m very pleased [about], and that’s football. I’m pleased we got three points on the board, and we look forward to the next game.”

Tru-Juice have attracted several top players to join their inaugural season, including Reggae Boyz Alex Marshall, Gadail Irving, and Tafari Chambers.

The Linstead based-club caught the eyes of many during their opening game when they thrashed reigning Caribbean Cup champions Mount Pleasant FA 4-0 and held last season’s semi-finalists, Montego Bay United, to a goalless draw.

Although starting on a positive note, Richards says they’re not placing too much pressure on themselves.

“Our objective is to play quality football and maximise on the points and [see] wherever that leads us,” he said. “Our aim is to compete. And competing can lead us to good places but as it relates to [the] objective [of] top six or whatever, if that should come then we are very welcoming for that but for now we’re taking it three games at a time.

“This is our first season. There are quite a number of teams that have been competing in this competition for some time so they have some experience. While we have experienced players, the club itself is in its first season so we continue to set different objectives at different points of the season, and we’ll see where that leads us.”

Mount Pleasant Head Coach Theodore Whitmore was pleased his team got off the mark after their 2-0 win over Dunbeholden at the Dunbeholden Sports Complex.

After losing their first two games of the season, goals from Trayvone Reid and Nicholas Nelson ensured the St Ann-based club picked up all three points.

“It doesn’t feel like three, it feels like six points,” Whitmore said. “I think we would have met our objective when we got two goals this afternoon; we didn’t concede, we kept a clean sheet, so I think it’s something that we can build on.

“When you look at the table and see Mount Peasant at the foot, nobody expects that. It wasn’t pleasing even for the fans that travel with us every Sunday, so it’s very pleasing [to beat Dunbeholden]. We look forward to the next one; and it gives us now a momentum going into the next game and into the semi-final of the Caribbean Cup.”

World.title: EU to offer single-market access to candidate countries
World.content:
"Earlier integration would open opportunities for Union businesses, strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependencies. The Commission will identify where verified regulatory alignment and enforcement capacity allow deeper participation in research, innovation and industrial cooperation, and wider market access. Priority should go to opportunities that advance accession preparations and meet shared economic and strategic needs."

The review, overseen by top von der Leyen advisor Alexandre Adam — a former aide to French President Emmanuel Macron — would radically overhaul the EU's approach to countries in its neighborhood. At present, almost all economic benefits of closer cooperation are reserved for members, but no new state has joined since Croatia in 2013.

As part of Adam's package of measures, Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro will be offered "road maps" designed to speed up the process of joining in the coming years. Others, like North Macedonia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Turkey, have seen the process drag on — with fears growing that they will become disengaged or gravitate closer to Russia or China.

Under the Commission's plan, economic benefits offered to candidate countries will depend on their support for the EU's foreign policy objectives, with single market access hinging on them not sharing key technologies with hostile states and trade rivals.

"As industrial and market integration deepens, participation in sensitive sectors must be accompanied by cooperation on investment screening, export controls, sanctions implementation and the protection of sensitive technologies," the review document reads.

"Assessments of access should consider strategic alignment, critical dependencies and the capacity to manage risks to infrastructure and supply chains. Where those conditions are not met, the scope of participation should be adjusted under the applicable instrument."

World.title: UK’s Burnham says he’ll consider push to rejoin EU
World.content:
The British prime minister said Labour ”could go all the way“ as it mulls what’s possible a decade on from the Brexit referendum.

LIVERPOOL, England — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham made clear that an attempt to rejoin the European Union could be among the options his government considers as it eyes a fundamental shift in the country’s relationship with the bloc.

Burnham told the governing Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool Tuesday that the Brexit settlement struck by the Conservatives had done “more harm than good” and said he would spell out “what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners” at a U.K.–EU summit later this year.

In a BBC interview, broadcast Wednesday, Burnham said: “We could look at what [former Chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way.”

World.title: Time to get tough on food, booze and tobacco
World.content:
Presented by EFPIA By CLAUDIA CHIAPPA with DOMINIC GIANNINI

Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.

SNEAK PEEK

— Don't shy away from regulating food, alcohol and tobacco to tackle Europe's biggest threat to society — chronic diseases — says the head of Austria's food and drugs agency.

— An expert panel in Germany hands down a proposal to reward pharmaceutical companies that invest in Germany through clinical trials or manufacturing.

— One MEP remains unconvinced on a critical patent proposal on the table for the Biotech Act following a roundtable of industry and European officials.

Welcome to Wednesday’s Morning Health Care! Seven coffees, two schnitzels, two paninis, a lemon tart and a heaping of scrambled eggs later, and that’s a wrap on our first 24 hours in Gastein. Another week like this and Claudia and I might need to take a closer look at the Commission’s heart health screening recommendations we’ve written so much about after we get back to Brussels …

Get in touch: [email protected], [email protected]. 

DRIVING THE DAY

RAMPING UP PREVENTION: Governments should focus on regulating key unhealthy ingredients instead of getting caught up in the “complex” debate on ultra-processed foods, according to Johannes Pleiner-Duxneuner, managing director of the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety.

Prevention: Preventing growing rates of chronic diseases is one of the main areas governments should focus on “because non-communicable diseases, diabetes, obesity are the main threats for our society,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the European Health Forum in Gastein, Austria.

But but but: discussions on prevention can get complicated, he said, for example when trying to tackle ultra-processed foods. The key is to keep it simple, Pleiner-Duxneuner said. “We should focus on sugar, salt, alcohol, tobacco. I think these are the main killers.”

Zooming out: Brussels is currently a hotspot for the prevention debate, with discussions on how to tackle ill health caused by industries such as food, alcohol and tobacco often heating up. Earlier this week, MEPs clashed over language describing the impact of alcohol on cancer in a parliamentary cancer report. Some lawmakers argued industry profits were being put before people’s health.

But it’s not just alcohol: Lawmakers are struggling to figure out how to nail down the best measures to reduce consumption of ultra-processed foods and tobacco. The debate on UPFs is gaining momentum, with the European Commission recently asking its Scientific Advice Mechanism to assess how UPFs should be defined, their health effects and consumption patterns. And tobacco regulation continues to divide countries as the EU mulls a proposal to raise taxes on cigarettes and set minimum levies for vapes, heated tobacco and nicotine pouches.

The sugar debate: More countries are introducing sugary drink taxes in an attempt to curb consumption amid soaring obesity rates, particularly among children. The measures are backed by the World Health Organization, which says “… taxes are one of the strongest tools we have for promoting health and preventing disease.” The German government is planning to introduce a new tax on sugary drinks starting in 2027, while the U.K., for example, has had one for years. Pleiner-Duxneuner said he’s a “fan” of the U.K.’s sugar tax: “From a scientific clinical point of view, there is no reason not to implement it in other European countries.”

Tricky: Though Austria does not currently have a sugar tax, the topic often enters the public and political debate — though it receives pushback from industry, Pleiner-Duxneuner said. “Definitely no one wants to damage the industry, so that's one of the reasons why it's not a hot topic at the moment,” he said. “But I think it is one of the tools that you can [use] to reduce sugar consumption.”

Don’t forget education: It’s key to pair regulation with educational programs targeting children, starting as early as kindergarten. “Austrian figures show that it's seven times more effective if you do education in kindergarten or early school pupils rather than doing it with teenagers,” he said. And it’s key to meet children where they are: social media. “This is something we're looking at — s also on social media, not only TV commercials.”

GERMANY

WHO’S GOING TO COUGH UP FOR THE BONUS? A proposal to reward pharmaceutical companies that invest in Germany, through clinical trials or manufacturing, has left the hardest question unanswered — how to pay for the industry incentives, our colleague Louis Westendarp writes in.

An expert panel handed over its plan on Tuesday to two state secretaries — one from the German Ministry of Economic Affairs and one from the Ministry of Health. The government promised to deliver the proposal by the end of the month, after concluding sweeping health care reforms in July, including cutting drug prices by more than doubling mandated discounts.

At the same time: Germany is under U.S. pressure to increase its drug prices, and many are watching to see if this proposal will also appease Trump administration officials. Closed-door talks between the two countries are ongoing.

Will it be enough? As our Berlin colleagues reported at the start of the month, the offer is to phase out the scheduled 8.5 percentage points increase in the manufacturer discount from 7 percent to 15.5 percent — with a 2 percentage point cut for adhering to collective bargaining agreements, 3 percentage points for local research and development, and 3.5 for German production.

The cost: The scheme costs approximately €1.3 billion, according to the National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Funds (GKV-Spitzenverband). However, it remains unclear who will cover this expense. The report merely outlined several financing options, also scooped by our Berlin colleagues.

Proposal 1: Pharmaceutical companies that do not meet the bonus criteria should bear the cost of the scheme through a higher price discount. However, the expert panel deemed this proposal "ineffective," according to the report.

Proposal 2: Funds for the bonus could be saved elsewhere within the statutory health insurance system. This would require a further review of the finance commission's report.

Proposals 3 and 4: The regulation could pay for itself through macroeconomic effects, or the bonus could be funded via the federal budget.

No decision reached: The matter has been left for others to decide — specifically, the coalition parties, people close to the panel told Louis. "We will now examine it in greater detail and proceed to implementation as quickly as possible," Frank Wetzel, State Secretary at the economic affairs ministry, said.

Ahem: It’s not the only tricky financial issue Germany is trying to resolve right now, with long-term care, pensions, and the fuel tax rebate also up for debate.

DRUG PRICING

BAND OF BROTHERS: Back at Gastein, Pleiner-Duxneuner revealed that Austria is working on a reimbursement model with Belgium, the Netherlands and other countries with similar pricing systems, as pharma companies were becoming increasingly willing to walk away from talks. Companies were instead opting to maintain higher prices in the U.S. to avoid Trump policies that copy lower prices in Europe, said Pleiner-Duxneuner.

Changing track: “In the past years, the companies were fighting actually to get access in Austria, and what we see more and more is that actually they're leaving the table: ‘No, we are not launching it with that price … otherwise we would have an average price that is ruining also the U.S. market price’,” Pleiner-Duxneuner told Morning Health Care. This has already happened for a handful of medicines including those for orphan diseases and cancer, he said.

** Every weekday afternoon, the Brussels Playbook Capitals newsletter draws on our reporting across national capitals to look ahead at what is shaping the EU agenda next. Sign up here.**

BIOTECH ACT

STAYING PUT: A roundtable of industry and European officials to thrash out the pros and cons of extending patents for certain biotech drugs failed to convince one of the MEPs critical of the proposal in the Biotech Act to change his mind.

What’s this about? Leading MEPs on the law hosted the meeting Tuesday to address concerns from some lawmakers that no independent impact assessment had been conducted on the bill. The proposed patent extension — known as a supplementary protection certificate — is one of the main sticking points in negotiations between MEPs. The one-year extension is designed to entice drug developers to test and manufacture in Europe.

No thanks: Socialists and Democrats MEP Tiemo Wölken — who is leading the legal affairs committee opinion on the law — said he didn’t hear anything to change his mind on granting patent extensions. “The Union cannot afford to grant additional patent protection without securing tangible benefits in return,” he told Morning Health Care. His amendments have sought to remove the patent offering.

Conditional: Some in industry have lobbied to remove the clinical trial and manufacturing conditions for the patent. “Multi-country clinical trials and the significant production within the Union are the only real added value in the Commission’s proposal, and we must safeguard them,” Wölken said. “Anyone seeking to weaken or remove these criteria is working against the Union’s interests.” He said it would have been good to hear from patient groups about the impacts as well.

They agree: Several NGOs expressed disappointment to Morning Health Care that they weren’t invited, arguing the panel was too industry-heavy. “We are particularly surprised and concerned that civil society representatives, especially patient representatives, were not invited to this meeting,” the European Patients’ Forum said. “Patients and their representatives have an essential role to play in this debate. We also have important perspectives to contribute on the Biotech Act and the extension of Supplementary Protection Certificates (SPCs), particularly as patients will be directly affected by its consequences.”

Patients first: The European Patients’ Forum wants to scrap the patent extension proposal, “because of its impact on timely patient access to medicines and the sustainability of healthcare systems,” it said. The EPF also doesn’t want clinical trial timelines to be further reduced so that patients’ rights and safety remain the priority.

Moving too fast: The forum also raised concerns about the pace of negotiations, as MEPs are trying to agree on a compromise text by December. “This is particularly important given the exceptionally fast pace of negotiations, which raises concerns that key issues may not receive the in-depth consideration they require, particularly in a broader political context where competitiveness is increasingly being prioritised over public health objectives,” EPF added. You can see all their asks here.

CLIMATE-HEALTH

INCREASED SPREAD: Climate change is spurring the spread of diseases like dengue and chikungunya through vectors such as mosquitoes, ticks, and bugs as temperatures warm and new places become at risk, delegates at Gastein were warned Tuesday.

Speedy: One mosquito in Europe moves 60 kilometers farther north each year, and outbreaks and local transmission of dengue and chikungunya are moving even faster, reaching up to 120 kilometers farther north than before, said Jan Semenza, an environmental epidemiologist at Heidelberg University. This is putting tens of millions more people at risk every year, he said.

You can’t say we didn’t know: The world might have been caught off guard by the coronavirus and the ongoing outbreak of the Bundibugyo ebolavirus in the Congo, but it can see the rise of vector-borne diseases, HERA Deputy Head Laurent Muschel told a panel at the European Health Forum in Gastein. This was growing “slowly but surely,” which means Europe shouldn’t be caught out, he said. “We have a bit of time, but not so much, and it's time to invest.”

Underprepared: Gaps in the European system included a lack of medical contingencies for most vector-borne diseases, including insufficient antivirals and vaccines that cover a broad spectrum, Muschel said. Diagnostics also needed to improve, he added.

WHAT WE’RE READING

A 1-year-old baby has been euthanized in the Netherlands, the Telegraph reports.

Novo to pay up to $2.6 billion for the rights to an experimental weight loss pill, reports Reuters.

World.title: EU accused of hiding environmental impact of data centers
World.content:
"If we do not make sure that these big power consumers are indeed in line with our overall objectives… then they will risk undermining our ability to live up to our own targets," the EU's energy chief, Dan Jørgensen, said in an interview with POLITICO.

According to the Commission's figures, Europe’s data centers used 20.7 terawatt-hours of electricity — about as much electricity as the entire nation of Croatia consumes — and more than 8 million cubic meters of water in 2025. That's a 26% increase in electricity use and 52% in water use from 2024.

But those numbers do not fully account for the sector's actual use, as the totals are the result of incomplete data collected by the Commission. The data has only been published in aggregate, following a 2024 law that banned Brussels and EU capitals from disclosing "all information and key performance indicators for individual data centers" amid lobbying from tech giants, which cited commercial interests.

Diego Solier, a conservative member of the European Parliament working on the EU's legislative push to boost the bloc's digital capacity, said Europe's data center expansion must be accompanied by reliable information for citizens and policymakers about how much energy and water is being used.

"Transparency should be the starting point," said Solier, who didn't comment on the complaint itself, which wasn't yet public. "At the same time, transparency must be proportionate, and should not require companies to disclose genuinely commercially sensitive information."

Right to know

Lighthouse Reports says the Commission "holds the primary responsibility [of] denying public knowledge of the effects of Europe's massive data center build-out," by allowing operators to keep details of their consumption under wraps and dodge scrutiny in the process — in breach of the Aarhus Convention, which the EU has been a party to since 2005.

World.title: Wie Merz in der Wirtschaft den Macron macht
World.content:

World.title: Chinese-run Brussels networking club raises intelligence concerns
World.content:
A Chinese-run networking club targeting business and political elites in Brussels bears the hallmarks of an influence and intelligence-gathering operation, a Western intelligence source has told Euronews.

 

The Global CEOs Dinner Club, which is now expanding to France, operates in a manner associated with China’s United Front, a Communist Party network used to promote Beijing’s interests abroad, according to the source.

The assessment comes as Belgium has recently been at the centre of several espionage probes launched by its Federal Prosecutor’s Office, including investigations into a former Chinese-Belgian researcher in the semiconductor industry and a Canadian national of Chinese origin working at NATO in Mons.

Yifei Yang, who runs the Global CEOs Dinner Club, studied in China and at a private European institute in Nice, France, before launching the organisation in Brussels last March.

French media outlet La Lettre reported last week that her activities had put at least one Western intelligence service on alert.

Asked by Euronews, one intelligence source would not confirm whether their service was investigating the case. However, after Yang’s activities were described to them, the source said they matched the modus operandi of China’s United Front.

The United Front is a decades-old Communist Party network known for promoting China’s interests through organisations and individuals abroad, while some of its activities have also been linked to the gathering of information for Chinese intelligence services.

Contacted by Euronews, Yang denied that China was behind the club, insisting that “we are neutral” and adding that its objective was to have an “impact on society” and “build sustainable business”.

Approached through Linkedin

Since last March, the Global CEOs Dinner Club has brought together business figures as well as people connected to Belgian and EU politics at events covering topics ranging from sustainability and diversity to technology and artificial intelligence.

On Wednesday evening, it was due to host a dinner entitled “China–EU EV Futures: Competition, Collaboration, and the Road Ahead” at a luxury Brussels hotel, bringing together business leaders, policymakers, technology executives and investors.

Guests included Hui Zhang, vice-president of Chinese electric vehicle maker NIO; Melanie Schuttenberg, a board member of Danish car components company TAJCO; and Ole Gerkensmeyer, CSO of Netherlands-based chipmaker Nexperia.

Yang said the organisation currently has 20 members from countries including France, Belgium, Denmark, Japan, China and Singapore. Annual membership costs €2,400 for individuals and €5,000 for companies.

“It is not all about business,” Yang told Euronews, describing the organisation as “value-driven”. She said 10% of its revenue goes to NGOs and charities.

The club’s website shows that speakers in recent months have included representatives from Belgian semiconductor research centre imec and Le Refuge, a shelter for LGBTQIA+ young adults.

Belgian senator Marie-Claire Mvumbi, who spoke at one of the club’s events on diversity, told Euronews that Yang had approached her through LinkedIn.

Mvumbi said between 30 and 50 people attended the event, which included discussions about diversity in business recruitment. “The event gave a good impression,” she said.

Yang says she hopes to expand the organisation into France and recently sent invitations for an event for female executives scheduled to take place in November at the luxury Le Meurice hotel in Paris.

World.title: Hungary cuts German activist Maja T.'s jail term over 2023 attacks at far-right rally
World.content:
A Budapest appeals court reduced the jail term on Wednesday for a German non-binary anti-fascist activist's sentence for participating in anti-Nazi violence from eight to seven years.

 

Maja T., 25, was found guilty in February of involvement in assaults in 2023 ahead of the annual "Day of Honour" in Budapest commemorating Nazi soldiers.

Prosecutors said the activist was part of a multinational far-left group that attacked nine people on the streets, including German and Polish citizens, whom they identified as far-right extremists.

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court of Appeal reclassified Maja T.'s role from co-perpetrator to accomplice, shortening the sentence by one year, the presiding judge said.

The ruling is final and not subject to further appeal.

The defendant entered the court led by guards on a leash amid faint cheers of "Maja" from the audience.

Maja T. attends a sentence appeal trial session at the Budapest-Capital Regional Court, 30 September, 2026 AP Photo

Ahead of the ruling, supporters put up banners near the court entrance demanding the release of the activist, amid a heavy police presence on surrounding streets.

Campaigners, including some German politicians, had questioned whether Maja T. would receive a fair trial, as the groups linked to the attacks were designated terrorist organisations last year by the former nationalist government of Viktor Orbán.

Multiple people accused of participating in the 2023 attacks have been put on trial in Hungary and Germany, with one receiving a five-year prison sentence in Germany.

Italy and France have refused to surrender two suspects to Hungary with courts in both countries citing the risk of "inhumane treatment" in prison.

In 2024, the German Constitutional Court found that Maja T. ran the risk of discriminatory treatment in Hungary as a non-binary person and should not be extradited.

But the ruling came hours too late to stop the handover.

Last year, Maja T. staged a 40-day hunger strike to protest the "unlawful handover" and "inhumane" prison conditions, an allegation denied by Hungary's prison service.
