World.title: Ninth-century Arabic silver coins found near Viking trading centre in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Experts believe they may have belonged to merchants travelling to or from the Viking Age port of Truso, which was situated nearby. The silver dirhams date back around 1,200 years, to the first half of the ninth century, before the founding of the Polish state. They may have remained in circulation until the turn of the 10th/11th century, the time of the settlement’s collapse. The discovery of the “new treasure” was announced last week by the Archaeological and Historical Museum in Elbląg. It did not reveal who had unearthed them, but said that the find had taken place during a legal search in a forest near the town of Młynary, just east of Elbląg. After conservation and processing work, the coins will be included in the collection of the museum, whose archaeologists will also visit the site hoping for further finds. The museum’s Jakub Jagodziński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the find consists of “six early medieval Arabic dirhams and two fragments of these silver coins”. He said that they are provisionally dated to the first half of the 9th century, but a more precise estimate will be possible after they are processed. The coins could have belonged to merchants travelling along the routes leading to or from Truso or to Prussian guards who later collected tolls on these routes, Jagodziński explained. Truso was a Viking Age port of trade set up by the Scandinavians on the shores of lake Druzno near the Vistula river delta. Established by the late 7th century and active until the early 11th century, its location enabled trade extending towards Kyivan Rus, Byzantium and the Islamic world. Historians knew of Truso’s existence because of the account of the Anglo-Saxon traveller Wulfstan of Hedeby. Centuries-long efforts to find the precise site proved fruitless until it was finally discovered in the early 1980s by the young archaeologist Marek Jagodziński, Jakub’s father. Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website. More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland. In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP. “Therefore, when hoards of Arab coins are discovered in Poland, they are divided into several pieces. Whole coins are also found, but much less frequently,” he explained. World.title: Poland offers to host facility producing Patriot missiles for Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the factory could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security. The news was revealed by deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who also confirmed that Poland would seek to establish a Patriot servicing and production facility even if it does not host Ukraine’s. Poland wants to host Patriot production Poland has proposed that the US and Ukraine launch joint production of Patriot missiles. Warsaw is citing security concerns and is proposing to host the facility in Poland instead of Ukraine: “If such a factory is planned to be built in… pic.twitter.com/syCkNt0o0V — Belsat in English (@Belsat_Eng) September 27, 2026 Patriot missile systems have been a key part of Ukraine’s defence against Russian aerial attacks. However, Kyiv has suffered from a shortage of missiles used in the system, prompting President Volodymyr Zelensky to appeal to allies to transfer their interceptors as well as to allow Ukraine to produce them itself. US President Donald Trump initially told Zelensky at a meeting in July that “we are gonna give you a licence to make Patriots”. However, he then backtracked on that offer later the same month. But, following weeks of uncertainty, on Friday last week Zelensky claimed that Trump had personally told him he had made a “final decision” to approve a licence for Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles. Washington has not confirmed that development. Asked about the issue on Saturday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told broadcaster TVN, “let’s see if it happens”. However, she added that, “we proposed that, if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in the so-called safe territory”. Poland is already the primary hub for military equipment, goods and people being transported in and out of its eastern neighbour. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that, regardless of where the plant serving Ukraine is located, Poland would also still seek to establish a facility for servicing and, eventually, production of Patriots. “What my interlocutors in Washington confirmed is that, even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, it does not change our efforts and does not rule out consent for Poland,” she said. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka was in Washington last week for talks with US officials. In May this year, another deputy defence minister, Cezary Tomczyk, told TVN that Poland had “received preliminary approval from the US State Department to produce missiles for Patriot systems”. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 In 2018, as part of its Wisła air defence programme, Poland signed a $4.75bn contract to purchase Patriot launchers and missiles from the US. In October 2023, the first Patriot systems procured from the US were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport. In December 2025, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries. Poland also has an agreement to domestically produce launchers for Patriot systems through cooperation between Polish state-owned defence contractor Huta Stalowa Wola SA and US defence giant Raytheon. Poland has announced a $1.2bn deal that will see a Polish state-owned defence firm manufacture 48 launchers for Patriot missile systems domestically in cooperation with US defence giant Raytheon https://t.co/PQOjKvhqYM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2024 The issue of Ukraine’s need for more Patriot missiles caused domestic political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition reacted angrily to reports that the government had handed over some interceptors to Ukraine. In July, the government confirmed that it had done so. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that only five missiles had been transferred to Ukraine. In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported that the Iran war had depleted America’s stockpile of Patriot missiles to 800 interceptors from roughly 2,300 before the war began. Last week, Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, confirmed that his country has also proposed that it could manufacture interceptors and perhaps even entire Patriot systems. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! One of the priests injured in a knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland last week – which left one of his colleagues dead and another fighting for his life in hospital – has delivered a homily calling for people to forgive the attacker and not to blame Ukrainians as a whole for his actions. “I ask you not to repay evil with evil, but with love, support, understanding and care,” said a visibly injured Father Adrian Mantykiewicz. “I ask you to respect and support each other as two brotherly nations.” 🙏 Poruszające słowa ks. Adriana po ataku nożownika w Opactwie w Jarosławiu. W swojej pierwszej homilii po napaści duchowny mówił o przebaczeniu, miłości do bliźniego i odpowiadaniu dobrem nawet na doznaną krzywdę. pic.twitter.com/zGEGvC5meB — Goniec.pl (@GoniecPL) September 28, 2026 On Thursday last week, a 31-year-old Ukrainian man, who can be named only as Ihor H. under Polish privacy law, entered the grounds of the Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław. Using a knife he took from a kitchen, he attacked five people before he was stopped. One priest, Stanisław Zbojnowicz, died from his injuries shortly afterwards. Another, Marek Pieńkowski, is still being treated in hospital. Ihor H. was arrested at the scene and, on Saturday, a court approved a request from prosecutors for him to be placed in detention for three months. For now, he is being held in a psychiatric facility, with prosecutors saying that he “displayed symptoms of mental illness”. President @Zelensky has condemned an "evil" knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland today, which left a priest dead and others injured Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk says the perpetrator will face the “full severity of Polish law” https://t.co/SIonlR4JpJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Saturday, in a church that is part of the Benedictine abbey complex, Mantykiewicz celebrated the Eucharist for Zbojnowicz. With bruising under his left eye and bandages on his head and hand, he delivered a homily in which he addressed the attack, its victims, and the perpetrator. “I am a disciple of my master, a disciple of my lord, and Christ teaches me love,” he said. “And from this place, as a disciple of Jesus Christ, I wish to say very clearly in my name, in the name of Father Marek, and in the name of Father Stanisław, that we forgive.” “I ask you to pray for our tormentor,” he continued. “He needs this prayer most of all. Because no matter what happened, we must overcome the evil that occurred here in our abbey with goodness, love, and forgiveness.” Mantykiewicz also appealed for people not to blame Ukrainians more broadly for the incident. There have been fears that the attack could prompt a backlash against Ukrainians, Poland’s largest immigrant group, who have already been experiencing a growing number of hate crimes this year. “I also want to ask you not to blame the nation from which the perpetrator came,” said the priest. “The evil was committed by a specific person…responsible for their own actions. It was not done by other people. It was one person, one person alone.” “Let us be disciples of Christ. Disciples who help others with love, care, respect, help and kindness,” he continued. “It does not matter who they are, what nation they come from, what religion they are, or what colour their skin is; they are human beings…and we must not deprive anyone of their dignity.” On Friday, the head of the Polish Catholic church’s council for migrants and refugees, Bishop Krzysztof Zadarko, gave a press conference at which he condemned the “outpouring of aggression and artificially stoked hatred towards Ukrainians that this event [in Jarosław] has fuelled”. “The church can only appeal to the consciences, primarily of Catholics and Christians, but also of all people, that this is not the right response; it is downright reprehensible, and incompatible with the Gospel,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF. “We are dealing with a tremendous tragedy, but shifting the blame of one person onto an entire society, ethnic group, or nationality is wrong,” he added. Agresja i niechęć do kogokolwiek jest nie do pogodzenia z wiarą chrześcijańską – mówił przewodniczący Rady KEP ds. Migrantów i Uchodźców bp Krzysztof Zadarko podczas konferencji prasowej przed 112. Światowym Dniem Migranta i Uchodźcy.https://t.co/M46RXggVTR pic.twitter.com/uZWodfR7sG — EpiskopatNews (@EpiskopatNews) September 25, 2026 Thursday’s attack caused widespread shock and mourning in Poland, and also prompted condolences from Ukraine, including President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said that “we are shocked by this evil”. On Saturday, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told broadcaster TVN that he had spoken with Ihor M.’s mother and was able to provide more information about him. He confirmed that the man had left Ukraine in 2022 and lived in Germany. Bodnar, however, said that media reports claiming Ihor M. had served in the Ukrainian military were false. Regarding the motive, Bodnar said that it appears Ihor M. “had some kind of mental illness”. He pledged that the Ukrainian authorities would cooperate and were “working on all the information we can provide to the Polish side”. World.title: Russia condemns Polish city’s “barbaric” removal of Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Russia has criticised the removal of a monument in the Polish city of Rzeszów expressing “gratitude” to the Soviet Red Army. It called the move “barbaric” and “sacrilegious”. The monument – part of which will be moved to a nearby Soviet cemetery and another to a museum – has been the subject of a long-running legal and political battle, amid wider debate in Poland about “decommunising” public spaces, especially in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 23 września 2026 r. w Rzeszowie (województwo podkarpackie), decyzją władz polskich i z naruszeniem dokumentów rosyjsko-polskich dotyczących ochrony obiektów dziedzictwa memorialnego, rozpoczęto proces demontażu pomnika wdzięczności żołnierzom… pic.twitter.com/HYuNeLG5dy — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) September 24, 2026 The Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army, standing 8.5 metres tall and weighing 6.6 tons, was erected in Rzeszów, southeastern Poland, shortly after the end of World War Two, when the Soviets had pushed Nazi Germany out of Poland and then installed their own communist government. It is located on Ghetto Victims Square, a public space also created after the war on the grounds of the city’s former Jewish cemetery, which had been destroyed by the German occupiers in 1942. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance, a state historical body, notes that the monument was erected just a few metres from where two Polish anti-communist resistance fighters who had been members of the wartime Home Army (AK) had been publicly hanged by the communists. The monument’s plinth featured bas-relief sculptures depicting Red Army Generals Ivan Konev and Karol Świerczewski, soldiers, and industrial and agricultural workers carrying a hammer and sickle. At the top of the 8.5-metre column was a statue of a woman and child. In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. That triggered a legal battle over the monument in Rzeszów. The government-appointed provincial governor and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body, moved to have it dismantled, arguing that the monument glorified communism. But city hall – led by left-wing mayor Tadeusz Ferenc, who had been a member of the communist party before 1989 – challenged the decision. It argued that the monument did not promote communism and noted that its name, referring to gratitude to the Red Army, was not an official one. In 2019, the provincial administrative court sided with the city and overturned the decision to remove the monument. However, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 prompted many Polish municipalities that had not removed Soviet-era monuments to begin doing so. In April 2022, Rzeszów’s current mayor, Konrad Fijołek, announced that his city’s monument would be taken from its current location and placed in a Soviet soldiers’ cemetery elsewhere in the city. “In principle, I am not in favour of dismantling or demolishing monuments, as they are a testament to history,” said the mayor. “But in light of the current wartime reality, this monument should not remain in its current location. But we are not barbarians; we will not demolish the monument, but relocate it.” However, the IPN opposed the idea of relocating the monument and refused to cover the costs of doing so. It wanted it to be eliminated entirely. Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We say ‘no’ to Russians who believe these lands somehow belong to their sphere of influence,” declared the Institute of National Remembrance https://t.co/aG9VQVlUQI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 12, 2025 As a result, the city is paying 156,000 zloty (€35,700) for the monument to be taken away, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. The bas-reliefs will go to the Soviet cemetery while the statue of mother and child will go to the city’s Museum of Technology and the Military. Work to remove the monument began this week and is expected to last until November. Once the above-ground section has been removed, a special conservation committee, including a representative of Poland’s Rabbinical Commission for Cemeteries, will determine how to proceed with the monument’s foundation. The beginning of the removal work prompted anger from Moscow, with the Russian embassy in Warsaw issuing a statement that called it a “sacrilegious step”. It demanded “the immediate cessation of work” and restoration of the monument to its previous state. “With regret, we must state once again: the barbaric policy of the Polish authorities, consisting of destroying everything that serves as evidence of the invaluable feat of the soldiers and officers of the Red Army in liberating Poland from Nazi occupation, is being continued at an ever faster pace,” they continued. Russia regards the Soviet Union’s driving Nazi Germany out of Central and Eastern Europe at the end of World War Two as a “liberation”. However, many in the region reject that term, given that it involved bringing their countries under brutal Soviet domination instead. In its statement, the Russian embassy also claimed that the actions in Rzeszów are a “violation of Russian-Polish documents concerning the protection of memorial heritage sites”. Moscow regularly claims that Poland’s removal of Soviet memorials violates a 1994 agreement between the two countries on respect for graves and other places of memory. It did so in August this year, when protesting the demolition of a monument in the town of Pyrzyce. However, Poland points out that the agreement relates to graves and war cemeteries, not separate monuments and symbols, which can be legally removed. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Rzeszów is also home to one of the famous – or infamous, depending on one’s perspective – communist-era monuments in Poland, the 38-metre-tall Monument to the Revolutionary Struggle. It has become a landmark of the city. In 2017, the IPN recommended that it be removed under the “decommunisation” law. The owners of the land upon which it sits also wanted to demolish it. However, mayors Ferenc and Fijołek sought to protect the monument, and their efforts succeeded last year, when it was added to Poland’s list of protected monuments, preventing it from being destroyed. World.title: British Pop Star Robbie Williams to Headline Colours of Ostrava 2027
World.content:
British pop star Robbie Williams will headline the opening day of Colours of Ostrava 2027, organisers have announced.

Williams will perform on Wednesday, July 21, at the Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex, marking his return to the Czech Republic after his recent concert at Prague’s O2 Arena.



The 2027 edition of Colours of Ostrava will run from July 21 to July 24. Williams is the first major act confirmed for the festival’s lineup.

“For me, Robbie Williams is, above all, a personality. He is someone you know, even if you aren’t necessarily a fan,” said Colours of Ostrava artistic director Filip Košťálek.

“Over more than three decades, he has managed to stay relevant, evolve and surprise audiences while remaining true to himself. And those are exactly the kind of personalities we want to bring to Colours.”

Košťálek said the festival is looking for artists with strong stories and songs who can create memorable moments for audiences.

Williams fits that profile after more than three decades at the centre of British pop. Since launching his solo career in the 1990s, following his departure from Take That, he has become one of the UK’s most successful solo artists.

His latest studio album, Britpop, was released in early 2025 after a delay. Williams had originally planned to release the record earlier but moved the date following the announcement of a new album by Taylor Swift.

The delay was also connected to Williams’ ambition to return to No. 1 on the UK album chart. The strategy paid off, with Britpop reaching the top of the chart and extending his record-setting run of No. 1 albums in the UK.

Williams has remained a major live attraction as well. His most recent Czech concert took place at Prague’s O2 Arena, where he combined songs from across his career with the humour and interaction that have become a defining part of his performances.

More artists for Colours of Ostrava 2027 are expected to be announced in the coming months.

World.title: Techno, Art and Live Performance Come Together at Strahov on October 10
World.content:
On October 10, the Prague electronic music collective EDEN will bring Rotten To The Core to Stadion Strahov for one of the collective’s largest and most ambitious events to date.

Running from 10pm until 7am, the night will bring together international and local DJs, dancers and visual artists for an event built around music, performance and visual art.



The lineup includes VLACE, SCHELLT, RiVid, 2NDRA and Mila (5), with the programme focused on techno and acid.

Among the artists, 2NDRA is a Prague-based schranz and techno producer and performer and one of the founders of EDEN Collective. RiVid, meanwhile, is a Czech-Japanese hard techno duo.

The event takes a broader approach to the club experience, combining the music programme with visual elements, art installations and live performances.

That approach comes at a time when electronic music events are becoming increasingly commercialised, while promoters and venues face rising production costs and growing regulatory pressures.

The event will take place beneath Strahov Stadium in Prague 6, continuing EDEN’s connection with unconventional venues and large-scale rave productions.

The collective previously hosted its 40-hour ALT BABYLON weekender in Prague in August, featuring dozens of local and international artists.

The event is for ages 18 and over, with tickets starting at CZK 300.

World.title: Václav Havel Would Be 90 This Year: From Playwright to President
World.content:
Václav Havel was one of the defining figures of modern Czech history.

Playwright, writer, dissident, political prisoner and, ultimately, the last president of Czechoslovakia and the first president of the Czech Republic, his life reflected some of the country’s most dramatic changes of the 20th century.

Born into a prominent Prague family, Havel experienced both privilege and political persecution. He became one of the leading voices of the opposition to communist rule and played a central role in the Velvet Revolution of 1989.



On October 5th, 2026, Havel would have turned 90. Here is a look at his life, political career and some of the places in Prague and beyond connected to him.

From a privileged Prague family to a banned writer

Havel was born in Prague on October 5, 1936, into a wealthy and well-connected family. His uncle, Miloš Havel, founded Barrandov Studios, while his grandfather was involved in construction and real estate.

His family’s position changed dramatically after the Communist Party took power in Czechoslovakia in 1948. Their property was confiscated, and Havel faced restrictions on his education and career because of his family background.

During the political liberalisation of the 1960s, Havel became increasingly involved in Prague’s theatre scene. He worked as a stagehand and later as a dramaturge, while also establishing himself as a playwright. His plays often explored power, bureaucracy and the absurdity of life under an authoritarian system.

The hopes of 1968

The Prague Spring of 1968 brought a period of political and cultural liberalisation to Czechoslovakia. Censorship was abolished, previously banned books began appearing in print and films that had been restricted were shown in cinemas again.

Havel embraced the new atmosphere and became increasingly active in public life. But the reforms ended abruptly when Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia on August 21, 1968.

Havel opposed the occupation and the return to political repression. He was subsequently banned from publishing and working in the theatre. For a period, he worked as a manual labourer at a brewery in Trutnov.

He later became one of the most prominent figures of the Czechoslovak dissident movement. He was a signatory of Charter 77, a civic initiative calling on the communist government to respect human rights, and was repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

From dissident to president

The communist regime collapsed in November 1989 following mass demonstrations across Czechoslovakia. Havel was one of the leading figures of the Civic Forum, the opposition movement that helped negotiate the peaceful transfer of power.

On December 29, 1989, he was elected president of Czechoslovakia.

Havel remained in office after the country split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, becoming the first president of the newly independent Czech Republic. During his political career, he supported the country’s integration into Western institutions, including NATO, and advocated closer ties with the European Union.

His presidency also left a visible mark on Prague Castle. Parts of the complex were opened to the public, while the South Gardens were restored following their pre-war design.

Life after Prague Castle

Havel left the presidency in 2003 but remained active as a writer and public figure. He continued to comment on political and social issues and maintained friendships with artists, intellectuals and international figures.

Among them was the Dalai Lama, who visited Havel in Prague on several occasions. Havel died on December 18, 2011, at his country house in Hrádeček, near the Krkonoše mountains.

Places connected to Václav Havel in Prague

Several Prague locations are closely connected to Havel and his family.

One is Lucerna Palace on Wenceslas Square, built by Havel’s grandfather. The complex includes the historic Lucerna Cinema, which has been operating for more than a century, as well as the famous Lucerna Café.

Prague Castle is another essential stop. Havel lived and worked there during his years as president and initiated several changes that made parts of the complex more accessible to the public.

Outside Prague, Havel was also closely associated with Lány Chateau, the traditional summer residence of Czech presidents. During his time there, he was known to visit the local pub and meet residents without the formality normally associated with a head of state.

World.title: Prague’s Kramář Villa to Open for Free Visits on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Kramář Villa will open to the public on October 3, giving visitors a chance to see inside one of the Czech government’s official residences.

Admission will be free.

The villa, located on Gogolova Street in Prague’s Letná district, is the official residence of the Czech prime minister. It was also the home of Karel Kramář, Czechoslovakia’s first prime minister, and his wife, Nadezhda.



Visitors during the open house will be able to take guided tours of the building and learn about its history, architecture and former residents. The tour will include parts of the villa that are normally closed to the public, including its living quarters and ceremonial rooms.

Built with a combination of Neo-Baroque and Art Nouveau influences, Kramář Villa has been one of Prague’s government residences since the early 20th century.

Its history is closely linked to Karel Kramář, who became the first prime minister of Czechoslovakia following the country’s establishment in 1918.

The open house will also include access to the villa’s garden. Located above the city, the grounds provide views across Prague and will remain open for longer than the villa itself.

The villa will welcome visitors from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on October 3. The garden will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

World.title: Czech Study Finds Supporting Homeless People Can Save Public Money
World.content:
A Czech experiment in which homeless people received CZK 100,000 with no conditions attached suggests that early financial support can reduce some of the costs associated with homelessness.

The project, known as New Leaf, was carried out by the Czech organization Neposeda in cooperation with researchers from Charles University.



The findings indicate that the state spends an average of about CZK 200,000 a year on each person experiencing homelessness, with healthcare, social services and police work accounting for a significant share of the total.

The researchers concluded that leaving people without support can ultimately be more expensive for public finances than providing targeted assistance.

How the New Leaf experiment worked

The project ran from summer 2024 until the end of 2025 and was inspired by a similar initiative in Canada.

Researchers focused on people who had been living on the streets for no more than two and a half years. The aim was to examine whether intervention at an earlier stage of homelessness could prevent longer-term problems.

Participants were divided into several groups. Forty people received CZK 100,000 without restrictions on how the money could be used. Another 20 were offered the support of a personal social worker instead, while 40 people formed a control group and received no additional assistance.

The study initially involved 100 people. One participant died from a serious illness shortly after the project began, leaving 99 participants in the final research sample.

The researchers tracked participants’ use of public services and their contact with state authorities, including emergency medical services, hospitals, outpatient healthcare, social services and police.

Healthcare accounts for the largest share

The study estimates that the state spends around CZK 200,000 annually on each homeless person.

Healthcare represented almost 43% of the estimated expenditure. Low-threshold services, which provide basic support and a safe place for people experiencing homelessness, accounted for around a quarter of the total.

Police work represented another 9%, or more than 18,000 crowns per person each year.

The wider cost to public finances

Data from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs recorded 11,641 homeless people in the Czech Republic in the previous year.

Based on the estimated annual cost per person, direct public expenditure associated with homelessness amounts to roughly 2.33 billion crowns a year.

World.title: Smartwings Cuts Prague Flights as Winter Schedule Shrinks
World.content:
Smartwings is reducing its winter flight schedule from Prague, with several routes being cancelled, frequencies cut and new connections postponed until spring 2027.

The biggest changes will affect Spain, a popular choice for Czech travelers looking for warmer weather during the autumn and winter months.

The airline will suspend flights between Prague and Valencia from November 2 until the beginning of March.

Flights to several other Spanish destinations will also be reduced. Smartwings will cut its Málaga service from two flights a day to one, while Barcelona will move from daily flights to four to six services a week.

Flights to Mallorca will be reduced from four per week to two. The Prague–Madrid route will continue, but flights will operate on an irregular schedule.

Smartwings is also suspending flights from Prague to Nice until early March.

New Prague routes pushed back

Several routes that were expected to launch this year will now have to wait until spring 2027.

The postponed connections include new services to Venice and Bergen, Norway. Smartwings has also delayed the return of flights to Brussels and Bucharest.

Both Brussels and Bucharest were suspended in the spring, with Smartwings originally planning to restore the routes in October.

Eurowings also reduces Prague services

Eurowings is making changes to its Prague schedule as well. The German carrier has cancelled its planned winter flights to Madeira, Portugal.

The route had been scheduled to return for the winter season, but Eurowings will instead offer tickets to Madeira through a partnership with Smartwings, which continues to operate flights to the Portuguese island.

Eurowings will also suspend its Prague–Stockholm service for most of January.

Higher fuel costs affect airline schedules

The changes come as airlines face higher operating costs linked to fuel prices.

According to Eurocontrol, the European organization responsible for coordinating air traffic management, jet fuel prices in Europe more than doubled between the beginning of the year and mid-September.

Airlines around the world have been adjusting schedules as fuel costs fluctuate amid the conflict in the Middle East. Route cancellations and reduced frequencies are among the measures carriers are using to adapt to changing market conditions.

World.title: Home Baking Returns to Czech Kitchens as Flour Sales Rise
World.content:
Home baking is gaining momentum in the Czech Republic, with online supermarket Rohlik.cz reporting a sharp increase in demand for baking ingredients this year.

Flour has been at the center of the trend. Sales of organic flour have risen by almost 72 percent compared with the previous year, while conventional flour sales increased by around 23 percent.



The change has also affected the balance of sales. Organic flour previously accounted for about 19 percent of flour purchases at Rohlik.cz. That figure has now climbed to almost 25 percent.

The figures suggest that customers are not simply buying more flour but are also paying greater attention to the type and quality of the ingredients they use.

Rohlik.cz CEO Miroslava Vopatová says baking continues to play a role in family life, particularly as an activity shared across generations. The supermarket has responded by offering products at different price points, from private-label options to organic and farm-produced ingredients.

Yeast sales tell a different story

The increase in demand for flour has not been mirrored by yeast.

Sales of yeast have been gradually falling since the surge in home baking during the coronavirus pandemic. One shift remains noticeable, however: shoppers are increasingly choosing fresh yeast rather than dried yeast.

Home baking in the Czech Republic is also strongly seasonal. Christmas remains the busiest period of the year, while a smaller increase usually occurs in March and April. Demand drops during the summer months.

For experienced bakers, the quality of the final product often depends on relatively simple details. Yeast dough needs enough time and warmth to rise properly, while rushing the process can affect the result.

The preparation of the filling matters as well. Curd cheese should be drained thoroughly before being added to a cake or pastry, reducing the risk of excess moisture making the dough soggy. Fruit fillings should also be sufficiently thick rather than watery.

These practical details can make a noticeable difference, particularly in traditional Czech pastries whose recipes are often passed down through families.

World.title: New Flights from Prague to Asia Boost Competition on Airfares
World.content:
Travelers flying from Prague this autumn have more options as airlines add capacity and new direct connections, particularly to Asia.

At the same time, increased competition is putting pressure on carriers to keep fares under control, according to data from Czech booking portal Letuška.cz.



The biggest changes are visible on long-haul routes. New services from Prague are making destinations in Asia more accessible, while airlines already serving the Czech market are responding with promotional fares.

“Thanks to high competition and new capacity from Prague, the autumn flight market offers very favorable travel conditions,” said Josef Trejbal, commercial director of Letuška.cz. He said the arrival of new Asian connections has helped revive demand for long-haul travel and encouraged established airlines to introduce more competitive offers.

Direct flights strengthen Prague’s links with Asia

Asia is once again attracting greater interest from Czech travelers. One factor is the growing number of direct or more convenient connections from Prague, which can reduce the need for lengthy transfers through major Middle Eastern hubs.

STARLUX Airlines, for example, is offering flights from Prague to Taipei from around CZK 21,000. The direct service provides an alternative to itineraries involving a stopover and can save travelers both time and, depending on the itinerary, money.

Another new option will be available from October 10, when flights to Hanoi are scheduled to begin on the Prague–Almaty–Hanoi route. Tickets listed through Letuška.cz start at around CZK 18,000.

The expansion comes as airlines compete more aggressively for passengers on long-haul routes departing from Prague.

Caribbean and Latin America see strong growth

Europe remains the most popular region for Czech travelers, but demand for long-haul destinations is also changing. According to Letuška.cz, Latin America and the Caribbean have recorded the sharpest year-on-year increases, with demand growing by hundreds of percent in some cases.

The Caribbean in particular has benefited from rising interest among travelers looking beyond Europe. Latin American destinations have also seen a significant increase in bookings compared with the same period last year.

The stronger demand is coinciding with changes in the competitive landscape. New routes from Prague are challenging airlines that have traditionally carried passengers to Asia and Australia through Middle Eastern hubs.

Major Gulf carriers including Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad are responding with promotional fares, adding further pressure to ticket prices.

World.title: Orbán’s friend Mészáros remains Hungary’s richest as Forbes publishes first-ever top 100 list
World.content:
Lőrinc Mészáros and his family remain by far the wealthiest Hungarians, with an estimated fortune of HUF 1,785.7 billion (EUR 4.87 billion), according to the Forbes Hungary 2026 rich list. This year’s ranking is the magazine’s first to feature the 100 richest Hungarians rather than 50, and is published as Hungary’s political and business landscape undergoes major changes.

Mészáros remains firmly at the top

Forbes Hungary has published its 2026 list of the country’s wealthiest people, expanding the ranking from 50 to 100 individuals and families for the first time. Lőrinc Mészáros and his family remain at the top, with an estimated fortune of HUF 1,785.7 billion.

The combined estimated wealth of the 100 people on the list is now approaching HUF 13,000 billion (EUR 35.5 billion), according to Forbes.

The ranking is based on financial reports from the most recently completed business year. As a result, Forbes notes that the list does not yet fully reflect the effects of the political changes that followed the April election.

The magazine says reviews, criminal proceedings, falling share prices and the establishment of a state asset recovery office are already pointing towards a new period in Hungary’s business world.

Have you read this? Legal threats fly as PM Magyar confronts Orbán-linked billionaire over motorway deal

Csányi, Felcsuti, Veres and Szíjj complete the top five

The five wealthiest Hungarians on the 2026 Forbes list are:

Lőrinc Mészáros and family – HUF 1,785.7 billion Sándor Csányi – HUF 649.7 billion Zsolt Felcsuti – HUF 587.6 billion Tibor Veres – HUF 567.7 billion László Szíjj – HUF 530.6 billion

Mészáros has therefore retained the top position, although Forbes says his estimated wealth increased by only HUF 39 billion this year – the smallest increase relative to his total fortune since he first appeared at the top of the list.

Last year, Forbes estimated his wealth at HUF 1,749.1 billion.

Jellinek ranks seventh, while Garancsi and Jászai remain in the top 15

Dániel Jellinek, owner of Indotek Group, ranks seventh with an estimated fortune of HUF 314.1 billion.

Jellinek was detained and subsequently placed under arrest in September in connection with a criminal investigation. The Forbes ranking, however, is based on the financial data and company valuations underlying its 2026 methodology.

His former wife, Kamilla Hermann, ranks 60th with an estimated HUF 59.8 billion.

István Garancsi, owner of Market Építő and Las Vegas Casino, ranks 10th with an estimated HUF 271.9 billion, while Gellért Jászai, head of 4iG, is 11th with HUF 254 billion.

István Tiborcz, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán, ranks 13th with an estimated HUF 185.6 billion.

The expansion to 100 names has also brought several figures onto the Forbes list for the first time. Árpád Habony ranks 52nd, while Mária Schmidt is 62nd and former defence minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky is 74th.

What could the political changes mean for Hungary’s billionaires?

Forbes describes this year’s ranking as a snapshot taken at the end of an era in which several business groups grew substantially through state-linked contracts and concessions.

The magazine says that the future of long-term state concessions could become a major issue for businesses closely associated with the previous system. It also raises questions about how companies that expanded in sectors heavily dependent on state contracts will perform in a more competitive environment.

Forbes further notes that businesses which previously benefited from preferential state financing, bond programmes or major public contracts are unlikely to be able to rely on the same conditions under the new government.

However, the 2026 ranking largely reflects the previous business year, meaning the longer-term impact of the political transition is not yet visible in full.

How does Forbes calculate the fortunes?

Forbes Hungary uses a methodology based on that of the US Forbes. Where possible, companies are valued using EBITDA – earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation – multiplied by an industry-specific valuation multiple.

Since its 2023 list, Forbes has used the average EBITDA of the previous three years rather than the latest figure alone. The magazine says this better reflects how companies have recently been valued in the Hungarian market.

For non-production businesses such as property developers, the calculation is primarily based on the value of the assets minus liabilities. Start-ups are assessed partly on the basis of investment received, while investment management companies are valued using their after-tax profit and an industry multiple.

Forbes also applies a standard 10% liquidity discount to private companies. Businesses heavily dependent on state contracts or holding state concessions are assessed on an asset basis with a significant discount, where their state exposure is considered substantial.

The magazine says its calculations were supported by data from company information providers Opten and Dun & Bradstreet, as well as Ingatlan.com, while valuation practices and exceptional cases were discussed with M&A advisers.

World.title: Hungary’s Semmelweis University breaks into world’s top 250 after major leap in global rankings
World.content:
Budapest’s Semmelweis University has climbed to 247th place in the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2027, making it the highest-ranked university in Hungary and Central and Eastern Europe.

Semmelweis University has made a major leap in the latest Times Higher Education (THE) global university rankings, entering the world’s top 250 universities for the first time. The Budapest-based medical university ranks 247th in the 2027 THE World University Rankings, up from 272nd last year.

The result also makes Semmelweis the highest-ranked university in both Hungary and Central and Eastern Europe.

The British-based Times Higher Education ranking is one of the world’s best-known university rankings. For its latest edition, THE assessed more than 20,000 higher education institutions from 118 countries and ranked around 2,200 of them.

Semmelweis particularly strong in research quality

THE evaluates universities across five broad areas: teaching, research environment, research quality, industry income and international outlook. Semmelweis performed particularly strongly in research quality, ranking 166th in the world in this category. It was also ranked 242nd for teaching.

According to the university, Semmelweis has placed within the top 25% of institutions worldwide in all five indicator groups.

THE also uses size-adjusted indicators, including the student-to-staff ratio, income per academic staff member and research citation impact. This is intended to prevent larger universities from gaining an advantage simply because of their size.

Semmelweis improved significantly in two of the five indicator groups and increased its score while maintaining its position in another.

More than one-third of students are international

Semmelweis Rector Béla Merkely attributed the university’s progress partly to the close relationship between its education, patient care and research activities, as well as its strong international presence.

The university has almost 16,000 students, more than one-third of whom are international, coming from nearly 130 countries around the world.

The number of international applicants is also rising. According to Semmelweis, applications for its English-language programmes increased by almost 40% this year, while its general medicine programme received roughly three times as many applications as available places.

The university has partnerships with a number of internationally recognised institutions, including the Karolinska Institute, Mayo Clinic, the University of Oxford, Heidelberg University, the National University of Singapore and Harvard University.

How other Hungarian universities performed

Several other Hungarian universities also appear in the THE 2027 rankings. The Óbuda University was placed in the 601–800 range, while the University of Debrecen and Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) were ranked between 801st and 1,000th.

The University of Szeged and University of Pécs both fell into the 1,001–1,200 range.

The Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences (MATE) and Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) were placed between 1,201st and 1,500th.

The Széchenyi István University, University of Pannonia, University of Miskolc and Pázmány Péter Catholic University were all ranked in the 1,501+ category.

Within Central and Eastern Europe, Semmelweis leads the regional rankings. The University of Tartu in Estonia is in the 301–350 range, Charles University in the Czech Republic in the 401–500 range, while Wrocław Medical University and Jagiellonian University in Poland are in the 501–600 range.

Oxford extends its record at the top

The University of Oxford remains at the top of the global ranking, extending its record to 11 consecutive years at No. 1, Telex reports. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) ranks second, while Princeton University and Stanford University share third place.

The top 10 consists exclusively of universities from the United States and the United Kingdom. For the first time, however, Asian universities collectively overtook European institutions in the rankings, with three Asian universities making the top 15.

University rankings come with caveats

University rankings have faced criticism in recent years because different ranking systems use different methodologies and attempt to compare institutions with very different profiles.

György Fábri, a lecturer at ELTE, previously argued that it was unrealistic to expect a Hungarian university to enter the top 100 of global rankings, pointing to the substantial financial gap between the world’s leading universities and Hungarian higher education.

He also described global university rankings as being particularly useful for international positioning and for showing roughly where an institution stands within the international research and higher education landscape.

Semmelweis itself has acknowledged the limitations of university rankings, noting that different methodologies can make comparisons between institutions with very different profiles difficult.

World.title: Hungary takes major step towards joining European Public Prosecutor’s Office
World.content:
Head of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), European Chief Prosecutor Laura Codruta Kovesi, has held talks on the technical details of Hungary’s membership of the EPPO with Justice Minister Márta Görög, Finance Minister András Kármán, Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai and Deputy Prosecutor General István Lajtár at the Ministry of Justice in Budapest, the ministry said on Tuesday.

The EPPO is an independent European Union body tasked with investigating criminal offences affecting the financial interests of the European Union, conducting prosecutions and bringing perpetrators to justice. These offences include budgetary fraud affecting the financial interests of the EU, active and passive corruption, embezzlement, money laundering, cross-border tax fraud and other connected offences.

In criminal cases falling outside the jurisdiction of the EPPO, the Hungarian Office of the Prosecutor General and the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will continue to act as public prosecutors, while criminal liability will continue to be determined by the Hungarian courts in accordance with the Hungarian legal system, the statement said.

The accession process involves significant professional, institutional and legislative tasks, which must be carried out “as soon as possible”, it added.

Legislative tasks will be carried out in two phases. In the first phase, the system for selecting the European Public Prosecutor and the delegated European Public Prosecutors will be established. This will require amendments to three acts. The relevant legislative package will be submitted to parliament as early as in 2026.

The aim is to establish a selection procedure that ensures the highest possible level of independence, objectivity and professional rigour. Due to the high professional standards required, the legislative process necessitates a longer preparation period, as the aim is to conduct wide-ranging consultations with the organisations concerned regarding the selection criteria and the details of the procedure, the ministry said.

World.title: Magyar government publishes list of 3,598 secretive resolutions issued since 2010
World.content:
The Hungarian government has published a list of so-called 2000-series government resolutions issued between 2010 and 2026, the Prime Minister’s Office told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) on Tuesday.

These decisions were previously not published in the Hungarian Gazette, but were sent directly to the government officials concerned. According to the list, the largest number of such resolutions were issued in 2021, during the coronavirus pandemic.

Most non-public decisions issued during 2021

A total of 3,598 so-called 2000-series government resolutions were issued over the past 16 years without being published in the Hungarian Gazette. These decisions, which were sent directly to those concerned, generally assigned tasks to specific government, law enforcement or other state officials.

The 2000-series government resolutions are not the same as government resolutions containing classified information, the Prime Minister’s Office said.

In recent years, the existence or contents of some 2000-series resolutions could only be learned from media reports. However, a complete annual breakdown of the resolutions had not previously been publicly available in one place.

Number of unpublished resolutions rose steadily

The newly published documents show that the government increasingly classified decisions as non-public over time. During the second Orbán government between 2010 and 2013, the number of non-public decisions ranged from 10 to 20 a year. This rose to 33 in 2014, after which the number continued to increase.

The highest number of non-public resolutions was recorded in 2021, during the coronavirus pandemic, when 679 government decisions were classified as 2000-series resolutions. A similarly high number was recorded in 2023, when 635 non-public government decisions were issued.

Full list available online

The annual lists of non-public government resolutions issued between 2010 and 2026 are now available on the government’s website. The documents can be accessed here.

World.title: Major development in the heart of Budapest as hospital goes through expansion and renovation
World.content:
A major transformation is under way at the Buda Health Centre. While the Budapest hospital’s nearly 90-year-old buildings have been completely modernised, a new hospital wing covering more than 22,000 square metres is also taking shape. Remarkably, patient care has continued throughout the large-scale construction project. The entire complex is scheduled to be completed in autumn 2027.

Old hospital buildings have been renovated

The comprehensive development has been under way since 2024 on the approximately 2.6-hectare site at the junction of Alkotás Street and Királyhágó Street, with construction carried out by Market Építő Zrt. The first major phase has already been completed: the ‘A’ building, constructed in 1939, and the ‘B’ wing, opened in 1973, have both been renovated.

The nearly century-old building was also structurally reinforced, including with jet grouting technology, while new insulation, modern windows and upgraded building services were installed. The operating theatres have also been modernised, making them suitable for the latest equipment, including robotic technology. The renovated buildings will once again house the publicly funded services of the National Centre for Spinal Disorders.

A new 22,600-square-metre wing is being built

At the same time, work is progressing rapidly on the new ‘C’ wing, comprising three underground car park levels, four patient-care floors and a mechanical plant level. The building will include consulting rooms, patient rooms, an outpatient and screening centre, and an emergency outpatient unit. Seven modern modular operating theatres are being built on the second floor, equipped with specialised medical gas supplies and sterile air-handling systems.

Around 17,000 cubic metres of concrete and 2,300 tonnes of reinforcing steel have been used for the structure. According to reports from Magyar Építők, work is currently progressing simultaneously on mechanical and electrical systems, floor screeding, painting and tiling.

Advanced technology will also improve energy efficiency

Critical hospital equipment must continue operating even in the event of a power failure. The new facility will therefore have multiple independent power supplies, automatic transfer switches, diesel generators and uninterruptible power supplies. Energy efficiency is also a key consideration. A ground-source heat pump system, rooftop solar panels and automatically controlled external shading will help reduce operating costs.

More on Budapest: Green light for 280 new Budapest homes as huge development acquires permits

Three buildings will become a single complex by 2027

The new wing will be connected to the renovated buildings by glazed links. The task involves more than simply creating physical access: the patient-flow, mechanical, electrical and building automation systems of the different buildings must also be integrated. The project’s location in a densely built-up part of Buda presents significant logistical challenges, while patient care must continue uninterrupted throughout the construction process.

Once the development is complete, the hospital’s total floor area will increase from approximately 18,000 to 35,500 square metres. The number of beds will rise from 150 to 250, operating theatres from seven to 17, and consulting rooms from 55 to 87. According to current plans, by autumn 2027 the historic buildings and the new wing will operate as a single, modern hospital complex.

World.title: China’s Ambassador Gong Tao: 77 years on a shared journey – Setting out anew with mutual understanding and friendship
World.content:
The past 77 years have witnessed China’s relentless pursuit of progress through trials and triumphs. Under the leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC), the Chinese people have opened a path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, achieving the historic transformation from national independence to prosperity and strength, while sustaining rapid economic growth and maintaining long-term social stability. The year 2026 marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the CPC and the opening year of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan. We are advancing Chinese modernization on all fronts through high-quality development, striving unremittingly for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and for the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.

Author: His Excellency Gong Tao, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

China’s high-quality development is people-centered. In December 2025, the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel in Xinjiang was opened to traffic. With an investment of RMB 6.08 billion and a total length of 22.13 kilometers, the tunnel cuts through the Tianshan Mountains at an elevation of more than 3,000 meters above sea level, closely linking northern and southern Xinjiang. A journey that once took seven hours now takes no more than 30 minutes, making travel and logistics much easier. As a local tour guide put it when introducing the tunnel: “Because the people need a good road like this, the motherland can make the mountains bow and the rivers yield. It is not that piercing through the Tianshan Mountains is easy; it is that the people are on the other side.” These words capture the underlying logic of Chinese modernization and the commitment of the CPC and the Chinese government to ensuring that development truly delivers for the people.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

China’s high-quality development is driven by innovation. In 2026, China continues making fresh progress in artificial intelligence, embodied robotics, computing power and commercial spaceflight, among other areas of innovation. Behind these remarkable achievements lies sustained investment in science and technology and a dynamic innovation ecosystem. China’s R&D intensity has surpassed the OECD average, with 77 percent of R&D investment coming from businesses. We have built an innovation ecosystem that is deeply integrated, open, inclusive and full of vitality. In Shenzhen’s Robot Valley, more than 200 robotics companies have gathered within a half-hour radius. It has become clear that decoupling benefits no one, and that a “small yard, high fence” strategy cannot hold back China’s technological innovation. China has always based its development on the strength and ingenuity of its people, while remaining open to international cooperation in science and technology.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

China’s high-quality development creates opportunities for the rest of the world. What China pursues has never been self-interest alone, but a community with a shared future for humanity in which all countries can thrive together. Committed to world peace, China has always approached international issues on their merits, acted on the principles of objectivity and justice, and actively explored solutions to hot-spot issues with Chinese characteristics. In September this year, President Xi Jinping put forward a four-point initiative on building a security architecture in the Middle East, contributing China’s solution to lasting stability in the region. On the Ukraine crisis, China remains committed to promoting peace talks and playing a constructive role in advancing a political settlement. Committed to global development, what China brings to the world is not shocks, but opportunities. By opening its vast market, driving industrial innovation, and maintaining stable supply chains, China is bringing greater certainty to the sluggish global economy. China’s economy continues to grow steadily—supported by the world’s largest and one of its most dynamic middle-income groups—making China an increasingly attractive market. In the first eight months of 2026 alone, China’s imports grew by more than 22 percent. Committed to upholding the international order, China has put forward the Global AI Governance Initiative and helped establish World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization in Shanghai, the first intergovernmental organization dedicated to AI, in an effort to bridge the global digital divide and promote fairer AI governance.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

This year marks the 77th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Hungary, with Hungary being one of the first countries to recognize the PRC. Having stood the test of time, China-Hungary relations have continued to grow in a sound and steady manner. Deepening our friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation has become a shared aspiration and consensus of our peoples.

Mutual respect is the political foundation of our bilateral relations. Despite our different histories, cultures and political systems, China and Hungary have always treated each other with mutual respect, understanding and trust, and regarded each other as reliable partners. China respects the choice of the Hungarian people, never interferes in Hungary’s internal affairs, and appreciates the adoption of friendly policies toward China by successive Hungarian governments, including their adherence to the One-China principle. Following the formation of Hungary’s new government and National Assembly, the leaders of our two countries have maintained friendly exchanges, charting the course for the future development of bilateral relations.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

Mutual benefit and win-win outcomes are defining features of our cooperation. Chinese businesses have invested in a wide range of areas in Hungary, creating tens of thousands of jobs and becoming an important force in driving local industrial upgrading, green development and economic growth. Chinese companies operating in Hungary are also contributing to local innovation, R&D and talent development, building close partnerships with universities such as the University of Debrecen and the University of Szeged. It is hoped that the Hungarian government will continue providing a sound business environment for Chinese businesses. Connectivity between our two countries has continued to improve, with 22 direct passenger flights per week connecting Budapest with seven Chinese cities and further strengthening Budapest’s role as an important hub between China and Europe. At the Budapest AI Summit earlier this month, leading Chinese AI companies, research institutes and universities took part, opening new opportunities for AI exchanges and cooperation between our two countries. Last week, the Hungarian side sent a delegation to the 5th Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou. Eleven Hungarian businesses as well as the Hungarian Innovation Agency participated in the event. I am confident that our two countries will achieve even greater results in emerging fields such as the digital economy and green trade.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

The deep roots of China-Hungary friendship among our peoples are one of its distinctive hallmarks. In November last year, I visited Perkáta in Fejér County, which forged friendly ties with Huaxiang in Beijing as early as 1960, becoming the first Hungarian township to establish a sister relationship with a Chinese counterpart. More than six decades on, the two sides have preserved this longstanding friendship and maintained close exchanges, writing a new and inspiring chapter in the history of China-Hungary friendship. To this day, Perkáta still has a Beijing Road, while its Hungary-China Friendship Agricultural Company has been operating for more than 50 years. Mr. Oláh István, mayor of Perkáta, will soon lead a delegation to visit Beijing, to renew cooperation in the new era. I would like to express my sincere appreciation to all friends who have supported and contributed to the China-Hungary friendship.

Photo: Embassy of the People’s Republic of China to Hungary

Looking back, the friendship between China and Hungary is deeply rooted in the mutual understanding and affinity between our peoples. Looking ahead, the greatest opportunities for our cooperation stem from our shared pursuit of development. Under the strategic guidance of our leaders, I am confident that China and Hungary will carry forward our traditional friendship, deepen political mutual trust and practical cooperation, strengthen people-to-people exchanges, and maintain close communication on international affairs. Together, we will keep our all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership in the new era strong and enduring, bringing greater benefits to our two peoples.

World.title: Georgian and Bulgarian nationals arrested: International burglary gang caught after targeting homes across Budapest – video
World.content:
Three Georgian and Bulgarian nationals have been arrested in Budapest after police linked them to nine daytime burglaries across six districts, with nearly HUF 17 million in suspected losses.

Police tracked suspicious Ukrainian-registered car

The three men — two Georgian nationals aged 28 and 30 and a 30-year-old Bulgarian citizen — were arrested in Budapest’s District V on 25 September by officers from the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK), with assistance from the Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK).

According to police, the men are suspected of committing burglaries on a commercial basis. They were questioned and taken into custody, while prosecutors requested their pre-trial detention. BRFK’s head of the Investigation Department, Lieutenant Colonel Sándor Gál, said the suspects had entered Hungary from Slovakia and carried out nine residential burglaries between 15 and 25 September.

The break-ins took place in six Budapest districts: I, II, III and XI on the Buda side, and XIII and XIV on the Pest side.

Police said the cases were linked by several similarities. All the burglaries took place during the daytime, and the suspects allegedly opened the entrance doors without causing visible damage. The stolen property included cash, jewellery, expensive watches and electronic devices. Police estimate the total damage at almost HUF 17 million.

CCTV footage led police to the suspects

Investigators suspected that the burglars were using a car to move around Budapest and transport the stolen goods. After reviewing CCTV footage from the areas around the burglaries, they noticed a dark blue Toyota RAV4 with Ukrainian registration plates, carrying three men.

On 25 September, police launched a targeted patrol operation in central Budapest to locate the vehicle. They eventually found the Toyota and, with the assistance of TEK officers, arrested the three suspects.

During searches of the men and the vehicle, investigators found specialised tools allegedly used for breaking into properties and opening locks, as well as substances suspected to be drugs. Some of the stolen items and cash were also recovered.

Police said the men had been staying in Hungary since 28 August.

Police suspect ‘travelling criminals’

According to Gál, investigators suspect the men may be so-called “travelling criminals” who enter a country, commit several offences and then move on. Police believe two of the three men actively participated in the burglaries, while the third acted as the driver.

The suspects refused to make statements or cooperate with investigators during questioning. A court has since ordered their detention for 30 days. Gál said police will also contact authorities in the suspects’ home countries and neighbouring states to establish whether they may have been involved in offences elsewhere.

He added that residential burglaries are not currently unusually common in Budapest, with statistics showing broadly stable numbers in recent years.

World.title: Busy autumn at Kempinski: ÉS Bisztró launches Sunday brunch as hotel spa wins prestigious award
World.content:
Autumn has brought several new developments to Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest, with ÉS Bisztró launching a new Sunday brunch concept and Kempinski The Spa being named Hungary’s Best Hotel Spa at the 2026 World Spa Awards.

New Sunday tradition at ÉS Bisztró

Since 20 September, ÉS Bisztró has been serving its new Sunday Brunch every Sunday from 11:30am to 4pm, offering guests a relaxed alternative to the traditional Sunday lunch.

The concept combines an à la carte brunch menu with some of the restaurant’s signature dishes, giving guests the freedom to put together their own Sunday meal. Options range from Eggs Benedict and oysters to Beef Wellington, Sunday roast and the restaurant’s iconic Tafelspitz.

The brunch is designed for a variety of occasions, whether it is a family lunch, a long gathering with friends or simply a leisurely Sunday afternoon. A live DJ provides the soundtrack throughout the afternoon, adding to the relaxed atmosphere.

Photo: ÉS Bistro, Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest

Guests can also choose from a dedicated drinks menu featuring Bellinis, Bloody Marys, martinis and champagne. Two-hour free-flow beverage packages are available as well, alongside soft drinks and mocktails.

The Sunday Brunch will run throughout the autumn-winter season, every Sunday from 11:30 AM to 4 PM. Guests arriving for brunch can also use the hotel’s underground garage free of charge during brunch hours.

Photo: ÉS Bistro, Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest

Kempinski spa takes home another major title

Meanwhile, Kempinski The Spa has once again been recognised at the World Spa Awards, taking the title of ‘Hungary’s Best Hotel Spa’ in the 2026 edition.

The award marks the sixth time the spa has received the distinction, according to Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest.

Spa Manager Katalin O’Nagy said the recognition was a tribute to the work of the spa’s therapists and reception team, highlighting their role in creating a welcoming and relaxing environment for guests.

Kempinski The Spa: Reception. Photo: Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest

The latest award adds another international accolade to Kempinski The Spa’s record and underlines the hotel’s focus on luxury wellness services in the Hungarian capital.

With a new Sunday brunch and another major spa award, Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest is entering the autumn season with both its dining and wellness offerings in the spotlight.

Kempinski Budapest The Spa: Relaxation Area. Photo: Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest

World.title: Turkey Freezes Former Minister’s Assets in Market Manipulation Probe
World.content:
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said on Tuesday that it had asked Turkish institutions to freeze all assets belonging to former Family and Social Policies Minister Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, as part of an investment fund investigation.

“As part of the fund investigation conducted by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office’s Terrorism Financing and Money Laundering Crimes Investigation Bureau, relevant institutions have been instructed regarding the freezing of all assets belonging to Ilyas Kaya and his wife, Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya,” it said.

The investigation into dubious capital market transactions has resulted in 51 people being remanded in custody. Turkish authorities previously ordered the liquidation of 130 funds managed by seven portfolio management companies after liquidity problems contributed to sharp market losses.

According to Reuters, the funds’ assets are worth around 18.8 billion euros, involving about 353,000 investors. Turkish television channel CNBC-e estimates the total at about 17.4 billion euros and the number of investors at more than 514,000.

Kaya, Turkey’s family and social policies minister from 2016 to 2018, resigned as a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, after allegations emerged about share transactions by her and her husband.

Following a cabinet meeting, Erdogan said the government would act against wrongdoing in the markets. “We neither violate people’s rights nor turn a blind eye when the rights of our citizens are violated,” he said on Tuesday.

Liquidation of funds does not mean that the investors’ money has been confiscated. Instead, banks are being tasked to deliver citizens’ money in these funds. Is Bank has been appointed to handle the liquidation of funds managed by Tera Portfoy, while state-owned Ziraat Bank will oversee funds belonging to the six other managers.

Opposition politicians allege that the couple invested around 2.9 million euros in shares of shipbuilder Ozata Denizcilik in April and later sold the shares for about 39.5 million euros. The figures have not been published by the authorities.

Media reported on Monday that the couple subsequently transferred around 39.5 million euros to an account designated by the Treasury and Finance Ministry. The reported payment has also not been publicly confirmed.

Kaya comes from a family with extensive experience of public office. Her brother, Omer Fatih Sayan, a former telecommunications regulator chief and deputy transport minister, was appointed to the Energy Market Regulatory Board in July.

Her sister, Ayse Hilal Sayan Koytak, previously ambassador to Kuwait and Bahrain, was appointed ambassador to Finland in September. Another sister, Nazmiye Sumeyye Sayan, previously served on Istanbul’s municipal council.

World.title: Tracing Illicit Cigarette Flows over Mountainous Bosnia-Montenegro Borderland
World.content:
To cross between the municipalities of Gacko and Pluzine, in Bosnia and Montenegro respectively, most local residents must drive at least 100 kilometres, crossing at the Deleusa-Vracenovici border crossing.

Not so for the cigarette smugglers.

They use an asphalt road linking the Gacko village of Lipnik with Ravno in Pluzine. It’s a distance of some 10 kilometres.

“It’s exclusively a smuggling road,” a security source in Bosnia told BIRN on condition of anonymity.

The terrain around the road is too steep for farming, and the road sees almost no other traffic.

According to the case files seen by BIRN, police believe the gangs smuggled the cigarettes from Montenegro into Bosnia via mountain passes and stashed them in and around Avtovac and Lipnik.

“Given that the territory of the municipality of Gacko borders Montenegro, specifically the municipality of Pluzine, it is possible to transport excise goods to stash locations in the areas of Avtovac and Lipnik within a short period of time,” one document states.

With Zirojevic and Miletic allegedly in charge, other members of the group monitored the movement of police or drove ahead of the contraband as reconnaissance, according to the documents. The files name 14 other individuals as involved, all from Gacko and neighbouring municipalities.

They used at least nine different vehicles and often switched licence plates.

“They drive like crazy,” said a source familiar with the police investigation. “They can be over the border and back in ten minutes.” Police nicknamed one of the drivers ‘Phantom’.

“He drives so fast that nobody can catch him in a police chase,” said the source.

The smugglers often targeted an evening gap in patrols when shifts change between 6 and 7 p.m.

According to sources familiar with the investigation, rather than rotating officers directly along the road, border police shift changes take place at fixed points further away, leaving the unofficial mountain crossing unmonitored for about an hour every day.

“And while the shift happens, they have done the job,” a source said.

From Lipnik and Avtovac, the cigarettes are transported deeper into Bosnia for sale through street vendors. This reporter found smuggled cigarettes for sale on the streets of Sarajevo for 4.5 Bosnian marks, or 2.25 euros. The price of the cheapest legally sold pack of cigarettes is 6.2 Bosnian marks, or 3.10 euros.
