World.title: I had to explain to a 24-year-old man why I didn’t want to be a trad wife. It’s exhausting
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGender Opinion I had to explain to a 24-year-old man why I didn’t want to be a trad wife. It’s exhausting Kayla Olaya Reporter September 30, 2026 — 7:30pm

September 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mosquitoes bit my legs while I stood, listening to a man my age politely explain how he wanted a trad wife. This man, a Polish 24-year-old working remotely as a coder in Thailand, the same holiday destination as mine, at the same accommodation and doing the same fitness camp, said he was saving as much money as he could so he could one day fully support a family. “If I invest my money well and don’t spend it, I can afford it,” he explained. “I want my wife to stay at home and look after the family,” he said, resolutely. Adobe Stock I replied: “I would hate that, relying on someone financially.” He stared awkwardly at me and said he disagreed because, as a man, he felt that was an imperative role.



Related Article Opinion

Sunday Life I spent years wishing I was smaller before learning the power of being a ‘jacked beast’ Kayla Olaya Reporter “I want my wife to stay at home and look after the family,” he said, resolutely. We stood there quietly for a bit. Despite clearly having things in common, I couldn’t think of anything else to say, and by now, my legs were covered in bites. I went back to my hut and we didn’t speak again for the rest of the trip. Maybe our difference of opinion was cultural. But in such a globalised society, where manosphere vitriol lands indiscriminately in the algorithms of Australians of all ages, I felt as though he was speaking a language I unfortunately recognised. It echoed right-wing extremist Andrew Tate’s world views. I remember when women raised the alarm about the self-proclaimed misogynist as he began gaining attention in 2022. I also remember thinking his short-lived prominence represented a small group of men without considering with whom the message was silently resonating.



Meeting young men while backpacking has been an interesting experience. I have found it’s best to avoid talking about politics of all forms – immigration, gender roles, various wars – and focus strictly on day-to-day activities after too many revealed themselves to be racist or misogynistic. I always returned home thinking young Australian men weren’t as extreme. These days, I find myself avoiding these topics in conversation with men my age as headlines of alleged schoolyard and sporting sexual assaults tell me it’s not safe here, either. Perhaps young men across the world saw Donald Trump become US president, despite boasting about grabbing women by their genitals, as a green light to speak of and view women as such. Trump continues to insult female journalists based on their looks, telling a Bloomberg reporter to be “quiet, quiet, piggy” when she asked about his relationship with paedophile Jeffrey Epstein last year. The alleged inappropriate sexual behaviour of a crew of Sydney Swans players made a media storm and brought into conversation – again – the attitudes young men have towards women. These behaviours riddle other codes, too.



Last November, Penrith Panthers player Brian To’o was caught allegedly making lewd remarks about teammates’ girlfriends on pictures he uploaded to his own Instagram story. To’o allegedly commented on one photo of skipper Nathan Cleary, “The Fowler Slayer”, about Matildas sensation and Manchester City player Mary Fowler. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Before his speech went viral, this boys’ school headmaster ran it past his daughter Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author As a young woman who has to navigate this world each day – reading it in the news, skirting around its edges while backpacking or having to screen it on dating apps – I am exhausted. I feel jaded. I wonder if I am part of the growing percentage of women choosing not to have babies if these are the fathers. The worst part? I feel I’m becoming numb to misogyny – a combination of being exposed to it more often and trying to avoid being upset by it. I am shown time and time again that hardly anything comes from the relentless headlines of the alleged rapes, killings and harassment of women. It’s devastating when I see that a study published in August found young men are increasingly holding hostile attitudes towards women.



When I talk about misogyny with young men – a few who hold manospheric views and most who don’t – I more frequently watch the topic glide over them with the same avoidance I am beginning to acquire. They’re tired, too. Maybe for the same reasons as me, maybe not. My colleague jokes that when she was a young woman, a red flag in young men “was if they couldn’t spell or if their favourite movie was The Shawshank Redemption” . Now, it’s if young men are looking for a “wifey” or “missus” in their Hinge profile. Before a date, I always check who the man follows on social media in case it’s right-wing provocateurs or hundreds of Instagram models. The Polish man who wants a trad wife stayed in a hut next to mine. Before the topic of gender roles came up, we shared our anxieties about living in a world overrun by technology, feeling helpless as the world burns around us and experiencing a sense of existential dread because AI has made us feel as though our contributions to society are meaningless. Yet, somehow, we were still worlds apart. Kayla Olaya is a culture reporter at The Sydney Morning Herald.

World.title: He stole his first instrument at the age of five. Eventually, all was forgiven
World.content:
Benjamin Clementine, 37, went from busking in the subways of Paris to becoming one of the most acclaimed artists in contemporary music.

Benjamin Clementine defied his family to forge his own musical destiny. The journey that followed has been far from easy.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Benjamin Clementine was five when an uncharacteristic act of resistance sealed his fate. Growing up in a household where instruments were forbidden, he became so entranced with the toy piano a classmate had brought to primary school that when she refused to let him play it, he took it – hoping to spend at least one evening at home with it – but was ordered to return it before he had the chance. How, he wondered, had this single-octave keyboard produced such an astonishing combination of sounds? “I was looking at this girl with that thing – I remember it like it was yesterday – and I asked her if I could play,” he says. “She said no. She just wouldn’t give it to me. I was so fascinated by this thing but sad that I couldn’t have it. When I looked at it, I got this good feeling I’d never felt before, outside of laughter with my siblings. It’s like how some kids feel when they find football or basketball or tennis.” Born and raised in London to a family of Ghanaian descent, the 37-year-old musician, composer and actor had almost no exposure to popular culture in his formative years. It was a strict, religious household. Non-Christian music was forbidden, as were instruments of any kind. His father, who had been a professor of mathematics in Liberia, was determined his son would study law. Somehow, despite his parents’ best attempts to shield him from the corrupting influence of secular music, Clementine, who will tour Australia for the first time this month, has become one of the most acclaimed voices in contemporary music. Unbound by genre, his compositions draw from a range of styles including classical, experimental and avant-garde. Poetry, literature and the writings of pioneering psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott also inform his work. Benjamin Clementine will tour Australia for the first time in October. Christophe Raynaud de Lage Speaking via Zoom from his home in California, his 193-centimetre frame curled into an armchair, Clementine says that when he brings his Back To Basics tour to Australia, it’ll just be him and his piano, which he usually plays barefoot. (He has likened this to the thrill of driving without shoes.) “Because I’ve never toured Australia, I want to show them my bare self, and it’s up to them to take me for who I am,” he says. “To be honest, I get tired of touring with so many people [in a back-up band].



“There’s always this offer of the Sydney Opera House. I would love to play there, but first I want to come in with a humble kind of approach. I don’t want to play in front of 5000 people right now in Australia; I want to play in front of 500 to 1000 people. My aim is to be intimate with people who are seeing me for the first time, so that we genuinely get to hear each other and smell each other. That’s what I’ve always done.” This pared-back approach is also a chance to reconnect with his musical roots, having taught himself to sing, compose and play a number of instruments. “Before all the tricks of production and frequencies and equalisation and compression, there’s just the song,” he says. “My greatest ability, from what I’ve been told, is to simply tell a story without noise. Over the years, I went from that to almost showing off through production – and sometimes you get lost in those things. I’m just tired of it. This is about going back to the fundamentals.” It’s not hard to see why critics frequently compare Clementine, with his powerful voice that shifts between delicate vulnerability and raw intensity, to Nina Simone. Many of their songs are self-contained stories, often containing social critiques. As one reviewer observed, each sings “as if all the world depended on it”. And they share a striking physicality that underscores a powerful stage presence. Clementine, who has modelled for Abercrombie & Fitch, has high, sharp cheekbones and an angular jawline. As The Guardian memorably put it, he “resembles an art deco illustration of himself”. Throughout his career, Clementine has amassed high-profile fans including Damon Albarn, Bjork and Paul McCartney. He met the latter after he was invited to perform on the TV music program Later... with Jools Holland. “Normally, I’m not fazed by anything when I’m performing but I could see Paul watching while I was playing and it was all a blur,” Clementine says. “Afterwards, I went to go to the loo and someone tapped me on the shoulder. It was Paul McCartney and I can’t remember exactly what he said but it was something like, ‘Oh, that was a great song’.” Having already recorded an EP, Cornerstone, he got to work on his first studio album, At Least For Now, released to wide acclaim in 2015. His subsequent albums, I Tell a Fly and And I Have Been received similar praise – including from the father who had been so reluctant to let him play music.



“He never said he was proud of me, but he showed me in his own way,” Clementine says. “Before he died, he said, ‘I like some of your songs’. It broke me down a little bit and I was in tears. For me, it was a huge compliment.” Now, as a father of three, Clementine understands his parents’ motivation in pushing him towards a career in law. Having fled political turmoil and material deprivation to build a stable life in London, they spent a fortune on his education, including boarding school. To them, it was incumbent upon their children to forge respectable careers. But fate intervened when his family moved to a house where an upright piano had been left behind. “They didn’t want me to play it because they knew it would pull my interest from my study,” he says. “And they were right: I was going to be a lawyer but then I decided not to do that. “After suffering themselves, and working hard to be accepted into society, you wouldn’t want your children [to experience similar hardships] … so there was resentment and anger,” he says. “They’re conservative; they do things the ‘correct’ way so it’s just embarrassing to have a child who has abandoned everything but doesn’t really know what he wants to do, other than going for whatever is ‘out there’. It’s a really hard thing for an immigrant parent to process that.” Naturally, music lessons were not an option, so Clementine taught himself to play piano by ear, and tried any instrument he could get his hands on. He spent hours in his local library, studying poetry, art and literature. (Sylvia Plath and William Blake are major influences, as is Nick Cave: “His music transports you to different places, and transcends different feelings and moments in time.”) He bought books with accompanying CDs to acquire the basics of French, Mandarin, German and Italian, among other languages. “I’ve always had a thing for languages and literature,” he says, paraphrasing a quote commonly attributed to Cicero. “‘Language without literature is like a body without a head’. I believe that literature is music in itself. It has melody and harmony, it’s atonal and tonal, it has rhythm. Now, I find myself writing and then applying it to common sounds. I change the accents on words and the intonation is determined by how I feel. I think that’s my personal secret in how I express what I want to say.”



Among his most popular songs are Cornerstone, which he performed on the Jools Holland show; I Won’t Complain, from his Mercury Prize-winning debut album At Least For Now; and Nemesis, used in the opening credits of Apple TV’s Morning Wars. He has also had supporting roles in the 2021 film Dune; Steve McQueen’s 2024 World War II drama Blitz; and Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series The Gentlemen. Clementine with Steve McQueen, who directed the 2024 film Blitz, in which he had a supporting role. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Does he believe the absence of formal music training allowed him the freedom to cultivate his unique sound? “If you’d asked me that question 10 years ago, I would have been arrogant,” Clementine admits. “I’d have said something like, ‘There’s no such thing as theory; we should all just receive music from our ears’. But as a 37-year-old man, I think theory is necessary. “Look, I’m happy with how I turned out. And I can read music now because I spent five years studying it myself, so I compose differently.” When Clementine was 16, his parents divorced: a huge shock in light of their devout Christianity. He lived with his father briefly, then his mother, before bouncing around Camden and crashing with mates. Not long after, he quit school.



At 19, he moved to Paris, primarily because it was close and contained a significant proportion of English-speaking residents. Much has been made of his time in the city, from periods of homelessness and stints in hostels to busking in the subway. But he’s reluctant to portray this as the first chapter of a rags-to-riches tale. He did, however, learn a lot about life while performing at train stations. Related Article Take 7 ‘Be careful who you surround yourself with’: Johnny Young’s prescient advice to Tina Arena “It was like Darwin’s survival of the fittest,” he says. “If I asked for money, I would only eat for a day but if I befriended somebody, I would eat for a week. I learned to be a better human. In England, I was still a boy.” Fellow buskers introduced him to popular music from the ’40s, ’50s and ’60s, including Nina Simone, Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen and The Beatles. “In that period, musicians had something they wanted to say and they had a melody to go with it,” he says. “But over the past 30 years, popular music has all been driven by the catchy phrase and the chorus. In the West, we’re obsessed with melody because it sells music. But melody has also plagued our music in the sense that people get away with saying nothing.” In France, Clementine became successful enough that he could afford to eat and pay his bills. Still, he refused regular requests from police to obtain a mandatory busking permit. “I didn’t want to succumb to the idea that I’m only worth a cent in the subway,” he says. “I never went to Paris to busk or make music. I knew that I was going somewhere.”

World.title: ‘Second-class citizens’: Liberals refuse to campaign after preselection snub
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaVictorian election ‘Second-class citizens’: Liberals refuse to campaign after preselection snub Angelica Snowden September 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Liberal Party is facing a backlash from its members in the must-win seat of Pakenham, who say they are unwilling to volunteer in the upcoming election campaign after party chiefs sidelined them from handpicking their candidate. Pakenham, in Melbourne’s outer south-east, is currently held by Labor’s Emma Vulin by just 0.39 per cent, making it one of the most marginal seats up for grabs at November’s state election. Candidates running for Pakenham (left to right): Alessandra Soliven for Labor, Radmila Dyson for the Liberal Party and Warren Pickering for One Nation. Ruby Alexander, Facebook Its status as a critical battleground has also been amplified by One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering also vying for the seat, as Pauline Hanson’s party seeks to capitalise on its surging popularity to win Victorian lower house seats for the first time. In 2022, Liberal candidate David Farrelly secured a swing of 1.8 per cent to the party, but just came up short.



The former long-time chair of Neighbourhood Watch in Cardinia sought to run again this year, as well as Maroondah City Council IT worker Monty Sodhi. But the party’s state executive decided against holding a local preselection and instead intervened to tap soccer club volunteer Radmila Dyson to be their candidate. Her preselection was confirmed on August 15, nine months after preselection applications closed in December. It also came after Labor chose 23-year-old Alessandra Soliven to replace incumbent MP Vulin – who will not recontest the seat after she was diagnosed with motor neurone disease – and Pickering entered the fray. David Farrelly (centre) secured a small swing to the Liberal Party, but ultimately fell short in the contest for Pakenham in the 2022 election. Eamon Gallagher Because marginally fewer than 40 members registered to vote for the Pakenham candidate, out of about 50 in the branch, the party’s state executive invoked a rule to bypass grassroots members and call in the preselection, according to an email seen by The Age sent to members by the Pakenham state electorate conference chair. The state executive – as well as a handful of branch office bearers – chose Dyson. A Liberal source, speaking anonymously to detail internal deliberations, said she was given special dispensation to run as a candidate because she had been a party member for less than a year.



Related Article Victorian election One Nation Victoria leader admits to drug use, drink-driving Four Pakenham branch members, also speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said Farrelly or Sodhi would have probably won a democratic vote. A senior party official added: “The whole thing was orchestrated so Monty and David couldn’t be elected.” “They didn’t want an Indian candidate running in a lower house seat,” the official alleged. “[The party] are trying to bring back people who have moved to One Nation, but in the meantime they have lost with the multicultural community and lost out on their heavy lifting on the ground.” Farrelly told The Age that members who otherwise would have volunteered for the party’s bid in the electorate “will not be volunteering any more”.



“I think the process the party engaged in right across the Victorian landscape for preselecting candidates failed drastically in a number of locations,” he said. “When you don’t have local members contributing to the vote, you’re not getting a true local representative and the membership voice isn’t being reflected through those candidates.” Radmila Dyson, the Liberal Party candidate for Pakenham. Facebook Asked how the party was tracking for volunteers to support Dyson, Farrelly said: “I wouldn’t know where that is up to now, and I haven’t been asked to help.” “That is unusual,” he said. “You normally ask everyone you can. Especially people with experience, and I’ve been a candidate and have worked on federal campaigns.”



Responding to a detailed list of questions about the preselection process, a Liberal Party spokesperson said:“The Liberal Party is excited to have Radmilla [sic] Dyson running in Pakenham.” Asked if she needed permission to run as a candidate because she only joined in August last year, the spokesperson said: “We do not comment on internal matters.” Typically, members of local branches are invited to attend a preselection conference and cast their ballot to choose the party’s candidate. A senior party source said local preselections went ahead in Williamstown, Frankston and Point Cook with just 19, 14 and 14 members allowed to cast votes alongside party chiefs. The party’s state executive also handpicked their preferred candidate – Moonee Valley councillor Samantha Byrne – in Niddrie in Melbourne’s north-west, the seat held by Premier Ben Carroll. That intervention also sparked a local backlash, with member Nigel Kibel sharing a post on Facebook declaring that “state executive deciding preselection is totally unacceptable”.



“Yesterday, the Liberal preselection in Niddrie took place, and once again it was determined that the locals did not have the numbers, so the state executive made the decision,” the July post read. “This occurred after the new state president, Brian Loughnane, said that local members would be included.” In Pakenham, Indian radio station Radio Haanji reported that Sodhi’s preselection bid had brought “hope for Australian-Indian political representation”. Pakenham hopeful Monty Sodhi. “As a member of the Sikh community, Sodhi has expressed an interest in representing Pakenham not only as a local resident but also … [as someone] who is running [for] an ultra-marginal seat and also one of the few Australian-Indian(s) seeking public office in Victoria,” the station said on Facebook. Sodhi declined to comment.



Related Article Opinion

Liberal Party The Liberal Party is shedding members in the west. The treatment of an Indian community candidate has been like a wrecking ball Chip Le Grand State political editor The party’s relationship with its Indian members was frayed earlier this year, after Dinesh Gourisetty was preselected to replace Moira Deeming on the party’s upper house ticket in the Western Metropolitan region, only to be dumped when it emerged he had given a character reference to a child abuser in 2024. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Gourisetty would not be welcome in her party room after the November election. This masthead previously reported that western suburbs branches shed members in the wake of the saga. Dyson, the party’s Pakenham candidate, co-founded the popular Officer City Soccer Club and remains its treasurer. According to property records, she owns a home in Beaconsfield, which sits just outside the Pakenham electorate. She has worked in her family business and is raising twins, according to the Pakenham Officer Star News. This masthead tried to contact her directly but she did not respond. A member of the Pakenham branch said they would not volunteer for the party’s relatively new recruit.



“There were two [candidates] more deserving than her. They are Monty Sodhi and David Farrelly,” the member said. “We have been ignored by the Liberal Party.” A second member, who joined the branch at the end of last year, also said they would limit the time they spent door-knocking in support of Dyson. “Why should we [go door-knocking]? We are not things to use and throw away,” they said. “[During preselection] I felt we are considered second-class citizens. If the party calls on us for fundraising, why not during the preselection.” A third member similarly expressed doubt about helping during the campaign. “They should have allowed us to vote … It’s disappointing. If it is a democracy, there should be a vote count.”

World.title: Third time’s a charm? McDonald’s to open new store in the heart of Newtown
World.content:
NationalNSWDevelopment Third time’s a charm? McDonald’s to open new store in the heart of Newtown Cindy Yin September 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hipsters will go head-to-head with Happy Meals in one of Sydney’s most vibrant entertainment strips after McDonald’s used a fast-track development process to take over the Oporto restaurant on Enmore Road. The fast-food chain’s move into the heart of the Newtown-Enmore nightlife precinct comes after an earlier bid to set up shop on King Street was rejected twice and met fierce resistance from residents. Newtown resident Lynn Stanton has lived in the area for more than 30 years, and said Enmore Road had always been a bit “quirkier” and more alternative than King Street. Nadir Tolj-Kinani Long-time Newtown resident Lynn Stanton, who is among locals opposed to the chain’s arrival in the suburb, said she had never eaten McDonald’s in her life, and wasn’t about to start any time soon. “I object to McDonald’s, full stop,” she said. “The way they’ve done it feels like coming through the back door so no one can even say they don’t like it … That’s wrong and spells greed and profit.”



McDonald’s on Friday began work at the Enmore Road site, one week after it abandoned a court case against the City of Sydney over the council’s refusal of a similar plan to build a store 500 metres away. At the time, the King Street proposal triggered a wave of backlash from residents, NSW Police, and business owners who said a McDonald’s store would erode the unique character of Newtown. Related Article City life Wondering where to go this evening? Here are the Sydney suburbs where the nighttime economy is booming McDonald’s was last in Newtown in 1998, when a restaurant opened in 1982 by rugby league great Ron Coote closed its doors. The multinational’s push into Newtown extends a citywide trend of fast food companies seeking to operate new outlets on local shopping strips despite community resistance. McDonald’s has made similar attempts to open in Crows Nest, Marrickville, Redfern, and the Central Coast, with mixed results. McDonald’s lodged the $1.2 million Enmore Road plan with the Inner West Council via the fast-tracked complying development certificate pathway on September 21. A private certifier, not council staff, approved plans the next day. Construction on internal alteration work and the fit-out began on September 25. There are no plans to install a drive-through.



Unlike a typical development application, CDCs combine planning and construction approval for more straightforward developments, but some have criticised the process over a perceived lack of council oversight and consultation. McDonald’s used the same pathway to win approval for a controversial plan to open an outlet in affluent Crows Nest this year. City of Sydney councillor Jess Miller said the fast-food chain’s use of the fast-tracked approval process could “really enrage people in the community”. “It means an application doesn’t go on exhibition, it doesn’t go to a local planning panel, none of the issues are ventilated. Rather than going through a transparent assessment and consultation process, CDCs can be approved via a check-a-box exercise.” McDonald’s is coming to bohemian Newtown, at the site of the former Oporto store on Enmore Road. Nadir Tolj-Kinani Heleana Genaus, secretary of the Newtown and Enmore Business Community, said reactions from local shop owners were mixed.



“The reluctance is there are plenty of fast-food multinational chains, and more emerging every day. But many are also providing low-cost options for consumers – a Big Mac is probably sitting more where people’s budgets are. “There’s no villain per se, and I don’t think it’s fair that McDonald’s is copping it because of that. They are just unemotionally responding to finding the right location to make some money,” she said. However, Inner West Greens councillor Liz Atkins said McDonald’s was “getting a foothold in the area after previous experiences of community backlash in Newtown and Marrickville.” The recognisable golden arches of McDonald’s will soon appear on a new site in Sydney’s inner west. Eamon Gallagher A council spokesperson said they had “no legal grounds” to refuse the McDonald’s application, as it had to comply with state government legislation.



McDonald’s said the start of construction represented a “multimillion-dollar investment into the local economy and creating over 130 jobs for construction workers and restaurant employees”. Related Article City life Why residents and police have joined forces to stop a McDonald’s at Redfern A company spokesman said the Enmore Road outlet, due to open later this year, would be operated by a local licensee committed to supporting the community. “McDonald’s Newtown was approved through a complying development certificate (CDC) as the restaurant met all necessary guidelines under relevant legislation. “We look forward to becoming part of the Newtown community when the restaurant opens.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘A cruel mess’: Families left in limbo as national autism scheme launches without Queensland
World.content:
NationalQueenslandDisability ‘A cruel mess’: Families left in limbo as national autism scheme launches without Queensland Courtney Kruk September 30, 2026 — 8:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Queensland government says its refusal to sign up to a new program for autistic children is in support of families, despite calls from across the sector to provide certainty for vulnerable kids removed from the NDIS. The first phase of Thriving Kids, a new system for children under nine with developmental delays or autism and low-to-moderate support needs, will launch on Thursday. The federal government says the NDIS alternative will initially include foundational supports, a digital resource hub, and national helplines to guide families. Federal Health Minister Mark Butler announced Thriving Kids, a new system for children under nine with developmental delays and autism, in August last year. The first phase of the program launches this week. Dominic Lorrimer Changes to NDIS access and assessment will not take effect until January 2028.



Queensland the lone holdout Queensland is the only state or territory yet to sign on to the program, with the Crisafulli government repeatedly criticising the scheme’s lack of detail and clear, long-term funding. Disability Services Minister Amanda Camm called Thriving Kids “a bad deal for children with a disability”, and said the LNP was prepared to take a stand, even if it was the only state to do so. Asked on Wednesday whether the government was considering an eleventh-hour agreement, Premier David Crisafulli said he remained “as strong and resolute as ever”. “We’re trying to get common sense out of Canberra to make sure [families] don’t fall through the cracks,” he said.



“We’ll keep working Canberra, [but] we want to see the details.” Related Article Hospitals Albanese ends hospital stalemate with $25b deal to move kids off NDIS A spokesperson for the federal government said while every other state and territory was finalising the implementation of Thriving Kids, Queensland had left families “rightly asking” what children’s services they could access. “Queensland joined every other state and territory earlier this year in signing a national agreement for foundational supports as part of the NHRA [National Health Reform Agreement] deal, as well as a heads of agreement on the national deal that includes Thriving Kids,” the spokesperson said. “The expectation now is those commitments are implemented so the benefits of the agreement can be realised.”



Greens state MP Michael Berkman labelled the situation “a cruel mess”, and said both Labor and the LNP had turned their backs on autistic people. “There’s still very little concrete information on what this Thriving Kids program would actually provide,” he said. Greens MP Michael Berkman says he’s concerned about the lack of detail around the Thriving Kids program. Joe Ruckli/Australian Financial Review “We’ve been told it will include online resources for parents, and there’s been talk of a lot of things it ‘may’ include, like school programs or social groups – all of which sounds pretty weak and undefined to me. “There’s also no information on what will happen to kids after they turn nine, and nothing on adults with autism who will be kicked off the NDIS at the end of next year.”



Related Article Disability Children won’t need an autism diagnosis to use Thriving Kids scheme Families and providers in the dark Brisbane mother Nicole Chesterton has been waiting almost two years to get her seven-year-old son assessed for autism. She was recently told her NDIS funding had been cut and that she wouldn’t be able to dispute it without a formal diagnosis. With the introduction of Thriving Kids looming, she’s even more uncertain about how her son will be supported. “[Under the NDIS] he was allocated around $17,000 a year to use on speech therapy, psychology, and all those allied health offerings,” she said.



“[Now] there’s no funding and I’m off the list. “I have no idea [what Thriving Kids will mean] … there’s no way to keep up with all the changes that they’re making.” Jodi Wolthers, chief executive of Parent to Parent Association Queensland – a support organisation for people with disabilities – said many families were feeling uncertain about what changes to the NDIS would mean in practice. Jodi Wolthers, chief executive of Parent to Parent Association Queensland. Inclusion Australia



“Our biggest concern is some parents we talk to have not heard of Thriving Kids,” she said. “At the same time, we are hearing from families whose young children are being exited from the NDIS. “The risk is that there is no Thriving Kids or other service for them to go to. There is no safety net. “In general, parents are concerned about the whole of the NDIS reform changes and what they will mean for their son/daughter and the impact on their family.” Soul Support provides disability services for children across south-east Queensland, Victoria and NSW.



Related Article Autism ‘We’re lost’: Families, staff devastated as specialist childcare centres close Managing director Breanna Jenkins said children with autism were already disadvantaged by current funding arrangements, and she worried that more would be left behind by a new, ill-defined program. “Who will be assessing the severity of these children and whether they’re eligible for Thriving Kids?” she said. “As we’ve seen with the NDIA [National Disability Insurance Agency] … it can be really challenging for [young people with autism] to get funding, and their funding can just be stripped away. “After how many years the NDIA has been around, we’re still ironing out key things about it … so it’s a real worry if we’re going to be putting up millions of people and families into Thriving Kids and all of these issues [remain].”



Vision Australia’s chief mission officer, Chris Edwards, said Thriving Kids raised questions for children with multiple disabilities and deteriorating conditions. “Where those supports are put into different lanes, that creates challenges to be able to provide a holistic support for a child to ensure they … actually start meeting developmental milestones,” he said. “All programs, whether it’s NDIS or Thriving Kids, should be accepting kids who have deteriorating conditions as early as possible so those interventions can become part of their norm.” What comes next? From Thursday, families of children with extra developmental needs can access expanded information and supports, including the new Thriving Kids Autism Helpline and a new online information hub, which Queenslanders will also be able to access.



The federal government said children with permanent and significant disability or high support needs will continue to access the NDIS. The full Thriving Kids program is expected by 2028. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Dally M awards 2026 LIVE updates: Early award winners; NRL counting underway; best of the red carpet
World.content:
It’s NRL Coach of the Year time, and the nominees are the Warriors’ Andrew Webster, the Dolphins’ Kristian Woolf, and Newcastle’s Justin Holbrook.

In the first real surprise of the night, considering Holbrook’s Knights went from the wooden spoon to the grand final in his first season in charge, the award goes to Webster – who guided the Warriors to a second-place finish on the regular season ladder.

In fairness the Dally M awards generally cover the regular season only – so Newcastle’s heroics in the finals, including knocking out the Warriors, were not a factor – but this is still a bit of a shock result.

The NRLW Coach of the Year goes to the Gold Coast Titans’ Karyn Murphy, who pips the Roosters’ John Strange and the Wests Tigers’ Craig Sandercock.

World.title: Hitting home owners is not the right strategy
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Hitting home owners is not the right strategy September 30, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. I am seriously confused. Inflation is too high so we need to increase interest rates so those fortunate enough to have a mortgage have to curtail their spending. The government then looks at measures to put more money into the economy in the guise of tax cuts or whatever may be effective in ensuring they may not lose votes. That, of course, may be inflationary ensuring another rate rise to curtail inflation.

How can the so-called money managers (Labor or Liberal) see this as a solution? How can no government economist (is this an oxymoron?) see that belting those who strive to buy their dream home is very narrowminded?

For goodness sake, increase the tax rates to reduce spending across the board.

David Raymond, Doncaster East RBA move is not fair

Raising interest rates has to be an inefficient means of combating inflation. Borrowers are the major cohort of those impacted by a rate rise – and that happens to be about a third of us.

The other two-thirds are basically unaffected by a rate rise. In effect, the Reserve Bank wants to control inflation by impacting only part of the community (″⁣RBA warns of more rate pain to come″⁣, 30/9).

Those unaffected go about buying their needs as they want to, making no impact on inflation other than perhaps creating demand – which may well contribute to inflation.

Why not make use of all of the population by altering taxation, in particular the GST. All of the population is then contributing to the lowering of inflation. And the government gets the benefit of reaping more dollars, lowering the deficit.

To disallow governments changing the GST at their whim, allow only the RBA make a directive to alter the GST rate similar to what it does now with interest rate changes.

Peter Randles, Mornington Don’t rely on ideology in a crisis

Let’s try and take the politics out of the rise in inflation and the rise in interest rates. RBA governor Michelle Bullock has put the primary cause at increased petrol prices which will soar if US President Donald Trump cuts diesel supply.

There is in my opinion an ideology that governments who don’t reduce income tax are inefficient. Ideology is not something to rely on in a crisis. The only people who have any sort of discretionary spending are higher-income earners. I suggest that the tax rate for people earning over $135,000 increase from 37¢ to 40¢ in the $1, which will decrease spending. It can be put in place for two years until things improve.

I am sure if Labor suggested it, the Coalition would throw a fit. But I can’t see the Coalition having anything better to suggest, other than get rid of Labor in 18 months.

John Rome, Mt Lawley, WA



Rise an ineffective tool

The Reserve Bank has failed to qualify why the latest increase is necessary. Hiding behind the stated goal that it is to reduce inflation is not a justification in itself, unless the RBA can demonstrate how increasing the cash rate will act to prevent institutions, industries and commerce from raising their prices.

Recent increases in the cash rate have clearly shown that it has done nothing to reduce inflation, nor will this latest increase.

David King, South Yarra Banks are the holders

As interest rates rise again, we see many articles regarding the plight of “mortgage holders”. Can we get the terminology right: the “holder” of the mortgage is the bank. The borrower pledges the right to the mortgaged property as security to the lender.

Angus McLeod, Cremorne A tradition we could do without

It’s reassuring to see that the Reserve Bank has observed the time-honoured Australian tradition of punishing the most vulnerable the most harshly.

Steve Walter, Newstead THE FORUM Funds and services

A shortage of staff at the new Footscray (″⁣New hospital, fresh crisis″⁣, 30/9) and Royal Children’s hospitals, a shortage of beds to house homeless people, childcare upheavals leaving families without places, roads across the state in poor condition, and public schools struggling for funds are all symptoms of the increasing need for better service delivery demanded by the community.

Also, the Middle East war and Reserve Bank interest rises are adding to the cost-of-living crisis that cannot be addressed unless governments have access to more funds either through borrowing or increasing taxes.

In debates surrounding the issues, the thought of paying higher taxes are excluded,

while ideology and self-interest dominate.

Whoever wins the next Victorian election has a massive challenge, and no simple solutions other than more funds will solve the problems. Let’s not be fooled by rhetoric and grandstanding by those seeking election.

Ray Cleary, Camberwell



Housing is key

The Age editorial (30/9) supporting an assertive homelessness outreach program points out that it is but one part of the whole. Housing is the issue, and the dream of home ownership is over for the foreseeable future for many Australians – a result of decades of policy neglect and failure from most governments.

The Age has a proud history of exposing government failures, and our housing crisis is fertile ground. All major parties should be asked to respond to the following assertions: Without serious government intervention, we will have a permanent under-class of citizens who cannot afford to purchase, struggle to pay private rents and cannot access public or social housing.

Band-aids applied for decades such as first home-buyers grants, selling scarce urban land for private development with paltry increases in public housing stock or encouraging superannuation funds to invest in social housing are not effective.

There is no substitute for adequate public funding for housing – as occurred from the 1940s to the 1970s – and credible analyses demonstrate significant net socio-economic benefits from such investment.

As Age columnist Ross Gittins has observed, this might smooth the impact of the cyclical nature of the private housing sector.

Norman Huon, Port Melbourne Billionaires aplenty

Your correspondent highlights the success of Australia’s super rich (Letters, 30/9). We are certainly doing very well in terms of wealth concentration. The United States has about 12 times Australia’s population (342 million v

28 million) and while we have about 180 billionaires, they have only about 1000.

Perhaps it is some kind of achievement in having twice as many billionaires per head of population as the US, the nation that is usually recognised as the leader of the Western world in terms of inequality.

Peter McCarthy, Mentone The peace supports

Politicians claim they want peace in the Middle East and stop there, as if everything would then be resolved and we can wash our hands of the situation.

Peace is not only the absence of war but requires actively putting in place the practical opportunity for prosperity, freedom and justice. Without these opportunities, peace is not only meaningless but will not last.

Roy Olliff, Mont Albert North Airport rail a waste

Why build airport rail when the Skybus takes, at most, 25 minutes from Southern Cross Station (“Carroll makes tracks in rush for airport rail by 2031”, 30/9)?

The train from Southern Cross to Sunshine station takes about 25 minutes. Another 10 minutes for the new line from Sunshine to the airport, and guess what? The bus is quicker. Do the maths: airport rail is a waste of money.

Peter Heffernan, Balaclava Careful with labels

I don’t doubt that Xi Jinping is a dictator, but is China an enemy state as Peter Hartcher asserts (Comment, 29/9)? There are many dictatorships around the world and many authoritarian states, but we usually manage cordial relations with them and avoid labelling them as enemies.

Even countries with whom we have had long-standing good relations can prove difficult at times. I think we do need to be cautious in our dealings with China. Alas, I also think we need to be cautious in our dealings with the United States in its current authoritarian phase. I don’t think it helps our efforts to maintain good relations to label them as enemies.

David Rose, Montrose



The benefits of trout

While it is true that trout are an invasive species, as your correspondent rightly says, (Letters, 29/9), brown and rainbow trout are almost certainly the only “pest” whose introduction has been, on balance, beneficial to Australia. Trout anglers are a large part of an industry that spends nearly

$11 billion annually and supports thousands of jobs in regional areas, all in pursuit of a fish that has had an almost negligible impact on our natural environment. Trout should not be considered as pests in the same context as other invasive species that have ravaged Australia.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully Children, ssshhhh

This may make me sound heartless, but maybe it’s time to ban children from libraries who don’t respect this sacred environment. While I have been studying and been respectful of the culture, some parents let their children run amok. It’s not an extension of school, children can be a nuisance and can disrupt the privilege of a quiet space. Kid-free zones may be a nice option.

Panagiota Frangopoulos, Malvern Neglected Footscray

As a 20-plus-year resident of the inner western suburbs of Melbourne and having founded the local community independents group (Voices of the Inner West of Melbourne), I’ve never seen our Footscray district area making news headlines as much for unfortunate reasons. The high-voltage powerlines through Yarraville residential streets, fast-tracked data centre developments, failed social support and safety in the Footscray urban area, and now the reporting on the dire situation at the Footscray Hospital (“Closed theatres, empty beds: The problems plaguing Melbourne’s new $1.5b hospital”, 30/9).

These examples speak to the widespread frustration of residents who have been feeling overlooked and taken for granted for many years – and now realising with this Victorian election that the district of Footscray is actually a marginal seat.

Anthony Warren, Seddon Superbug super scary

Amid the many alarming stories in The Age yesterday, one stood out: “Ultimate Superbug: New form of antibiotic resistance uncovered” (30/9).

Science reporter Angus Dalton’s overview revealed 10 of Victoria’s 14 independent research institutes will close because of the “slow strangulation of the research sector by flat state and federal funding”.

I’d always assumed wealthy pharmaceutical companies in Australia – and throughout the world – would help fund such vital research but ironically, antibiotics are deemed “the opposite of a profitable blockbuster drug”.

While experts express concern about the prospective fatal intrusion AI will create, who’s worried about an emerging “ultimate superbug” resistant to existing antibiotics that is a genuine threat to human lives?

Regrettably, it seems, no one.

Sally Davis, Malvern East Plight of the humble bee

While walking the dogs recently, I noticed some bees, but so few it seems that they can afford to

be selective, feeding only on lavender bushes.

In the evenings, with the light of Jupiter standing in for the Moon, I have recently seen swarms of what I guess must be bogong moths landing on and feeding on the streetside bottlebrushes (″⁣After catastrophic decline, the bogong moth is springing back″⁣, 29/9). They are so small though, possibly offering only tiny snacks for any of Sydney’s micro bats?

I can remember much larger moths in the past with these markings, that with their wings extended could cover a child’s hand. With councils tending to replace all-year-round flowering natives like bottlebrushes with northern hemisphere deciduous trees (bare in winter), what hopes remain for these and other nocturnal nectar feeders and pollinators?

Garry Dalrymple, Earlwood, NSW



Hive of humanity

Can you imagine how insufferable people would be if they only spoke after checking with artificial intelligence? They would always be right and no one would have differing opinions, anecdotal incidents to relate, and creativity would be lost because everyone would be attuned to what AI thinks is the correct fashion.

Empathy and sympathy, love and affection may become scripted, but will we recognise the falsity of it?

Our eyes, ears need to absorb natural things before they become overwhelmed by unnatural ones. The simple touch of a human or animal is enough to trigger all sorts of endorphins in our brain.

I can’t see an AI machine doing that without us popping a pill to activate it. Unless we have proper human interaction, it will become a short, boring grey life we lead.

Our biggest data centre is the 8 billion real people in the world.

Sharing each other’s feelings and experiences is our primary weapon against AI.

Greg Tuck, Warragul Sketchy planning

We seem to be very good at drawing the Airport Rail Link. Just not very good at building it.

Ron Mather, Melbourne Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Finances

Why do we need politicians and economists while we have the Reserve Bank governing our lives?

Richard Sykes, Bell Park



When Australia’s underlying rate of inflation is nearly the same as Puerto Rico’s, you know we are definitely on the path to becoming a banana republic.

Martin Newington, Aspendale It might be tough, but I still remember running a business and having a mortgage when the Reserve Bank raised the interest rate to 17.5 per cent.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Furthermore

Two signs seen in a cafe in Scotland – ″⁣Dogs Welcome” and “Unsupervised children will be given a triple shot macchiato and a free kitten”.

Kathy Keech, Beaumont, SA Somewhere in Russia, there must be people who are different from Vladimir Putin. Pity we only ever get to see Putin’s cruel excesses.

John Walsh, Watsonia When we read that OpenAI promises to do better after the Medicare hack, is the statement coming from company human management or its machine?

Tim Nolan, Brighton



So Donald Trump has changed the name of artificial intelligence to super intelligence. He may have considered the name, supreme intelligence, but I believe he’s saving that title for himself.

Henry Herzog, St Kilda East Did anyone else have a metacarpal moment of Mark Latham v John Howard when Donald Trump took to Adam Scott with a mild case of attempted dislocation of his shoulder?

David West, Essendon Your correspondent (letters, 29/9) laments the lack of genuine original thought and ideas in letters to the editor. I agree, but around 3000 years ago it was said: ″⁣There is nothing new under the sun″⁣ (Ecclesiastes 1:9). Keep trying, though.

John Massie, Middle Park George Orwell’s novel, 1984, should be renamed 2084.

Kerrin Adams, Greensborough

World.title: ‘I want to apologise for all this’: Stawell Gift winner apologises after losing title over drug test
World.content:
SportAthleticsWorld athletics championships ‘I want to apologise for all this’: Stawell Gift winner apologises after losing title over drug test Michael Gleeson Updated September 30, 2026 — 7:59pm ,first published 6:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The men’s winner of this year’s Stawell Gift, Olufemi Komolafe has been stripped of the title and his prizemoney over a failed drug test. Komalafe has apologised for his accidental breach which saw him fail a doping test after the prestigious Easter Monday 120m sprint. He will lose the title and the $40,000 winner’s cheque. Olufemi Komolafe when he won the Stawell Gift in April. Getty Images “I want to apologise for all this. I won’t keep the title of Stawell Gift winner, but the experience of winning it was invaluable, and I’m eager and confident that I can take it to the next level when I return,” Komalafe said in a message to friends. Komalafe failed a drug test after inadvertently taking a banned substance contained in ADHD medication. He has received a 12-month ban, reduced from the standard four years after Sport Integrity Australia accepted the use was inadvertent and Komalafe co-operated fully with authorities.



He won the race in April off five metres in a time of 12.03 seconds. Jake Ireland, who came second and will be elevated to winner, said it was not the way he wanted to be called a Stawell Gift winner. Jake Ireland (wearing the white singlet) running at Stawell in April. He’s now the retrospective winner of this year’s Gift. Getty Images “Ninety percent of winning is crossing the line and celebrating with your family and friends,” Ireland said. “I certainly don’t feel like a winner, maybe that’s the competitor in me. I was not first over the line.



“I suppose this year has got an asterisk to it. I would hate to come across as gloating or rubbing it in. “It was not like a blatant cheating where it’s deliberate; it was accidental. I feel for him, too, I know he is in a horrible place.” Olufemi Komolafe collected $40,000 as winner of the Stawell Gift. Luke Hemer, Stawell Gift Stawell Gift Event Management said it was aware of a matter relating to the 2026 Stawell Gift that was now being examined by Sport Integrity Australia processes. “[We] respects the integrity of this process, including the rights of all parties involved,” the organisation posted on Instagram.



“The integrity of competition is fundamental to the Stawell Gift. SGEM is committed to providing a fair and level playing field for every athlete and respects the established processes for dealing with matters of this nature.” Loading The Victorian Athletic League’s statement said it could “confirm an integrity issue and process is underway with an athlete related to the 2026 Stawell Gift”. “We can’t comment at this stage until the process is completed by Sport Integrity Australia,” it added. World.title: Our five favourite luxury homes by the coast for sale
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes by the coast for sale Shona Hendley September 30, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether it’s the sound of crashing waves, the water views, the salt air, or the outdoor lifestyle, there’s nothing quite like living in or visiting your holiday home by the coast. Open-plan living, indoor-outdoor flow and natural textures—here are five of our favourite luxury homes by the coast, now on the market. 35 Salonika Street, Sorrento VIC Featuring a palette of natural stone, French oak timber and handmade Krause bricks, this Sorrento home makes a stylish impression.



Designed to capture natural light through large windows, the open-plan kitchen, living, and dining areas open onto an al fresco area for indoor-outdoor entertaining. Outside, there’s an additional private deck, pool and spa, and a dedicated gym at the rear of the home. Situated only a short walk from Sorrento’s main street, you have coastal living at your fingertips. 14 Seaview Crescent, Stanwell Park, NSW



With an elevated position and panoramic Pacific Ocean views, this South Coast home is highly desirable. In addition to the views, the property is close to the beach and to Stanwell Park village. But you may not want to leave the property. With the in-ground pool and spa, a Balinese-style hut, multiple outdoor terraces and tropical landscaping, you have resort-style living right in your backyard. Other features include the designer kitchen, a master suite with a balcony, a four-car garage and a wine cellar. 18 Park Road, Sorrento VIC



This contemporary coastal home features expansive living and dining areas and indoor-outdoor spaces. With a north-facing, undercover deck featuring a plumbed barbecue kitchen and a pizza oven overlooking a heated pool and landscaped gardens, you can enjoy the outdoors year-round. Inside, the home is set up for convenience with hydronic heating, heated towel rails, recycler heating and cooling, double glazing and two gas fireplaces. With five bedrooms, four bathrooms and well-thought-out zoning, the home is well suited for family holidays.



11 Burns Street, Byron Bay, NSW This brand-new double-storey residence in Byron Bay features a contemporary coastal design, ideal for either a permanent family home or a holiday home investment. With a north-facing orientation, the home has plenty of natural light throughout, highlighted in the open-plan kitchen and dining area, which is located in the heart of the home. Outside, a covered entertainment terrace features retractable awnings, a built-in barbecue, and a large family-sized swimming pool.



Other highlights include multiple living zones, a private main bedroom suite with a walk-in robe and en suite, solar panels and proximity to the Byron Bay township and beaches. 92 Cabana Boulevard, Benowa Waters QLD Designed by Stuart Osman, this waterfront home offers coastal living on the Nerang River. The property’s outdoor features make the most of the natural setting and are a definite highlight. These include an infinity pool and spa, two oversized 4.5-metre pivoting umbrella shades, waterside and poolside fire pit zones with built-in bench seating, electric retractable awnings with integrated LED lighting, and outdoor heaters and fans.



And if you like water sports, there is a 10-metre (approximately) pontoon with a jet-ski launch, offering direct access to the Broadwater. The interiors are also impressive, with the tech-savvy home using Google Home integration to control the lighting, fountain and custom wine cellar, and featuring a dedicated media room with surround sound.
