World.title: I had to explain to a 24-year-old man why I didn’t want to be a trad wife. It’s exhausting
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGender Opinion I had to explain to a 24-year-old man why I didn’t want to be a trad wife. It’s exhausting Kayla Olaya Reporter September 30, 2026 — 7:30pm

September 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mosquitoes bit my legs while I stood, listening to a man my age politely explain how he wanted a trad wife. This man, a Polish 24-year-old working remotely as a coder in Thailand, the same holiday destination as mine, at the same accommodation and doing the same fitness camp, said he was saving as much money as he could so he could one day fully support a family. “If I invest my money well and don’t spend it, I can afford it,” he explained. “I want my wife to stay at home and look after the family,” he said, resolutely. Adobe Stock I replied: “I would hate that, relying on someone financially.” He stared awkwardly at me and said he disagreed because, as a man, he felt that was an imperative role.



Related Article Opinion

Sunday Life I spent years wishing I was smaller before learning the power of being a ‘jacked beast’ Kayla Olaya Reporter “I want my wife to stay at home and look after the family,” he said, resolutely. We stood there quietly for a bit. Despite clearly having things in common, I couldn’t think of anything else to say, and by now, my legs were covered in bites. I went back to my hut and we didn’t speak again for the rest of the trip. Maybe our difference of opinion was cultural. But in such a globalised society, where manosphere vitriol lands indiscriminately in the algorithms of Australians of all ages, I felt as though he was speaking a language I unfortunately recognised. It echoed right-wing extremist Andrew Tate’s world views. I remember when women raised the alarm about the self-proclaimed misogynist as he began gaining attention in 2022. I also remember thinking his short-lived prominence represented a small group of men without considering with whom the message was silently resonating.



Meeting young men while backpacking has been an interesting experience. I have found it’s best to avoid talking about politics of all forms – immigration, gender roles, various wars – and focus strictly on day-to-day activities after too many revealed themselves to be racist or misogynistic. I always returned home thinking young Australian men weren’t as extreme. These days, I find myself avoiding these topics in conversation with men my age as headlines of alleged schoolyard and sporting sexual assaults tell me it’s not safe here, either. Perhaps young men across the world saw Donald Trump become US president, despite boasting about grabbing women by their genitals, as a green light to speak of and view women as such. Trump continues to insult female journalists based on their looks, telling a Bloomberg reporter to be “quiet, quiet, piggy” when she asked about his relationship with paedophile Jeffrey Epstein last year. The alleged inappropriate sexual behaviour of a crew of Sydney Swans players made a media storm and brought into conversation – again – the attitudes young men have towards women. These behaviours riddle other codes, too.



Last November, Penrith Panthers player Brian To’o was caught allegedly making lewd remarks about teammates’ girlfriends on pictures he uploaded to his own Instagram story. To’o allegedly commented on one photo of skipper Nathan Cleary, “The Fowler Slayer”, about Matildas sensation and Manchester City player Mary Fowler. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Before his speech went viral, this boys’ school headmaster ran it past his daughter Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author As a young woman who has to navigate this world each day – reading it in the news, skirting around its edges while backpacking or having to screen it on dating apps – I am exhausted. I feel jaded. I wonder if I am part of the growing percentage of women choosing not to have babies if these are the fathers. The worst part? I feel I’m becoming numb to misogyny – a combination of being exposed to it more often and trying to avoid being upset by it. I am shown time and time again that hardly anything comes from the relentless headlines of the alleged rapes, killings and harassment of women. It’s devastating when I see that a study published in August found young men are increasingly holding hostile attitudes towards women.



When I talk about misogyny with young men – a few who hold manospheric views and most who don’t – I more frequently watch the topic glide over them with the same avoidance I am beginning to acquire. They’re tired, too. Maybe for the same reasons as me, maybe not. My colleague jokes that when she was a young woman, a red flag in young men “was if they couldn’t spell or if their favourite movie was The Shawshank Redemption” . Now, it’s if young men are looking for a “wifey” or “missus” in their Hinge profile. Before a date, I always check who the man follows on social media in case it’s right-wing provocateurs or hundreds of Instagram models. The Polish man who wants a trad wife stayed in a hut next to mine. Before the topic of gender roles came up, we shared our anxieties about living in a world overrun by technology, feeling helpless as the world burns around us and experiencing a sense of existential dread because AI has made us feel as though our contributions to society are meaningless. Yet, somehow, we were still worlds apart. Kayla Olaya is a culture reporter at The Sydney Morning Herald.

World.title: He stole his first instrument at the age of five. Eventually, all was forgiven
World.content:
Benjamin Clementine, 37, went from busking in the subways of Paris to becoming one of the most acclaimed artists in contemporary music.

Benjamin Clementine defied his family to forge his own musical destiny. The journey that followed has been far from easy.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Benjamin Clementine was five when an uncharacteristic act of resistance sealed his fate. Growing up in a household where instruments were forbidden, he became so entranced with the toy piano a classmate had brought to primary school that when she refused to let him play it, he took it – hoping to spend at least one evening at home with it – but was ordered to return it before he had the chance. How, he wondered, had this single-octave keyboard produced such an astonishing combination of sounds? “I was looking at this girl with that thing – I remember it like it was yesterday – and I asked her if I could play,” he says. “She said no. She just wouldn’t give it to me. I was so fascinated by this thing but sad that I couldn’t have it. When I looked at it, I got this good feeling I’d never felt before, outside of laughter with my siblings. It’s like how some kids feel when they find football or basketball or tennis.” Born and raised in London to a family of Ghanaian descent, the 37-year-old musician, composer and actor had almost no exposure to popular culture in his formative years. It was a strict, religious household. Non-Christian music was forbidden, as were instruments of any kind. His father, who had been a professor of mathematics in Liberia, was determined his son would study law. Somehow, despite his parents’ best attempts to shield him from the corrupting influence of secular music, Clementine, who will tour Australia for the first time this month, has become one of the most acclaimed voices in contemporary music. Unbound by genre, his compositions draw from a range of styles including classical, experimental and avant-garde. Poetry, literature and the writings of pioneering psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott also inform his work. Benjamin Clementine will tour Australia for the first time in October. Christophe Raynaud de Lage Speaking via Zoom from his home in California, his 193-centimetre frame curled into an armchair, Clementine says that when he brings his Back To Basics tour to Australia, it’ll just be him and his piano, which he usually plays barefoot. (He has likened this to the thrill of driving without shoes.) “Because I’ve never toured Australia, I want to show them my bare self, and it’s up to them to take me for who I am,” he says. “To be honest, I get tired of touring with so many people [in a back-up band].



“There’s always this offer of the Sydney Opera House. I would love to play there, but first I want to come in with a humble kind of approach. I don’t want to play in front of 5000 people right now in Australia; I want to play in front of 500 to 1000 people. My aim is to be intimate with people who are seeing me for the first time, so that we genuinely get to hear each other and smell each other. That’s what I’ve always done.” This pared-back approach is also a chance to reconnect with his musical roots, having taught himself to sing, compose and play a number of instruments. “Before all the tricks of production and frequencies and equalisation and compression, there’s just the song,” he says. “My greatest ability, from what I’ve been told, is to simply tell a story without noise. Over the years, I went from that to almost showing off through production – and sometimes you get lost in those things. I’m just tired of it. This is about going back to the fundamentals.” It’s not hard to see why critics frequently compare Clementine, with his powerful voice that shifts between delicate vulnerability and raw intensity, to Nina Simone. Many of their songs are self-contained stories, often containing social critiques. As one reviewer observed, each sings “as if all the world depended on it”. And they share a striking physicality that underscores a powerful stage presence. Clementine, who has modelled for Abercrombie & Fitch, has high, sharp cheekbones and an angular jawline. As The Guardian memorably put it, he “resembles an art deco illustration of himself”. Throughout his career, Clementine has amassed high-profile fans including Damon Albarn, Bjork and Paul McCartney. He met the latter after he was invited to perform on the TV music program Later... with Jools Holland. “Normally, I’m not fazed by anything when I’m performing but I could see Paul watching while I was playing and it was all a blur,” Clementine says. “Afterwards, I went to go to the loo and someone tapped me on the shoulder. It was Paul McCartney and I can’t remember exactly what he said but it was something like, ‘Oh, that was a great song’.” Having already recorded an EP, Cornerstone, he got to work on his first studio album, At Least For Now, released to wide acclaim in 2015. His subsequent albums, I Tell a Fly and And I Have Been received similar praise – including from the father who had been so reluctant to let him play music.



“He never said he was proud of me, but he showed me in his own way,” Clementine says. “Before he died, he said, ‘I like some of your songs’. It broke me down a little bit and I was in tears. For me, it was a huge compliment.” Now, as a father of three, Clementine understands his parents’ motivation in pushing him towards a career in law. Having fled political turmoil and material deprivation to build a stable life in London, they spent a fortune on his education, including boarding school. To them, it was incumbent upon their children to forge respectable careers. But fate intervened when his family moved to a house where an upright piano had been left behind. “They didn’t want me to play it because they knew it would pull my interest from my study,” he says. “And they were right: I was going to be a lawyer but then I decided not to do that. “After suffering themselves, and working hard to be accepted into society, you wouldn’t want your children [to experience similar hardships] … so there was resentment and anger,” he says. “They’re conservative; they do things the ‘correct’ way so it’s just embarrassing to have a child who has abandoned everything but doesn’t really know what he wants to do, other than going for whatever is ‘out there’. It’s a really hard thing for an immigrant parent to process that.” Naturally, music lessons were not an option, so Clementine taught himself to play piano by ear, and tried any instrument he could get his hands on. He spent hours in his local library, studying poetry, art and literature. (Sylvia Plath and William Blake are major influences, as is Nick Cave: “His music transports you to different places, and transcends different feelings and moments in time.”) He bought books with accompanying CDs to acquire the basics of French, Mandarin, German and Italian, among other languages. “I’ve always had a thing for languages and literature,” he says, paraphrasing a quote commonly attributed to Cicero. “‘Language without literature is like a body without a head’. I believe that literature is music in itself. It has melody and harmony, it’s atonal and tonal, it has rhythm. Now, I find myself writing and then applying it to common sounds. I change the accents on words and the intonation is determined by how I feel. I think that’s my personal secret in how I express what I want to say.”



Among his most popular songs are Cornerstone, which he performed on the Jools Holland show; I Won’t Complain, from his Mercury Prize-winning debut album At Least For Now; and Nemesis, used in the opening credits of Apple TV’s Morning Wars. He has also had supporting roles in the 2021 film Dune; Steve McQueen’s 2024 World War II drama Blitz; and Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series The Gentlemen. Clementine with Steve McQueen, who directed the 2024 film Blitz, in which he had a supporting role. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Does he believe the absence of formal music training allowed him the freedom to cultivate his unique sound? “If you’d asked me that question 10 years ago, I would have been arrogant,” Clementine admits. “I’d have said something like, ‘There’s no such thing as theory; we should all just receive music from our ears’. But as a 37-year-old man, I think theory is necessary. “Look, I’m happy with how I turned out. And I can read music now because I spent five years studying it myself, so I compose differently.” When Clementine was 16, his parents divorced: a huge shock in light of their devout Christianity. He lived with his father briefly, then his mother, before bouncing around Camden and crashing with mates. Not long after, he quit school.



At 19, he moved to Paris, primarily because it was close and contained a significant proportion of English-speaking residents. Much has been made of his time in the city, from periods of homelessness and stints in hostels to busking in the subway. But he’s reluctant to portray this as the first chapter of a rags-to-riches tale. He did, however, learn a lot about life while performing at train stations. Related Article Take 7 ‘Be careful who you surround yourself with’: Johnny Young’s prescient advice to Tina Arena “It was like Darwin’s survival of the fittest,” he says. “If I asked for money, I would only eat for a day but if I befriended somebody, I would eat for a week. I learned to be a better human. In England, I was still a boy.” Fellow buskers introduced him to popular music from the ’40s, ’50s and ’60s, including Nina Simone, Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen and The Beatles. “In that period, musicians had something they wanted to say and they had a melody to go with it,” he says. “But over the past 30 years, popular music has all been driven by the catchy phrase and the chorus. In the West, we’re obsessed with melody because it sells music. But melody has also plagued our music in the sense that people get away with saying nothing.” In France, Clementine became successful enough that he could afford to eat and pay his bills. Still, he refused regular requests from police to obtain a mandatory busking permit. “I didn’t want to succumb to the idea that I’m only worth a cent in the subway,” he says. “I never went to Paris to busk or make music. I knew that I was going somewhere.”

World.title: ‘Second-class citizens’: Liberals refuse to campaign after preselection snub
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaVictorian election ‘Second-class citizens’: Liberals refuse to campaign after preselection snub Angelica Snowden September 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Liberal Party is facing a backlash from its members in the must-win seat of Pakenham, who say they are unwilling to volunteer in the upcoming election campaign after party chiefs sidelined them from handpicking their candidate. Pakenham, in Melbourne’s outer south-east, is currently held by Labor’s Emma Vulin by just 0.39 per cent, making it one of the most marginal seats up for grabs at November’s state election. Candidates running for Pakenham (left to right): Alessandra Soliven for Labor, Radmila Dyson for the Liberal Party and Warren Pickering for One Nation. Ruby Alexander, Facebook Its status as a critical battleground has also been amplified by One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering also vying for the seat, as Pauline Hanson’s party seeks to capitalise on its surging popularity to win Victorian lower house seats for the first time. In 2022, Liberal candidate David Farrelly secured a swing of 1.8 per cent to the party, but just came up short.



The former long-time chair of Neighbourhood Watch in Cardinia sought to run again this year, as well as Maroondah City Council IT worker Monty Sodhi. But the party’s state executive decided against holding a local preselection and instead intervened to tap soccer club volunteer Radmila Dyson to be their candidate. Her preselection was confirmed on August 15, nine months after preselection applications closed in December. It also came after Labor chose 23-year-old Alessandra Soliven to replace incumbent MP Vulin – who will not recontest the seat after she was diagnosed with motor neurone disease – and Pickering entered the fray. David Farrelly (centre) secured a small swing to the Liberal Party, but ultimately fell short in the contest for Pakenham in the 2022 election. Eamon Gallagher Because marginally fewer than 40 members registered to vote for the Pakenham candidate, out of about 50 in the branch, the party’s state executive invoked a rule to bypass grassroots members and call in the preselection, according to an email seen by The Age sent to members by the Pakenham state electorate conference chair. The state executive – as well as a handful of branch office bearers – chose Dyson. A Liberal source, speaking anonymously to detail internal deliberations, said she was given special dispensation to run as a candidate because she had been a party member for less than a year.



Related Article Victorian election One Nation Victoria leader admits to drug use, drink-driving Four Pakenham branch members, also speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said Farrelly or Sodhi would have probably won a democratic vote. A senior party official added: “The whole thing was orchestrated so Monty and David couldn’t be elected.” “They didn’t want an Indian candidate running in a lower house seat,” the official alleged. “[The party] are trying to bring back people who have moved to One Nation, but in the meantime they have lost with the multicultural community and lost out on their heavy lifting on the ground.” Farrelly told The Age that members who otherwise would have volunteered for the party’s bid in the electorate “will not be volunteering any more”.



“I think the process the party engaged in right across the Victorian landscape for preselecting candidates failed drastically in a number of locations,” he said. “When you don’t have local members contributing to the vote, you’re not getting a true local representative and the membership voice isn’t being reflected through those candidates.” Radmila Dyson, the Liberal Party candidate for Pakenham. Facebook Asked how the party was tracking for volunteers to support Dyson, Farrelly said: “I wouldn’t know where that is up to now, and I haven’t been asked to help.” “That is unusual,” he said. “You normally ask everyone you can. Especially people with experience, and I’ve been a candidate and have worked on federal campaigns.”



Responding to a detailed list of questions about the preselection process, a Liberal Party spokesperson said:“The Liberal Party is excited to have Radmilla [sic] Dyson running in Pakenham.” Asked if she needed permission to run as a candidate because she only joined in August last year, the spokesperson said: “We do not comment on internal matters.” Typically, members of local branches are invited to attend a preselection conference and cast their ballot to choose the party’s candidate. A senior party source said local preselections went ahead in Williamstown, Frankston and Point Cook with just 19, 14 and 14 members allowed to cast votes alongside party chiefs. The party’s state executive also handpicked their preferred candidate – Moonee Valley councillor Samantha Byrne – in Niddrie in Melbourne’s north-west, the seat held by Premier Ben Carroll. That intervention also sparked a local backlash, with member Nigel Kibel sharing a post on Facebook declaring that “state executive deciding preselection is totally unacceptable”.



“Yesterday, the Liberal preselection in Niddrie took place, and once again it was determined that the locals did not have the numbers, so the state executive made the decision,” the July post read. “This occurred after the new state president, Brian Loughnane, said that local members would be included.” In Pakenham, Indian radio station Radio Haanji reported that Sodhi’s preselection bid had brought “hope for Australian-Indian political representation”. Pakenham hopeful Monty Sodhi. “As a member of the Sikh community, Sodhi has expressed an interest in representing Pakenham not only as a local resident but also … [as someone] who is running [for] an ultra-marginal seat and also one of the few Australian-Indian(s) seeking public office in Victoria,” the station said on Facebook. Sodhi declined to comment.



Related Article Opinion

Liberal Party The Liberal Party is shedding members in the west. The treatment of an Indian community candidate has been like a wrecking ball Chip Le Grand State political editor The party’s relationship with its Indian members was frayed earlier this year, after Dinesh Gourisetty was preselected to replace Moira Deeming on the party’s upper house ticket in the Western Metropolitan region, only to be dumped when it emerged he had given a character reference to a child abuser in 2024. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Gourisetty would not be welcome in her party room after the November election. This masthead previously reported that western suburbs branches shed members in the wake of the saga. Dyson, the party’s Pakenham candidate, co-founded the popular Officer City Soccer Club and remains its treasurer. According to property records, she owns a home in Beaconsfield, which sits just outside the Pakenham electorate. She has worked in her family business and is raising twins, according to the Pakenham Officer Star News. This masthead tried to contact her directly but she did not respond. A member of the Pakenham branch said they would not volunteer for the party’s relatively new recruit.



“There were two [candidates] more deserving than her. They are Monty Sodhi and David Farrelly,” the member said. “We have been ignored by the Liberal Party.” A second member, who joined the branch at the end of last year, also said they would limit the time they spent door-knocking in support of Dyson. “Why should we [go door-knocking]? We are not things to use and throw away,” they said. “[During preselection] I felt we are considered second-class citizens. If the party calls on us for fundraising, why not during the preselection.” A third member similarly expressed doubt about helping during the campaign. “They should have allowed us to vote … It’s disappointing. If it is a democracy, there should be a vote count.”

World.title: Firefighters battle blaze at Auckland Coca-Cola factory
World.content:
About 50 firefighters were deployed to a Coca-Cola production building in Auckland's Mount Wellington on Wednesday.

Fire and Emergency Northern shift manager Nadine Davies said 10 crews responded to a blaze on the second floor of the site on Carbine Road. She said the first crews arrived at 4:18pm.

The blaze was extinguished, and all crews had left the scene by 8:45pm.

A fire investigator attended the scene, and it was not being treated as suspicious.

The building had been handed over to its owners.

World.title: Tararua Health can deliver safe services to the community, director insists
World.content:
Tararua Health Group can deliver safe health services to the community, despite a critical audit from the Ministry of Health, says its director.

The audit of Dannevirke Community Hospital found there was not a safe and sustainable roster for doctors, nurses and healthcare assistants.

A Ministry of Health spokesperson said the inspection report was currently being written and will contain details of issues that were identified.

Tararua Health director Mark Wills told Checkpoint the hospital was one and a half nurses short, and did not have sufficient doctor coverage at the time the review was issued.

He said one doctor left, and cover had been arranged by a doctor who was on the day shift and also agreed to be on-call for the night shift - but auditing staff found that was not suitable.

Audio player for " Tararua Health Group on notice after Dannevirke Hospital " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/health/1665135%2Ftararua-health-can-deliver-safe-services-to-the-community-director-insists

Tararua Health Group on notice after Dannevirke Hospital Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

Wills said he did not believe staffing levels were unsafe before the audit was announced.

"We weren't aware that they were considered to be unsafe staff levels - we had a view that we had sufficient nursing staff and that we were recruiting additional nursing staff.

"We're not arguing with their view, but that is their view."

He said he had taken the feedback on board and had now appointed more nurses.

Tararua Health Group also owns Pahīatua Medical centre, where half a dozen staff have tendered resignations over workload and safety concerns.

Wills said the difficulties did not reflect a pattern of behaviour, but it was very hard to recruit.

"If there are people out there who want to actually join the Pahīatua Medical Centre and contribute towards serving that community we would be very grateful for their interest."

When asked why so many staff had left, Wills said there were "lessons to be learned for everyone".

"Obviously some of those staff have left for sound reasons, where they're moving out of the territory or retiring or whatever, but I think we'd also admit that there's some that have left that we would have rather not lost."

Wills is also the founder and chief executive of OmniHealth, which is the parent company for Tararua Health Group.

That company also owns Taitoko Health clinic in Levin, where the last GP serving at the clinic has resigned.

He was asked whether OmniHealth was the problem, and whether it was running the staff too leanly for commercial reasons.

"No, certainly not, I would refute that vehemently - there's an absolute need for more staff in our sector and we are continually hunting for staff. I have heard recently that 60 percent of the general practices in New Zealand are looking for GPs right now."

World.title: 'Significant change': NZ Film Commission scraps major source of funding for organisations
World.content:
A major source of public funding for film and screen sector organisations is set to end after more than two decades of it being offered.

The New Zealand Film Commission (NZFC) announced on Wednesday that its annual Core Funding Programme would cease when contracts expired on 30 June 2027.

The programme currently provided over $1 million in support to 10 industry groups, including the Screen Producers Guild and the actors' union Equity.

Film Commission chief executive Annie Murray said the commission would be directing public funding towards fewer, but "higher-impact investments".

"We recognise that this is a significant change for the organisations involved, particularly given the programme's long history. Our responsibility is to regularly review our programmes, carefully prioritise public funding and make deliberate choices about where NZFC investment can have the greatest impact for New Zealand film.

"This decision is about ensuring that NZFC's public investment supports the New Zealand screen industry as effectively as possible, now and into the future."

Murray said affected organisations had known the programme was at risk.

"It's a tough day for the screen sector; we acknowledge that.

"We've been signalling this decision for the past year and we've now communicated the decision with eight months' notice.

"We're under no illusion that this is a significant decision that will impact these organisations. But the Film Commission is in a constrained funding environment. We have to look for where we can have the greatest impact with the limited funds we've got."

She said the commission's public funding had been cut by 5 percent this financial year after a two percent cut the previous year, and they were expecting another 5 percent cut next year.

"Our sources of funding have been frozen for many years, and the impact of inflation means we can do less with the money we have than we could 10 years ago.

"We are looking for other sources of funds for New Zealand films, seeking investors, and looking to New Zealanders, New Zealand organisations, and expats offshore to see if they might want to support New Zealand film."

The commission said its Core Funding Programme had existed in different forms for more than two decades.

World.title: Explainer: What you need to know about road rules changing on 1 October
World.content:
Explainer - Road rules are changing from Thursday. Here's what you need to know.

Four new rules that come into effect on 1 October include changes to overtaking, where e-scooters can travel and where children can ride their bikes.

"These changes are about fixing the basics: safer streets, clearer rules, and less bureaucracy getting in the way of everyday travel," Transport Minister Chris Bishop said in announcing the changes earlier this year.

Okay, what are the changes?

The new rules:

require a minimum passing gap of 1.5 metres when drivers pass other road users who are not driving a motor vehicle

allow children up to 12 years old to ride bikes on footpaths and allow parents or caregivers to ride with them

allow people to ride e-scooters in cycle lanes

require road users to give way to buses leaving bus stops

The Government sought feedback from the public on possible transport changes earlier this year, Bishop said, and received about 6000 responses.

There are changes for bike lanes. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Changes for families biking together

One big change is for families who go cycling with young children.

Originally, it was proposed children 12 and under only could use footpaths, but that has been extended to allow their parents or caregivers to accompany them.

"One of the strongest messages we heard was that allowing children to ride on footpaths only solves half the problem if the grown-up riding with them still has to use the road," Bishop said.

"That's why we've adapted the proposal to allow parents and caregivers to ride alongside children on the footpath.

"Keeping kids safe while they're learning to ride is common sense. This change strikes the right balance between protecting young cyclists and ensuring footpaths remain safe for everyone who uses them."

Some submitters to the proposal have worried about possible impacts on pedestrian safety, especially for the elderly or disabled.

Overtaking gap rule simplified

The changes also simplified overtaking-gap rules when passing cyclists, pedestrians, horse riders and any other road users who are not driving a motor vehicle.

NZTA says that drivers must leave a distance of at least 1.5 metres when passing those other road users who are travelling in the same direction as them, in the same lane.

"If you can't pass safely, slow down and wait behind them until you can," NZTA notes on its website. "Take extra care when passing them as the wind gust from your vehicle could affect their balance."

"Instead of different distances in different circumstances, drivers will be required to leave a minimum gap of 1.5 metres when overtaking," Bishop said.

"That's clearer for drivers and safer for everyone."

E-scooters can now use bicycle lanes. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

New rules for e-scooters and bus stops

E-scooters will now be allowed to use cycle lanes.

E-scooters have been allowed to ride on the footpath and the road, but it has been illegal to ride in the cycle lanes.

This only applies to e-scooters that are not considered a motor vehicle, NZTA says. (You can get in the weeds of the details about how exactly that is decided here.)

A fourth rule also clarifies when drivers must give way to buses, which hadn't previously been laid out.

On roads with a 60km/h or lower speed limit, if bus drivers are leaving a bus stop, the side of the road or moving out of a bus lane, other drivers must give way to the bus.

The bus driver must indicate their intention to move for at least three seconds, giving other drivers time to react and bus drivers time to check the way is clear, NZTA says.

One change that was mooted but did not go forward was to give councils more power to fine people for parking on grass berms.

"We also heard strong views on the proposal relating to parking on berms, which would have given councils greater powers to fine the owners of vehicles parked on berms," Bishop said.

"After considering the feedback, we've decided not to proceed because it became clear the proposal wouldn't solve the underlying problem."

World.title: How are GPs and nurses dealing with ADHD diagnoses so far?
World.content:
It's been nearly eight months since GPs and nurse practitioners were given the authority to diagnose and prescribe medicine for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults.

The February rule change was made to tackle the massive backlog of patients, who were sometimes waiting longer than a year for a diagnosis when only psychiatrists and paediatricians had that power.

But with GP clinics already understaffed and overwhelmed with patients, there was concern about how GPs and nurse practitioners would manage the extra workload.

At Family Health Matters in Auckland's Glenn Innes, nurse practitioner Michal Noonan had a waitlist of patients wanting ADHD assessments months before she could start offering them.

She began offering diagnoses in March, a month after the changes come into effect, and said since then there has been a steady flow of demand from both enrolled patients, and people outside the clinic.

"People have been waiting a really long time to be assessed, they've often thought that they've got ADHD, but the cost in the past has been just out of reach for most people, now there is another option, while it is still costly, it's significantly more accessible for more people, but people just want to get started and want to get cracking along."

GPs and nurse practitioners learning to balance the load

Noonan said the past seven months have been a learning curve.

She and the one other nurse practitioner offering the service at their clinic have had to think carefully about how to balance their workloads.

"We kind of set up that we would do two to three ADHD things in a week per person, so that it didn't have such a huge impact upon our enrolled population, and our other work that of course continues on and has been really busy because of winter and the flu season."

After finding their feet, they decided to bring in a psychologist and a psychology intern to help handle the paperwork and other admin that comes with an ADHD diagnosis.

At Hobsonville Family Doctors, Dr Torrance Merkle is offering ADHD diagnoses alongside his normal duties. He also offers assessments at Beehyve, an online telehealth platform specialising in ADHD.

Assessments typically take between 90 minutes and two hours of a health professional's time.

But that doesn't take into account the paperwork and administrative steps, with patients first submitting a pre-assessment questionnaire that must be reviewed by someone in the clinic.

Originally Merkle was doing four assessments per week, two at his Hobsonville Clinic, and two online via Beehyve.

However he has now cut down to one assessment per week, to ensure workload is manageable.

"I think in general practice we do want to help people but do you have to be really cautious of how much time and energy you spend each day with patients and you do have to save some for yourself because the whole health sector is under strain, particularly general practice.

"I do feel guilty and it's not ideal that my normal patients have to wait two weeks to see me at the moment, I wish I could see everyone within a day or two."

Despite the busy workload, Merkle said the changes he had seen an ADHD diagnosis make in patient's lives had made the work more than worth it.

"The improvements that people get and the amount of life changing that happens from sorting ADHD out, it's one of the most impactful things we can do in medicine and it's super rewarding.

"You really do get that feeling of I've actually made a difference in this person and family's life this week and that's definitely one of the main motivators."

Wait times down, but cost remains a barrier

Merkle and Noonan agree the changes seem to be cutting down the long wait times for assessments, with wait times at their clinics at no more than a few weeks.

However, it's the cost that remains a barrier for many patients.

Due to the time a diagnosis takes, an assessment at Family Health Matters comes in around $1200.

At Hobsonville Doctors a 90-120 minute assessment will set you back $800.

Costs vary from clinic to clinic, but all come in well under the price of a psychiatry appointments, which can cost upwards of $2000.

Despite the price of a GP or nurse practitioner being more affordable, Noonan said the bill still makes getting a diagnosis inaccessible for many.

"That still doesn't address the issue we have predominantly with our some of Māori and Pacific whānau, that's still out of reach for many whānau. I think we need to maybe think about how we do that."

Dr Luke Bradford says the high cost of ADHD assessments is still an issue. Supplied

Royal New Zealand College of GPs president Dr Luke Bradford said he was confident that as time went on, the backlog of patients waiting for a diagnosis would be solved with the February changes.

"Before this change people were typically waiting six to twelve months for a private assessment, that is much shorter now, people are being seen much quicker so that's good."

However, Bradford agreed that the high cost of assessments was still an issue.

"The issue is accessibility and affordability. That's a societal question, at what point is the payment for this diagnosis the responsibility of the individual versus the responsibility of society and therefore out of the health budget and that's a different discussion."

How widely are ADHD assessments being offered by GPs and nurse practitioners?

There's no record of exactly how many GPs and nurse practitioners have opted into delivering ADHD assessments and prescriptions, with many patients left stumped in February, when they were turned away from their local GP clinic which was not choosing to offer the service.

Bradford said there had been an enthusiastic uptake of GPs offering assessments so far, but it wasn't something that all GPs wanted to do.

RNZCGP believes between 75 and 100 have started diagnosing and prescribing for ADHD.

Healthpoint, which lists over 1000 of the country's clinics, had only 34 currently recorded as offering the service.

Bradford said he expects the number to increase as time goes on.

"There was a lot of pressure in January and a lot of feeling that wasn't going to change anything overnight. We always knew that, we knew that the GPs would take time to build their skills, build their service provision."

As for the workload, Bradford said there have been no concerns raised with him.

He said like any other specialist service, it was a GP's choice to the offer assessments.

"These are GPs who are choosing to do it as a special interest, there a whole heap of other special interests that GPs do that take longer and have set aside clinical time and that's what we're seeing is GPs are choosing to set aside time for this because they're interested in it."

World.title: Naked residents and dangerous dogs: The perils of the political door knock
World.content:
There are just 38 days to go until the general election and until then, you can be sure that political candidates will be pounding the pavement and knocking on thousands of doors as they seek to win votes.

While they might be able to reach far greater numbers of potential people through advertising or social media campaigns, the candidates that RNZ spoke to are adamant there is nothing quite like a face-to-face conversation to try and gain votes.

The political door-knock is also the source of countless memorable yarns - from dangerous dogs to constituents answering the door in various states of undress.

Audio player for " Political candidates go door-knocking in hunt for support " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1663770%2Fnaked-residents-and-dangerous-dogs-the-perils-of-the-political-door-knock

Political candidates go door-knocking in hunt for support Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Despite the miserable weather, ACT Party leader David Seymour set a ferocious pace as went door-to-door through Auckland's Mission Bay to endorse his new candidate for the Tāmaki electorate James Christmas on Saturday.

On a good day, he said people will answer the door half the time, that the hit rate is about one in four. But the responses were largely positive.

"It's a real antidote to social media. When you get out and talk to people, even today, we've had pretty good political support, but even if they're not hanging out to vote for us, they're still very positive and friendly," Seymour said.

"I think that's a really nice thing that more people need to see. Because you go on a Facebook comment section, bloody hell, it makes you fear for humanity and democracy."

Seymour reckoned he had knocked on about 15,000 doors during the course of his political career, and he said he had become an expert in all manner of latches, door knobs, knockers and doorbells.

"This is an old tactic - I always go to the very back first so that if someone did want to cause trouble, you haven't alerted them to your presence and then left them between you and the road."

Another thing he has learned: never assume how people might vote based on their place of residence.

"When I was first door knocking down the bottom of Baradine College, I knocked on the nunnery and I found three hardcore ACT voting nuns. So you should never judge a book by its cover."

While he found the experience of door-knocking overwhelmingly positive, Seymour has had a few close scrapes.

"I was knocking on a door with this huge front yard and a big stone wall and I heard this ferocious dog coming so I hoofed it, leapt the fence, tore my pants and then I looked around and despite the huge noise it was a tiny little thing."

On the other side of the political divide, Labour's deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni was equally adamant about the importance of door knocking.

"I think you shouldn't underestimate the importance of face to face - kanohi ki te kanohi - New Zealanders still appreciate it. And there's nothing more persuasive than having someone in front of you having a genuine conversation talking about things that matter to you."

Even if they made it clear they were not going to give her their vote, people were by and large very polite, although not always entirely presentable.

"We had to walk past a bedroom window to get to the main entrance and unfortunately the window was open and someone was putting their pants on.

"In that situation I said to my volunteer with me, 'just pretend you didn't see that and to save embarrassment for that person and also ourselves'."

National MP Cameron Brewer door-knocking in Greenhithe. RNZ / Matthew Theunissen

Catching someone just after they have hopped out of the shower is another occupational hazard for the door knocker, as National Party MP Cameron Brewer discovered when RNZ joined him on a door-knock on the streets of Greenhithe in his Upper Harbour electorate.

Nonetheless, a key advantage that door knocking had over other forms of campaigning was that people remembered, said Brewer.

"I remember at primary school - or even in adulthood - who came to my place of business, who came to my primary school, and you never forget.

"People still say to me, 'you knocked on my door, remember what we talked about?' And I'm like, 'yes, I do'. And they say, 'so what have you done about it?' I said, 'we're looking into that issue. Just give it to me again. Was it traffic?' 'No, it wasn't traffic!'."

Brewer had also had his fare share of awkward encounters.

"Sometimes there's a bit of cuddling on the couch watching Netflix. One's kind of in a bit of a predicament there as to whether they kind of try to tiptoe away, which might even look worse - a peeping tom kind of comes to mind - or whether you just kind of back yourself and knock on the door and look the other way."

Brewer said campaigners were also being briefed about the potential perils of "smart doorbells".

"Normally these days when you push them, they start recording and... sometimes someone might be in Singapore listening and watching," he said.

"If you're an ill-disciplined candidate that has big opinions about people's gardens or wants to exchange a bad taste joke with the volunteer or whatever, that quip could be recorded. And so smart doorbells are a bit of an occupational hazard."

Not that he would ever say a bad word about one of his constituent's gardens. "My constituents are world class and we know that because they vote very well every election."

He said some of his colleagues had not quite finessed the art of the door-knock. He recounted a story that John Banks told him about a door-knock he did with his then-colleague Paul Goldsmith.

"Banksy rang me up and he said, 'Cam, he knocked on this door and it was quite a challenging neighbourhood and this young woman came to the door and she was holding a crying baby and had a toddler kind of wrapped around her leg and she was very busy and looked exhausted'."

Goldsmith reportedly said: "'Would you like to eradicate socialism?' That's typical Goldie," said Brewer.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said relationships developed on doorsteps were vital for good politics.

"One of my favourite things is talking to people who think that they hate me," she laughed.

"I think when you wear away the concept of each other that we may be holding in our minds and you come back down to the brass tacks of the things that we have in common, you'll find most New Zealanders want more affordable lives, not just for themselves, but for their fellow New Zealanders.

"They want greater job opportunities for all of us. They want healthy nature and they want honest politics.

World.title: Central Otago council dumps plans to truck human waste to local farm
World.content:
Central Otago District Council has dumped plans to truck treated human effluent onto nearby farmland.

The council has been grappling with how to deal with a growing volume of sludge, with staff warning bags containing thousands of cubic metres of dried sludge needed a new home.

The original plan was to dump the sludge on land near Lauder using a non-notified consent that already allows Wānaka's sludge to be disposed there.

The proposal triggered outrage from locals and Federated Farmers who were worried about the potential impact on their water and health.

But council staff changed their recommendation on Tuesday after discovering the Lauder site might not be able to handle all of its sludge due to the capacity already committed to Wānaka's waste, and the potential savings for ratepayers were less than expected.

Instead, councillors voted to send the sludge to Winton landfill in Southland at a meeting on Wednesday.

Earlier this year, 20,0000 cubic metres of sludge was discovered to have built up in the Cromwell treatment ponds.

If not acted upon, the council said it would reduce the pond capacity and performance, which could trigger nitrogen limits and require "significantly more costly treatment upgrades".

The council said the Lauder site operator had advised that it had already committed capacity to waste from Wānaka and there was a risk some of the geobags from Cromwell might not meet requirements.

The cost of removing and transporting the Cromwell waste to Winton as well as pond desludging was expected to be just over $3 million - which was more than a million dollars below the pre-tender estimate.

Council Three Waters general manager Julie Muir said the priority was having a clear, reliable plan in place.

"At this time, we'd rather have certainty than chase a saving that might not hold up," she said.

"Getting the Cromwell ponds sorted before winter is the focus, and landfill is the option we can rely on to get that done."

Federated Farmers Otago president Anna Gillespie welcomed the Central Otago District Council's decision.

"It's heartening that councillors have heeded the anger and strong warnings from rural residents in Lauder and the wider Manuherekia catchment," she said.

"The understandable motivation was to save ratepayers' money in these tough times but that cannot be at the expense of the environment and water quality in a sensitive catchment.

"Council officers warned of rural community fightback and potential for delays to the urgent programme of work to deal with sludge at both the Cromwell and Alexandra treatment plants."

Gillespie said Federated Farmers still questioned the science and modelling behind the consent granted to spread effluence sludge from Wānaka at the former sheep and beef farm at Lauder.

World.title: Stawell Gift winner suspended for 12 months after positive drug test
World.content:
This year's Stawell Gift men's winner, Olufemi "Femi" Komolafe, has been suspended for 12 months after testing positive for ADHD medication.

The 21-year-old set a new personal best to claim his first major title in April this year, and also claimed the $40,000 prize for placing first in the annual 120-metre handicapped sprint.

Komolafe was given a 5-metre handicap in this year's race, starting behind all but one of his opponents in the final.

But Sports Integrity Australia has handed down a 12-month ban, confirming Komolafe had tested positive for the banned medication.

ADHD medications are banned in sport for their potential performance-enhancing effects, with athletes only able to use them if they have a medical diagnosis and it is part of treatment.

Stawell Gift organisers have not confirmed whether Komolafe will be asked to return his winnings or whether he will be stripped of his title.

The ban comes as Sports Integrity Australia expresses concerns over the prevalence of athletes using ADHD medications without a formal diagnosis.

In July, its chief executive, Sarah Benson, said she was seeing a "significant number" of inadvertent doping violations from high-level Australian athletes using ADHD medication.

Dr Benson said the consequences are severe for athletes found breaching the rules.

"Since these medications could be abused by athletes for performance improvement reasons, the tough reality is that they are banned under the World Anti-Doping Code if the athlete does not have a formal diagnosis," Dr Benson said.

"Under the Code, this is true even if they establish their diagnosis after the positive test, and they face a ban of one to four years."
