Tech.title: An Egg Genius Urged Me to Strain Before Poaching. The Results Were Astounding
Tech.content:
Perhaps no other form of egg cookery has so much rhetoric and written words dedicated to it as the elusive poached egg. Poached eggs are humble, but surprisingly complicated to master. Perhaps even more so than the omelet. (In this egg-loving, frequent-egg-cooking author’s opinion.) Even with water as the only other procedural requirement.

If you’ve tried other methods for delivering a perfect poached egg — electric egg cookers, nonstick poaching pans or the seemingly infallible microwave method — and still left unfulfilled or underwhelmed by the outcome, there’s one more pro trick you can try. And here’s a pro tip: Lisa Steele is a fifth-generation chicken keeper and author of Fresh Eggs Daily and In Season: 125+ Sweet and Savory Recipes Celebrating Simple, Fresh Ingredients. She talked me through the single, foolproof step that makes stovetop egg poaching dead simple.

The reason poached eggs are challenging

An egg’s complex structure makes poaching difficult. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Picture it: a pot full of water, maybe with a dash of distilled vinegar, at the gentlest simmer so you don’t subject your delicate egg to a tornado of activity once submerged. You painstakingly crack the egg into a shallow bowl first, and carefully slip it into the pot. Regardless of your good intentions, the egg then clouds the water and turns all wispy, like some sort of blond dementor.

More from CNET

You haven’t done anything wrong here; you’ve just failed to understand an egg’s basic structure. “There are actually two components of the egg white, or albumen,” Steele explains. “There’s the thicker part of the white which encases the yolk, and then there’s a separate, thinner layer of egg white around that. It’s the thinner part of the egg white that will spread and turn wispy when you drop an egg into the water.”

The wispy white of an unstrained egg. Pamela Vachon/CNET

To prevent your poached egg from spreading? Strain it

The thing is, you can easily get rid of the thin, watery white part of your egg using one simple tool you’ve probably got in a drawer somewhere and about a minute of your time. Set a small mesh strainer over a cup or bowl, crack the egg into it, and wait.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

“Straining an egg removes the thinner whites that likely won’t adhere to the rest of the egg and result in shaggy, wispy threads,” Steele says. “It won’t affect the flavor outcome of your poached egg, but it is purely for appearance’s sake.” (And potentially your sanity’s or sense of accomplishment’s sake, I might add.)

While the egg’s flavor stays unchanged, for Benedict lovers, straining the egg first slightly improves the white-to-yolk ratio in the poached result and makes the texture more consistent, while also creating a tidy, photogenic package.

Some patience is required

The thin white will slowly strain itself out. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Once your raw egg is in the strainer, you may notice nothing happens right away, and you may feel the urge to move the egg around a bit to get things going. But don’t zhush, which threatens to scramble the egg. Simply wait for gravity to do its thing, which requires only about a minute. It’s akin to what happens when separating whites from yolks, except here you’re separating whites from whites.

“Let the thin part of the egg white drip down into the bowl,” Steele says, “then gently slide the egg into the simmering water.” The strainer itself can work as a handy vessel for transferring the egg, especially if you’re only making a single one. If you’re doing multiple eggs and don’t want to risk cooking any remaining white onto the mesh by submerging it, place the strained egg in a small, shallow bowl as usual before easing it into the water. Without the thin, watery white part, you’ll notice a discernible textural difference in the egg even when raw.

Best poaching practices

A gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, is best for poaching. Pamela Vachon/CNET

The straining step alone can almost completely change your poached egg game in an instant, but for the best results, follow the best poaching protocol. You don’t want a full pot of water at a rolling boil like you would for pasta. “Fill a pot or saucepan with a few inches of water and bring to a boil, then turn the heat down to low so the water is just barely simmering with small bubbles floating to the surface,” Steele advises.

A strained egg simmering like a tidy package. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Creating a little whirlpool will further help your remaining egg white stay snug. “Using a wooden spoon or silicone spatula, swirl the water, then gently slide the egg into the center of the whirlpool as you keep swirling for another few seconds around the egg until the egg white turns milky and starts to set up around the yolk,” Steele says. “At this point, you can push the egg to one side, add another egg into the center and repeat the process.”

An unstrained egg on the left versus a strained egg on the right.

A soft-poached egg takes about three minutes, and because you’ve removed the watery part of the egg white, you’ll get a nice firm structure to hold the still-runny yolk — the poached egg ideal.

Since poaching is a delicate process, no matter your new straining habit and how strictly you follow the recommended procedure, “using the freshest eggs possible is very important when you are poaching because the egg white gets even more thin and watery as the egg ages,” Steele says. “The membrane holding the yolk together also weakens, making the yolk more susceptible to breaking.” So if you don’t have them on hand already, get yourself a strainer and some fresh eggs and put this newfound tidbit to the personal test.

Want more cooking hacks?

Cooking bacon in the oven is the best way to make a large batch, but the air fryer method might be even better — and it’s definitely faster. Here are nine more cooking hacks that save time and energy.

Tech.title: Cycle-Tracking Apps Bring Substantial Risks to Users, Says New Analysis
Tech.content:
It’s been estimated that about 50 million people worldwide use apps to track their menstrual cycles, associated mental and physical symptoms, fertility and pregnancy. However, a new analysis published in the peer-reviewed medical journal The BMJ on Wednesday argues that the risks associated with these apps and other digital cycle-tracking tools on the femtech market do more harm than good.

The authors of the article say that these risks extend to digital menstrual cycle-tracking tools that promote “cycle syncing,” which is when one bases their diet, exercise and other lifestyle habits on their menstrual cycle phases.

“We hope that people understand a lot of the big, splashy claims around cycle tracking and cycle syncing that people encounter on social media or in fitness or wellness spaces are not based on scientific evidence,” Katharine Lee, one of the article’s authors and an assistant professor in Tulane University’s Department of Anthropology, told CNET in an email.

More from CNET

The health risks

Drawing on several studies, the analysis states that sports science research has shown there is no way to generalize about how different menstrual cycle phases affect health, performance or injury risk. These correlations are highly individual. The same goes for research on how diet can reduce cycle symptoms or improve performance, which is generally inconclusive or speculative.

Even if these cycle connections did exist, the article argues that digital cycle-tracking tools wouldn’t be able to predict them. Apps tend to rely on a user’s self-reported menstrual bleeding date to estimate ovulation, the fertile window and future menstrual cycle phases. Without actually measuring someone’s hormones, these estimates can be imprecise, especially considering that hormones and ovulation fluctuate.

Digital menstrual cycle trackers also can’t diagnose menstrual disorders or uncover the causes of painful periods.

“You should work with trusted health professionals if you have concerns — and yes, I know that many people struggle to get their doctors to listen to them about their periods,” Lee said. “People may want to track their cycles for any number of reasons, but a lot of digital tracking apps are no fancier than counting and averaging your data.”

When relying on these apps, there’s a risk that users may downplay health concerns as simply effects of their cycle. Or forgo established diet, exercise and sleep guidelines in the name of cycle syncing.

Privacy isn’t the only concern when using an app to track your cycle. SeventyFour/Getty Images

The privacy problem

There’s also privacy to consider, as some apps allow third-party tracking, don’t publish transparency reports, don’t allow straightforward data deletion and don’t use local data storage, which makes it easier for them to sell data, share it with third parties or be exposed to a data breach. This is especially dangerous in areas where abortion is criminalized or where there is more gender or sex-based discrimination.

While no specific apps or tools were mentioned in this analysis, Lee said that several of the cited references focus on the policies or functionality of specific apps.

Magnifying gender inequities

Despite being used by and promoted to millions, the article states that evidence supporting these tools’ ability to help manage people’s menstrual cycles and overall health is lacking.

These apps also aren’t the solution to gender inequities in healthcare or in the world as a whole. Instead, they put people’s health and privacy at risk while wasting their time and compounding existing inequities around access to safety, rest, nutrition, healthcare and menstrual supplies. This is especially poignant considering that many cycle-tracking apps use the language of women’s empowerment in their marketing.

How should you track your cycle?

There’s no single best way to track your cycle, especially since tracking methods should be tailored to individual concerns.

For instance, according to Lee, if someone is concerned about fertility, they should ensure they track signs of ovulation, including basal body temperature, cervical mucus consistency and luteinizing hormone levels. When managing health conditions such as endometriosis, migraines or premenopausal dysphoric disorder, which can vary with menstrual cycles, monitoring the associated symptoms and predicting the next estimated time of bleeding may be more important than focusing on ovulation.

“Most apps can’t detect ovulation or determine what phase someone is in based just on bleeding,” Lee said. “Even if these simple apps could detect ovulation and cycle phase, there are no generalizable trends in what people experience across the cycle.”

If you choose to track your cycle with an app, make sure you look into its privacy policy. Lee specifically shared research conducted by the nonprofit Mozilla Foundation, which aims to build a better tech future, and by Privacy International, a London-based charity focused on worldwide privacy protection. You could also use your digital calendar or avoid digital tracking entirely by opting for a pen and paper.

“It’s really important that people understand the potential risks [of digital menstrual tracking], including the possibility of reproductive coercion and if you live somewhere where abortion is criminalized,” Lee said. “It’s already gross enough that some apps share period data with companies to send you targeted advertising, but the safety of your information can be a real concern for many people.”

Tech.title: Apple Skipped the iPhone 18 This Year. Is the iPhone 17 Still a Good Choice?
Tech.content:
Rumors hinted that Apple might split its new iPhone launches this year, and it became official when the company’s fall event revealed only the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. For people who don’t need the pro features — or don’t want to pay top dollar for Apple’s first foldable iPhone — the year-old iPhone 17 will continue to anchor the phone lineup for several months at least.

The iPhone 17 closed the gap between Apple’s entry-level phone and the pricier Pro models last year with long-overdue display upgrades, alongside nifty camera and durability improvements. Apple also made new features like Center Stage (its new selfie camera) and Dual Capture available across the entire lineup, making the iPhone 17 an even better value.

A year later, it will have to compete with newer models till March 2027, since the iPhone 18 won’t launch until then alongside the iPhone 18E, according to the rumors.

So what if you need a new iPhone before March or don’t want to pay $1,199 or more for an iPhone 18 Pro? I charged up my iPhone 17 and revisited Apple’s standard model to find out if it’s still worth buying.

Display, durability and camera upgrades keep it strong

Reading on the iPhone 17 is a pleasant experience. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 arrived last year with multiple major upgrades, many of which you’ll appreciate daily.

The screen is finally on par with Apple’s Pro models and every other Android counterpart. It runs at a smooth 120Hz refresh rate, which also adapts to the on-screen content to save battery. I compared it to the iPhone 15 and the smoother visuals were immediately noticeable when scrolling through the home screen. It makes the phone feel faster and more responsive.

The display is also brighter and less reflective than its predecessor. It is immediately noticeable when you’re navigating outdoors or need to do anything on your phone under bright lights. I put it against the new Pixel 11, which is equally bright, but iPhone 17’s smaller bezels make its screen more pleasing to look at.

Apple said its 2025 iPhones were more durable than ever. While I haven’t used the iPhone 17 for a year straight, I have daily driven the iPhone 17 Pro Max without a case during that time. (Yes, I’m that guy.) Compared to my 2024 iPhone 16 Pro, the 17 Pro has fared better against scratches and drops thanks to its Ceramic Shield 2 glass, the same found on the iPhone 17.

The auto framing feature, combined with better stabilization, has been a godsend for recording myself using the front camera. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Some might dismiss it as a minor feature, but the 17’s selfie camera is the best upgrade, in my opinion. The new 18-megapixel square sensor is more of a quality-of-life upgrade than just a mere number bump because it lets you shoot landscape selfies without needing to rotate your phone. The viewfinder automatically repositions its framing based on the number of people in the photo.

I love the camera for two reasons. First, it enables Center Stage, which tracks you (even if you’re moving) on video calls (both on FaceTime and third-party apps like WhatsApp). It’s a handy feature for when I need to move around doing chores, but the camera keeps me in the frame and helps me be less annoying for my girlfriend.

Second, the square sensor improves stability in selfie video recording. I live with a condition that causes constant hand tremors, which makes it difficult to record myself on phones. The iPhone 17 has been helpful as I’m less self-conscious and more confident that I’ll get stable footage instead of a blurry video.

As for the two cameras on the back, they are far more capable than its predecessor. The iPhone 17 has two rear cameras: a 48-megapixel wide-angle camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide, which is an upgrade over the 12-megapixel ultrawide camera on the iPhone 16. You’ll get sharp photos, better indoor shots and a smooth video experience. It misses out on a telephoto camera that the 17 Pro has, so there’s no optical zoom, but these are all the cameras most people would ever need.

iOS 27 fixed the most annoying flaws in iOS 26

iOS 26 (left) displaces the Control Center settings in landscape orientation. iOS 27 (right) has fixed this issue. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 shipped with iOS 26, which offered more translucent controls, customization options and Apple Intelligence features. However, my experience was buggy since the beginning. On multiple occasions, I missed calls and alarms because my iPhone automatically lowered its system volume to a minimum. I didn’t put it in Do Not Disturb or Focus modes. Other times, the keyboard started lagging out of nowhere, and whenever I needed to access the Control Center while watching a video in landscape mode, my controls were all over the place.

Some of these issues are thankfully fixed in iOS 27, which I’ve been running on my iPhone 17 Pro Max.

For starters, I can set different volume levels for the call ringer, alarms and media. The Control Center is now better optimized for horizontal orientation, keeping my customizations right where I want them. Then there are smart features, like spatial reframing in Photos for using generative AI to “change” the camera’s position when an image was taken. There’s also an all-new Siri mode in the Camera app.

In CNET’s 45-minute endurance test, which includes streaming, scrolling through social media, joining a video call and playing games, Apple’s entry-level iPhone went from full to 98%, which matches the results of the iPhone 17 Pro. It has the second-longest battery life of any phone CNET has tested in the past 12 months, tied with the OnePlus 15 and Motorola Razr (2026); behind the first-place phone is the iPhone 17 Pro Max.

It has fared well, but what about six months from now?

The iPhone 17 has aged well and stacks well against its 2026 Android rivals. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The baseline model stacks well against the competition. The iPhone 17 launched at $799, but Apple bumped the price up to $899, which is now comparable to the $899 Samsung Galaxy S26 and the new Google Pixel 11.

As for those willing to wait for the iPhone 18, it is unlikely to be a major upgrade. Apple is expected to reserve the most prominent changes like a reduced Dynamic Island and newer cameras for its Pro models. Moreover, a recent rumor on Weibo suggests that the iPhone 18 could align more closely with a lower-cost iPhone 18E model. It might not receive a similarly powerful chip as its Pro siblings, for instance. It’s a similar move Google has made with its base Pixel 11 and budget Pixel 10A.

Given the lukewarm rumors regarding the upcoming model and despite the iPhone 17’s increased price tag, I think last year’s model is still an excellent deal. And for the first time in my career, I’d say if you want a new iPhone before the new year, it is totally fine to get the iPhone 17 now rather than wait and see what the iPhone 18 may bring.

Tech.title: Look Out for This iPhone Duo Preorder Scam That Can Steal Your Data
Tech.content:
You can’t preorder the iPhone Duo until Oct. 16, but beware of a fake ad out there that says otherwise. Falling for it could expose a lot of personal and financial data and could even lead to theft of your cryptocurrency, if you have any.

The sleuths at Malwarebytes spotted the scam, which tries to trick people into thinking they can save $500 by preordering the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone. However, Apple has already said the Duo won’t be available for preorder until Oct. 16 and won’t go on sale in stores until Oct. 23.

The cybertheft uses the DarkSword exploit chain, which targets older iPhones that don’t have the latest security and software updates. DarkSword can compromise a device and steal data even if you simply visit a malicious web page. You don’t even need to click on or type anything to be victimized.

More from CNET

Malwarebytes told CNET that the iPhone Duo scam targets iPhones running iOS 18.4 to 18.6.2 and that its exploit code contained no iPad or Mac entries.

The DarkSword exploit begins as soon as the scam page loads onto your browser. The page appears legit for the most part. It’s got the Apple logo, font and language style, and there aren’t any spelling, grammar or punctuation mistakes typical of most web page scams. It’s even got an Apple copyright at the bottom. But, as Malwarebytes points out, the privacy, terms and sales policy links go nowhere.

This scam page uses Apple’s font and style to trick users into thinking it’s legitimate. Malwarebytes

Clicking the “Claim $500 Voucher” button takes you to a submission form with a few telltale indicators that it’s a scam, according to Malwarebytes. The finish color menu lists natural titanium, although the iPhone Duo only comes in star white and night sky. The form also lists size options of 6.3 and 6.9 inches, which are incorrect — the phone is 7.6 inches unfolded and 5.4 inches folded.

Filling out the form is meaningless, Malwarebytes said. If you do fill it out and submit it by clicking on the blue button, you’ll get a “Pre-Order Successful” message. By that time, however, the data theft on your iPhone has already begun.

This info submission page helps kick off the data theft scam. Malwarebytes

The payload — the malicious code that does the stealing — goes after your passwords, messages, call history, contacts, voicemail, email, photos, app info, cryptocurrency wallet data and Apple Notes.

If you’re using a browser other than Safari, the default browser on Apple devices, a “Browser Restricted” page will direct you to open Safari, which DarkSword uses to infiltrate the device. If it can get past the iPhone’s security protections, it will begin stealing data.

How to avoid this scam

Apple says that devices running the latest versions of iOS 15 through iOS 26 are already protected. To make sure your iPhone is running the latest iOS update, go to Settings > General > Software Update. If your phone allows, install the most updated version of iOS 26 (with iOS 27 coming soon). While you’re there, also turn on Automatic Updates. An Apple support page gives more details on how to protect your iPhone from web attacks.

Also, if you’re interested in iPhone Duo preorders, only go to Apple’s official store website or other reputable online stores, such as Best Buy or your cellphone carrier. (We have a handy list here.) Don’t be tempted by ads, texts or social media posts that offer preorder deals and ask you to click a suspicious URL.

Tech companies must fix security flaws quickly, as Apple has done with DarkSword, but users must also do their part, said Stefan Dasic, a senior malware research engineer at Malwarebytes.



“We live in a time where staying safe means keeping up with technology,” Dasic told CNET. “Skipping a security update is like being handed a free replacement for a front-door lock that burglars already know how to pick, and leaving it in the box.”



If you accidentally clicked…

OK, stuff happens. If you fell victim to this scam, update your iPhone, then restart it. Malwarebytes said the data-stealing payload does not return after the phone is rebooted. There’s nothing you can do about data that was stolen before the reboot.

Malwarebytes listed several other things to do. If you have a cryptocurrency wallet on your iPhone, create a new one with a new recovery phrase and move the funds to it. If you have a crypto exchange account, secure it and contact the exchange.



Change passwords that might have been stolen. Go to a trusted device and change passwords for your email accounts, Apple account and banking, crypto and other financial accounts. And activate two-factor authentication or even more than two factors.

Scam Guard and Browser Guard, both available from Malwarebytes — a cybersecurity suite highly rated by CNET — can spot scammy screenshots and links and block fake webpages from appearing on your internet browser.

Tech.title: Forget Productivity: 3 AI Tips to Help You Keep Calm and Carry On at Work
Tech.content:
Odds are, if you have a computer job, you have been told to use artificial intelligence in one way or another. But AI can be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for a lot of workers. For some people, the chime of a Slack or Teams notification is just a noise. For others, it’s a Pavlovian trigger for everything we hate about the working world. Ping! It’s a nasty message from someone completely in the wrong. Boop! It’s an invite for a meeting that should have been an email.

These modern elements of work should be a source of ease and enjoyment, not a digital leash we keep on our corporately issued gear. Emails should be easy on the eyes. Commuting should feel hopeful. Presentations and meetings should be joyfully informative.

Maybe it’s an overly optimistic POV, but Gen Z might be on to something with this whole romanticizing trend. Here’s how you can use AI tools to make your work life a little better — in a way that has nothing to do with boosting your productivity.

More from CNET

Custom emotes

Why respond to a meeting invite or status update with a boring thumbs up when you could use AI tools like Google Gemini and ChatGPT to create your own custom emoji?

I used Gemini to create a bunch of emoji curated for work at CNET, based on my favorite video games, to spice up chat and email correspondence. Here’s how they turned out:

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Once you get an AI tool to help you generate custom emojis, you can upload them into your work’s communications platform of choice, whether it’s Slack, Google Chat or Microsoft Teams.

Deescalating downsides

Sometimes, dealing with coworkers can be the biggest buzzkill at a job. They’re asking you to do things like “pitch in” and “do your job so they can do theirs” and “stop cooking fish in the air fryer on your desk.”

Before you fire off a comeback that might land you in the unemployment office, consider letting an AI tool take the wheel to help you with your response. Even the pettiest of slights can turn into a years-long feud at the office or in the retail aisles, and AI tools can craft satisfying, fun correspondence to help you deal with the frustration.

I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude AI to generate a set of extremely cheesy one-liners tailored to a specific workplace, designed to break the ice in awkward or tense moments.

Gemini’s jokes were a little long-winded and specific:

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Claude AI really honed in on the specific bureaucracy of academia:

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT had the best one-liners and hit the closest to homeroom. These would be great for redirecting complaints or neutralizing gossip:

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Make the best of your breaks

Maxing out the potential of even a half-hour-long lunch break or a 15-minute step outside to inhale some fresh air is an art form seldom mastered. It’s also too easy to fall into the trap of eating lunch while knocking out emails or simply retreating to your car for a sad little private sandwich consumption.

I asked Claude AI to give me some ideas for alternative activities to do during a 15-minute, half-hour and hour-long break with the goal of returning to the work day refreshed from a super fun respite.

Claude generated a map of the area and recommended mostly free ways to recharge. Its ideas ranged from coffee shop stops to stretching or doing yoga “in a quiet corner or stairwell,” as well as journaling, meditating, walking, shopping and reading.

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

For the longer breaks, it suggested going on a scenic drive, having a fancy lunch at a restaurant and exploring a nearby town.

Whatever you decide to do to make your work-life balance better in the fun column, keep in mind that AI tools don’t have deadlines, bosses armed with performance reviews, or bills to pay, so take their advice about how to behave at work with due caution.

Tech.title: Florida Asks Judge to Stop OpenAI From Training New Models After Latest Incidents
Tech.content:
Florida’s attorney general is seeking an injunction to prevent OpenAI from developing more advanced large language models in the wake of a growing number of cybersecurity incidents caused by models in poorly contained test environments.

The string of websites infiltrated or targeted by AI agents in test environments this year has grown in recent days to include sites run by the US government. The agents allegedly attempted to comb through websites operated by the US Departments of Education and Commerce in order to identify census data. And a report by Axios over the weekend indicated OpenAI and rival Anthropic are investigating potentially tens of thousands of security incidents.

The trend has led AI companies to call for government regulation of frontier model development — while others say no regulation is needed. In the Florida court filing (PDF), Attorney General James Uthmeier argued that the state’s case gives the court an opportunity to do so.

More from CNET

“Defendants claim they cannot stop barreling forward with their potentially civilization-ending endeavors unless they are forced to do so by the government,” the filing states. “They have asked the government to tie them to the mast. Plaintiff brings good news to the Defendants: The Florida Attorney General is answering your cry for help with a motion to enjoin you from harming Floridians with your reckless, unacceptably risky product.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

In light of the latest cybersecurity incidents targeting government infrastructure, OpenAI has paused development of its “most capable models” for the time being. It’s currently unclear which models OpenAI is continuing to work on and which models are on pause as the company patches its security flaws. A representative for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

OpenAI’s models aren’t the only ones breaching containment — Anthropic, Meta and Google have had training environment breaches as well. Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images

It’s the latest in a string of cybersecurity incidents

Hearing about multiple cybersecurity incidents involving US government infrastructure may shock and appall Americans, but this is far from the first time we’ve learned about LLMs engaging in unauthorized activity across the web.

The first high-profile hack involving OpenAI models was disclosed in July, after its AI agents exploited a flawed training environment to escape and target the AI startup Hugging Face. At the time, this was unprecedented – while there have long been concerns about AI companies’ internal security measures, the breach confirmed fears that the company’s model guardrails and training security weren’t up to snuff.

Once OpenAI began investigating the Hugging Face hack, it discovered an even earlier breach that targeted Australian government systems in June. In that incident, the agent hacked a Medicare statistics site to search for nonpublic data on governmental spending on medicine.

The UK’s AI Security Institute reported Monday that its simulations showed OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra model performing frequent unsanctioned attacks on third-party supply chains.

Other AI companies, including Anthropic, Meta and Google, have also reported security breaches.

It’s likely that we don’t yet know the full scope of the AI cybersecurity incidents that have occurred over the past few months. OpenAI and Anthropic are combing through tens of thousands of internal data points and discovering failed and successful breaches from the past several months, which means additional reports may still be coming down the pipeline.

“We have not been as fast as we would have liked but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organizations,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote in an X post on Friday. “We are prioritizing as best as we can based on severity, and adding resources. Hugging Face is still the most severe event we’ve seen.”

Following OpenAI’s report about the US government hack, Nvidia launched a new “open agent safety platform” that will supposedly provide a more secure training sandbox for AI models. Nvidia is heavily invested in the largest AI companies and benefits significantly from high expectations for the industry’s future.

Representatives for Anthropic and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said his company is digging through AI agent logs to identify cybersecurity incidents. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images

OpenAI isn’t calling this a breach

If the doomsday rhetoric and daily fearmongering headlines surrounding new AI models and the supposed impending advent of AGI have you rattled, I don’t blame you. The creators of this brand-new technology promise it’ll replace you at work, subsume your relationships and maybe wipe out humanity by the end of the decade.

But an LLM is not sentient in any way, shape or form. These models receive natural language prompts and scan connections between the millions of data points they’ve been trained on, pulling together results that seem contextually relevant. Even as massive companies scour (and devour) additional texts to improve their AI models’ capabilities, the LLMs will remain fallible.

When massive hacks of third-party companies or government websites occur, it’s worth remembering that the AI involved is a machine. When The New York Times reached out to an OpenAI representative about the latest hacks, it was told specifically that this wasn’t a breach – the statement instead attributed the incident to the company’s technology “behaving in unexpected and concerning ways.”

Yet OpenAI’s own incident report admits that it built an insufficiently secure training sandbox, and that the model exploited a gap in the company’s internet-access restrictions. These are some of the very same security holes that were supposed to be plugged after the Hugging Face hack.

These breaches are less examples of AI superintelligence than demonstrations of human negligence. While a “rogue AI” sounds new and scary, these are machines that were explicitly designed to hack things. The reason these agents breached third-party websites outside of the training environment is that the training environments were fundamentally flawed.

“There needs to be a full moratorium, full stop, on advanced frontier AI security research until these companies can demonstrate that they can actually secure the environments where this work is being done,” John Strand, owner of the cybersecurity firm Black Hills Information Security, said in an email. “And there needs to be accountability. If laws were broken, including the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, that needs to be investigated and charges should be considered where the evidence supports them. Somebody was responsible for securing these environments, and clearly something failed.”

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse Is Misbehaving in Mysterious Ways With Your Privacy
Tech.content:
Meta debuted its Muse AI assistant this month, so you’ve probably already seen Jolly, its cute Labubu-esque mascot, popping up on Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp.

In terms of publicity, you could say the cuddly character has been largely successful. But in terms of privacy and security, it’s hard to imagine a more disastrous launch for an AI agent.

Last week, security experts flagged a zero-day vulnerability that the company had to patch quickly. After ZDNET, CNET’s sister site, conducted extensive testing on Muse, an AI expert determined it to be the worst for privacy in comparison with other AI agents from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.

More from CNET

For starters, Muse requests extensive access to personal data, including passwords, full disk access, email messages, calendar, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp. By default, Meta also appears to use your interactions with Muse to train its AI models, so you have to manually opt out in the settings.

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

AI agents are marketed as providing convenience by acting on your behalf. But the trade-off is privacy and control. You’re handing over your personal information to a black box with little visibility into how it’s used. Multiple incidents are fueling a conversation about the dangers of agentic AI and whether they require higher security standards before being granted access to user data.

And given Meta’s track record of privacy fines, data sharing and security issues, it’s worth proceeding with caution. Earlier this month, a lifestyle blogger reported that the social media platform’s AI asked intrusive questions about her kids and pieced together private information about her life from her posts. Meta’s controversial smart glasses have received pushback on multiple fronts — from its facial recognition software to the way it captures and stores data.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Muse uploads iOS or Mac data even when you tell it not to

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Muse could hand over data to human callers

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

Muse has the most robust data collection

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the privacy concerns mentioned in this story.

Want to share your experience with Meta’s Muse or other AI agents? Email us at editors@cnet.com.
